_meta.purpose: Canonical, machine-readable knowledge base for Clue. The app reads this for the explorative Feed, the immersive layered Reader, the Learn loop (Discover / Review / Quiz), the Library, and Debate mode. A few cards a day, remembered for good — starting at the very basics and going as deep as you like.
_meta.status: SEED CONTENT — hand-curated to exercise the engine, weighted toward foundations you can build on. Economics and political economy are presented as competing theories and traditions, not settled truth. Every card should be re-verified and the set expanded (target: hundreds of cards, many sourced to specific papers/books with working links).

schema.fields: ordered list for the Library + the Me radar; each {id,label,blurb,icon,color}.
schema.depths: legend for a card's `depth`: fact (a single finding/date) | concept (a foundational idea) | book (a whole-book insight) | event (a dated event).
schema.cards: the knowledge units {id,field,depth,level,title,fact,detail,src,year,tags,layers,deploy,counter,quiz,xref,prereq,media,kind}. `fact` is the one-line hook shown in the Feed. `layers` is the progressive-depth model: an ordered list of {d,t,body} the Reader peels open one at a time. `detail` is a fallback when `layers` is absent. `deploy` = how to use it in an argument. `counter` = the honest steelman/caveat (also used in Debate mode). `quiz` is optional {q,choices,answer}.
schema.src: v3: array of evidence ids — see evidence.json. Replaced the old inline `source` object so every source is logged once and reused.
schema.xref: v3: array of card ids this card CONNECTS TO (the mental web). Rendered as 'Connects to' chips in the Reader.
schema.prereq: v3: array of card ids this card BUILDS ON. Rendered as 'Builds on' chips; will gate unlock order in the pedagogy engine (Phase 3).
schema.media: v3: array of {type:'equation'|'image'|'figure'|'map', tex|src, caption, alt}. Equations render as plain TeX until KaTeX lands (Phase 2).
schema.kind: v3 (optional): content type beyond depth — 'date' (rendered: shows a big date headline via `when`, free text like '14 Jul 1789', falling back to `year`) | 'language' | 'symbol' (reserved).
schema.layers: each layer is {d:'gist'|'basics'|'deeper'|'debate', t:short title, body:text}. The Reader always opens at the gist (the hook) and lets you reveal the next layer. The 'debate' layer is where a theory is shown as contested — who disputes it and why.
schema.motions: debate topics for Debate mode {id,text,fields}. The app pulls your LEARNED cards in those fields as evidence (deploy) and rebuttals (counter).
schema.evidence.json: separate registry: id -> {who,year,title,where,url,kind,strength}. `strength` describes how thick the evidence is, concretely.
schema.glossary.json: separate registry: id -> {term,symbol,def,field}. Inline tap-tooltips arrive in Phase 2.

rules.accuracy: Prefer robust, widely-accepted facts. Name the source (author/year/work). Avoid bare 'studies show'.
rules.honesty: Every card carries a `counter` — the strongest objection or caveat. This trains steelmanning and keeps the app from teaching one-sided talking points.
rules.pluralism: For economics, politics and philosophy especially, present ideas as theories within a tradition, name the school, and show what rival schools say. No model is the last word.

cards.title: The fall of Constantinople
cards.fact: In 1453 Ottoman forces took Constantinople, ending the Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire.
cards.detail: Sultan Mehmed II's army breached the great walls after a siege, aided by massive cannon. The city became the Ottoman capital. It is conventionally taken to mark the end of the Middle Ages and helped push scholars and trade routes westward — one spur for the Renaissance and for Europe's search for new sea routes.
cards.deploy: A clean marker for the end of the medieval order and the rise of the Ottomans as a Mediterranean great power.
cards.counter: Periodisation is a convenience: little changed overnight, and '1453 = end of the Middle Ages' is a tidy Eurocentric label.

quiz.q: What ended in 1453 with the fall of Constantinople?
Which Ottoman sultan led the army that captured Constantinople in 1453?
What technological factor is most often credited with letting the Ottomans break through Constantinople's famously strong walls?

A history exam states that the fall of Constantinople occurred 'roughly N centuries before the year 2000.' Using the actual year of the event, what whole number should N be (rounded to the nearest century)?

cards.title: The French Revolution begins
cards.fact: On 14 July 1789 a Paris crowd stormed the Bastille, igniting the French Revolution.
cards.detail: Fiscal crisis, a rigid estates system and high bread prices brought down the absolute monarchy. The Revolution produced the Declaration of the Rights of Man, a republic, the Terror, and ultimately Napoleon — spreading the language of citizenship, rights and nationalism across Europe.
cards.deploy: The hinge between divine-right monarchy and a modern politics of rights and citizenship.
cards.counter: Liberation and violence rode together — the Declaration of Rights sat beside the Terror. Its universalism was tested hardest in the colonies: enslaved Haitians took 'liberty and equality' at their word and revolted in 1791, winning independence in 1804. C.L.R. James ('The Black Jacobins') put that Haitian Revolution at the centre, and Michel-Rolph Trouillot argued European histories largely silenced it; the exclusion of women and the enslaved from French citizenship was no footnote.

quiz.q: The storming of the Bastille (14 July 1789) began which event?
Which 1791 slave uprising in a French colony took the Revolution's promise of liberty and equality at its word and won independence in 1804?
Which combination of pressures is most accurate as the immediate backdrop to the monarchy's collapse in 1789?
choices: Government bankruptcy, a rigid system of estates, and high bread prices
A foreign invasion, plague, and naval defeat
Rapid industrialization, urban factory strikes, and railway debt
Religious schism, a disputed succession, and a crop surplus

quiz.q: The storming of the Bastille (1789) and Haitian independence (1804) are both used as Revolution-era markers. How many years separate those two events?

cards.title: Humans land on the Moon
cards.fact: On 20 July 1969, Apollo 11 landed the first humans on the Moon.
cards.detail: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the surface while Michael Collins orbited above. The feat was as much Cold War contest as science — a demonstration of capability against the Soviet Union after Sputnik (1957) and Gagarin (1961).
cards.deploy: A peak example of what concentrated state funding and a clear goal can achieve in a few years.
cards.counter: It was driven by superpower rivalry as much as curiosity; crewed deep-space flight largely stalled once the point was made.

quiz.q: Which mission first landed humans on the Moon (1969)?
Which Apollo 11 crew member stayed in lunar orbit while his two colleagues walked on the surface?
Counting from the launch of Sputnik, the first artificial satellite that triggered the space race, how many years later did humans first walk on the Moon?
Which framing best captures why crewed deep-space missions largely stalled after the first Moon landings?
choices: The effort was driven by superpower rivalry, so motivation dropped once dominance was demonstrated
The Moon was found to be made of unusable material
International treaties banned all further crewed spaceflight
Rocket technology was destroyed and could not be rebuilt

cards.title: China's reform and opening up
cards.fact: From 1978, China's 'reform and opening up' under Deng Xiaoping rebuilt a poor planned economy into the world's factory.
cards.detail: At the 1978 third plenum the CCP began 'reform and opening up': de-collectivising farms, allowing private business, inviting foreign investment and creating special economic zones — while keeping one-party rule. The World Bank credits the era with lifting almost 800 million people from extreme poverty. How to read it is contested, and the label you pick is the bias: Beijing calls it 'socialism with Chinese characteristics' (the Party steering, not retreating); economists Ha-Joon Chang and Joe Studwell argue the real engine was state-directed industrial policy, land reform and cheap directed credit, not free markets; the economist Martin Ravallion finds the biggest early poverty fall (1978–84) came from de-collectivising farms, before global trade took off.
cards.deploy: A test case in development economics — was the driver the market, the state, or both? Name the reading you mean rather than assuming 'markets won'.
cards.counter: It also brought steep inequality (documented by Branko Milanović and Thomas Piketty), heavy environmental damage, repressed independent labour and no political opening — and the common Western 'free-market triumph' telling understates how much the state directed the whole process (the 'Beijing Consensus' reading).

quiz.q: The World Bank credits China's post-1978 reforms with…
choices: Lifting ~800 million people out of extreme poverty

quiz.q: What name does Beijing officially give to its post-1978 model, signaling the Party steering rather than retreating from the economy?
According to economist Martin Ravallion's analysis, which change drove the largest early fall in extreme poverty (1978-84), before export-led trade took off?
choices: Opening coastal special economic zones to foreign factories

quiz.q: The World Bank credits China's reform era with lifting almost 800 million people from extreme poverty. Rounded to the nearest hundred million, how many people (in millions) is that?

cards.title: China's party-state
cards.fact: China is a one-party state: the Communist Party sits above the government, the courts and the army.
cards.detail: The People's Republic is a Leninist party-state. The CCP — not the state — holds ultimate authority: it runs parallel structures throughout government, controls the military and courts, and selects leaders internally through 'democratic centralism'. Under Xi Jinping, power has re-centralised around the top leader.
cards.deploy: Essential for reading Chinese politics: 'the government' is subordinate to the Party, so Western state-vs-society models fit poorly.
cards.counter: One-party doesn't mean monolithic — there are factions, technocratic competence and local experimentation; and the model leans heavily on continued growth for legitimacy.

quiz.q: In China's system, ultimate authority rests with…
A foreign analyst wants to understand why a Chinese court ruled a certain way on a politically sensitive case. Which approach best fits how power actually flows in China?
choices: Look for guidance or pressure from the Communist Party, since the judiciary sits below the Party
Treat the court as fully independent of political bodies, as in a separation-of-powers system
Assume the National People's Congress overruled the court, since the legislature outranks the Party
Assume the army directed the verdict, since the military controls the courts

quiz.q: What is the name of the internal Party principle by which leaders are selected and decisions are made centrally rather than through open public elections?
Which claim is consistent with the idea that a one-party state need not be monolithic?
choices: Rival factions, technocrats and local policy experiments coexist within the single ruling party
Multiple parties compete in genuinely contested national elections
The government routinely overrides the Party on major policy
An independent judiciary checks the Party's decisions

cards.title: China's 'century of humiliation'
cards.fact: China frames 1839–1949 as a 'century of humiliation' — and it still shapes its foreign policy.
cards.detail: From the First Opium War (1839) to 1949, China suffered military defeats, 'unequal treaties', lost territory and foreign extraterritoriality. The CCP makes this narrative central: national rejuvenation means never being humiliated again. It frames disputes over Taiwan, the South China Sea and sovereignty as righting historical wrongs.
cards.deploy: Decodes Chinese rhetoric: many positions are cast as recovering from a century of foreign domination, not as naked expansion.
cards.counter: The narrative is also a state-curated tool — it can justify assertiveness and recast criticism as renewed 'humiliation'.

quiz.q: China's 'century of humiliation' refers to…
choices: ~1839–1949 of foreign defeats and unequal treaties

quiz.q: If a narrative dates a 'century of humiliation' from an opening war in 1839 to a founding moment in 1949, how many years does that span cover?
Which 1839 conflict is treated as the starting point of China's 'century of humiliation'?
How does the 'century of humiliation' framing typically reshape the meaning of a present-day Chinese claim over disputed territory?
choices: It recasts the claim as recovering from past foreign domination rather than as new expansion
It presents the claim as a purely commercial dispute with no historical dimension
It frames the claim as a concession China is offering to former colonial powers
It treats the claim as irrelevant to national identity or sovereignty

cards.title: How China's state is structured
cards.fact: China's state runs through tiered 'people's congresses', from the local level up to the National People's Congress.
cards.detail: Formally, the National People's Congress (NPC) — the world's largest legislature (~2,900 delegates) — is the supreme organ of state power. It elects the president and decides the State Council (the government), meets briefly each spring (the 'Two Sessions'), and leaves a Standing Committee to act between sessions. Below it sit people's congresses at province, prefecture/city, county and township levels, each overseeing the government at its tier. Running in parallel at every level is a CCP committee that sets direction — so the state and the Party form two interlocking hierarchies.
cards.deploy: Gives you the real map of Chinese governance: a layered congress-and-government system shadowed at each level by a Party committee.
cards.counter: China-law scholars like Murray Scot Tanner argue the NPC has gained real legislative substance; sceptics such as Minxin Pei note it has never rejected a Party bill, so its role is mainly to ratify and consult, not to legislate as a Western parliament would.

quiz.q: China's supreme organ of state power is…

A short annual meeting of China's national legislature passes a slate of laws and budgets, then disbands for the year. Which body handles legislative business during the long gaps between these sessions?
choices: The Standing Committee of the National People's Congress
The State Council acting as a substitute legislature

quiz.q: Roughly how many delegates make up the National People's Congress, the world's largest legislature?
What is the popular nickname for the brief springtime period when the National People's Congress and the advisory conference meet at the same time?

cards.title: How China appoints its officials
cards.fact: Most senior officials in China aren't elected — they're selected and promoted by the Party through the 'nomenklatura' system.
cards.detail: The CCP's Organization Department manages a 'nomenklatura' — roughly the top several thousand party-state posts (ministers, provincial leaders, even major university and state-enterprise heads). Cadres are appointed and promoted on assessed criteria: loyalty to the Party, ideological standing and measured performance (historically growth and stability targets), alongside patronage networks. A typical career climbs the rungs — county, then a city (e.g. mayor or city party secretary), then a province — before a few reach the Central Committee, the Politburo, and its Standing Committee, which the Central Committee formally 'elects' but the leadership in practice selects.
cards.deploy: Explains how China picks its rulers: an internal Party personnel system that rewards measured performance and loyalty — often described as 'political meritocracy'.
cards.counter: Daniel A. Bell ('The China Model') and Eric Li defend it as a political meritocracy that filters for competence over decades; Minxin Pei argues the targets invite gaming and faked data, and that loyalty and factional patronage increasingly outweigh merit near the top.

quiz.q: Senior Chinese officials are chosen mainly by…
Which Party body manages the list of senior party-state posts and decides who is appointed to them?
A provincial governor in China posts strong official GDP growth figures and is promoted. A critic of the appointment system would most likely warn that:
choices: The performance targets invite gaming and faked data, so the numbers may not reflect real competence
Promotion ignores measured performance entirely and rests only on seniority
Such officials are chosen by direct popular vote rather than the Party
Provincial leaders cannot be promoted to national bodies under any circumstances

quiz.q: Which career path best matches the typical upward climb of a senior Chinese cadre under this system?
choices: County post, then a city role, then a province, then potentially national Party bodies
A single national appointment by popular election with no prior local posts
Direct entry to the Politburo Standing Committee from a university position
Rotation only within one ministry from entry to retirement

cards.title: Where Chinese voters actually vote
cards.fact: Chinese voters directly elect only the lowest levels — village committees and county/township congresses; everything above is indirect.
cards.detail: Under the 1987 Organic Law, villages directly elect village committees and chiefs — China's main experiment in grassroots elections. County, district and township people's congresses are also directly elected. But every level above (city, province, NPC) is elected indirectly by the congress one tier below, and the CCP pre-approves candidate nominations throughout. In a village, an elected committee operates alongside the appointed village Party secretary, who often holds the real authority.
cards.deploy: Shows where direct voting exists in China (the grassroots) and where it stops (everything above the county).
cards.counter: Scholars of Chinese village elections like Kevin O'Brien saw genuine grassroots accountability and a training ground; others note that CCP candidate-vetting and the parallel village Party secretary cap how much the elected committee actually decides.

quiz.q: In China, directly-elected bodies exist mainly at the level of…
A Chinese citizen wants a direct vote on who sits in their provincial people's congress. Under the post-1987 system, what happens?
choices: They cannot vote directly; provincial congress members are chosen by the congress one tier below
They vote directly, the same as for the village committee
They vote directly only if they hold Party membership
They submit candidate nominations that the province then ratifies by referendum

quiz.q: In a Chinese village, an elected committee operates alongside an appointed official who often holds the real authority. What is that official's role?
Which year's Organic Law established direct election of village committees and chiefs, China's main experiment in grassroots elections?

cards.title: 'Whole-process people's democracy'
cards.fact: The CCP calls China a democracy — 'whole-process people's democracy' — judged by results, not by multiparty elections.
cards.detail: Introduced by Xi Jinping in 2019 and written into law in 2021, 'whole-process people's democracy' is the Party's own democratic theory. It claims democracy runs through the entire cycle of governance — consultation, decision, management and oversight, via the people's congresses and the political consultative conference — rather than ending at the ballot box. Its test of success is consequentialist: how well government improves citizens' lives, not whether power alternates between parties.
cards.deploy: Lets you engage Chinese politics on its own terms: it doesn't claim to be a liberal democracy but defines democracy as effective, consultative governance under Party leadership.
cards.counter: Beijing and scholars like Zhang Weiwei argue outcome-based, consultative democracy suits China and delivers; democracy researchers like Larry Diamond counter that without competitive elections, a free press or any way to remove rulers, it is authoritarianism relabelled.

quiz.q: 'Whole-process people's democracy' judges success mainly by…
choices: How well government improves citizens' lives

quiz.q: Two governments are compared under the 'whole-process people's democracy' standard. Which feature would that doctrine count as the strongest evidence of being democratic?
choices: Consultation, policy delivery and oversight that measurably improved citizens' living standards
A surprise transfer of power to an opposition party after a close election
Multiple independent parties competing on a national ballot
An independent press that freely criticizes the head of state

quiz.q: Which democracy researcher argues that, lacking competitive elections, a free press, or any means to remove rulers, China's model is authoritarianism relabelled?
Xi Jinping introduced 'whole-process people's democracy' in 2019, and it was written into law in 2021. How many years elapsed between its introduction and its codification in law?

cards.title: How the CCP's ideology references Marx
cards.fact: The CCP's official ideology is Marxism–Leninism — adapted, it says, to China through a lineage ending in 'Xi Jinping Thought'.
cards.detail: The Party's guiding ideology runs Marxism–Leninism → Mao Zedong Thought → Deng Xiaoping Theory → the Three Represents → the Scientific Outlook on Development → Xi Jinping Thought, all under 'socialism with Chinese characteristics'. The bridge to markets is the doctrine of the 'primary stage of socialism': China is still building its productive forces, so markets and private enterprise are tools on a long road to communism. From Marx it keeps historical materialism (the economic base shapes society), class analysis, and the Party as a vanguard; Xi Jinping Thought is presented as 'Marxism for the 21st century'.
cards.deploy: Explains how a market-driven economy squares with a Communist Party: the 'primary stage of socialism' frames markets as a means, with the Party steering toward communism.
cards.counter: The Party calls it living Marxism, creatively applied. Yasheng Huang ('Capitalism with Chinese Characteristics') argues it is really capitalism under a socialist label; Marxist critics like David Harvey see private capital, billionaires and deep inequality as a betrayal of Marx's classless aim; others read the Marxist vocabulary mainly as cover for the Party's monopoly on power.

quiz.q: How does CCP doctrine square markets with Marxism?
choices: Via the 'primary stage of socialism' — markets as a tool toward communism

quiz.q: Which CCP doctrine claims China is still building its productive forces, framing markets and private enterprise as tools on a long road to communism?
Which idea, inherited from Marx, does CCP doctrine retain when it holds that the economic base shapes society?

Counting Marxism-Leninism as the first link, the CCP's ideological lineage runs Marxism-Leninism, Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development, and Xi Jinping Thought. At which position in that chain does Xi Jinping Thought sit?

cards.title: China's growth model
cards.fact: China grew by investing and exporting at a scale no big economy had tried — and now struggles to rebalance toward consumption.
cards.detail: The boom ran on extraordinarily high investment and savings (gross savings around 43% of GDP), a large manufacturing export sector (exports ~20% of GDP), and state-owned enterprises (~40% of GDP) alongside a dynamic private sector — financed largely by state-directed bank credit. It built world-class infrastructure fast, but kept household consumption a low share of GDP and bred overcapacity and debt. Since the 2010s, plans have aimed to 'rebalance' toward consumption and services — slowly.
cards.deploy: Explains both China's speed and its strains: an investment-and-export engine that's powerful but hard to turn toward consumer-led growth.
cards.counter: Sustainability is debated: Justin Yifu Lin (ex-World Bank chief economist) points to continued tech upgrading and catch-up, while Michael Pettis stresses the property bust, debt and demographics and calls the investment model exhausted. The same state direction is credited for coordination and blamed for misallocation.

quiz.q: China's growth has leaned most heavily on…
According to the card, China's manufacturing export sector amounted to roughly what share of GDP during the boom?
China's high-investment, export-heavy model was financed largely through which channel?
choices: Deep foreign equity markets buying domestic shares

quiz.q: Which economist stresses China's property bust, debt and demographics and argues the investment-led growth model is exhausted?

cards.title: China's hukou system
cards.fact: Where you're registered in China sets your access to schools, healthcare and benefits — the hukou system.
cards.detail: Hukou registers every citizen as rural or urban and to a specific place; public services — schooling, healthcare, housing support — are tied to your registered locality. Roughly 200–300 million rural migrants work in cities but can't easily get urban services for themselves or their children, creating a large internal-migrant underclass (the 'floating population'). Reforms have eased registration in smaller cities, but big-city hukou stays hard to obtain.
cards.deploy: Explains a core source of Chinese inequality and the 'floating population': rights and services follow your registration, not where you live and work.
cards.counter: Beijing presents hukou as orderly urbanisation without sprawling mega-slums; the geographer Kam Wing Chan, who studies it, calls it institutionalised discrimination that makes rural migrants second-class citizens in the cities.

quiz.q: China's hukou system mainly determines…
choices: Access to local public services by registered locality

quiz.q: What is the common name for the large group of rural migrants working in Chinese cities without local urban registration?
A worker born in a rural county moves to Shanghai and works there for 10 years. Under the hukou system, where can her child most reliably access free public schooling?
choices: In Shanghai, because she has worked there over five years
In any city the family chooses, since residence sets eligibility
In her registered rural locality, not in Shanghai
Anywhere in China, because schooling is a national entitlement

quiz.q: If a city has 9 million residents and 3 million of them are migrants who hold no local urban hukou, what percentage of residents lack local urban registration?

cards.title: China's hidden local-government debt
cards.fact: Chinese cities funded their boom by borrowing through off-the-books companies — now a major debt risk.
cards.detail: Local governments can't easily run deficits or raise much tax, yet were tasked with growth and infrastructure. Many borrowed via 'local government financing vehicles' (LGFVs) — state-owned companies that take loans and issue bonds, typically using land-use rights as collateral and repaying from land sales (60–80% of local revenue in 2018). This funded rapid building but piled up large, partly hidden debts; the IMF estimated LGFV debt near $8 trillion (about 47% of GDP) by end-2023. When property prices and land sales fell, repayment became a systemic worry.
cards.deploy: Explains how China's infrastructure was financed — and why local-government and property debt is now a central economic risk.
cards.counter: Nicholas Lardy argues the mostly-domestic, state-owned debt is manageable and restructurable; Michael Pettis sees years of misallocated investment and a slow-burning drag on growth.

quiz.q: Chinese local governments largely funded infrastructure by…
choices: Off-budget financing vehicles backed by land sales

quiz.q: What asset did Chinese local government financing vehicles most commonly pledge as collateral, with sales of it providing the bulk of local revenue?
If a country's GDP is 20 trillion dollars and hidden local financing-vehicle debt equals 47% of GDP, how many trillion dollars is that debt?
Why did the local-government debt model become a systemic worry around 2022 to 2023?
choices: Foreign creditors suddenly demanded repayment in dollars
Falling property prices and land sales cut off the main repayment source
The central government banned all local borrowing overnight
Interest rates on national treasury bonds spiked sharply

cards.title: How China is divided up
cards.fact: China has 34 provincial-level units — provinces, autonomous regions, municipalities and two special regions.
cards.detail: There are 22 provinces (China also claims Taiwan as a 23rd), 5 'autonomous regions' for large minority populations (Xinjiang, Tibet, Inner Mongolia, Guangxi, Ningxia), 4 directly-governed municipalities (Beijing, Shanghai, Tianjin, Chongqing), and 2 special administrative regions (Hong Kong, Macau) under 'one country, two systems'. Below provinces sit prefectures, counties and townships — the rungs officials climb.
cards.deploy: The basic political map of China — and why 'autonomous region' and 'SAR' flag special arrangements for minority areas and for Hong Kong/Macau.
cards.counter: 'Autonomous' is largely nominal — real authority stays with the central Party; and Taiwan's status and the degree of Hong Kong's autonomy are sharply contested.

quiz.q: Xinjiang, Tibet and Inner Mongolia are classed as China's…
Adding China's directly-governed municipalities and its special administrative regions together, how many provincial-level units does that come to?
What constitutional formula governs the arrangement under which Hong Kong and Macau are special administrative regions?
A foreign firm wants to base in a city governed directly by the central government rather than sitting under a province. Which is a valid choice?

cards.title: The line that splits China in two
cards.fact: A line drawn in 1935 still splits China: about 94% of people live on the eastern half.
cards.detail: The Hu Huanyong line (Heihe–Tengchong line) runs diagonally from Heihe in the northeast to Tengchong in the southwest. East of it lies 43% of the land but ~94% of the people — the fertile, watered, coast-facing lowlands. West of it lies 57% of the land (Tibet, Xinjiang and other dry, mountainous regions) with only ~6%. Despite decades of 'develop the west' drives, the divide has barely moved since 1935.
cards.deploy: A single line that explains China's population, farming, cities and even its development politics.
cards.counter: It's a striking regularity, not destiny — infrastructure, water-transfer projects and urbanisation are slowly testing whether the line can shift.

quiz.q: China's Hu line marks that ~94% of people live…
choices: In the eastern half of the country

quiz.q: If 94% of a country's people live on the eastern side of a dividing line that covers 43% of its land area, what percentage of the population lives on the western side?
Which two cities give the Hu line its endpoints, one in the northeast and one in the southwest?
Based on the population split the Hu line describes, which best characterises the western side of the line?
choices: Densely populated coastal lowlands with intensive farming
The most urbanised and industrialised part of the country
Slightly less crowded but otherwise similar to the east
Sparsely populated, dry and mountainous, covering most of the land

cards.title: China's giant city-clusters
cards.fact: China's economy clusters into a few giant city-regions, each bigger than most countries.
cards.detail: Growth concentrates in planned megaregions: the Pearl River Delta / Greater Bay Area (Guangzhou–Shenzhen–Hong Kong; ~86 million people, manufacturing and tech), the Yangtze River Delta (Shanghai–Suzhou–Hangzhou; finance and trade), and Jing-Jin-Ji (Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei; politics and heavy industry). Cities are informally ranked in 'tiers', and the state deliberately steers people and industry into these clusters.
cards.deploy: Shows where China's people and wealth actually concentrate — a handful of coastal city-clusters, not evenly across the provinces.
cards.counter: Concentration drives growth but widens the coastal–interior gap and strains the hukou system as migrants pour into tier-1 cities.

quiz.q: Which is a major Chinese megaregion?
Which Chinese megaregion is anchored by Shanghai, Suzhou and Hangzhou and is known for finance and trade?
A foreign electronics firm wants to set up volume hardware manufacturing near a dense supplier base and major tech companies. Which Chinese city-cluster best fits that need?
choices: The Pearl River Delta / Greater Bay Area (Guangzhou-Shenzhen-Hong Kong)
An inland province far from the coastal clusters

quiz.q: If a megaregion holds 86 million people and a separate cluster holds 64 million, how many million people live in the two combined?

cards.title: The Sunni–Shia split
cards.fact: Islam's main split — Sunni and Shia — began as a 7th-century dispute over who should lead after Muhammad.
cards.detail: When Muhammad died in 632 with no agreed successor, Muslims divided: most (Sunnis) accepted leaders chosen by the community; a minority (Shia, 'partisans of Ali') held that leadership belonged to Muhammad's family through his cousin and son-in-law Ali. The two share Islam's core but differ on authority, law and ritual; the killing of Ali's son Hussein at Karbala (680) deepened it. Sunnis are ~85% of Muslims worldwide, Shia ~15% — but Shia are the majority in Iran and Iraq.
cards.deploy: A key to reading the region: many 'sectarian' conflicts are power struggles wearing a Sunni/Shia label.
cards.counter: Calling every conflict 'ancient sectarian hatred' misleads — Sunni and Shia have long coexisted, and the split is frequently politicised by modern states, not a constant of history.

quiz.q: The Sunni–Shia split originally arose over…
choices: Who should lead the community after Muhammad

quiz.q: The Shia branch of Islam holds that leadership after Muhammad belonged to his family through which cousin and son-in-law?
If Sunnis make up about 85 percent of the world's roughly 1.9 billion Muslims, approximately how many Sunni Muslims is that, in billions?
Why do historians warn against framing every Sunni-Shia conflict as 'ancient sectarian hatred'?
choices: The two groups disagree on every point of doctrine, so coexistence has never occurred
The split is recent and dates only to the 20th century
Sunni and Shia have long coexisted, and modern states frequently politicise the divide for power
Sunni and Shia are actually two separate religions with no shared scripture

cards.title: Oil and the rentier state
cards.fact: Many Middle Eastern states live off oil revenue, not taxes — which reshapes the deal between rulers and ruled.
cards.detail: Gulf states (Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait, Qatar) are 'rentier states': most government income comes from selling oil and gas, not taxing citizens. With little taxation there's little leverage to demand representation — rulers fund generous welfare and public jobs in exchange for political quiet ('no taxation, no representation'). Oil also made the region strategically vital, pulling in outside powers, and gave producers leverage through OPEC.
cards.deploy: Explains both the durability of Gulf monarchies and why outside powers stay so invested in the region.
cards.counter: The model is strained — low oil prices, youth unemployment and the energy transition push states (e.g. Saudi 'Vision 2030') to diversify and, cautiously, to tax; and political scientists like Michael Herb question how tightly oil really locks in autocracy.

quiz.q: A 'rentier state' funds itself mainly from…
In the classic rentier-state bargain, what do rulers offer citizens in exchange for political quiet?
choices: Generous welfare and public-sector jobs funded by oil revenue
Lower oil exports to keep domestic prices high
Stronger parliaments with the power to tax
Free elections in return for higher income taxes

quiz.q: What is the name of the Saudi diversification programme aimed at reducing dependence on oil revenue?
A rentier government takes 92 percent of its revenue from oil sales and the remaining 8 percent from a new tax. If total revenue is 250 billion dollars, how many billion dollars come from the tax?

cards.title: The Israeli–Palestinian conflict
cards.fact: Two peoples claim national rights in one land — the core of the Israeli–Palestinian conflict.
cards.detail: Both Jews and Palestinian Arabs claim the land between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean. Modern Zionism and Arab nationalism collided under Ottoman then British rule; the 1948 creation of Israel was, for Israelis, independence, and for Palestinians the 'Nakba' — over 750,000 displaced. Wars in 1948 and 1967 left Israel governing the West Bank and Gaza; disputes centre on borders, settlements, refugees, Jerusalem and security. A 'two-state solution' along the 1967 lines has been the main proposed framework but remains unrealised.
cards.deploy: Lays out the conflict's structure — competing national claims to the same land — without scoring it for either side.
cards.counter: Almost every fact here is narrated differently by each side; even basic terms ('occupation', 'terrorism', 'self-defence') are contested, so treat any single-source account with care.

quiz.q: The 'two-state solution' refers to…
choices: An Israeli and a Palestinian state side by side

quiz.q: What Arabic word do Palestinians use for the displacement of over 750,000 people around the 1948 creation of Israel?
After which year's war did Israel come to govern the West Bank and Gaza?
Why should a single-source account of this conflict be treated with caution?
choices: All the historical facts are fully agreed and only opinions differ
Even basic terms like 'occupation' and 'self-defence' are narrated and contested differently by each side
Reliable written records of the events do not exist
Only one of the two peoples actually claims the land

cards.title: The Iran–Saudi rivalry
cards.fact: Iran and Saudi Arabia wage a cold war across the Middle East — usually through proxies.
cards.detail: Since Iran's 1979 revolution, Shia-led Iran and Sunni-led Saudi Arabia have competed for regional leadership. They rarely fight directly; instead they back opposing sides in Syria, Yemen, Iraq, Lebanon and elsewhere, turning local conflicts into proxy battlegrounds. The rivalry blends sect (Shia vs Sunni), nationalism (Persian vs Arab) and raw power politics; a 2023 China-brokered deal restored diplomatic ties and cooled it.
cards.deploy: A master key to many regional wars: ask which side Tehran and Riyadh are backing.
cards.counter: Framing it as purely 'Shia vs Sunni' overstates religion — it's also Persian–Arab and great-power rivalry, and the two have periodically sought détente.

quiz.q: The Iran–Saudi rivalry is mostly fought…
choices: In direct war between their armies

quiz.q: Which country brokered the 2023 deal that restored diplomatic ties between Iran and Saudi Arabia?
Why is calling the Iran-Saudi rivalry purely a 'Shia vs Sunni' religious conflict an oversimplification?
choices: It also involves Persian-Arab and great-power rivalry, and the two states have periodically pursued detente
Neither country has a Shia or Sunni majority population
The rivalry began only after 2010 with no earlier dispute
Both governments are officially secular and reject any religious identity

quiz.q: A new civil conflict erupts in a Middle Eastern state with both Shia and Sunni factions. Based on the Iran-Saudi proxy pattern, what is the most likely outcome?
choices: Tehran and Riyadh back opposing local sides, turning it into a proxy battleground
Iran and Saudi Arabia jointly send troops to end the fighting quickly
Both powers stay neutral because the conflict is purely internal
Saudi Arabia and Iran each invade directly with their own armies

cards.title: The Scramble for Africa
cards.fact: In the 1880s, European powers carved up almost all of Africa among themselves — often by lines on a map.
cards.detail: At the Berlin Conference (1884–85), European states set rules for claiming African territory, accelerating a 'Scramble' that by 1914 left only Ethiopia and Liberia uncolonised. Borders were drawn for European convenience — straight lines cutting across peoples and merging rivals — and economies were reorganised to extract raw materials. Those imposed borders and extractive patterns outlived empire and still shape African states.
cards.deploy: The root behind many of Africa's borders, ethnic tensions and commodity-export economies — designed externally, not grown.
cards.counter: How much it explains is itself a named debate: dependency theorists like Walter Rodney ('How Europe Underdeveloped Africa') blame colonial extraction for lasting underdevelopment; institutional economists like Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson point to the extractive institutions it left behind; others weigh pre-colonial states, geography and post-1960 choices too.

quiz.q: The 1884–85 Berlin Conference…
choices: Set rules for Europeans to partition Africa

quiz.q: By 1914, only how many African states had escaped European colonisation?
Name either of the two African states that remained uncolonised by 1914.
A scholar argues Africa's lasting underdevelopment stems from colonial extraction draining wealth to Europe. Which thinker's tradition does this best match?
choices: Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson on extractive institutions
Theories that pre-colonial states and geography matter more

cards.title: The Sahel
cards.fact: The Sahel is the dry belt below the Sahara — and one of the world's most stressed regions.
cards.detail: A semi-arid band running ~5,900 km from the Atlantic to the Red Sea, the Sahel (Mali, Niger, Burkina Faso, Chad and others) sits between desert and savanna. Rainfall is low and erratic, droughts recur, and the population is growing fast — squeezing land and water and fuelling herder–farmer conflict. By 2021 the Sahel accounted for a large and rising share of the world's terrorism deaths, making it both a humanitarian and a security crisis.
cards.deploy: Explains why the Sahel is a flashpoint: climate stress + fast population growth + weak states + spreading insurgency.
cards.counter: Reducing it to terrorism and famine misses local politics and resilience; and the biggest militarised response — France's Operation Barkhane (2014–2022) — is now widely judged a failure, including by French analysts, having left jihadist control wider than before.

quiz.q: The Sahel is best described as…
choices: A semi-arid belt south of the Sahara

quiz.q: The Sahel belt stretches roughly how many kilometres from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea?
The Sahel is a transitional band between which large desert to its north and savanna to its south? Name the desert.
Which combination best explains why the Sahel became a major flashpoint?
choices: Climate stress and erratic rainfall, fast population growth, weak states, and spreading insurgency
Abundant rainfall, shrinking population, strong central states, and lasting peace
Oil wealth, low population, foreign investment, and stable borders
High mountains, dense rainforest, isolation, and absence of conflict

cards.title: The Sahel's turn from France to Russia
cards.fact: Since 2020, coups across the Sahel have thrown out French troops and turned toward Russia.
cards.detail: A wave of military coups hit Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger from 2020. The juntas blamed France and the West for failing to stop jihadist insurgencies, expelled French and Western forces, quit the regional bloc ECOWAS, and formed the Alliance of Sahel States — bringing in Russian military contractors instead. It marks a sharp unwinding of post-colonial Western influence in the region.
cards.deploy: Captures the Sahel's geopolitical realignment: out with France and ECOWAS, in with juntas and Russia.
cards.counter: The juntas — Mali's Assimi Goïta, Burkina Faso's Ibrahim Traoré, Niger's Abdourahamane Tchiani — and pan-Africanist supporters frame it as reclaiming sovereignty from France; ECOWAS, Paris and rights groups like Human Rights Watch counter that jihadist violence has worsened and that the Russian forces (Wagner/Africa Corps) replacing the French committed documented massacres such as Moura, Mali (2022).

quiz.q: After their coups, Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger…
choices: Expelled French forces and turned toward Russia

quiz.q: After their coups, Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger quit which West African regional bloc?
accept: Economic Community of West African States

quiz.q: Which sequence correctly describes the Sahel juntas' realignment after 2020?
choices: Expelled French and Western forces, left ECOWAS, and brought in Russian military contractors
Invited more French troops, joined the EU, and expelled Russian advisers
Kept French forces, deepened ECOWAS ties, and rejected all foreign militaries
Allied with the United States, joined NATO, and banned Russian contractors

quiz.q: Rights groups documented a 2022 massacre by Russian (Wagner) forces in which Malian town?

cards.title: Françafrique
cards.fact: 'Françafrique' is the name for France's continued grip on its former African colonies after independence.
cards.detail: After 1960 France kept deep influence over its former colonies: the CFA franc pegged to the French franc (now euro) under French oversight; defence pacts that brought frequent French military interventions; an opaque presidential 'African Cell'; and personal networks linking elites. Critics coined 'Françafrique' for this clientelist, often corrupt system. It has weakened lately — budget limits, public scrutiny and rivals (China, Russia) — with Sahel states now expelling French troops.
cards.deploy: Explains how formal independence in 1960 left real economic and military dependence — and why anti-French feeling now runs high in the Sahel.
cards.counter: The historian François-Xavier Verschave coined Françafrique; economists Ndongo Samba Sylla and Fanny Pigeaud attack the CFA franc as a colonial leash. Its defenders — the French Treasury and the regional central banks (BCEAO/BEAC) — credit the peg with low inflation and convertibility, and note that blaming Paris alone lets local elites off the hook.

quiz.q: 'Françafrique' refers to…
choices: France's continued post-independence sway over former African colonies

quiz.q: Which feature is a core pillar of the Francafrique system as it operated after 1960?
choices: A currency (the CFA franc) pegged to the French franc and later the euro under French oversight
A free-trade bloc giving former colonies tariff-free access to all EU markets
A shared parliament in Paris where African states held voting seats
A French commitment to never station troops on the African continent

quiz.q: What is the name of the opaque advisory unit inside the French presidency that historically managed relations with former African colonies?
How do defenders of the CFA franc, such as the regional central banks, typically justify the currency peg?
choices: It delivers low inflation and guaranteed convertibility
It lets member states print money freely to fund deficits
It floats against the euro to boost export competitiveness
It removes all French involvement in monetary decisions

cards.title: Libya after Gaddafi
cards.fact: Libya went from one of Africa's richest states to a fractured war zone after Gaddafi fell in 2011.
cards.detail: Muammar Gaddafi ruled Libya for 42 years on oil wealth and tight control. In 2011, Arab Spring protests and a NATO-backed uprising toppled and killed him — but no stable order replaced him. Rival governments and militias fought two civil wars, the country split between east and west, and Libya became a major transit route for migrants heading to Europe. Oil still flows, but power is contested.
cards.deploy: A cautionary case on regime change: removing a dictator without a workable successor state can produce lasting collapse.
cards.counter: The 2016 UK House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee found the intervention had no plan for the aftermath, and Barack Obama called that failure his 'worst mistake'; interventionists counter that Gaddafi had so hollowed out the state that collapse was likely regardless.

quiz.q: Since Gaddafi's fall in 2011, Libya has…
choices: Fractured into rival governments and civil war

quiz.q: Gaddafi ruled Libya for 42 years and was toppled in 2011. In what year did he originally take power? Give the year.
Which Western military alliance backed the 2011 uprising that helped topple Gaddafi?
Which lesson best captures why Libya is cited as a cautionary tale about regime change?
choices: Removing a dictator without a workable plan for the successor state can produce lasting collapse
Air power alone is always sufficient to install a stable democracy
Oil-rich states are immune to civil war after a leadership change
Foreign intervention reliably shortens the duration of internal conflict

cards.title: The Hijra and year one of the Islamic calendar
cards.fact: 622 CE: Muhammad's migration (the Hijra) from Mecca to Medina marks year 1 of the Islamic calendar.
cards.detail: Facing persecution in Mecca, Muhammad and his followers relocated to Yathrib (Medina), where the first Muslim community and polity took shape. The Islamic lunar calendar (AH, 'after Hijra') counts from this year — not from Muhammad's birth or the first revelation.
cards.deploy: A reminder that the world's major calendars start from different events — dating itself encodes a worldview.
cards.counter: The year is firm, but precise days are reconstructed from later sources.

quiz.q: The Islamic calendar counts its years from…
In what year CE does the Hijra fall, the event that marks year 1 of the Islamic calendar? Give the year.
By its older name, to which city did Muhammad migrate during the Hijra, the place later called Medina?
The Islamic calendar's year 1 is fixed to which event?
choices: Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina

cards.title: Sykes–Picot carves up the Middle East
cards.fact: 1916: the secret Sykes–Picot agreement split the Ottoman Middle East into British and French spheres.
cards.detail: During WWI, Britain and France (with Russian assent) secretly agreed how to divide the Ottoman Arab lands. The mandates and borders that followed — Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, Palestine — were drawn largely in European capitals, cutting across communities. The legacy still shapes Middle Eastern politics and grievances.
cards.deploy: Concrete evidence that many modern state borders were imposed from outside, not grown organically.
cards.counter: Later deals (San Remo, the mandate system) reshaped the lines; blaming all regional conflict on one 1916 map oversimplifies.

quiz.q: The 1916 Sykes–Picot agreement secretly divided…
choices: the Ottoman Middle East between Britain and France

quiz.q: The 1916 Sykes-Picot agreement divided the Arab lands of which collapsing empire?
Besides Britain, which European power was the other main signatory that gained a sphere of influence under the 1916 Sykes-Picot agreement?
In what year was the secret Sykes-Picot agreement made? Give the year.

cards.title: The founding of the People's Republic of China
cards.fact: 1 October 1949: Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China.
cards.detail: After decades of warlordism, Japanese invasion and civil war, the Communists under Mao defeated the Nationalists (who fled to Taiwan). The new state launched land reform and later the Great Leap Forward and Cultural Revolution; from 1978 Deng Xiaoping's reforms opened the economy that made China a superpower.
cards.deploy: The starting point for understanding modern China's politics, economy and rise.
cards.counter: 1949 is a founding, not a steady state: Maoist and reform-era China differ so sharply they are almost different systems.

quiz.q: What was founded on 1 October 1949?
When the Communists won the Chinese Civil War in 1949, where did the defeated Nationalist government retreat to and continue ruling?
Which sequence correctly orders these episodes of PRC history from earliest to latest?
choices: Great Leap Forward, Cultural Revolution, Deng's economic reforms
Cultural Revolution, Great Leap Forward, Deng's economic reforms
Deng's economic reforms, Great Leap Forward, Cultural Revolution
Great Leap Forward, Deng's economic reforms, Cultural Revolution

quiz.q: If the People's Republic of China was proclaimed in 1949 and Deng Xiaoping's economic reforms began in 1978, how many years of Maoist-era rule preceded the reform period?

cards.title: The Year of Africa
cards.fact: 1960, the 'Year of Africa': 17 African countries gained independence from colonial rule.
cards.detail: In a single year a wave of mostly French and British colonies became sovereign states — Nigeria, Senegal, Mali, the Congo and others. Independence often came with borders inherited from the colonisers and economies built to export raw materials, shaping later challenges (including across the Sahel).
cards.deploy: Shows how recent decolonisation is — within living memory — and how colonial borders and economies outlast empire.
cards.counter: Formal independence didn't end external influence: Cold War rivalry, debt and 'Françafrique' ties kept shaping these states.

quiz.q: Why is 1960 called the 'Year of Africa'?

In the 'Year of Africa', 17 colonies became independent. If a textbook listed 23 colonies that were still ruled at the start of that year, how many of those 23 would remain colonised at year's end, assuming all 17 came from this group?
Which feature of newly independent African states in 1960 is best explained as a direct inheritance from the colonial period?
choices: Borders drawn by European powers that cut across ethnic groups
Membership in the United Nations Security Council
Universal adoption of a single indigenous official language

quiz.q: What term names the continuing web of political, military and economic ties through which France kept influence over its former African colonies after independence?

cards.title: The fall of the Berlin Wall
cards.fact: 9 November 1989: the Berlin Wall fell, symbolising the end of the Cold War division of Europe.
cards.detail: Mounting protest and a botched East German announcement sent crowds to the checkpoints; the guards stood aside. Within a year Germany was reunified and by 1991 the Soviet Union had dissolved. In the dominant Western telling it marked the triumph of liberal democracy and the 'end of history' (Francis Fukuyama). Seen from Moscow it reads differently — the 'common European home' Gorbachev hoped for never arrived, and Putin later called the Soviet collapse 'the greatest geopolitical catastrophe' of the century; many East Germans, too, recall loss alongside liberation.
cards.deploy: A hinge date — and a test of whose story you tell: Western triumph, Russian catastrophe, or Eastern dispossession.
cards.counter: The triumphal reading curdled: NATO expansion, the chaos of Russia's 1990s 'shock therapy', authoritarian revival and the 2008 crash all complicated any 'liberalism won' story — and reunification itself, for many in the East, was no simple homecoming.

quiz.q: The fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) symbolised…
choices: the end of the Cold War division of Europe

quiz.q: Which political scientist argued that the post-1989 triumph of liberal democracy marked 'the end of history'?
The Berlin Wall fell in 1989 and the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991. How many years separated these two events?
How did Vladimir Putin later characterise the collapse of the Soviet Union, illustrating that 1989-91 is read very differently from Moscow?
choices: As 'the greatest geopolitical catastrophe' of the century
As the inevitable triumph of liberal democracy
As the realisation of the 'common European home'

cards.title: The prisoner's dilemma
cards.fact: Two people each acting in their own interest can both end up worse off than if they'd cooperated.
cards.detail: In the classic setup two suspects each do better by betraying the other no matter what the other does — so both betray, and both get a worse outcome than mutual silence. The individually rational move is collectively self-defeating. It models arms races, price wars, overfishing and climate inaction.
cards.deploy: The sharpest illustration that 'everyone acting rationally' need not produce a good outcome — a core case for coordination and rules.
cards.counter: Real life is rarely one-shot or anonymous; repetition, reputation and communication can rescue cooperation.

quiz.q: In a one-shot prisoner's dilemma, two self-interested players tend to…
choices: Both defect, ending up worse off

quiz.q: In a one-shot prisoner's dilemma, why does each player betray rather than stay silent?
choices: Betraying yields a better payoff regardless of what the other player does
Players cannot communicate so they choose randomly
Mutual silence is forbidden by the rules of the game
Betraying always gives both players the highest possible joint payoff

quiz.q: Which feature of repeated interactions, absent from a single anonymous round, is most credited with letting cooperation emerge?
Which real-world situation is NOT a standard example of prisoner's-dilemma logic, where individual rationality undermines a better collective outcome?
choices: A buyer choosing the cheapest of several identical products
Two firms cutting prices in a price war
Nations refusing to cut emissions while others pollute
Fishers each overharvesting a shared fishery

cards.title: Nash equilibrium
cards.fact: A Nash equilibrium is a situation where no player can do better by changing their move alone.
cards.detail: Named after John Nash, it is the resting point of a game: given what everyone else is doing, no one gains by deviating unilaterally. A game can have one, many, or no equilibria in pure strategies. Crucially, an equilibrium can be stable yet bad for everyone — mutual defection in the prisoner's dilemma is a Nash equilibrium.
cards.deploy: Lets you predict where strategic interactions settle — and show that a stable outcome isn't necessarily efficient or fair.
cards.counter: It assumes rational, payoff-maximising players who know the rules; real people misjudge, learn, and care about fairness.

quiz.q: At a Nash equilibrium…
choices: no player gains by changing strategy alone

quiz.q: Two firms each choose a price. Neither can raise its profit by changing its own price while the other holds steady, yet both would earn more if they jointly charged higher prices. What does this scenario illustrate?
choices: A Nash equilibrium that is not the jointly best outcome
A situation with no Nash equilibrium
A game that must have multiple equilibria

quiz.q: What is the technical term for a single player switching to a different move on their own, while everyone else keeps their move fixed?
A coordination game has these pure-strategy Nash equilibria: (Left, Left) and (Right, Right). How many pure-strategy Nash equilibria does it have?

cards.title: Repeated games and tit-for-tat
cards.fact: If a game is played again and again, cooperation can become rational — strategies like 'tit-for-tat' reward it and punish betrayal.
cards.detail: When players keep meeting, today's betrayal invites tomorrow's retaliation. In Axelrod's tournaments the simple 'tit-for-tat' rule — start nice, then copy the opponent's last move — did remarkably well. Repetition, reputation and a long 'shadow of the future' turn the prisoner's dilemma's logic around.
cards.deploy: Explains how cooperation emerges without a central enforcer — among firms, nations, even unrelated animals.
cards.counter: It needs a credible future: if the end is known and near, cooperation can unravel backwards from the final round.

quiz.q: Why can repetition sustain cooperation in a prisoner's dilemma?
In a tit-for-tat strategy, what move does a player make in the very first round, before seeing any of the opponent's choices?
Two suppliers know they will trade for exactly 10 fixed rounds and both know the count. Standard reasoning predicts cooperation tends to collapse. Which mechanism drives that collapse?
choices: Backward induction from the known final round, where there is no future to protect
Tit-for-tat punishing the wrong player by mistake
An increase in the number of available strategies
The disappearance of any Nash equilibrium in the game

quiz.q: Playing a one-shot prisoner's dilemma against the SAME opponent five separate times in a row counts as how many repetitions of the game?

media.caption: Valid: if the premises hold, the conclusion must.

cards.title: Valid vs true: the shape of an argument
cards.fact: An argument can be perfectly valid yet completely false — validity is about form, not facts.
cards.detail: An argument is valid if its conclusion must be true whenever its premises are — the logic holds regardless of content. It is sound only if it is valid AND its premises are actually true. 'All cats are robots; Felix is a cat; so Felix is a robot' is valid but unsound.
cards.deploy: Lets you separate two different complaints: 'your logic doesn't follow' vs 'your premise is false'.
cards.counter: Validity is necessary but cheap; in real debate the action is usually whether the premises are true, which logic alone can't settle.

quiz.q: An argument is valid when…
choices: if the premises are true, the conclusion must be too

quiz.q: Consider: 'All birds can fly; a penguin is a bird; therefore a penguin can fly.' How is this argument best classified?
What single term describes an argument that is valid AND has all true premises?
An argument has true premises and a true conclusion, but the conclusion does not actually follow from those premises. What can you correctly say about it?
choices: It is invalid, so it cannot be sound
It is valid because the conclusion is true
It is sound because all the statements are true

media.caption: Modus ponens (and modus tollens: P→Q, ¬Q ⊢ ¬P).

cards.title: Modus ponens and modus tollens
cards.fact: Two reliable inference rules: affirm the 'if' (modus ponens) or deny the 'then' (modus tollens).
cards.detail: Modus ponens: from 'if P then Q' and 'P', conclude 'Q'. Modus tollens: from 'if P then Q' and 'not Q', conclude 'not P'. Both are valid forms — the backbone of everyday and mathematical reasoning. Popper's falsification is modus tollens: if a theory predicts Q and we observe not-Q, the theory fails.
cards.deploy: Names the moves so you can check whether a conclusion actually follows — and spot when someone only looks like they're using them.
cards.counter: Garbage in, garbage out: a valid form with a false 'if…then' premise still gives you nothing.

quiz.q: Modus tollens reasons from 'if P then Q' and 'not Q' to…
Given 'If it rained, the ground is wet' together with the observation 'It rained,' which named inference rule lets you conclude 'the ground is wet'?
A scientist's theory predicts a comet will appear in March. March passes with no comet. By which valid form does this observation refute the theory?
choices: Modus tollens: from 'if theory then Q' and 'not Q', conclude 'not theory'
Modus ponens: from 'if theory then Q' and 'theory', conclude 'Q'
Affirming the consequent: from 'if theory then Q' and 'Q', conclude 'theory'
Denying the antecedent: from 'if theory then Q' and 'not theory', conclude 'not Q'

quiz.q: Starting from 'If the alarm works, the light blinks' and the fact that 'the light is not blinking,' what conclusion does modus tollens deliver?

media.caption: Invalid — Q can have other causes.

cards.title: Affirming the consequent
cards.fact: 'If P then Q; Q; therefore P' is a fallacy — a true consequence doesn't prove the cause.
cards.detail: Affirming the consequent confuses 'P implies Q' with 'Q implies P'. 'If it rained, the street is wet; the street is wet; so it rained' ignores sprinklers and hoses. It is one of the commonest reasoning errors — including in reading evidence: a result merely consistent with a theory doesn't confirm it.
cards.deploy: A precise label for a very common bad move — useful when someone treats 'consistent with' as 'proves'.
cards.counter: Such inferences can still raise the probability of P (that's Bayesian evidence) — they're just not deductively valid.

quiz.q: 'The street is wet, so it must have rained' commits which error?
A diagnostic theory predicts that a patient with disease D will have an elevated marker M. A patient is found to have elevated M, and the doctor concludes the patient has D. What is the logical flaw?
choices: Other conditions could also raise M, so observing M does not establish D
The theory failed to predict M, so the observation is irrelevant
Elevated M actually makes D less likely, not more
The conclusion is valid because the prediction came true

quiz.q: Affirming the consequent mistakenly treats 'P implies Q' as though it also licensed which converse claim?
Which inference is deductively VALID rather than an instance of affirming the consequent?
choices: If it rained, the street is wet; the street is not wet; so it did not rain
If a number is divisible by 4, it is even; this number is even; so it is divisible by 4
If she studied, she passed; she passed; so she studied
If the engine is on, the light is lit; the light is lit; so the engine is on

cards.title: What a proposition is
cards.fact: A proposition is a statement that's either true or false — logic's basic building block.
cards.detail: Logic works with propositions: declarative statements that bear a truth value, not questions, commands or exclamations. 'Snow is white' is a proposition; 'Close the door!' isn't. Different sentences can express the same proposition, and propositions are what we combine and reason about.
cards.deploy: The first move in any logical analysis: isolate the actual truth-apt claims before judging an argument.
cards.counter: Natural language is messy — vagueness, context and words like 'I' or 'now' mean real sentences don't always map to one fixed proposition.

media.caption: Each proposition is true (⊤) or false (⊥).

quiz.q: Which of these is a proposition?
From this list, how many items are propositions: 'Water boils at 100 C at sea level', 'What time is it?', 'Turn left at the corner', '7 is a prime number', 'Ouch!', 'Paris is the capital of Spain'?
Why do the sentences 'It is raining' (English) and 'Il pleut' (French) count as expressing the same proposition?
choices: They are different sentences that carry the same truth-evaluable content
They contain the same number of words
They are both questions about the weather
A proposition must be written in exactly one language

quiz.q: What property must a declarative statement have to qualify as a proposition: that it bears a definite ____ value?

cards.title: The five connectives
cards.fact: Five little symbols build every compound statement: not, and, or, if–then, if-and-only-if.
cards.detail: Propositional logic joins propositions with connectives: ¬ (not), ∧ (and), ∨ (or), → (if…then), ↔ (iff). Each is truth-functional — the truth of the whole depends only on the truth of its parts. They are the grammar of formal reasoning.
cards.deploy: Lets you translate tangled prose into precise structure you can actually test.
cards.counter: The logician's '→' isn't everyday 'if': 'if P then Q' counts as true whenever P is false, which feels odd (the 'paradoxes of material implication').

media.caption: not, and, or, if–then, iff.

quiz.q: The symbol ∧ means…
The connective written as the double-headed arrow, read 'if and only if', is called by what one-word abbreviation?
What does it mean to say a connective like 'and' is truth-functional?
choices: The truth value of the compound depends only on the truth values of its parts
The connective can join only true statements
The connective always produces a true result
Its meaning changes depending on the topic of the sentences

quiz.q: Under the logician's material conditional, the statement 'If 2 is odd, then the moon is made of cheese' is evaluated as:
choices: True, because the antecedent (2 is odd) is false
False, because the moon is not made of cheese
Neither true nor false, because the two parts are unrelated
False, because both parts are false

cards.title: Truth tables
cards.fact: A truth table lays out a statement's truth for every combination of its inputs.
cards.detail: List every true/false combination of the variables, then compute the compound's value in each row. For n variables there are 2ⁿ rows. Truth tables define each connective exactly and let you check equivalence and validity mechanically — no intuition required.
cards.deploy: The brute-force lie detector for propositional arguments: build the table and read off the answer.
cards.counter: They blow up fast — 2ⁿ rows — so they're impractical for many variables, and don't extend to 'all/some' (quantified) statements.

media.tex: P \wedge Q:\ TT\to T,\ TF\to F,\ FT\to F,\ FF\to F
media.caption: The truth table for AND.

quiz.q: A truth table for a statement with 3 variables has how many rows?
A compound proposition is built from 5 distinct variables. How many rows does its complete truth table require?
What is the main reason truth tables cannot be used to test an argument like 'All cats are mammals; Felix is a cat; so Felix is a mammal'?
choices: It uses quantifiers (all/some), which truth tables do not handle
It has too few variables to fill a table
Its conclusion is false, so no table applies
Truth tables only work for statements that are always true

quiz.q: Building a full truth table and checking that the conclusion is true in every row where all premises are true is a mechanical test for what property of an argument?

cards.title: Tautology and contradiction
cards.fact: Some statements are true no matter what (tautologies) and some are false no matter what (contradictions).
cards.detail: A tautology is true in every row of its truth table (e.g. P ∨ ¬P — 'either it's raining or it isn't'). Its opposite is a contradiction (always false); everything else is contingent (depends on the facts). Tautologies are the logical truths — true by form alone.
cards.deploy: Separates claims true by logic alone from claims that actually say something about the world.
cards.counter: Logical truth isn't informative truth — a tautology tells you nothing about reality, which is why 'it is what it is' explains nothing.

media.caption: Law of excluded middle — a tautology.

quiz.q: A tautology is a statement that is…
Which statement is a contradiction (false in every possible situation)?
A statement whose truth depends on the actual facts, neither always true nor always false, is called what?
A truth table for a formula built from 3 distinct atomic variables has how many rows?

cards.title: De Morgan's laws
cards.fact: 'Not (A and B)' equals 'not A or not B' — negation flips and/or.
cards.detail: ¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q, and ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q: pushing a negation inside a bracket swaps AND with OR. The rule is everywhere — simplifying logic, database queries and programming conditions.
cards.deploy: A reliable rewrite for negating compound conditions correctly — vital in code and contracts alike.
cards.counter: Easy to misapply: people negate 'A and B' to 'not A and not B' (wrong) instead of 'not A or not B'.

media.caption: Negation swaps AND and OR.

quiz.q: 'Not (rich and famous)' is equivalent to…
'It is not the case that the file exists or the user is logged in' is equivalent to which condition?
choices: The file does not exist AND the user is not logged in
The file does not exist OR the user is not logged in
The file exists AND the user is logged in
The file does not exist OR the user is logged in

quiz.q: When you push a negation inside a bracket, AND turns into which connective?

cards.title: The contrapositive
cards.fact: 'If P then Q' is identical to 'if not Q then not P' — its contrapositive.
cards.detail: A conditional and its contrapositive are logically equivalent: (P → Q) ≡ (¬Q → ¬P). 'If it's a dog, it's a mammal' equals 'if it's not a mammal, it's not a dog'. Beware the converse (Q → P) and inverse (¬P → ¬Q) — those are NOT equivalent to the original.
cards.deploy: A proof tool: when a conditional is hard to show directly, prove its contrapositive instead.
cards.counter: The common error is swapping in the converse — 'if it's a mammal it's a dog' — which simply doesn't follow.

media.caption: A conditional equals its contrapositive.

quiz.q: The contrapositive of 'if P then Q' is…
choices: if not P then not Q
if not Q then not P

quiz.q: For the conditional 'if it rains, the ground is wet', what is the name of the form 'if the ground is wet, then it rained' that is NOT logically equivalent to it?
Which statement is logically equivalent to 'if a number is divisible by 6, then it is even'?
choices: If a number is not even, then it is not divisible by 6
If a number is even, then it is divisible by 6
If a number is not divisible by 6, then it is not even
If a number is divisible by 6, then it is odd

quiz.q: The form '(not P) implies (not Q)', built by negating both parts of 'if P then Q' without swapping them, is called what?

cards.title: Disjunctive syllogism
cards.fact: Either P or Q; not P; therefore Q — reasoning by elimination.
cards.detail: A valid rule: from 'P ∨ Q' and '¬P', conclude Q. 'It's in the kitchen or the garage; it's not the kitchen; so the garage.' It's how you reason by ruling options out.
cards.deploy: Formalises elimination — rule the alternatives out and the survivor follows.
cards.counter: It needs a genuine, complete 'or': if the disjunction misses a third possibility, eliminating one option doesn't establish another.

media.caption: Disjunctive syllogism (valid).

quiz.q: From 'P or Q' and 'not P', you may conclude…
Given 'the suspect fled by car or by train' and 'the suspect did not flee by train', what validly follows?
choices: The suspect did not flee by car

quiz.q: Disjunctive syllogism only works if the starting 'or' lists every real possibility. Naming a fake either/or that omits other options is which informal fallacy?
Why does 'X is in folder A, B, or C; X is not in folder A; therefore X is in folder B' FAIL as a valid disjunctive syllogism?
choices: Eliminating one of three options leaves two survivors, not one, so B is not forced
The disjunction was not really true to begin with
Disjunctive syllogism cannot use the word 'folder'
You must always eliminate the last option, not the first

cards.title: Hypothetical syllogism
cards.fact: If P then Q, and if Q then R — so if P then R. Conditionals chain.
cards.detail: From 'P → Q' and 'Q → R', conclude 'P → R'. 'If I oversleep I miss the train; if I miss the train I'm late; so if I oversleep I'm late.' It's the engine of step-by-step deductive chains.
cards.deploy: Justifies stringing implications into a chain — the backbone of multi-step proofs and arguments.
cards.counter: Real conditionals carry hidden exceptions, so long chains accumulate 'other things being equal' caveats and can break in practice.

media.tex: P \rightarrow Q,\ Q \rightarrow R \vdash P \rightarrow R
media.caption: Conditionals chain (valid).

quiz.q: From 'P→Q' and 'Q→R' you can conclude…
You know 'If it rains, the match is cancelled' and 'If the match is cancelled, we get refunds.' Which conclusion is validly chained?
choices: If it rains, we get refunds
If we get refunds, it rained
If it doesn't rain, we get no refunds
If the match is cancelled, it rained

quiz.q: Hypothetical syllogism links conditionals end to end into a single longer conditional. What is the one-word name for this property, where the consequent of one implication feeds the antecedent of the next?
Starting from 'P1 → P2' and adding P2 → P3, P3 → P4, on up to P7 → P8, all chained by hypothetical syllogism, how many conditional premises in total are needed to validly conclude 'P1 → P8'?

cards.title: Denying the antecedent
cards.fact: 'If P then Q; not P; therefore not Q' is a fallacy — P isn't the only road to Q.
cards.detail: Denying the antecedent invalidly infers ¬Q from a conditional plus ¬P. 'If you're a ski instructor you have a job; you're not a ski instructor; so you have no job' — but you could have another job. It mirrors affirming the consequent; both confuse a conditional with a biconditional.
cards.deploy: Names a common slip: 'the cause didn't happen, so the effect can't' ignores other causes.
cards.counter: If the 'if' really means 'if and only if' (a biconditional), then denying the antecedent does work — so check whether 'if' means 'only if'.

media.caption: Invalid — other causes can give Q.

quiz.q: 'If P then Q; not P; so not Q' is…
'If a number is divisible by 4, it is even. 17 is not divisible by 4, therefore 17 is not even.' What is wrong with this reasoning?
choices: It denies the antecedent — being divisible by 4 isn't the only way to be even
Nothing; it is valid because 17 really is odd

quiz.q: Denying the antecedent becomes a valid inference only if the conditional is actually which two-directional connective, where P and Q each imply the other?
Which argument is logically VALID rather than a case of denying the antecedent?
choices: If P then Q; not Q; therefore not P
If P then Q; not P; therefore not Q
If P then Q; Q; therefore P
If P then Q; not P; therefore Q

cards.title: Quantifiers: all and some
cards.fact: Two quantifiers extend logic from 'this' to 'all' and 'some': ∀ (for all) and ∃ (there exists).
cards.detail: Propositional logic can't capture 'all men are mortal'. Predicate logic adds quantifiers over a domain: ∀x P(x) ('every x is P') and ∃x P(x) ('some x is P'), where P is a predicate. This is 'first-order logic', the workhorse of modern mathematics.
cards.deploy: Lets you state and test general claims ('all', 'some', 'none') precisely, not just single facts.
cards.counter: Quantifier order matters and trips people up: '∀x∃y loves(x,y)' (everyone loves someone) is not '∃y∀x loves(x,y)' (someone is loved by all).

media.caption: for all x, P(x);  there exists x, P(x).

quiz.q: The symbol ∀ means…
Quantifiers belong to the branch of logic that extends propositional logic by adding predicates and a domain of objects. What is the standard name for this branch?
Over the domain {1,2,3,4,5,6}, let P(x) mean 'x is even'. How many of the domain's elements are witnesses that make ∃x P(x) true?

cards.title: Negating quantifiers
cards.fact: To negate 'all', say 'some… not'; to negate 'some', say 'none'.
cards.detail: Negation flips quantifiers: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x) ('not everything is P' = 'something isn't P'), and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x) ('nothing is P' = 'everything is not-P'). It's De Morgan's laws lifted to quantifiers — and the key to disproving universal claims.
cards.deploy: The rule for correctly contradicting sweeping claims: the opposite of 'all are' is 'at least one isn't', not 'none are'.
cards.counter: The everyday slip is negating 'all swans are white' to 'no swans are white' — the real negation is just 'some swan isn't white'.

media.caption: Negation swaps ∀ and ∃.

quiz.q: The negation of 'all A are B' is…
What is the correct negation of 'Every student passed the exam'?
choices: At least one student did not pass
