quiz.q: Pushing a negation through a quantifier turns 'for all' into 'there exists' (and vice versa) while negating the inside. This rule is the quantified version of which named pair of laws?

cards.title: The power of a counterexample
cards.fact: One counterexample is enough to demolish a 'for all' claim.
cards.detail: Because ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x), disproving a universal needs just a single failing case. 'All swans are white' dies the moment you find one black swan. Proving a universal takes a general argument; disproving it takes one example — an asymmetry at the heart of testing ideas.
cards.deploy: The cheapest refutation in the toolkit: to kill a sweeping claim, find one clear exception.
cards.counter: It only refutes strictly universal claims — against 'most' or statistical claims, a single exception proves little.

media.plain: one x with ¬P(x) ⇒ not all are P
media.caption: A single counterexample refutes a universal.

quiz.q: To disprove 'all A are B' you need…
choices: one A that is not B

quiz.q: Someone claims 'every prime number is odd.' What is the fastest way to refute this?
choices: Point out that 2 is a prime number that is even
Prove that infinitely many primes are odd
Show that most primes are odd
Argue that the claim is too broad to be useful

quiz.q: The negation of 'for all x, P(x)' equals 'there exists an x such that not-P(x).' What is the name for the symbol meaning 'there exists'?
To disprove a strictly universal claim of the form 'all X are Y' with certainty, what is the minimum number of valid counterexamples required?

cards.title: Aristotle's syllogism
cards.fact: All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; so Socrates is mortal — the classical syllogism.
cards.detail: A categorical syllogism reasons from two premises using 'all', 'some' and 'no' to a conclusion. Aristotle catalogued the valid forms (like 'Barbara': all M are P, all S are M, so all S are P) and the four proposition types (A, E, I, O). It's logic's oldest formal system and the ancestor of predicate logic.
cards.deploy: The original template for valid deductive argument — still the cleanest illustration of form over content.
cards.counter: Syllogistic logic is limited — it struggles with relations and multiple quantifiers — which is why Frege's predicate logic superseded it.

media.tex: \text{All } M \text{ are } P;\ \text{all } S \text{ are } M \;\therefore\; \text{all } S \text{ are } P
media.plain: All M are P; all S are M ∴ all S are P
media.caption: The 'Barbara' syllogism.

quiz.q: A categorical syllogism reasons using…
Premises: 'All metals conduct electricity' and 'All copper objects are metals.' Which conclusion validly follows in syllogistic form?
choices: No copper object is a non-metal

quiz.q: How many distinct proposition types (A, E, I, O) does Aristotle's categorical logic use?
Whose system of predicate logic, handling relations and multiple quantifiers, superseded the limited reach of categorical syllogistic logic?

cards.title: Proof by contradiction
cards.fact: Prove something by assuming the opposite and deriving an absurdity (reductio ad absurdum).
cards.detail: To prove P, assume ¬P and show it forces a contradiction; since the assumption breaks logic, P must hold. It's how we prove √2 is irrational and that there's no largest prime. The trigger is a contradiction — a statement and its negation both true.
cards.deploy: A powerful move when direct proof is hard: attack the negation and watch it self-destruct.
cards.counter: Constructive (intuitionist) mathematicians distrust it for existence claims — showing 'not-not-P' isn't the same as building a P.

media.caption: Reductio ad absurdum.

quiz.q: Proof by contradiction works by…
choices: assuming the opposite and reaching an absurdity

quiz.q: To prove by contradiction that there is no smallest positive rational number, what should you assume at the start?
choices: Assume that a smallest positive rational number does exist
Assume that all rational numbers are positive
Assume that the smallest positive rational equals 1
Assume that rationals cannot be ordered

quiz.q: What is the Latin name for proof by contradiction, meaning 'reduction to the absurd'?
Why do constructive (intuitionist) mathematicians distrust proof by contradiction for existence claims?
choices: Showing 'not-not-P' does not actually build or exhibit a P
It relies on premises that are never true
It can only handle finite cases
It requires a base case that is hard to verify

cards.title: Proof by induction
cards.fact: To prove a statement for all whole numbers, prove it for 1 and that each case implies the next.
cards.detail: Mathematical induction: show the base case (n=1) holds, then show that if it holds for n it holds for n+1. Like dominoes — knock the first and prove each topples the next, and all fall. It proves infinitely many cases in two finite steps.
cards.deploy: The standard way to prove a universal claim over the integers — sums, inequalities, algorithm correctness.
cards.counter: It only works over well-ordered, step-by-step domains (the naturals); a wrong base case or a gap in the step silently breaks the whole proof.

media.caption: Base case + inductive step.

quiz.q: Mathematical induction proves a claim for all n by…
choices: proving a base case and that n implies n+1

quiz.q: An induction proof shows the base case n=1 and that each case implies the next. Using that domino logic, how many of the cases n=1, n=2, ..., n=100 are thereby established?
A student proves a statement holds for n=1 but forgets to show that holding for n implies it holds for n+1. What is wrong with the proof?
choices: Without the inductive step, nothing guarantees the claim for n=2 and beyond
Nothing — verifying the base case alone is sufficient
The base case should have started at n=0 instead
The proof is valid but only for even numbers

quiz.q: Mathematical induction is guaranteed to work only over a domain with what ordering property, possessed by the natural numbers, that lets you always step to a unique next element?

cards.title: Formal vs informal fallacies
cards.fact: A fallacy is a broken argument — and the sneaky ones aren't about form but content.
cards.detail: Formal fallacies fail by structure (like affirming the consequent). Informal fallacies fail by content or context: the logic can look fine while the move is illegitimate — a distraction, a smuggled assumption, a shifted meaning. Spotting them is core to clear thinking and honest debate.
cards.deploy: A checklist for pressure-testing arguments: is this valid in form, and free of informal tricks?
cards.counter: 'That's a fallacy!' is itself overused — naming a fallacy doesn't refute a claim (the 'fallacy fallacy'); a badly-argued point can still be true.

quiz.q: Informal fallacies fail because of…
choices: their content or context, not form

quiz.q: Someone argues badly for a claim using a textbook fallacy. What follows about the claim itself?
choices: Nothing - the claim could still be true; the bad argument just fails to establish it
The claim is automatically false because the argument was fallacious
The claim becomes unfalsifiable until a new argument is given
The claim is proven true, since pointing out a fallacy proves the opposite

quiz.q: What is the name for the mistake of treating a claim as refuted merely because one argument for it was fallacious?
'All cats are mammals; Rex is a mammal; therefore Rex is a cat.' Which category does this error belong to?
choices: Formal fallacy - the deductive structure is invalid
Informal fallacy - it relies on emotional content
Informal fallacy - a word shifts meaning between premises
Not a fallacy - the conclusion follows necessarily

cards.title: Straw man
cards.fact: Straw man: beat a distorted version of your opponent's argument instead of the real one.
cards.detail: You swap someone's actual position for a weaker, exaggerated caricature, refute that, and claim victory. 'You want some immigration limits? So you'd ban all foreigners!' The real argument stands untouched. Its honest opposite is steelmanning — engaging the strongest version.
cards.deploy: Name it to force a return to what was actually claimed — then steelman instead.
cards.counter: Not every restatement is a straw man; sometimes you fairly draw out an implication. The test: would the other side accept your version?

quiz.q: A straw man argument…
choices: misrepresents the opponent's view to attack it

quiz.q: What is the honest opposite of straw-manning, where you engage the strongest version of an opponent's argument?
A colleague says 'We should add a few safety checks before launch.' You reply: 'So you want to delay the product forever and bankrupt the company?' Which test best shows this is a straw man?
choices: The colleague would reject your version as not what they claimed
Your version is longer than the original statement
You raised your voice while replying
The colleague has no expertise in safety

quiz.q: When is restating an opponent's position NOT a straw man?
choices: When you fairly draw out an implication they would accept as their own
Whenever your restatement is shorter than theirs
Whenever you disagree with the original position
When you attack the person's motives instead of the wording

cards.title: Ad hominem
cards.fact: Ad hominem: attack the arguer instead of the argument.
cards.detail: You dismiss a claim by pointing at the person — their character, motives or group — rather than engaging the reasoning. 'You'd say that, you're a banker.' Whether they're a banker has no bearing on whether the argument is sound. (It's not the same as a mere insult.)
cards.deploy: Separates the messenger from the message — a claim's truth doesn't depend on who says it.
cards.counter: Questioning a source's credibility or bias when weighing testimony (not proof) is legitimate — that's evidence assessment, not a fallacy.

quiz.q: An ad hominem attacks…
choices: the person rather than the argument

quiz.q: 'Dr. Lee's study on diet should be ignored - she's overweight herself.' Why is this an ad hominem rather than a fair point?
choices: Her body weight has no bearing on whether the study's reasoning and data are sound
Studies on diet can never be evaluated by anyone
Personal remarks are always insults and insults are always fallacies
Only doctors are allowed to comment on diet studies

quiz.q: Which of these is a LEGITIMATE move, not an ad hominem fallacy?
choices: Doubting a paid witness's testimony because they were hired by one side
Rejecting a math proof because its author once lied about something unrelated
Dismissing an economic argument because the speaker is wealthy
Ignoring a safety report because the engineer dresses oddly

quiz.q: Questioning a source's credibility or bias is legitimate when you are weighing what kind of claim - not proof, but what?

cards.title: False dilemma
cards.fact: False dilemma: forcing two options when more exist.
cards.detail: An argument frames a choice as 'either A or B' when other possibilities — or middle grounds — are available. 'You're either with us or against us.' It treats contraries (which can both be false) as if they were exhaustive contradictories.
cards.deploy: Crack a forced 'either/or' open by naming the third option it's hiding.
cards.counter: Some choices really are binary (a switch is on or off); calling every either/or a 'false dilemma' is itself lazy.

quiz.q: A false dilemma…
choices: presents only two options when more exist

quiz.q: 'Either we cut the whole program or the budget collapses.' What is the most direct way to expose this as a false dilemma?
choices: Name a third option, such as cutting only part of the program
Point out that the speaker is biased
Show the speaker once made a different argument
Argue that budgets are too complicated to discuss

quiz.q: A false dilemma treats two options as exhaustive when they are not. What does it mistake contraries (which can both be false) for?
choices: Contradictories, where exactly one must be true
Synonyms that mean the same thing

quiz.q: Why is 'a light switch is either on or off' NOT a false dilemma?
choices: The two options really are exhaustive - there is no third state
Light switches are too simple to reason about
Any statement framed as either/or is automatically valid
It mentions a physical object rather than a political view

cards.title: Slippery slope
cards.fact: Slippery slope: claim one small step must lead to a disastrous end — without showing why.
cards.detail: The argument asserts that allowing A will inevitably cascade to extreme outcome Z, treating each link as automatic. 'If we allow X, soon we'll have total chaos.' It's fallacious when the chain of causation is merely asserted, not demonstrated.
cards.deploy: Demand the mechanism: which step actually forces the next, and how likely is each?
cards.counter: Some slopes are real — precedents and feedback can cascade; the fallacy is only when the inevitability is claimed without evidence.

quiz.q: A slippery-slope argument claims…
choices: one step inevitably leads to an extreme outcome, unproven

quiz.q: A senator argues: 'If we let stores stay open one hour later, soon they'll be open all night, then crime will skyrocket, then the whole neighborhood collapses.' What makes this a slippery-slope fallacy rather than a sound prediction?
choices: Each step is asserted to follow automatically, with no evidence that one stage actually forces the next
It predicts a bad outcome rather than a good one
It involves more than two steps in the chain
It concerns a change to existing store hours

quiz.q: To rebut a slippery-slope argument, you should demand that the speaker show this for each link in the chain: what actually forces the next step. What single word names the thing being demanded?
Why is a slippery-slope argument NOT always a fallacy?
choices: Real precedents and feedback effects can genuinely make one step cascade into the next
Long chains of reasoning are always more reliable than short ones
Predicting disaster is a valid way to win any debate
Any claim about the future is automatically true

cards.title: Begging the question
cards.fact: Begging the question: assuming the very thing you're meant to prove.
cards.detail: The conclusion is smuggled into the premises, so the argument only 'works' for someone who already agrees. 'The Bible is true because it's the word of God, and we know that because the Bible says so.' (In logic, 'begs the question' means circular — not 'raises the question'.)
cards.deploy: Check whether a premise secretly restates the conclusion — circular arguments persuade no one not already convinced.
cards.counter: All valid deductions are 'contained' in their premises; the specific fault is using the conclusion itself as a premise, which can be subtle.

media.caption: The conclusion is its own premise.

quiz.q: Begging the question means…
choices: assuming the conclusion in the premises

quiz.q: Which statement begs the question?
choices: This essay is the best in the class because no other essay is as good as it
This essay scored highest because three independent judges rated it first
This essay is well-written, so it probably deserves a good grade
This essay arrived late, which usually lowers the grade

quiz.q: In everyday speech people misuse 'begs the question' to mean 'prompts the further question.' In logic, what one-word adjective describes the actual flaw of an argument that begs the question?
A valid deduction's conclusion is in some sense 'contained' in its premises, yet that alone is not the fallacy of begging the question. What specifically is the fault?
choices: Using the conclusion itself as one of the premises that is supposed to support it
Deriving a conclusion that nobody had thought of before
Drawing a conclusion that is broader than any single premise
Relying on more than two premises to reach the conclusion

cards.title: Equivocation
cards.fact: Equivocation: sliding between two meanings of the same word mid-argument.
cards.detail: A key term shifts sense between the premises and the conclusion, so the argument only appears to connect. 'Nothing is better than eternal happiness; a ham sandwich is better than nothing; so a ham sandwich is better than eternal happiness.' 'Nothing' changed meaning.
cards.deploy: Pin down definitions: make each key word hold one fixed meaning throughout.
cards.counter: Words genuinely have multiple senses; the fallacy is the illegitimate switch, not ambiguity itself, which careful definition resolves.

quiz.q: Equivocation is…
choices: using a key word in two different senses

quiz.q: 'A feather is light; what is light cannot be dark; therefore a feather cannot be dark.' Which word is used equivocally to make this seem valid?
What is the most effective way to neutralize an equivocation? Answer with a short phrase naming what you must fix for each key term.
Why does the mere fact that a word has several meanings NOT by itself constitute the fallacy of equivocation?
choices: Ambiguity is normal; the fault is illegitimately switching senses mid-argument, which a fixed definition prevents
Words with multiple meanings can never appear in a valid argument
Equivocation only occurs with numbers, not words
A word's meaning is always fixed by its first appearance in any text

cards.title: Appeal to authority
cards.fact: 'An expert said so' isn't proof — especially the wrong expert.
cards.detail: Citing authority turns fallacious when the authority is irrelevant, biased or speaking outside their field — or when 'an expert says X' is treated as conclusive rather than as evidence. A Nobel physicist's view on nutrition carries no special weight.
cards.deploy: Weigh expertise by relevance and consensus, not fame — and treat authority as evidence, not proof.
cards.counter: Deferring to genuine, relevant expert consensus is rational, not fallacious — you can't verify everything yourself; the fault is misplaced or overstated authority.

quiz.q: Appeal to authority is fallacious when…
choices: the authority is relevant and expert
the authority is irrelevant or treated as proof

quiz.q: A celebrated chemist endorses a particular brand of running shoe as biomechanically superior. Why is treating this endorsement as proof an appeal to authority?
choices: The chemist is speaking outside their field, so their fame gives the claim no special weight
Chemists are never trustworthy on any subject
Endorsements of products can never contain true claims
Running shoes cannot be evaluated scientifically at all

quiz.q: When is deferring to an expert RATIONAL rather than fallacious?
choices: When you rely on relevant expert consensus you can't feasibly verify yourself
When the expert is the most famous person available regardless of field
When a single expert's opinion is treated as final and beyond question
When the expert's view contradicts the available evidence

quiz.q: The card warns against weighing expertise by fame. By which TWO qualities should an expert's testimony instead be judged? Give one of the two as a single word.

cards.title: It's all bits
cards.fact: Everything in a computer — text, images, sound — is ultimately just numbers in binary (0s and 1s).
cards.detail: A bit is one on/off switch; eight bits make a byte. Numbers are written in base 2; text maps characters to numbers (ASCII/Unicode); images are grids of numbers for colour; sound is numbers sampled over time. The machine only ever shuffles patterns of bits — meaning is something we layer on top.
cards.deploy: Demystifies computers: no magic, just a very fast machine moving 0s and 1s under layers of convention.
cards.counter: 'It's all just bits' is true but unhelpful for understanding software — the interesting structure lives in the abstractions above.

quiz.q: At the lowest level, a computer stores text and images as…
A standard byte is made of how many bits?
How many distinct values can a single group of 4 bits represent?
A program displays a photo of a sunset. How does the image actually exist inside the machine?
choices: As a grid of numbers encoding colours, with meaning supplied by the software that interprets them
The computer stores the literal colours of light and shows them directly
As text describing the scene that the screen reads aloud
Images are the one data type a computer stores without converting to numbers

cards.title: Big-O: how algorithms scale
cards.fact: Big-O notation describes how an algorithm's cost grows as the input gets bigger — not how fast it runs today.
cards.detail: An algorithm is a step-by-step recipe. Big-O captures scaling: O(n) doubles work when input doubles; O(n²) quadruples it; O(log n) barely grows. For large inputs a better Big-O beats a faster computer — an O(n log n) sort crushes an O(n²) one on a million items, whatever the hardware.
cards.deploy: Explains why 'use a better algorithm' often beats 'buy a faster computer' as data grows.
cards.counter: Big-O hides constant factors and real-world effects; for small inputs a 'worse' algorithm can be faster in practice.

quiz.q: Big-O notation describes an algorithm's…
choices: How its cost scales with input size

quiz.q: An algorithm runs in O(n^2). If the input size triples, roughly how many times more work does it do?
For a step that runs on a million items, which growth rate would you most prefer, assuming the hidden constants are similar?
Big-O can be misleading for small inputs because it hides the multiplier attached to each operation (the per-step overhead). What is this hidden quantity called?

cards.title: The halting problem
cards.fact: Some problems are provably impossible for any computer: no program can decide, in general, whether another program will halt.
cards.detail: Alan Turing proved in 1936 that there is no general algorithm to decide whether an arbitrary program halts or loops forever — the halting problem. It set a hard limit on computation, echoing Gödel's incompleteness: formal systems and machines alike have questions they can't answer from the inside.
cards.deploy: Shows that 'undecidable' is a real, proven category — some questions have no algorithmic answer, however much power you throw at them.
cards.counter: Undecidability is about the general case; many specific instances are perfectly decidable, and approximations often suffice.

quiz.q: The halting problem shows that…
choices: No program can decide in general whether any program halts

quiz.q: Who proved in 1936 that no general algorithm can decide whether an arbitrary program halts?
Which statement correctly describes the scope of the halting problem's impossibility result?
choices: No single algorithm can decide halting for every possible program and input, though many specific cases can be settled
It is impossible to tell whether any individual program will halt, even with the program in front of you
Halting can be decided, but only on computers with unlimited memory
The result applies only to programs written in old programming languages

quiz.q: The halting result is often paired with which logician's incompleteness theorems, which show formal systems contain truths they cannot prove from within?

cards.title: Law of large numbers (and the gambler's fallacy)
cards.fact: Averages settle down over many trials — but a fair coin has no memory, so 'due' outcomes are a fallacy.
cards.detail: The law of large numbers says the average of many independent trials converges to the true probability — flip a fair coin enough and heads approaches 50%. But each flip is independent: a run of tails doesn't make heads 'due'. Confusing the long-run average with short-run correction is the gambler's fallacy.
cards.deploy: Two lessons in one: trust large samples, and never expect chance to 'balance out' in the short run.
cards.counter: Convergence can be slow and assumes independence; with dependence or fat tails the average stays unstable far longer than intuition expects.

quiz.q: After five tails in a row, the chance of heads on a fair coin is…
A fair six-sided die has just rolled four 6s in a row. What is the probability the next roll is a 6? Give the decimal value.
What is the name of the mistaken belief that a run of one outcome makes the opposite outcome 'due' on the next independent trial?
Which assumption is essential for the law of large numbers to guarantee that the running average converges to the true probability?
choices: The trials are independent of one another
Earlier results gently pull later results back toward the mean
The sample stays small enough to avoid drift
Each outcome has already balanced out within the first few trials

cards.title: The central limit theorem
cards.fact: Add up many small independent effects and you tend to get a bell curve — the normal distribution.
cards.detail: The central limit theorem says sums or averages of many independent influences converge to a normal (Gaussian) shape, whatever the underlying distribution. That's why heights, measurement errors and sample averages cluster symmetrically around a mean — and why the bell curve and the standard deviation are everywhere in statistics.

media.caption: Whatever you start with, the averages of many draws pile up into this bell.

cards.deploy: Explains why so many quantities are bell-shaped, and licenses much of standard statistics.
cards.counter: It fails when effects aren't independent or one factor dominates — then you get fat tails (power laws), where rare extremes are far commoner than the bell curve predicts.

quiz.q: The central limit theorem says sums of many independent effects tend toward a…

A factory's daily output is the sum of contributions from 500 independent workers, none dominating. By the central limit theorem, the distribution of total daily output across many days should look approximately:
choices: Bell-shaped (normal), regardless of each worker's individual output pattern
Uniform, since each worker contributes equally on average
Heavily right-skewed, because sums can only grow
Identical in shape to one worker's output distribution

quiz.q: A single die roll has standard deviation about 1.71. If you average 36 independent rolls, the standard deviation of that average is the single-roll SD divided by sqrt(n). What is the SD of the average of 36 rolls?

The central limit theorem breaks down when one factor dominates or effects are dependent, producing distributions where rare extreme events are far more common than a bell curve predicts. What name is given to this fat-tailed family of distributions?

cards.title: Correlation isn't causation
cards.fact: Two things moving together may share a hidden common cause rather than one causing the other.
cards.detail: Ice-cream sales and drownings rise together — because both rise with summer heat, a confounder. To infer cause you need more: a plausible mechanism, controlled experiments (randomisation breaks confounding), or careful natural experiments. 'X correlates with Y' is the start of an investigation, not its conclusion.
cards.deploy: A precise check on causal claims from observational data — ask 'what's the confounder?' and 'was it randomised?'
cards.counter: Overused as a thought-stopper: correlation is real evidence, and good design (instrumental variables, natural experiments) can infer causation without a lab.

quiz.q: Ice-cream sales correlate with drownings mainly because…
choices: Both rise with summer heat (a confounder)

quiz.q: Cities with more storks recorded also tend to have more human births. Both rise because larger cities have more of everything. What is the single-word term for such a hidden third variable that drives two correlated quantities without either causing the other?
A study finds people who take vitamin pills live longer. Before concluding the pills extend life, the strongest single move to rule out hidden common causes would be to:
choices: Run a randomised controlled trial assigning pills or placebo by chance
Collect more years of the same observational data
Survey participants on whether they believe the pills work
Check that the correlation is statistically significant at p < 0.05

quiz.q: Why is randomly assigning who receives a treatment so powerful for establishing causation?
choices: It breaks the link between the treatment and any confounders, since assignment no longer depends on them
It guarantees the treatment and control groups have identical outcomes
It removes all measurement error from the experiment
It makes the correlation between treatment and outcome larger

cards.title: Good names are the cheapest documentation
cards.fact: Code is read far more often than it's written, so clear names are the highest-leverage documentation there is.
cards.detail: A variable called daysSinceLastLogin needs no comment; d needs a paragraph. Good names state intent — what something is or does — so the next reader (often you, months later) doesn't have to reverse-engineer it. Renaming for clarity is one of the safest, most valuable edits you can make.
cards.deploy: The simplest lever for maintainable software: spend the extra seconds naming things well.
cards.counter: Names can't carry everything; over-long or 'clever' names hurt as much as cryptic ones — the goal is clarity, not length.

quiz.q: Clear names matter most because code is…
choices: Read far more often than it's written

quiz.q: A function is named processData. Following the principle that names should state intent, the best improvement would be:
choices: validateAndStripInvalidRows, naming what it actually does
doStuff, since shorter names are always better
pd, to save typing for the next reader

quiz.q: Good names are called the cheapest documentation a programmer can write. What asymmetry makes spending extra seconds on a clear name pay off so reliably?
choices: Code is read far more often than it is written, so each reader saves the cost
Clear names make programs execute measurably faster at runtime
Long descriptive names compress better in version control
Compilers reward intent-revealing names with fewer warnings

quiz.q: Why can a name like maximumRetryCountBeforeConnectionAbortHandlerInvocation be as harmful as a name like x?
choices: Excessive length obscures meaning and adds reading effort, defeating the goal of clarity
Long names are rejected by most compilers
Long names always run slower at execution time
It duplicates knowledge, violating the single-source-of-truth rule

cards.title: Don't repeat yourself (DRY)
cards.fact: Every piece of knowledge should have one authoritative place in the code.
cards.detail: When the same logic is copied in several spots, changing it means finding every copy — and missing one creates bugs. DRY says capture it once (a function, a constant, a single source of truth) so a change happens in exactly one place. It's about duplicated knowledge, not just identical text.
cards.deploy: Explains why copy-paste programming rots: each duplicate is a future inconsistency waiting to happen.
cards.counter: Premature DRY is its own trap — forcing unlike things to share code creates tangled coupling. A little duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction.

quiz.q: DRY is mainly about avoiding duplication of…
A tax rate of 0.2 is hardcoded in seven different functions. The DRY-aligned fix is to:
choices: Define it once as a named constant and reference that everywhere
Add a comment next to each copy reminding developers to update all seven
Leave it duplicated, since each function is independent
Rename each copy so they are easier to find later

quiz.q: A validation rule is copy-pasted into 9 places. A requirement change forces an edit, but a developer updates only the copies they remember, leaving 2 untouched. How many of the 9 sites now hold the outdated, inconsistent logic?
Two unrelated features happen to share five identical lines today. Aggressively merging them into one shared function risks which problem warned against by experienced engineers?
choices: Tight coupling between things that may need to change independently — the wrong abstraction
Violating the single source of truth for genuinely shared knowledge
Making each feature impossible to compile separately
Reducing the total line count too much

cards.title: Code is for humans: manage complexity
cards.fact: The hard part of programming isn't writing code — it's keeping complexity low enough to keep changing it.
cards.detail: As software grows the limit isn't the computer but the human: how much you can hold in your head. Small functions, clear boundaries between parts, and hiding details behind simple surfaces keep local changes local. The aim is code you can safely modify without understanding all of it at once.
cards.deploy: Reframes 'good code' as 'code that's cheap to change' — the real cost is maintenance, not the first draft.
cards.counter: Abstraction has a price: too many layers can obscure as much as sprawl. The skill is matching structure to the problem, not maximising either.

quiz.q: As software grows, the main constraint is…
choices: Human ability to understand and change it

quiz.q: Two implementations pass identical tests. One is a single 400-line function; the other is several small functions with clear boundaries. By the principle that good code is code that's cheap to change, which is better and why?
choices: The small-functions version, because future changes can stay local without reloading the whole thing into your head
The single function, because fewer functions means fewer places for bugs to hide
They are equal, since both pass the same tests so quality is identical
The single function, because inlining everything always runs faster

quiz.q: What is the name for the design technique of hiding a component's internal details behind a simple interface so callers don't need to know how it works?
A team keeps adding abstraction layers, yet the code becomes harder to follow. What does this illustrate about managing complexity?
choices: Abstraction has a cost; structure should match the problem rather than be maximised
Abstraction is always harmful and should be removed entirely
The team simply needs more layers until clarity returns
Complexity only ever comes from the hardware, not from design choices

cards.title: Octopuses have three hearts
cards.fact: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood.
cards.detail: Two branchial hearts pump blood through the gills; one systemic heart sends it to the body. The blood carries oxygen with copper-based haemocyanin (blue) rather than iron-based haemoglobin (red), which works better in cold, low-oxygen water.
cards.deploy: A vivid example that evolution finds many independent solutions to the same problem (oxygen transport) — there is rarely one 'right' design.
cards.counter: It's a trade-off, not strictly 'better': haemocyanin carries less oxygen than haemoglobin at warm temperatures.

quiz.q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
An octopus's blue blood carries oxygen using…

An octopus has branchial hearts that pump blood through its gills and one systemic heart for the rest of the body. If you observed an animal with the same arrangement but with four gill-serving (branchial) hearts plus one systemic heart, how many hearts would it have in total?
Which metal is at the core of haemocyanin, the oxygen-carrying pigment that gives octopus blood its blue colour?
Octopuses transport oxygen with copper-based haemocyanin while many other animals use iron-based haemoglobin. What does this contrast best illustrate about evolution?
choices: Evolution can reach different, trade-off-laden solutions to the same problem rather than one optimal design
Whichever pigment carries more oxygen always wins out everywhere
Blue blood is universally superior to red blood
Oxygen transport can only evolve once in any lineage

cards.title: A day on Venus is longer than its year
cards.fact: Venus takes longer to spin once than to orbit the Sun.
cards.detail: Venus rotates once every ~243 Earth days but orbits the Sun every ~225 Earth days — and it spins backwards (retrograde). So by the sidereal definition, its 'day' outlasts its 'year'.
cards.deploy: Everyday intuitions ('a day is shorter than a year') are local conventions, not universal truths.
cards.counter: It depends on the definition: a solar day on Venus (sunrise to sunrise) is ~117 Earth days, because the retrograde spin and orbit partly cancel.

quiz.q: Venus rotates once every about 243 Earth days and orbits the Sun every about 225 Earth days. By how many Earth days does one sidereal Venusian day exceed one Venusian year?
What single word describes Venus's rotation, meaning it spins in the opposite direction to most planets?
On Venus a solar day (sunrise to sunrise) is about 117 Earth days, far shorter than its 243-day sidereal rotation. Why is the solar day shorter?
choices: Its retrograde spin and its orbital motion partly cancel, so the Sun returns to the same place sooner
Venus speeds up its rotation during daytime
The Sun physically moves faster across Venus's thick atmosphere
Solar and sidereal days are the same thing measured twice

cards.title: The Year Without a Summer (1816)
cards.fact: In 1816 a volcano half a world away caused snow in June and famine across the Northern Hemisphere.
cards.detail: The 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora in Indonesia — the largest in recorded history — threw sulfate aerosols into the stratosphere, dimming the sun and crashing temperatures. Crops failed across Europe and North America. The gloom of that summer also gave us Mary Shelley's 'Frankenstein'.
cards.deploy: A single physical event can cascade into global social, economic and even cultural effects.
cards.counter: Attribution is partly confounded by an overlapping solar minimum (the Dalton Minimum); the volcano was the main driver but not the only one.

quiz.q: Which Indonesian volcano erupted in 1815, the largest eruption in recorded history, triggering the global cold spell of the following year?
How did the 1815 volcanic eruption in Indonesia cause crop failures in Europe and North America the next year?
choices: Sulfate aerosols reached the stratosphere and dimmed sunlight, lowering temperatures worldwide
Lava flows physically reached the Northern Hemisphere and buried farmland
Ash blocked shipping lanes so food could not be delivered
The eruption shifted Earth's orbit slightly farther from the Sun

quiz.q: Which famous novel did Mary Shelley begin during the gloomy, storm-bound summer of 1816?

cards.title: Honey effectively never spoils
cards.fact: Sealed honey can stay edible for thousands of years — pots found in Egyptian tombs were still good.
cards.detail: Honey's very low water content, acidity, and the trace hydrogen peroxide released by an enzyme (glucose oxidase) make it hostile to microbes. Kept sealed and dry, it lasts indefinitely.
cards.deploy: Preservation can be a property of chemistry, not refrigeration — a clean counterexample to 'all food rots'.
cards.counter: Only while sealed: add water (or contamination) and honey will ferment. Crystallisation is normal and reversible, not spoilage.

quiz.q: A friend leaves a jar of honey open in a humid kitchen for months and it starts to bubble and smell of alcohol. What has most likely happened?
choices: It absorbed water and the diluted honey fermented
The sugar oxidised into pure ethanol on contact with air
It froze and the ice crystals trapped yeast
The acidity rose until it self-pasteurised

quiz.q: Honey contains an enzyme that releases small amounts of hydrogen peroxide, helping kill microbes. Name that enzyme.
Which observation is normal for old, properly sealed honey rather than a sign that it has spoiled?
choices: It has turned partly solid and grainy (crystallised)
A fuzzy mould layer has grown on top
It has separated into a watery, bubbling layer

cards.title: Some infinities are bigger than others
cards.fact: There are strictly more real numbers than whole numbers — infinity comes in different sizes.
cards.detail: Cantor's diagonal argument (1891) shows you can't list all real numbers even with an infinite list: given any list, you can build a real number missing from it. So the reals are 'uncountable' and outnumber the (countable) integers.
cards.deploy: Stops loose appeals to infinity: 'infinite' does not mean 'all the same' or 'anything goes'.
cards.counter: Whether there's a size strictly between the integers and the reals (the Continuum Hypothesis) is provably undecidable in standard set theory (Gödel 1940, Cohen 1963).

quiz.q: Cantor's diagonal argument shows the real numbers are…
choices: The same size as the integers

quiz.q: Which set is the 'bigger', uncountable infinity?
Using the same diagonal idea, why can't you list all infinite binary strings (each an endless sequence of 0s and 1s)?
choices: Given any list, you can flip the nth digit of the nth string to build a string that differs from every listed one
Because there are only finitely many such strings
Because each string has the same number of 0s as 1s
Because the strings can be paired one-to-one with the integers

quiz.q: What single word describes an infinite set whose members can be put in a complete one-to-one list with the positive integers?
What is the name of the question (undecidable in standard set theory) of whether any infinity lies strictly between the size of the integers and the size of the reals?

cards.title: Gödel's incompleteness theorems
cards.fact: Any consistent maths system rich enough for arithmetic contains true statements it can never prove.
cards.detail: Gödel (1931) showed such a system can't be both complete and consistent, and can't prove its own consistency from within. Truth outruns provability.
cards.deploy: A hard limit on formal systems — useful against claims that 'anything true can, in principle, be proven'.
cards.counter: Routinely overstated. It applies to specific formal systems, not to 'all reasoning'; it does not imply 'nothing is knowable' or license mysticism.

quiz.q: Someone claims their formal arithmetic system is both consistent and able to prove every true arithmetic statement. What does Gödel's first incompleteness theorem say about this?
choices: It is impossible: a consistent system rich enough for arithmetic must have true statements it cannot prove
It is fine as long as the system also proves its own consistency
It is possible only if the system has finitely many axioms
It is possible because completeness automatically follows from consistency

quiz.q: Which of these is a correct application of Gödel's incompleteness results?
choices: A sufficiently strong formal system cannot prove its own consistency from within itself
No statement in mathematics can ever be proven
Human reasoning is bounded by exactly the same limits as any machine
All of mathematics is therefore false or meaningless

quiz.q: In what year did Gödel publish his incompleteness theorems?

cards.title: The base-rate fallacy
cards.fact: A 99%-accurate test for a rare disease is wrong most of the time it says 'positive' — because ignoring how rare the disease is flips the odds.

layers.body: When a disease is rare, even an excellent test produces mostly false alarms — there are vastly more healthy people to misclassify than sick people to catch. The fallacy is to read '99% accurate' as '99% chance I'm sick', forgetting how uncommon the disease is to begin with: its base rate.

The fix is Bayes' theorem, and it falls straight out of what 'conditional probability' means. The chance of two things both happening can be written two ways: \(P(A \cap B) = P(A\mid B)\,P(B)\), and equally \(P(A \cap B) = P(B\mid A)\,P(A)\). Set them equal and divide by \(P(B)\): \(P(A\mid B) = \dfrac{P(B\mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}\) — that is Bayes, derived in one line. Let \(A\) be 'sick' and \(B\) be 'tests positive'. The denominator \(P(+)\) counts every positive test, true and false: \(P(+) = P(+\mid\text{sick})\,P(\text{sick}) + P(+\mid\text{healthy})\,P(\text{healthy})\). The base rate \(P(\text{sick})\) sits right there in the formula — and quietly dropping it is the fallacy.

Plausible numbers: 1 in 100 people has the disease (base rate 1%); the test is 99% sensitive (it flags 99% of sick people) and 95% specific (a 5% false-alarm rate). Picture 10,000 people. About 100 are sick, so ~99 test positive. The other 9,900 are healthy, and 5% of them — 495 people — test positive anyway. That is 99 + 495 = 594 positive tests, of which only 99 are truly sick: \(99/594 \approx 0.167\). So a positive result means roughly a 1-in-6 (about 17%) chance of actually being sick — not 99% — because the 9,900 healthy people throw off far more false alarms than the 100 sick people give true hits.

media.say: the chance you're sick given a positive test is the test's hit-rate times how common the disease is, divided by how often anyone tests positive.
media.caption: Bayes' theorem — the base rate P(sick) is the term the fallacy forgets.
Of 10,000 people, 594 test positive — but only 99 are actually sick (~17%).

cards.deploy: Demand the base rate before accepting 'the test/study says X' — an accuracy figure on its own can badly mislead.
cards.counter: It is no licence to dismiss tests: a higher base rate (testing people with symptoms, not everyone), a more specific test, or simply repeating it swings the odds back. Kahneman and Tversky showed even doctors fall for the fallacy; Gerd Gigerenzer found that stating it in natural frequencies — '99 of 594', as above — largely cures it.

quiz.q: For a rare condition, a positive result on a highly accurate test is…

A disease affects 1 in 1000 people. A test has a 5% false-positive rate and catches everyone who has the disease (no false negatives). Out of 10000 randomly screened people, how many test positive in total?
In that same screening of 10000 people (10 true positives among about 510 total positives), roughly what percent of people who test positive actually have the disease?
Which change does NOT improve the chance that a positive result reflects a real case?
choices: Screening an even broader healthy population, lowering the share who truly have the disease
Testing only people who already show symptoms
Using a more specific test with fewer false positives
Repeating the test and requiring a second positive

cards.title: Simpson's paradox
cards.fact: A trend can hold in every subgroup yet reverse when the groups are combined.
cards.detail: In Berkeley's 1973 graduate admissions, men appeared admitted at higher rates overall, yet within most departments women were admitted at equal-or-higher rates — women applied more to competitive departments. Aggregation flipped the picture.
cards.deploy: Aggregate numbers can mislead — always ask whether a confounder is hiding inside the average.
cards.counter: Which view is 'correct' isn't a rule of thumb; it depends on the underlying causal structure, which the data alone can't settle.

quiz.q: A drug shows a higher recovery rate than placebo in mild cases and also in severe cases, yet a lower overall recovery rate when all patients are pooled. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The drug was given disproportionately to severe cases, who recover less often regardless
The drug is genuinely harmful and the subgroup results are measurement errors
Recovery rates cannot differ between subgroups and the pooled group
The placebo had an unlisted active ingredient

quiz.q: Treatment B cures 90 of 100 mild patients and 40 of 100 severe patients. What is treatment B's overall cure rate across all 200 patients, as a percentage?
When a subgroup trend reverses after the groups are aggregated, the hidden variable that simultaneously affects both group membership and the outcome is called what?

cards.title: Entropy and the arrow of time
cards.fact: In an isolated system, entropy never decreases — which is why time has a direction.
cards.detail: The second law of thermodynamics: usable energy disperses; ordered states drift toward disorder. It's why heat flows hot→cold and why a smashed cup never reassembles.
cards.deploy: Rules out perpetual-motion and 'free lunch' schemes — there's always a cost paid somewhere.
cards.counter: Local order can increase (life, fridges, crystals) as long as total entropy rises — a frequent misuse is citing the second law against evolution.

quiz.q: A household refrigerator keeps its interior colder than the room, decreasing the entropy inside the fridge. Why does this not violate the second law of thermodynamics?
choices: The fridge dumps more entropy into the surrounding room than it removes inside, so total entropy rises
The second law applies only to gases, not to cold air
Electrical energy is exempt from the second law
The interior is not truly isolated, so the law does not apply to it at all

quiz.q: Which law of thermodynamics states that the entropy of an isolated system never decreases?
Someone claims biological evolution is impossible because it produces increasingly ordered organisms while the second law demands rising disorder. What is the flaw in this argument?
choices: Earth is not an isolated system; it receives energy from the Sun, so local order can increase while total entropy rises
Evolution does not actually increase the order of organisms
The second law only constrains heat engines, never living matter
Entropy can decrease in any system as long as it is alive

cards.title: The speed of light is the same for everyone
cards.fact: Light travels at the same speed for all observers, no matter how they move.
cards.detail: Einstein's 1905 special relativity takes this as a postulate. The consequences are strange but measured: moving clocks run slow (time dilation), moving lengths contract, and simultaneity is relative.
cards.deploy: Shows 'common sense' about absolute time and simultaneity is simply wrong — verified by GPS, particle accelerators, atomic clocks.
cards.counter: Newtonian mechanics remains an excellent approximation at everyday speeds; relativity refines it, it doesn't make it 'useless'.

quiz.q: A spaceship moving at 0.9c shines a laser forward. An observer on the ground measures the speed of the emitted light. What value do they get?
choices: c, the same as the ship's crew measures
1.9c, the ship's speed plus light speed
0.1c, light speed minus the ship's speed
0.9c, the same as the ship's speed

quiz.q: What name is given to the effect by which a clock moving relative to an observer is measured to tick more slowly?

Two lightning strikes that are simultaneous for an observer on a train platform are NOT simultaneous for a passenger on a fast-moving train. This illustrates which consequence of light's invariant speed?

media.caption: The more precisely you fix position (Δx), the less precisely momentum (Δp) is fixed.

cards.title: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle
cards.fact: You cannot know a particle's exact position and momentum at the same time.
cards.detail: The product of the uncertainties in position and momentum has a hard floor (Δx·Δp ≥ ħ/2). It's a feature of nature, not a limit of our instruments.
cards.deploy: There are fundamental, not merely practical, limits to measurement.
cards.counter: Frequently abused by analogy ('the observer changes everything') in social or business arguments where it simply doesn't apply.

quiz.q: The uncertainty principle states the product of position and momentum uncertainties is at least h-bar/2, where h-bar is about 1.05e-34 J*s. If a particle's position uncertainty is 1e-9 m, what is the minimum possible momentum uncertainty, in kg*m/s? Give your answer in units of 1e-26 (i.e. divide the result by 1e-26).
Why is it incorrect to say the uncertainty principle is just a result of clumsy measuring instruments that disturb the particle?
choices: The limit is a fundamental property of nature, holding even for an ideal, perfectly gentle measurement
Better instruments have already eliminated the uncertainty in modern labs
It applies only to electrons, where instruments are unavoidably crude
The principle describes calculation rounding errors, not physical measurement

quiz.q: Which pair of physical quantities does Heisenberg's principle say cannot both be known to arbitrary precision at the same time, with their uncertainties bounded by h-bar/2?

cards.title: We can still see the Big Bang's afterglow
cards.fact: The whole sky glows faintly at ~2.7 K — leftover heat from the early universe.
cards.detail: Penzias and Wilson detected the cosmic microwave background in 1964 (published 1965), a relic of when the universe cooled enough for light to travel freely ~380,000 years after the Big Bang. It's some of the strongest evidence for the hot Big Bang model.
cards.deploy: The Big Bang is evidence-backed, not mere speculation — we literally observe its relic radiation.
cards.counter: 'Big Bang' describes the expansion from a hot, dense state — it does not claim to explain the ultimate origin or 'what banged'.

quiz.q: Why is the relic radiation now seen at microwave wavelengths rather than as the intense visible/infrared glow it once was?
choices: The expansion of the universe has stretched (redshifted) the light to longer wavelengths, cooling it to ~2.7 K
Interstellar dust absorbs all the original visible light, re-emitting only microwaves
Earth's atmosphere filters out everything except the microwave band
The radiation was emitted as microwaves from the very first instant of the Big Bang

quiz.q: The event that released the cosmic microwave background — when the universe first cooled enough for light to travel freely as atoms formed — is known by what term?

Penzias and Wilson detected the background radiation in 1964. If a similar relic had instead been confirmed in 1989 by a satellite mission, how many years later than the original detection would that be?

cards.title: Moving clocks run slow
cards.fact: Moving clocks run slow — and GPS has to correct for it every day.
cards.detail: If the speed of light is the same for everyone, then time itself must stretch: a clock moving fast (or sitting deeper in gravity) ticks slower than one at rest. It's tiny at everyday speeds but real — fast-decaying muons reaching the ground, atomic clocks flown around the world, and astronauts ageing a few milliseconds less all confirm it, and GPS satellites would drift kilometres off without relativistic corrections.
cards.deploy: The most concrete proof that time is relative, not absolute — your phone's navigation depends on it.
cards.counter: It's only sizeable near light-speed or strong gravity; at human speeds the effect is real but minuscule, which is why intuition misses it.

quiz.q: Time dilation means a fast-moving clock…
choices: Runs slow relative to one at rest

quiz.q: Two identical atomic clocks start synchronized. One flies fast around the world and returns. Compared with the clock that stayed home, the travelled clock will read:
choices: Exactly the same — speed cannot affect a clock's mechanism
Stopped, because it briefly reached relativistic speed

quiz.q: Using the time-dilation factor 1/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2), a clock moving at 0.6c (so v^2/c^2 = 0.36) ticks slow by this factor. For every 1 second on the moving clock, how many seconds elapse for a stationary observer?
What short-lived subatomic particle, produced high in the atmosphere, reaches the ground in far greater numbers than classical physics predicts — a direct everyday confirmation of time dilation?

cards.title: The universe's heat death
cards.fact: If entropy always rises, the universe drifts toward a cold, featureless 'heat death'.
cards.detail: Run the second law forward forever: usable energy keeps dissipating until temperature differences vanish and no work is possible — maximum entropy, the 'Big Freeze'. Proposed by Lord Kelvin in 1852, it implies a far-future universe of near-uniform cold, perhaps after 10^100 years, once even black holes have evaporated.
cards.deploy: Takes the arrow of time to its cosmic conclusion — order is borrowed, and the loan eventually comes due.
cards.counter: It assumes the universe keeps expanding and that entropy is even well-defined for the whole cosmos (including gravity) — both are debated, and the timescale is so vast as to be almost meaningless.

quiz.q: The 'heat death' of the universe is a state of…
choices: Maximum entropy and no usable energy

quiz.q: Why does maximum entropy imply that no useful work can be extracted in the far future 'heat death'?
choices: Work requires a temperature or energy difference to flow across, and in uniform equilibrium no such differences remain
All energy has been destroyed, leaving nothing to power any process
Gravity has pulled all matter into a single point, halting all motion
The total energy of the universe has dropped to absolute zero everywhere

quiz.q: Which physicist proposed the idea of the universe's heat death in 1852?
The heat-death timescale is often quoted as about 10^100 years. Expressed as a power of ten, what is the exponent of that number of years?

cards.title: Quantum entanglement
cards.fact: Entangled particles stay linked across any distance — yet you still can't send a message faster than light.
cards.detail: Two particles can be 'entangled' so that measuring one instantly fixes the state of the other, however far apart — Einstein's 'spooky action at a distance'. Bell-test experiments confirm the correlations are real and can't be explained by hidden pre-set values. But because each result looks random on its own, entanglement can't transmit information faster than light; it underpins quantum computing and cryptography.
cards.deploy: The sharpest break with classical intuition — reality's correlations are non-local, yet relativity's speed limit still holds.
cards.counter: 'Instant link' is easily over-hyped: no usable signal travels faster than light, so it enables no sci-fi communication.

quiz.q: Quantum entanglement allows…
choices: Correlations across distance, but no faster-than-light signal

quiz.q: Why can't entangled particles be used to send a message faster than light, even though measuring one instantly fixes the other's state?
choices: Each individual measurement outcome looks random, so no controllable information is encoded in a single particle's result
The entanglement breaks the instant either particle is observed, before any data can be read
Light-speed signalling is only forbidden for charged particles, not entangled ones
The two particles must be brought back together to compare results, which takes longer than light travel

quiz.q: What kind of experiment rules out the idea that entangled particles simply carry pre-set 'hidden' values, confirming the correlations are genuinely quantum?
Einstein famously dismissed the instantaneous correlation between entangled particles as 'spooky action at a ___' — fill in the missing word.

cards.title: Dark energy
cards.fact: Most of the universe is 'dark energy' — and it's pushing the cosmos apart faster and faster.
cards.detail: Since 1998, supernova measurements have shown the universe's expansion is accelerating, driven by a mysterious 'dark energy' that makes up ~68% of everything (dark matter ~27%, ordinary matter just ~5%). Its nature is unknown — a cosmological constant, or something stranger — and the cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure independently support it.
cards.deploy: A humbling headline: about 95% of the universe (dark energy plus dark matter) is stuff we can't directly see or explain.
cards.counter: 'Dark energy' is a placeholder for an unknown — some physicists suspect it signals that our theory of gravity is incomplete rather than a real new substance.

quiz.q: Dark energy is associated with…
If dark energy is about 68% of the universe and dark matter about 27%, what percentage is the ordinary matter we can directly see and explain?
What observation, beginning in 1998, first provided strong evidence for dark energy?
choices: Distant supernovae appeared dimmer than expected, implying the cosmic expansion is speeding up
Galaxies were found rotating faster at their edges than their visible mass allows
The Sun's neutrino output was measured to be lower than predicted
Light from distant stars was seen bending around the Sun during an eclipse

quiz.q: What is the name for the simplest candidate explanation of dark energy, a constant vacuum energy term Einstein originally introduced into his field equations?

cards.title: Gutenberg's printing press (~1440)
cards.fact: Cheap printed books in the 1400s helped trigger the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution.
cards.detail: Movable-type printing in Europe (~1440) collapsed the cost of copying text. Literacy spread, ideas travelled faster than authorities could suppress them, and standardised knowledge accumulated.
cards.deploy: Information technology reshapes who holds power — a historical anchor for arguments about the printing press / internet / AI.
cards.counter: Printing predates Gutenberg in East Asia (Bi Sheng's movable type ~1040, Korean metal type earlier). His contribution was the European system and its economics, not the raw idea.

quiz.q: Whose movable-type printing in East Asia, around 1040, predates the European press by roughly four centuries?
Which historical development is most directly credited to the spread of cheap printed books in 1400s Europe?
choices: The Protestant Reformation, as dissenting ideas spread faster than authorities could suppress them
The fall of the Western Roman Empire to invading tribes
The construction of the first Gothic cathedrals across France
The establishment of the first transatlantic trade routes to the Americas

quiz.q: If the European movable-type press dates to about 1440 and Bi Sheng's movable type in China to about 1040, how many years earlier was the Chinese invention?

cards.title: The Black Death (1347–1351)
cards.fact: A plague that killed a third or more of Europe also raised the wages of those who survived.
cards.detail: With labour suddenly scarce, surviving workers could demand more, accelerating the decline of serfdom in parts of Western Europe. Catastrophe restructured the economy.
cards.deploy: Shocks can shift the balance of power between labour and capital — scarcity changes bargaining position.
cards.counter: The 'wages rose' story varies sharply by region and institutions; in places elites tightened controls instead. Single mechanisms oversimplify.

quiz.q: Why did wages rise for surviving workers in parts of Western Europe after the Black Death?
choices: Labour became scarce, so survivors could demand more for their work
Governments passed laws mandating higher minimum pay for peasants
A flood of New World silver inflated all prices and wages together
Surviving workers were better educated and thus more productive

quiz.q: If a region had 6 million people before the Black Death and the plague killed one third of them, roughly how many people survived?
The bargaining power of surviving labourers helped accelerate the decline of which medieval system that bound peasants to a lord's land?

cards.title: The Peace of Westphalia (1648)
cards.fact: The 1648 treaties ending the Thirty Years' War are often called the birth of the sovereign state.
cards.detail: They're cited as the origin of 'Westphalian sovereignty' — the principle that states are supreme within their own borders and don't answer to outside authority.
cards.deploy: A foundational reference for debates about national sovereignty vs international intervention.
cards.counter: Historians (e.g. Andreas Osiander) argue the 'Westphalian myth' is a 19th-century back-projection; the treaties didn't actually establish modern sovereignty as commonly claimed.

quiz.q: What principle, named after the 1648 treaties, holds that a state is the supreme authority within its own borders and answers to no outside power?
The Thirty Years' War ended with the 1648 treaties. In what year did that war begin?
What is the central claim of historians like Andreas Osiander who speak of a 'Westphalian myth'?
choices: The treaties did not actually establish modern sovereignty; that reading is a later back-projection
The treaties were never signed and the war continued for decades afterward
The treaties created a single European empire rather than separate states
The treaties applied only to maritime law and not to land borders

cards.title: The Thucydides Trap
cards.fact: When a rising power threatens a ruling one, the result is often war.
cards.detail: Graham Allison studied 16 cases over 500 years and found war in 12. Named after Thucydides' line that it was the rise of Athens, and the fear it caused in Sparta, that made war inevitable. Applied today to the US and China.
cards.deploy: A structured frame for great-power-rivalry arguments — names the mechanism (fear of a shifting balance).
cards.counter: Beyond the contested case selection (4 of 16 avoided war, and 'often' is not 'inevitable'), the frame itself is disputed: Xi Jinping flatly rejects it — 'there is no Thucydides Trap' — and liberal and constructivist scholars argue deep economic interdependence and nuclear deterrence make structural war far from fated. Reaching for the 'trap' already takes the anxious US vantage point as the neutral one.

quiz.q: A historian replicates the Thucydides Trap method on a new dataset of 25 rising-power-vs-ruling-power cases and finds the same war rate Graham Allison reported (war in 12 of 16 cases). To the nearest whole number, how many of the 25 cases would end in war?
In the original ancient analogy, which rising power's growth and the fear it provoked was said to make war with Sparta unavoidable?
Which objection to the Thucydides Trap rests on conditions specific to the modern era rather than on disputing how the 16 historical cases were counted?
choices: Deep economic interdependence and nuclear deterrence make a structural war between great powers far from fated
Only 12 of the 16 cases actually ended in war, so the pattern is weaker than claimed
The set of 16 cases was chosen in a way that biases the result

cards.title: Chokepoint: the Strait of Hormuz
cards.fact: Roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes through one narrow strait.
cards.detail: About 20–21 million barrels a day move through the Strait of Hormuz between the Persian Gulf and open ocean — a single point of geographic leverage.
cards.deploy: Physical geography concentrates strategic power — concrete grounding for arguments about energy security.
cards.counter: Shares and volumes shift; new pipelines and changing demand steadily reduce any one chokepoint's leverage.

quiz.q: If about 20 million barrels of oil pass through the Strait of Hormuz each day and global oil consumption is roughly 100 million barrels per day, what percentage of world oil consumption transits the strait?
The Strait of Hormuz connects the open ocean to which body of water bordered by major oil exporters?
Why does the strategic leverage of a maritime chokepoint like Hormuz tend to weaken over time?
choices: New pipelines and shifting demand reroute flows around the single point
Narrow straits gradually widen through erosion, easing congestion
International law eventually bans any state from interdicting shipping there
Oil tankers are steadily replaced by smaller vessels that need no strait

cards.title: Mackinder's Heartland theory (1904)
cards.fact: Whoever controls the Eurasian 'Heartland' could dominate the world — a classic land-power doctrine.
cards.detail: Halford Mackinder argued that control of inner Eurasia (the 'World-Island') was the key to global power, because it was beyond the reach of sea power.
cards.deploy: The founding lens of geopolitical 'land power vs sea power' thinking — still echoed in analyses of Russia and Central Asia.
cards.counter: Airpower, nuclear weapons, and globalised trade undercut pure land-centric determinism; geography constrains but doesn't dictate.

quiz.q: Who formulated the 1904 theory that whoever controls inner Eurasia could dominate the world?
What was Mackinder's core reasoning for why the Eurasian Heartland was the pivot of world power?
choices: It lay beyond the reach of sea power, making it a secure base for land power
It held the largest share of the world's oil and gas reserves
Its coastlines gave the easiest access to global maritime trade routes
Its dense population could field the world's largest navy

quiz.q: Mackinder gave inner Eurasia a name to capture its size and centrality. What did he call it?

cards.title: Rimland: the reply to Heartland
cards.fact: The rival to Heartland theory: control the coastal 'rim' of Eurasia, not its core.
cards.detail: Nicholas Spykman (1940s) inverted Mackinder: power lies not in the inaccessible Eurasian Heartland but in the 'Rimland' — the densely populated coastal fringe (Europe, the Middle East, South and East Asia). 'Who controls the Rimland rules Eurasia.' It shaped US Cold War containment, which ringed the Soviet and Chinese landmass with alliances and bases.
cards.deploy: Decodes US grand strategy: containment and the alliance network around Eurasia's rim are Rimland thinking in action.
cards.counter: It's a doctrine, not a law — air power, nuclear weapons and economics complicate any neat 'geography decides power' story. It also has a target's-eye flip side: what Washington calls 'containment', Moscow and Beijing read as hostile encirclement, and revisionist historians (the Wisconsin School around William Appleman Williams) cast US Cold War strategy as expansionist, not merely defensive.

quiz.q: Spykman's Rimland theory says power lies in…
Which strategist argued in the 1940s that power lay in Eurasia's coastal fringe rather than its core?
Which US Cold War policy is best understood as Rimland theory put into practice?
choices: Containment, ringing the Soviet and Chinese landmass with alliances and bases
Massive retaliation, threatening nuclear strikes against any aggression
Detente, easing tensions through arms-control treaties
Non-alignment, avoiding commitments to either bloc

quiz.q: A revisionist (Wisconsin School) reading of US Cold War strategy reframes the same alliance network around Eurasia's rim as what, rather than as defensive containment?
choices: An expansionist project, read from Moscow and Beijing as hostile encirclement
A purely economic free-trade arrangement with no military purpose
An accidental byproduct of decolonization with no grand design
A short-lived experiment quickly abandoned after 1950

cards.title: The security dilemma
cards.fact: Arming to feel safer can make everyone less safe — the 'security dilemma'.
cards.detail: Even with no aggressive intent, one state's defensive build-up looks threatening to others, who arm in response, leaving all less secure — a spiral driven by fear and uncertainty about intentions (Herz, 1950; Jervis). It's a core reason rising-power tensions (the Thucydides Trap) can escalate without anyone actually wanting war.
cards.deploy: Explains how war can come from fear, not aggression — and why signalling restraint and intentions matters so much.
cards.counter: It's not inevitable: arms control, transparency, and clearly non-threatening 'defensive' postures can defuse the spiral; not every build-up is misread.

quiz.q: The 'security dilemma' is when…
choices: Defensive arming makes others feel threatened, spiralling insecurity

quiz.q: Country A doubles its missile-defence and naval forces purely to feel safer, with no plans to attack anyone. Country B sees this and races to build up its own forces, and now both feel more threatened than before. This outcome is the central mechanism of which concept?

What emotion or psychological state, combined with uncertainty about others' true intentions, is identified as the main driver that turns one state's defensive build-up into an escalating arms spiral?
Which measure is LEAST likely to defuse a security-dilemma spiral between two states?
choices: Secretly accelerating a weapons programme while denying it
Adopting a visibly defensive, non-threatening posture

cards.title: The Malacca dilemma
cards.fact: Most of East Asia's oil squeezes through one narrow strait — the 'Malacca dilemma'.
cards.detail: The Strait of Malacca, between Malaysia and Indonesia, is the world's busiest — around 80% of China's imported crude passes through it, plus much of Japan's and Korea's trade. China's reliance on a single chokepoint a rival navy could blockade is its 'Malacca dilemma' (Hu Jintao's term, 2003), and a driver of overland pipelines, a bigger navy and the Belt and Road.
cards.deploy: A concrete lens on China's strategy: much of its energy security hangs on a strait it doesn't control.
cards.counter: A blockade would be an act of war with huge costs to all sides, so the vulnerability is more strategic anxiety than likely event — and alternatives (pipelines, reserves) are being built.

quiz.q: The 'Malacca dilemma' refers to…
choices: East Asia's reliance on one strait for oil and trade

quiz.q: Suppose a country imports 12 million barrels of crude oil per day, and 80% of it passes through a single strait. How many million barrels per day flow through that strait?
Which two countries border the strait through which roughly 80% of China's imported crude oil passes?
Building overland pipelines, expanding the navy, and pursuing the Belt and Road initiative are best understood as China's attempts to do what?
choices: Reduce dependence on a single maritime chokepoint a rival navy could blockade
Increase the share of oil shipped through the Strait of Malacca
Lower its total demand for imported energy

cards.title: When populations shrink
cards.fact: The demographic transition's final twist: much of the world is now ageing and shrinking.
cards.detail: Past the transition, fertility in many countries has fallen below replacement (~2.1). Japan, South Korea, much of Europe and now China face ageing and then shrinking populations — fewer workers supporting more retirees, strained pensions and slower growth. South Korea's fertility (~0.7) is the world's lowest. Migration can offset it but is politically fraught.
cards.deploy: Reframes the population debate: for a growing share of the world the worry is too few people, not too many.
cards.counter: It's uneven — much of sub-Saharan Africa is still growing fast — and forecasts are uncertain. The 'crisis' framing is also contested: degrowth and ecological economists (Jason Hickel) argue a smaller population eases planetary limits and isn't inherently catastrophic, and feminist demographers warn that 'too few babies' rhetoric instrumentalises women's fertility and fuels coercive pronatalism. Whether decline is a problem depends on whether endless growth is the goal.

quiz.q: Below-replacement fertility leads to…
If each woman has on average 0.7 children over her lifetime, then for every 1000 women in one generation, roughly how many daughters are born in the next (assuming about half of births are girls)?
A country's total fertility rate sits steadily at 1.4 children per woman (well below the replacement rate of about 2.1), with little migration. What is the most likely long-run demographic outcome?
choices: The population ages and then shrinks

quiz.q: Name the region frequently cited as the main exception to global population decline because its population is still growing rapidly.

cards.title: The demographic transition
cards.fact: As countries develop, they shift from high birth-and-death rates to low — then they age.
cards.detail: Falling child mortality and development first cause a population boom, then birth rates fall and the population stabilises and greys, raising the ratio of retirees to workers.
cards.deploy: Explains why growth slows and why ageing (China, Japan, Europe) reshapes economies and pensions.
cards.counter: Trajectories vary widely; immigration, policy, and culture can speed up, slow down, or reverse parts of the transition.

quiz.q: In the demographic transition, why does a population typically boom BEFORE birth rates fall?
choices: Death rates (especially child mortality) drop first, while birth rates stay high for a while
Birth rates rise sharply before death rates change
Immigration always surges at the start of development
Retirees suddenly outnumber workers early on

quiz.q: In a small town, there are 600 working-age adults and 150 retirees. What is the ratio of retirees to workers, expressed as retirees per worker (to two decimals)?
What word describes the late stage of the demographic transition in which the share of older people rises and the population 'greys'?

cards.title: Natural selection
cards.fact: Heritable variation plus differential survival produces design without a designer.
cards.detail: Darwin (1859): organisms vary, some variations are inherited, and those that aid survival and reproduction become more common over generations — yielding apparent design.
cards.deploy: Complexity can arise from blind, cumulative processes — the canonical answer to 'it looks designed, so it was designed'.
cards.counter: Selection is one mechanism among several. Genetic drift, gene flow, and sheer contingency also shape evolution; not every trait is an adaptation.

quiz.q: Natural selection requires variation that is…
A population of cave fish lives in total darkness for thousands of generations and gradually loses its eyes. Which option best explains how natural selection could drive this loss?
choices: Eyes are costly to build, so individuals born with reduced eyes left more offspring in the dark
The fish consciously stopped using their eyes, so the trait faded
Living in darkness directly damaged the eye genes of each fish
An external designer optimized the fish for cave life

quiz.q: Name the 19th-century naturalist whose 1859 book set out the theory that heritable variation plus differential survival produces apparent design.
Why is 'this trait helps the organism, so it must be an adaptation built by selection' an unreliable inference?
choices: Traits can also spread by drift, gene flow, or contingency, so not every helpful-looking trait was shaped by selection
Selection never produces helpful traits, only harmful ones
Adaptations always reduce an organism's survival
Heritable variation plays no role in evolution

cards.title: You're about half bacteria (by cell count)
cards.fact: Your body holds roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells — about 1:1, not the old '10:1'.
cards.detail: A 2016 re-estimate put it near 38 trillion bacteria to 30 trillion human cells. The widely-repeated '10 times more bacteria than your own cells' was never well-founded.
cards.deploy: Doubles as a fact and a myth-correction — a clean way to show how a 'known' figure can be wrong.
cards.counter: These are estimates with wide ranges and they vary person to person; function matters more than raw counts.

quiz.q: If a person has about 36 trillion bacterial cells and 30 trillion human cells, what is the ratio of bacterial to human cells, rounded to one decimal place?
The popular claim that the human body holds '10 times more bacteria than its own cells' was overturned by a 2016 re-estimate. What did the corrected figure show?
choices: The numbers of bacterial and human cells are roughly equal, about 1 to 1
Human cells outnumber bacteria by about 10 to 1
There are essentially no bacterial cells in a healthy body
Bacteria outnumber human cells by about 100 to 1

quiz.q: Beyond raw cell counts, what aspect of the body's bacteria do scientists say matters more for health, given that counts vary widely between people?

cards.title: CRISPR: programmable gene editing
cards.fact: Since 2012 we've been able to cut and edit DNA at a chosen spot, cheaply and precisely.
