cards.detail: Doudna and Charpentier showed the bacterial CRISPR-Cas9 system can be guided by a custom RNA to cut DNA wherever you point it (Nobel Prize 2020). It transformed biotech almost overnight.
cards.deploy: Cheap, precise editing changes every debate about medicine, agriculture, and 'designer' organisms.
cards.counter: Off-target edits and the ethics of heritable (germline) changes remain serious, unresolved caveats.

quiz.q: In the CRISPR-Cas9 system, what type of guide molecule is customized to direct the Cas9 protein to cut DNA at a chosen location?
CRISPR gene editing was demonstrated in 2012 and its developers won the Nobel Prize in 2020. How many years passed between the demonstration and the Nobel award?
Which concern is the most serious unresolved caveat specifically tied to making CRISPR edits that would be passed on to a person's children?
choices: Heritable germline edits raise unresolved ethical questions because the changes affect future generations who cannot consent
The edits are far too expensive to ever attempt in humans
Cas9 can only cut RNA, never DNA, so the edits do not last
Germline edits are guaranteed to be perfectly accurate, removing all risk

cards.title: Evolution by pure chance
cards.fact: Evolution isn't only survival of the fittest — pure chance ('genetic drift') also shapes which genes survive.
cards.detail: Beyond selection, gene frequencies wander randomly across generations through sheer sampling luck — who happens to reproduce. This 'genetic drift' is strongest in small populations, where it can fix or erase a gene regardless of fitness, and (per Kimura's neutral theory) it drives much molecular evolution. Selection and drift act together, not in opposition.
cards.deploy: Corrects the 'everything is an adaptation' reflex — much genetic change is just noise, not design.
cards.counter: Drift and selection are partners, not rivals; their relative weight depends on population size, and teasing them apart is genuinely hard.

quiz.q: Genetic drift changes gene frequencies through…
choices: Random chance, especially in small populations

quiz.q: Two isolated populations of a beetle carry a neutral color gene at 50% frequency. One population has 20 beetles, the other has 20,000. In which is the gene's frequency more likely to swing dramatically by chance alone over a few generations, and why?
choices: The 20-beetle population, because sampling luck has a bigger effect when fewer individuals reproduce
The 20,000-beetle population, because more individuals means more random change
Both equally, because drift ignores population size
Neither, because a neutral gene cannot change frequency

quiz.q: Whose neutral theory holds that genetic drift, rather than selection, drives much of molecular evolution?
How should genetic drift and natural selection be understood in relation to each other?
choices: As partners acting together, with their relative weight depending on population size
As strict opposites, where one being active means the other is switched off
As the same process described with two different names
As forces that only operate in different species, never the same one

cards.title: What your microbes do for you
cards.fact: Your resident microbes earn their keep — digesting fibre, making vitamins and training your immune system.
cards.detail: Gut microbes ferment dietary fibre into short-chain fatty acids, help synthesise vitamins (K and several B's), and help calibrate the immune system, while crowding out invaders. Disruption ('dysbiosis') — e.g. from broad-spectrum antibiotics — is associated with conditions from inflammatory bowel disease to metabolic problems, though much of the 'gut–brain' story is still emerging.
cards.deploy: Reframes microbes as partners, not passengers — and explains why broad antibiotics have side effects.
cards.counter: The field is hot and over-hyped: many microbiome–disease links are correlations, and popular 'gut–brain axis' claims often run ahead of the evidence.

quiz.q: A well-supported role of the gut microbiome is…
choices: Digesting fibre and training the immune system

quiz.q: A patient on a two-week course of broad-spectrum antibiotics develops diarrhoea and a yeast infection. Which microbiome mechanism best explains why wiping out resident gut bacteria can cause this?
choices: Losing the resident bacteria removes their crowding-out of potential invaders, letting opportunistic organisms overgrow
Antibiotics directly damage the lining of the gut wall, exposing nerves
The body compensates by producing excess stomach acid
Antibiotics block the synthesis of dietary fibre in the colon

quiz.q: Gut microbes ferment dietary fibre into a class of molecules that nourish colon cells. What is the general name for these molecules (the 4-letter abbreviation is fine)?

A study finds people with inflammatory bowel disease tend to have lower gut bacterial diversity, but cannot show the low diversity came first. In one word, what kind of relationship has the study actually demonstrated, as opposed to causation?

cards.title: The gene-edited babies line
cards.fact: In 2018 a scientist edited the genes of babies — crossing a line the field had agreed not to.
cards.detail: CRISPR can edit body cells (somatic) to treat one patient, or the germline (eggs, sperm, embryos), whose changes pass to all descendants. In 2018 He Jiankui announced gene-edited twins in China; the work drew near-universal condemnation and a prison sentence — it was unsafe, the consent forged, the ethics indefensible. Most countries ban heritable germline editing while allowing somatic gene therapies.
cards.deploy: Marks the bright line in gene editing: treating a patient vs. permanently altering the human lineage.
cards.counter: The line is contested at the edges — a 2017 US National Academies report cautiously allowed heritable editing in principle for serious disease, so 'never' isn't a settled consensus.

quiz.q: The 2018 He Jiankui case involved editing…

A clinic uses CRISPR to edit blood stem cells removed from an adult with sickle-cell disease, then returns them to that same patient. Why is this widely permitted while editing an embryo is mostly banned?
choices: The edits affect only that patient's body cells and are not passed to any children
Blood stem cells cannot be permanently altered, so the change is temporary
Sickle-cell disease is the only condition for which gene editing is legal
Editing adults requires no consent, simplifying the ethics

quiz.q: What is the term for the reproductive-cell lineage (eggs, sperm, embryos) whose edits are inherited by all of a person's descendants?

He Jiankui announced the gene-edited twins in 2018. A US National Academies report had cautiously discussed allowing heritable editing the year before, in 2017. How many years before the announcement was that report published?

cards.title: Wolves reshaped Yellowstone
cards.fact: Reintroducing wolves in 1995 rippled all the way down to the rivers.
cards.detail: With wolves back, elk grazed differently, letting willow and aspen recover, which helped beavers and stabilised some streambanks — a 'trophic cascade' from a top predator.
cards.deploy: Top predators have outsized, system-wide effects — a memorable case that removing one species isn't a local change.
cards.counter: The popular 'wolves changed the rivers' story is partly overstated; recovery had multiple drivers and the magnitude is debated.

quiz.q: A top predator's return alters the behaviour of its prey, which changes the vegetation, which in turn affects other species and even streambanks. What two-word ecological term names this top-down chain of effects?
After wolves returned to Yellowstone, willow and aspen along streams recovered. What was the most direct mechanism linking the wolves to that plant recovery?
choices: Elk changed how and where they grazed, reducing browsing pressure on young trees
Wolves fertilised the soil with carcasses, directly feeding the trees
Wolves ate the beavers that had been eating the saplings
Wolf urine raised water tables along the streams

quiz.q: Wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone in 1995. How many full years had passed by the year 2025?

cards.title: Planetary boundaries
cards.fact: Scientists have mapped nine limits for a stable planet — and we've crossed several.
cards.detail: The framework defines a 'safe operating space' across climate, biodiversity, the nitrogen and phosphorus cycles, freshwater, land use, and more. A 2023 update found six of nine boundaries transgressed.
cards.deploy: Moves environmental debate from 'climate only' to a systems view of multiple, interacting limits.
cards.counter: The specific boundary values carry real uncertainty, and some boundaries are global while others are really regional — the numbers are estimates, not constants.

quiz.q: The planetary-boundaries framework defines nine limits for a stable planet, and a 2023 update found six of them already transgressed. How many of the nine limits were still within the safe operating space?
Which statement best captures why the planetary-boundaries framework is more than a restatement of climate change?
choices: It treats climate as one of several interacting limits, alongside things like biodiversity loss and the nitrogen and phosphorus cycles
It replaces climate targets with a single combined pollution index
It argues climate change is not actually a planetary boundary
It applies only to freshwater and land-use change, not the atmosphere

quiz.q: Some planetary boundaries are genuinely global while others are really driven by local conditions, and the threshold values themselves carry uncertainty. In one word, what does this make the published boundary numbers, rather than fixed constants?

cards.title: Half the nitrogen in you came from one factory process
cards.fact: The Haber-Bosch process (1909) pulls nitrogen from the air to make fertiliser — and now feeds roughly half the world.
cards.detail: Before it, crop yields were capped by natural nitrogen. Synthetic ammonia broke that ceiling; a large share of the nitrogen atoms in your body passed through this industrial reaction.
cards.deploy: One chemical process underpins modern food security — a striking dependency to put on the table.
cards.counter: It's double-edged: the same nitrogen runoff drives algal blooms, dead zones, and potent nitrous-oxide emissions.

quiz.q: Before synthetic ammonia, what was the main ceiling on crop yields?
choices: The amount of nitrogen available from natural sources
The lack of mechanical harvesting equipment
A shortage of suitable seed varieties

quiz.q: Which gas, a far stronger greenhouse gas than CO2, is released as a side effect of heavy nitrogen fertiliser use?
A region grows enough food for 8 million people. If the same fraction depends on synthetic-nitrogen fertiliser as for the world overall (roughly half), how many of those people depend on it?

cards.title: Reinforcing vs balancing feedback
cards.fact: Two loop types explain most system behaviour: one amplifies, one stabilises.
cards.detail: Reinforcing (positive) loops compound — interest, viral spread, arms races. Balancing (negative) loops push back toward a target — a thermostat, hunger, market correction.
cards.deploy: Lets you name why something grows explosively or stays stubbornly stable instead of hand-waving.
cards.counter: Real systems chain many loops with delays; reading off a single loop usually misleads.

quiz.q: A thermostat that switches the heater off as room temperature approaches the set point is an example of which loop?
choices: A delay-free open loop with no feedback

quiz.q: What single word describes a feedback loop that compounds its own output, like compound interest or viral spread?
Why does reading off a single feedback loop usually mislead when analysing a real-world system?
choices: Real systems chain many loops together with time delays
Feedback loops only exist in engineered, not natural, systems
A single loop always switches sign over time
Balancing loops cancel reinforcing loops exactly

cards.title: The tragedy of the commons — and its rebuttal
cards.fact: Shared resources get overused when each user pockets the gain but shares the cost — yet communities often solve this without the state or markets.
cards.detail: Hardin (1968) argued a shared pasture is doomed to overgrazing. Elinor Ostrom (Nobel 2009) then documented many real communities that govern shared fisheries, forests and irrigation sustainably through their own rules.
cards.deploy: Carries its own counter-argument: useful whether you're arguing for regulation OR for local self-governance.
cards.counter: Hardin overgeneralised from a model; Ostrom showed the 'tragedy' is not inevitable when users can communicate and make binding rules.

quiz.q: Which economist won a Nobel for documenting communities that sustainably govern shared resources through their own rules?
What incentive structure drives overuse of a shared resource in the tragedy-of-the-commons argument?
choices: Each user keeps the full gain but spreads the cost across everyone
Each user pays the full cost but shares the gain equally
Users gain and lose in exactly equal proportion
The resource regenerates faster than anyone can extract it

quiz.q: According to Ostrom's findings, what key ability lets users avoid the 'tragedy' and govern a shared resource without the state or markets?

cards.title: Heavy tails: when the average lies
cards.fact: Wealth, city sizes, and word frequencies follow heavy-tailed distributions where a few cases dominate.
cards.detail: In a power-law-like distribution, the 'typical' value and the average can be wildly different — think the 80/20 rule. A handful of extreme cases carry most of the total.
cards.deploy: Warns against reasoning from the mean in unequal systems — 'average income' or 'average user' can be meaningless.
cards.counter: True power laws are statistically hard to distinguish from lognormal distributions, and the label is often slapped on data that doesn't fit it.

quiz.q: Suppose 1000 customers spend a total of $2,000,000, but following an 80/20 pattern, 20% of customers account for 80% of spending. How many dollars do that top 20% of customers spend in total?
In a heavy-tailed distribution like wealth or city sizes, why can the average be a misleading summary?
choices: A few extreme cases dominate the total, so the mean sits far from the typical value
The distribution has no defined total, so any average is invalid
Every value is identical, making the mean equal to the median
The values are negative, so the average is meaningless

quiz.q: Which other distribution is statistically hard to distinguish from a true power law, making the 'power law' label often unreliable?

cards.title: Why the rich get richer
cards.fact: Why do a few get so much? Often because 'the rich get richer' — preferential attachment.
cards.detail: Power-law distributions frequently arise from one simple rule: the more you already have, the more you attract. New web pages link to already-popular pages; citations flow to already-cited papers; wealth begets wealth. Barabási and Albert (1999) showed this 'preferential attachment' generates the heavy-tailed, 'scale-free' patterns seen across many networks.
cards.deploy: A mechanism behind heavy tails: unequal outcomes can emerge from a neutral 'rich-get-richer' process, not just from differences in merit.
cards.counter: It's one route to power laws, not the only one; real systems mix it with chance, fitness and resets, so pure preferential attachment rarely fits perfectly.

quiz.q: Preferential attachment ('rich get richer') tends to produce…
What family of statistical distributions, marked by heavy tails and 'scale-free' structure, does a rich-get-richer growth process typically generate?
A new node joins a growing network and attaches to existing nodes with probability proportional to how many connections each already has. Which node is MOST likely to gain the new connection?
choices: The node that already has the most connections
The node that joined the network most recently
Every existing node, with exactly equal probability
The node with the fewest connections, to balance the network

quiz.q: Under preferential attachment, attachment probability is proportional to a node's current connection count. In a network, node A has 30 links and node B has 6 links. How many times more likely is a new node to attach to A than to B?

cards.title: Where to push a system
cards.fact: There are places to push a system for big change — and the obvious ones are usually the weakest.
cards.detail: Donella Meadows ranked twelve 'leverage points' for intervening in a system. Tweaking numbers (taxes, subsidies) is low leverage; changing feedback loops and rules is stronger; the highest leverage is shifting the system's goals and the underlying paradigm. People sense these points but often push them the wrong way.
cards.deploy: A change toolkit: stop fiddling with parameters and aim at goals and mindsets, where leverage is greatest.
cards.counter: High-leverage points (paradigms) are exactly the hardest to move and easiest to get catastrophically wrong; the ranking is a heuristic, not a formula.

quiz.q: In Meadows' framework, the highest-leverage intervention is…
choices: Changing the system's goals or paradigm

quiz.q: Which researcher ranked twelve 'leverage points' for intervening in a system, from adjusting numbers up to shifting paradigms?
A city wants to durably reduce car dependence. Ordered from lowest to highest leverage in Meadows' framework, which sequence is correct?
choices: Raise the fuel tax; rewrite zoning rules; redefine the city's goal from car throughput to people's access
Redefine the city's goal; rewrite zoning rules; raise the fuel tax
Rewrite zoning rules; raise the fuel tax; redefine the city's goal
Raise the fuel tax; redefine the city's goal; rewrite zoning rules

quiz.q: Meadows' leverage points are numbered so that lower numbers mean higher leverage, with the most powerful being shifting the underlying paradigm. If the list runs from 12 (weakest) down to 1 (strongest), what number corresponds to the highest-leverage intervention?

cards.title: Governing the commons
cards.fact: Elinor Ostrom showed communities can govern shared resources themselves — and found the rules that make it work.
cards.detail: Against the idea that commons inevitably collapse, Ostrom's fieldwork on fisheries, forests and irrigation found communities sustainably self-governing for generations. Her eight design principles include clear boundaries, rules fitted to local conditions, participation in rule-making, monitoring, graduated sanctions, cheap conflict resolution and nested governance. She won the 2009 Nobel in economics.
cards.deploy: The empirical rebuttal to 'tragedy of the commons': self-organised governance is a real third option beyond the state and the market.
cards.counter: Her principles aren't a guarantee — they work best for bounded, local resources; scaling them to global commons like the climate is far harder.

quiz.q: Ostrom showed commons can be sustained by…
choices: Community self-governance with the right rules

quiz.q: Whose fieldwork on fisheries, forests, and irrigation systems demonstrated that communities can sustainably self-govern shared resources, earning a 2009 Nobel in economics?
A village irrigation cooperative wants to follow Ostrom's design principles. Which practice best fits her principle of 'graduated sanctions'?
choices: First-time over-users get a small warning, while repeat offenders face steadily harsher penalties
Anyone who breaks a rule even once is permanently banned from the system
Rule-breakers are reported to a distant national authority for prosecution
All members pay the same flat fee regardless of how much water they take

quiz.q: Ostrom distilled her findings into a well-known set of numbered design principles for enduring commons institutions. How many such principles are in this set?

cards.title: Climate tipping points
cards.fact: Push a natural system too far and it can flip — abruptly, and sometimes for good.
cards.detail: Some Earth systems have thresholds where change becomes self-reinforcing: melting ice exposes dark water that absorbs more heat; a drying Amazon can flip toward savanna; the Atlantic overturning circulation (AMOC) could slow sharply. Past a tipping point the shift can be fast and effectively irreversible, and crossing one can nudge others — a cascade.
cards.deploy: Why climate risk isn't smoothly proportional: some changes don't ease back once you stop pushing.
cards.counter: Exact thresholds are uncertain and hotly debated — some 'tipping' claims outrun the evidence, and timescales range from years to centuries.

quiz.q: A climate 'tipping point' is…
choices: A threshold past which change is self-reinforcing and often irreversible

quiz.q: What is the name of the large-scale Atlantic ocean current system, abbreviated AMOC, whose sharp slowing is treated as a potential climate tipping point?
Sea ice melts, exposing dark open water that absorbs more sunlight, which warms the region and melts still more ice. What kind of process makes this a candidate tipping mechanism?
choices: A stabilizing negative feedback that restores equilibrium
A purely linear response proportional to forcing
A one-off shock with no further consequences

quiz.q: Which statement best captures why crossing a climate tipping point is more worrying than ordinary warming?
choices: The shift can be rapid and effectively irreversible even if the original push is removed
It always reverses fully within a single year once emissions stop
It only changes one isolated system and never affects any other
Its threshold and timing are precisely known well in advance

cards.title: Keystone species
cards.fact: Some species hold a whole ecosystem together — far out of proportion to their numbers.
cards.detail: A 'keystone species' has an outsized effect relative to its abundance (Robert Paine, 1969). Remove sea otters and urchins strip the kelp forests; remove the ochre sea star and mussels crowd everyone out; remove wolves and herbivores reshape the land. Like the keystone of an arch, pull it and the structure can collapse.
cards.deploy: Explains why protecting one species can matter for a whole ecosystem — and why Yellowstone's wolves rippled so far.
cards.counter: The label is overused (200+ claimed keystones) and context-dependent; real food webs are messier than a single linchpin.

quiz.q: A keystone species is one that…
choices: Has an outsized effect relative to its abundance

quiz.q: A small predatory snail makes up under 1% of the biomass on a rocky shore, yet removing it lets one mussel species blanket the rock and cut the number of resident species from 15 to 8. What does this most strongly suggest about the snail?
choices: It is a keystone species, since its effect on the community far exceeds its abundance
It is a dominant species, since it controls the most biomass
It is an invasive species, since it suppresses native mussels
It is a generalist, since its loss has little measurable effect

quiz.q: Which ecologist introduced the keystone species concept, based on experiments removing the ochre sea star (Pisaster) from rocky tidepools?

If a tidepool holds 18 species while a keystone predator is present, but collapses to a stable 7 species after the predator is removed, how many species are lost as a direct consequence of the removal?

cards.title: Fertiliser's dead zones
cards.fact: The fertiliser that feeds the world also chokes its waters — creating ocean 'dead zones'.
cards.detail: Nitrogen and phosphorus runoff from farms (and sewage) over-fertilise rivers, lakes and coasts. The nutrients trigger algal blooms; when the algae die and decompose they strip oxygen from the water, creating hypoxic 'dead zones' (like the Gulf of Mexico's) where fish can't survive. It's the downstream cost of Haber–Bosch abundance.
cards.deploy: The other half of the fertiliser story: the reactive nitrogen that feeds billions also pollutes the water that receives the runoff.
cards.counter: It's manageable, not inevitable — better nutrient timing, buffer strips and treatment cut runoff; the obstacle is mostly cost and governance, not chemistry.

quiz.q: Eutrophication creates 'dead zones' by…
choices: Nutrient runoff → algal blooms → oxygen depletion

quiz.q: In a coastal bay receiving heavy farm runoff, what is the correct ordering of events that produces a hypoxic dead zone?
choices: Nutrient influx, then algal bloom, then algae die and decompose, then oxygen is depleted
Oxygen depletion, then algal bloom, then nutrient influx, then fish die
Algae die, then nutrient influx, then oxygen rises, then bloom forms
Fish die first, releasing nutrients that fuel a bloom that adds oxygen

quiz.q: Besides nitrogen, which other plant nutrient running off from farms and sewage is the main driver of eutrophication?

Water with dissolved oxygen below 2 mg/L is considered hypoxic. If a river measures 9 mg/L upstream of farmland but only 1.5 mg/L in the bloom-affected estuary, by how many mg/L has the dissolved oxygen dropped?

cards.title: Comparative advantage
cards.fact: Two countries can both gain from trade even if one is better at making everything.
cards.detail: Ricardo (1817): what matters is opportunity cost, not absolute skill. Each side specialises where it gives up the least, and total output rises. It's the core case for trade.
cards.deploy: The standard answer to 'they can make it cheaper, so trade hurts us' — gains come from specialisation, not from winning at everything.
cards.counter: Named critics — Friedrich List in the 1840s, Ha-Joon Chang today — argue infant industries need protection to ever become competitive; and the clean result assumes full employment and mobile resources while ignoring distribution: trade can raise the total yet leave specific workers and regions worse off.

quiz.q: Comparative advantage says gains from trade come from differences in…
A country should specialise where it has the lowest…
In one hour, Country A can make 6 shirts or 3 computers; Country B can make 2 shirts or 4 computers. For Country A, what is the opportunity cost of producing one computer, measured in shirts?
Country A can make 6 shirts or 3 computers per hour; Country B can make 2 shirts or 4 computers per hour. According to comparative advantage, who should specialise in computers?
choices: Country B, because it gives up only 0.5 shirts per computer versus A's 2 shirts
Country A, because it can also make more shirts overall
Neither, because A is not absolutely better at everything
Country B, because it has the higher absolute computer output regardless of opportunity cost

quiz.q: Which classical economist set out the theory of comparative advantage in 1817, arguing that opportunity cost rather than absolute skill drives the gains from trade?

cards.title: Externalities
cards.fact: When a cost or benefit lands on third parties, the market price gets it wrong.
cards.detail: Pollution is the classic case: a factory's price doesn't include the harm downstream. Pigou (1920) proposed taxing the activity to make the price tell the truth.
cards.deploy: Justifies carbon taxes, congestion charges, and the like: prices need correcting when costs spill over.
cards.counter: Coase (1960) showed that with clear property rights and low bargaining costs, private parties can fix externalities without taxes — the right remedy depends on the situation.

quiz.q: A chemical plant's production imposes pollution costs on a downstream town that the plant never pays. Why does the unregulated market price of the chemical end up too low?
choices: It reflects only the plant's private costs, leaving out the external cost borne by third parties
It includes the town's cleanup costs, which inflate the apparent supply
It overstates demand because buyers value pollution
It double-counts the social cost, pushing the price below marginal benefit

quiz.q: Which economist argued in 1960 that, with clearly defined property rights and low bargaining costs, private parties can resolve an externality without government taxes?

A factory's private cost of making a tonne of product is 80 dollars, but its pollution imposes an external cost of 35 dollars per tonne on others. What is the Pigouvian tax per tonne that makes the price reflect the full social cost?

cards.title: Loss aversion
cards.fact: Losing $100 hurts about twice as much as gaining $100 feels good.
cards.detail: Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory (1979) showed people don't weigh outcomes by final wealth but by gains and losses from a reference point — and losses loom larger. It helped found behavioural economics.
cards.deploy: Undercuts the assumption that people are cool rational maximisers — framing a choice as a loss vs a gain changes behaviour.
cards.counter: The exact 2:1 ratio varies by context and there's ongoing replication debate; it's a robust tendency, not a fixed constant.

quiz.q: Losing a dollar hurts about twice as much as gaining one feels good. In a 50/50 gamble with a possible $60 loss, what is the smallest win amount at which a typical loss-averse person breaks even and would accept the bet?
A gym advertises the same monthly fee two ways. Which framing best exploits loss aversion to maximise sign-ups?
choices: Pay $30 a month and keep your fitness
Don't lose the $30 a month you waste staying unfit
Join the average member who works out twice a week

quiz.q: In prospect theory, outcomes are judged as gains and losses relative to a baseline rather than as final wealth. What is the name for that baseline?

cards.title: Hume's is–ought gap
cards.fact: You can't logically derive what ought to be purely from what is.
cards.detail: Hume (1739) noticed writers slide from describing facts ('is') to prescribing duties ('ought') without justifying the jump. Facts alone don't entail values.
cards.deploy: A precision tool for spotting when an opponent smuggles a value claim in under cover of 'the science says'.
cards.counter: Some philosophers (ethical naturalists) argue the gap can be bridged; it's a powerful warning, not a settled proof that values float free of facts.

quiz.q: Which argument commits Hume's is-ought fallacy by deriving a value conclusion from purely factual premises?
choices: Eating meat causes suffering, so if suffering matters morally we ought to reduce meat consumption
Humans have always eaten meat, therefore eating meat is morally permissible
If we ought to minimise suffering, and factory farming maximises it, we ought to oppose factory farming
Lying erodes trust, and since we value trust, we should avoid lying

quiz.q: When someone commits Hume's gap, what kind of claim is illegitimately concluded from purely factual premises: one about what is the case, or one about what should be done?
Which group of philosophers most directly challenges the is-ought gap by arguing moral facts can be derived from natural facts?

cards.title: Falsifiability
cards.fact: A claim that nothing could ever disprove isn't really scientific.
cards.detail: Popper argued the mark of a scientific theory is that it sticks its neck out — it forbids certain observations, so it could be proven wrong. 'What would change your mind?' is the key question.
cards.deploy: A sharp test against unfalsifiable claims ('it's true, you just can't see the evidence').
cards.counter: Kuhn and Lakatos showed real science doesn't work by naive falsification — a failed prediction is often blamed on auxiliary assumptions, not the core theory.

quiz.q: For Popper, a scientific theory must be…
By Popper's criterion, which claim is LEAST scientific (unfalsifiable)?
choices: Heavy objects fall at g in a vacuum
Whatever happens was meant to be
Water boils at 100°C at sea level

quiz.q: By Popper's falsifiability criterion, which of these is the most scientific statement?
choices: Everything happens for a reason we can't always understand
Some events are influenced by unmeasurable forces
History unfolds according to a hidden purpose

quiz.q: Which two philosophers are most associated with the objection that scientists rescue a failing theory by blaming auxiliary assumptions rather than abandoning its core?
A fortune teller predicts 'something significant will affect your life this year.' Why does this fail Popper's test?
choices: No possible outcome could count as the prediction failing
It was not published in a peer-reviewed journal
It relies on statistics rather than observation
It has not yet been repeated by other fortune tellers

cards.title: Rawls's veil of ignorance
cards.fact: To find fair rules, choose them not knowing who you'll be in the society.
cards.detail: Rawls (1971): behind a 'veil' that hides your wealth, talents, race and class, you'd pick principles that protect everyone — because you might end up at the bottom.
cards.deploy: A portable fairness test for any institution or policy: would you accept it not knowing your place in it?
cards.counter: Nozick and others reject the setup: why assume people behind the veil would be so risk-averse (favouring the worst-off) rather than gambling on the average?

quiz.q: Behind the veil of ignorance, choosers are imagined to favour rules that protect the least advantaged because they might end up there. What single word names this strategy of guarding against the worst possible position?
Using the veil-of-ignorance test, which tax policy would a chooser most likely endorse if they knew nothing about their future income?
choices: One that funds a strong safety net in case they end up poor
One that abolishes all taxes to maximise top earners' wealth
One that taxes only the bottom income bracket
One designed by sampling current voters' preferences

quiz.q: Which philosopher most prominently objected that there is no good reason to assume people behind the veil would be so risk-averse rather than gambling on the average outcome?

cards.title: The median voter theorem
cards.fact: In a simple two-way majority vote, the middle voter decides — so parties drift to the centre.
cards.detail: If opinion lines up on one axis and the winner needs a majority, the option preferred by the median voter beats all others. Candidates converge toward that voter to win.
cards.deploy: Explains why rival parties can end up sounding alike — a clean model for centrist convergence.
cards.counter: It assumes one dimension, two options, and full turnout. Primaries, multidimensional issues, and abstention routinely break it.

quiz.q: A new candidate is choosing where to stand on a single left-right policy line. Their opponent has already locked in a position slightly right of the electorate's midpoint. To maximize their chance of winning a two-way majority vote, where should the new candidate position themselves?
choices: Just to the left of the opponent, capturing the median and everyone to the left
Far left, to lock in the most committed base voters
Far right, to outflank the opponent on their own side
Exactly mirroring the opponent's position to look consistent

quiz.q: Seven voters have ideal points on a 0-to-10 line at positions 1, 2, 3, 6, 8, 9, and 10. In a one-dimensional majority vote, what is the position of the voter whose preference is decisive?
Name one of the core assumptions of the simple median voter model whose violation (for example by multi-issue politics or low participation) typically causes the result to break down.

cards.title: Duverger's law
cards.fact: Winner-take-all elections tend to produce two big parties; proportional systems produce many.
cards.detail: Under first-past-the-post, votes for small parties are 'wasted', so voters and donors consolidate around two contenders. Proportional representation rewards smaller parties, so more survive.
cards.deploy: Shows that party systems are shaped by the voting rules, not just by the electorate's views — institutions matter.
cards.counter: It's a tendency, not an iron law: the UK and India sustain strong regional/third parties under the same rules.

quiz.q: A country switches from first-past-the-post to proportional representation. Based on the institutional logic of how electoral rules shape party systems, what is the most likely change to its party landscape?
choices: More small parties survive and win seats
The two largest parties consolidate into one
Voter turnout automatically falls to near zero

quiz.q: Under first-past-the-post, what term describes a vote cast for a small party that wins no seat and so effectively counts for nothing — the mechanism that pushes voters to consolidate around two contenders?

Strong regional and third parties persist in countries like the UK and India despite their use of winner-take-all elections. What does this best illustrate about the relationship between electoral rules and party numbers?
choices: The two-party outcome is a strong tendency rather than a guaranteed law
Proportional representation must secretly be in use there
Electoral rules have no effect on party systems at all
Winner-take-all rules reliably produce many parties

cards.title: The collective action problem
cards.fact: Even when everyone would benefit, large groups often fail to act — because each person can free-ride.
cards.detail: Olson (1965): if you'll get the benefit whether or not you contribute, the rational move is to let others do the work. So big diffuse groups under-organise while small concentrated interests punch above their weight.
cards.deploy: Explains why concentrated lobbies beat diffuse majorities, and why obvious public goods get under-provided.
cards.counter: Selective incentives, social pressure, leadership, and repeated interaction (Ostrom) routinely overcome free-riding — it's a hurdle, not a wall.

quiz.q: A policy would give each of 30 million consumers about 4 dollars a year in lower prices, while costing 200 firms roughly 600,000 dollars each. Which side is more likely to organize effectively to influence the outcome, and why?
choices: The firms, because their stake is large and concentrated while consumers' is tiny and diffuse
The consumers, because they vastly outnumber the firms
Neither, because both groups face identical incentives
The consumers, because their total benefit far exceeds the firms' total cost

quiz.q: What is the term for a benefit (such as a member-only service or perk) offered specifically to those who contribute, used to overcome free-riding by rewarding participation rather than the whole group?

Which scholar's work on how communities self-organize to manage shared resources — through monitoring and repeated interaction — is the standard counterpoint to the claim that diffuse groups inevitably fail to act?

cards.title: Arrow's impossibility theorem
cards.fact: No voting system can be perfectly fair — Arrow proved it's mathematically impossible.
cards.detail: Arrow's impossibility theorem (1951): with three or more options, no ranked voting method can satisfy a short list of reasonable conditions at once — no dictator, respect unanimity, and 'independence of irrelevant alternatives'. Every ranked system trades something off (and has a spoiler effect). It's a foundational result in social choice.
cards.deploy: Ends the hunt for a 'perfect' voting system — the real question is which trade-offs you accept, not whether you can avoid them.
cards.counter: It applies to ranked orderings; rated systems (approval, score voting) that use grades rather than rankings sidestep the exact theorem, so it's not a counsel of despair.

quiz.q: Arrow's impossibility theorem shows that…
choices: No ranked voting rule can meet all fairness criteria at once

quiz.q: Arrow's impossibility theorem proves that no ranked voting method can simultaneously satisfy its short list of fairness conditions. Which design choice lets approval and score voting sidestep the exact theorem?
choices: They use independent grades or ratings rather than a single ranked ordering of all options
They require a dictator to break every tie
They restrict every election to exactly two candidates
They forbid voters from expressing any preference at all

quiz.q: Arrow's theorem applies once there are at least how many distinct options or candidates on the ballot?
Arrow's condition that says adding or removing a losing, non-competitive option should not flip the group's ranking of the others — the one closely tied to the spoiler effect — is known by what name?

cards.title: Proportional representation's trade-off
cards.fact: Proportional representation trades the stability of two big parties for fuller representation.
cards.detail: Where winner-take-all tends toward two parties (Duverger), proportional representation allocates seats in line with vote share, so smaller parties win seats and parliaments hold many. That mirrors diverse views more faithfully and wastes fewer votes, but usually means coalition governments — more inclusive, sometimes less decisive. It's the central trade-off in electoral-system design.
cards.deploy: Frames the electoral-system choice: representativeness (PR) versus governability and clear accountability (FPTP) — no free lunch.
cards.counter: It's a tendency, not a law: PR systems vary hugely (thresholds, district size) and many are perfectly stable; 'PR equals chaos' is a caricature.

quiz.q: Compared with winner-take-all, proportional representation tends to produce…
A country switches from a winner-take-all system to proportional representation. Which outcome is the most likely consequence?
choices: Single-party majority governments become more frequent
Coalition governments become more common as more parties win seats
Voter turnout is guaranteed to fall sharply
The total number of legislative seats must shrink

quiz.q: In a 200-seat parliament elected by pure proportional representation, a party wins 23% of the national vote. Ignoring any threshold and rounding to the nearest whole seat, how many seats does it receive?
Which political scientist's name is attached to the principle that single-member winner-take-all districts tend to produce a two-party system?

cards.title: You never test one idea alone
cards.fact: A failed experiment never cleanly refutes a single hypothesis — you always test a whole bundle.
cards.detail: The Duhem–Quine thesis: any prediction leans on a web of auxiliary assumptions (the instrument works, no other forces, the background theory holds). When a test fails, logic alone can't say which link broke — you can always save the core idea by blaming an auxiliary. This complicates Popper's clean falsification and feeds Kuhn's picture of theories defended within a 'paradigm' until anomalies pile up.
cards.deploy: A check on naive falsification: 'the experiment disproved it' is rarely as clean as it sounds.
cards.counter: It can be overstated into 'anything goes' — in practice scientists do reach justified verdicts; the holism is real but not paralysing.

quiz.q: The Duhem–Quine thesis says a failed test…
choices: Can't pinpoint which assumption failed — you test a whole web

quiz.q: An astronomer predicts a planet's position using Newtonian mechanics, but the telescope reading disagrees with the prediction. Per the Duhem-Quine thesis, what can logic alone NOT determine?
choices: Which specific assumption (the theory, the instrument, or a background condition) is the one at fault
Whether the telescope produced a reading at all
Whether the astronomer recorded the number correctly

quiz.q: Whose model of science describes theories being defended within a 'paradigm' until anomalies accumulate, a view the Duhem-Quine holism is often said to support?
The Duhem-Quine thesis most directly complicates which philosopher's idea?
choices: Bacon's inductive method as pure enumeration

cards.title: The naturalistic fallacy
cards.fact: Calling something 'natural' doesn't make it good — and defining 'good' as any natural property is a trap.
cards.detail: G.E. Moore's naturalistic fallacy (1903): you can't define 'good' as identical to a natural property (pleasure, survival, what evolution favours), because his 'open question' always remains — 'this is pleasant, but is it good?' still makes sense, so the two aren't the same. It's cousin to Hume's is–ought gap and to the everyday 'appeal to nature' (natural = better).
cards.deploy: Disarms 'it's natural, therefore good/right' arguments — and warns against reading ethics straight off biology.
cards.counter: Ethical naturalists reject Moore's argument and hold that moral facts can be natural facts; the 'fallacy' label is itself contested (Frankena).

quiz.q: The 'naturalistic fallacy' warns against…
choices: Equating 'good' with a natural property (e.g. 'natural = good')

quiz.q: Which philosopher introduced the naturalistic fallacy, in his 1903 work Principia Ethica?
Someone argues, 'Refined sugar is bad for you because it isn't natural, while honey is natural and therefore healthy.' Which everyday reasoning error is this?
Moore's 'open question argument' shows that 'good' cannot just mean 'pleasant' because which question still makes genuine sense?
choices: 'This act is pleasant, but is it good?'

cards.title: Nozick's reply to Rawls
cards.fact: Nozick's reply to Rawls: a just outcome is whatever free exchanges produce — even if unequal.
cards.detail: In Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), Robert Nozick countered Rawls with an 'entitlement theory': holdings are just if they were acquired and transferred justly, whatever pattern results. His 'Wilt Chamberlain' example: if fans freely pay to watch a star, the resulting inequality is just, and forcibly redistributing it violates liberty. He defends only a 'minimal state'.
cards.deploy: The libertarian counterweight to Rawls: justice as fair process and liberty, not as a fair distribution pattern.
cards.counter: Egalitarians like G.A. Cohen argue that 'just steps' ignore tainted starting points (conquest, slavery) and that pure process can entrench injustice; Nozick's initial-acquisition principle is the weak link.

quiz.q: Nozick's entitlement theory judges a distribution by…
choices: Whether it arose through just acquisition and free transfer

quiz.q: What is the name of Nozick's celebrated thought experiment in which fans freely pay a basketball star to watch him play, producing a just inequality?
On Nozick's entitlement theory, which feature makes a distribution of holdings just?
choices: Each holding was acquired and transferred through just steps, regardless of the final pattern
The final pattern leaves no one below a guaranteed minimum
The distribution maximizes total happiness across society
The least advantaged are made as well off as possible

quiz.q: Nozick argues that only what kind of state is justified, one limited to protecting against force, theft and fraud and enforcing contracts?

cards.title: What economics is about
cards.fact: Economics starts from one awkward fact: we have unlimited wants and limited means.
cards.detail: Because you can't have everything, every choice means giving something up. Economics studies how people and societies handle those trade-offs — and the cost of any choice is the best alternative you gave up (its opportunity cost).
cards.deploy: Reframes almost any policy fight as 'what are we giving up?' rather than just 'is this nice?'.
cards.counter: The scarcity frame can hide questions of power and distribution — who decides what's scarce, and for whom.

quiz.q: The opportunity cost of a choice is…
choices: The best alternative you gave up

quiz.q: Economics begins from the problem of…
A student has a free evening and chooses to study instead of either going to a concert (which she values most among the alternatives) or sleeping early. What is the opportunity cost of studying?
choices: Both the concert and sleeping early combined
Nothing, since the evening was free

quiz.q: Economics exists as a discipline because human wants are unlimited but the means to satisfy them are limited. What single word names this fundamental condition?
Which objection best captures a limitation of framing every social problem purely as 'scarcity and trade-offs'?
choices: It can obscure questions of power and distribution — who decides what counts as scarce, and for whom
It assumes resources are unlimited rather than limited
It only applies to money and ignores time
It makes opportunity cost impossible to define

cards.title: Supply and demand
cards.fact: In the basic model, price isn't set by cost or fairness — it's where supply meets demand.
cards.detail: When price rises, buyers want less and sellers offer more; the price settles where the two meet. It's a powerful starting model — but it assumes competition, good information and flexible prices that real markets often lack.
cards.deploy: Explains how a price emerges from supply and demand — and why interventions like caps or subsidies ripple into quantity (shortages or surpluses), not just price.
cards.counter: Perfect competition is rare; with market power, information gaps or sticky prices the simple model can mislead.

quiz.q: In the basic model, the market price settles where…
In a market, demand is Qd = 100 - 2P and supply is Qs = 10 + P, where P is price. At the equilibrium price, what quantity is traded (in units)?
A government sets a price ceiling well below the equilibrium price for a good. According to the basic supply-and-demand model, what is the most likely result?
choices: A shortage, because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
A surplus, because sellers offer more than buyers want
No change, because price caps only affect fairness, not quantity
Higher quality, because sellers compete harder

quiz.q: The basic supply-and-demand model can mislead when one buyer or seller is large enough to influence the price on their own. What two-word term describes such an actor's ability to move the price?

cards.title: What GDP measures
cards.fact: GDP measures the money value of what a country produces — and quietly leaves a lot out.
cards.detail: GDP totals the market value of a country's output. It misses unpaid work, ignores distribution, and treats some harms as gains — which is why 'growth' is one of economics' biggest arguments.
cards.deploy: Cuts through 'the economy grew, so we're better off' — ask what the number counts and what it omits.
cards.counter: For all its flaws, GDP tracks real things — jobs, output, tax revenue — and no rival measure has cleanly replaced it.

quiz.q: GDP does NOT directly count…
A country's GDP rises sharply in a year when a major oil spill triggers a costly cleanup paid for with new contracts. Why might this rise be misleading as a sign of improved wellbeing?
choices: GDP can count spending to repair harm as added output, treating some damage as a gain
GDP excludes all government spending, so the cleanup would not appear
GDP only counts exports, so domestic cleanup is irrelevant
GDP automatically subtracts environmental damage from output

quiz.q: GDP totals the market value of output but assigns no value to a parent caring for their own children at home. What category of activity does GDP systematically miss for this reason?

Two countries each produce a total output worth 600 billion dollars. In Country A, one household captures 500 billion and the rest share 100 billion; in Country B output is shared evenly. Since GDP ignores distribution, by how many billion dollars do their GDP figures differ?

cards.title: Why 'political economy'?
cards.fact: Before it was 'economics', it was 'political economy' — and the politics never really left.
cards.detail: The classical writers studied 'political economy' — wealth and its distribution between classes. Around 1900 the field rebranded as 'economics' on the model of physics, pushing power to the margins; 'political economy' names the traditions that keep it central.
cards.deploy: Reminds an opponent that 'just the economics' is rarely just the economics.
cards.counter: Naming the politics doesn't settle the facts — efficiency and distribution can still be studied with evidence.

quiz.q: Classical writers like Smith and Ricardo studied wealth and its distribution between classes under a two-word name for the field — one that kept power and politics central. What was that name?
Around 1900 the field rebranded from 'political economy' to 'economics', modelling itself on a particular natural science. Which science was the model, and what was a consequence?
choices: Physics — and questions of power and class were pushed to the margins
Biology — and the field became focused on evolution of firms
Chemistry — and it emphasised the mixing of inputs
Astronomy — and it focused on long-run cycles

quiz.q: Which statement best reflects a fair counterpoint to the claim that 'just the economics' always hides politics?
choices: Naming the politics doesn't settle the facts — efficiency and distribution can still be examined with evidence
Economics has no political content whatsoever, so the worry is baseless
Only political economy uses evidence; mainstream economics does not
Because politics is everywhere, no economic claim can ever be tested

cards.title: The rival schools
cards.fact: There is no single 'economics' — there are rival schools that disagree about how the economy works.
cards.detail: Economics is plural: classical, Marxian, neoclassical, Keynesian, monetarist, Austrian, behavioural and ecological schools give different answers to the same questions. The mainstream is one paradigm among several, not the last word.
cards.deploy: Whenever someone says 'economists agree', ask which economists — the field is plural.
cards.counter: Pluralism can tip into 'anything goes'; some claims really are better supported by the evidence than others.

quiz.q: A friend says 'all economists agree that the central bank should cut interest rates.' Which response best reflects the pluralist view of economics?
choices: Ask which school they mean — Keynesians, monetarists and Austrians often draw opposite conclusions from the same situation
Agree, since monetary policy is the one area where every school converges
Point out that economics is a settled science, so dissent is just error
Reply that only behavioural economists are qualified to judge interest rates

quiz.q: Name the school of economic thought, named after the writer who built on the labour theory of value, that analyses the economy through class conflict and the dynamics of capital.
Which statement captures the 'counter' caution about economic pluralism?
choices: Treating every school as equally valid risks 'anything goes' — some claims are still better supported by evidence than others
Pluralism proves that no economic claim can ever be tested against evidence
Once you accept many schools exist, the mainstream school must be discarded
Disagreement among schools means economic data is always fabricated

cards.title: Adam Smith and the invisible hand
cards.fact: Smith argued a butcher feeds you not from kindness but from self-interest — and somehow it works.
cards.detail: Smith (1776) argued self-interested exchange, coordinated 'as if by an invisible hand', can benefit all, powered by the division of labour. But he also rooted society in sympathy and distrusted merchants — he's far more nuanced than the caricature.
cards.deploy: Useful against caricatures of 'capitalism = greed is good' — even Smith didn't say that.
cards.counter: Smith still defended self-interest and markets as broadly benign — he isn't the proto-socialist some make him either.

quiz.q: Smith's 'invisible hand' is the idea that…
Smith's butcher example is meant to show that:
choices: Self-interested exchange, not benevolence, is what reliably gets your dinner on the table
Butchers are uniquely generous and supply meat out of kindness
Markets fail whenever participants act in their own interest
Central planners must direct the butcher to supply the right amount of meat

quiz.q: Besides self-interest, Smith grounded human society in a moral sentiment he wrote a whole book about. What is that sentiment?
In which year did Smith publish 'The Wealth of Nations', where the invisible-hand argument appears?

cards.title: The division of labour
cards.fact: Smith watched a pin factory and saw the secret of modern wealth: split the job up.
cards.detail: Splitting work into specialised steps multiplies output — Smith's pin factory is the classic example. But he and later Marx warned it can also deskill and alienate the worker.
cards.deploy: Explains assembly lines, supply chains and outsourcing — and their human downside.
cards.counter: Specialisation also lifted billions out of subsistence; the gains are real, not just the costs.

quiz.q: Suppose one worker doing every step of pin-making alone produces 20 pins a day. If splitting the work into specialised steps raises output to 4,800 pins per worker per day, by what factor did per-worker output increase?
Modern global supply chains, where a single product is assembled from components made in many specialised factories worldwide, are a large-scale application of which idea?
choices: The invisible hand of price signals only

quiz.q: What one-word term did Smith and later Marx use for the worker's sense of disconnection and loss of skill that repetitive, fragmented work can cause?

cards.title: Ricardo and the logic machine
cards.fact: David Ricardo turned economics into a machine of pure logic — and reached unsettling conclusions.
cards.detail: Ricardo built ruthless logical models: comparative advantage, the theory of rent (landlords gain as population grows), and a labour theory of value later taken up by Marx and dropped by the mainstream.
cards.deploy: Shows distribution-as-class-conflict has deep roots inside classical economics, not just in Marx.
cards.counter: The labour theory of value faces hard problems (capital, time, skill) that marginalism was designed to solve.

quiz.q: Ricardo's theory of comparative advantage implies that a country should specialise in and export the goods in which it:
choices: Has the lowest relative (opportunity) cost, even if a trading partner is better at making everything
Has an absolute productivity lead over every other country
Employs the most workers per unit of output

quiz.q: According to Ricardo's theory of rent, which class captures a growing share of income as population rises and less-fertile land is brought into use?
The labour theory of value, which Ricardo developed and Marx later adopted, was largely abandoned by the mainstream because it struggled to account for the role of:
choices: Capital, time and differences in skill in determining prices
Population growth in raising land rents

cards.title: Where does value come from?
cards.fact: Is a thing valuable because of the work in it, or because of how much you want it?
cards.detail: Classical economists and Marx located value in labour; marginalists from the 1870s relocated it in usefulness at the margin. The mainstream took the second path — but the first still frames profit as extraction rather than reward.
cards.deploy: Lets you locate an argument: profit-as-reward (marginalist) vs profit-as-extraction (Marxian).
cards.counter: Marginalism resolved real puzzles — like why water is cheap and diamonds dear — that the labour theory struggled with.

quiz.q: A factory owner sells goods for far more than the wages and materials cost. A labour-theory-of-value advocate and a marginalist describe the gap differently. Which pairing is correct?
choices: Labour view: extraction of unpaid worker effort; marginalist view: reward for supplying a scarce, useful factor
Labour view: reward for risk-taking; marginalist view: theft from consumers
Labour view: a market accident; marginalist view: surplus value taken from labour
Both views: the gap is purely a measurement error in accounting

quiz.q: Marginalists located a good's value not in the labour embodied in it but in its usefulness at the margin. Give the one-word-or-two concept naming the usefulness of one more unit.
Air is essential to life yet free, while a signed first-edition novel is inessential yet pricey. Why does this pattern favour the marginalist account of value over the labour theory?
choices: Value tracks the usefulness of the last available unit, and one more breath of abundant air is worth almost nothing while a scarce book is not
Value tracks the total hours of labour, so air took longer to produce
Value tracks how essential a good is overall, which predicts air should be priciest
Value tracks the raw materials consumed, which are higher for air

cards.title: The marginal revolution (1870s)
cards.fact: In the 1870s economics quietly changed its mind about what value even is.
cards.detail: Around 1871–1874, Jevons, Menger and Walras relocated value in marginal utility, founding neoclassical economics and shifting the field from class and distribution toward individual optimisation and equilibrium.
cards.deploy: Explains why mainstream economics talks about utility and equilibrium rather than class.
cards.counter: The marginalist tools genuinely unified price theory and remain the workhorse of applied economics.

quiz.q: Name any one of the three economists credited with independently founding the marginalist (neoclassical) approach to value in the early 1870s.
Taking the midpoint of the marginal revolution as 1872, how many full years separate 1872 from the year 2026?
After the marginal revolution, the central questions of mainstream economics shifted away from one focus and toward another. Which shift describes it?
choices: From class and the distribution of output toward individual optimisation and equilibrium
From individual choice toward the labour embodied in commodities
From equilibrium analysis toward the historical study of class conflict
From price theory toward the moral philosophy of just wages

cards.title: Marx's Capital
cards.fact: Marx didn't just dislike capitalism — he tried to reverse-engineer its hidden machinery.
cards.detail: Marx (1867) argued workers produce more value than their wage ('surplus value'), the source of profit and capital; competition drives accumulation, crises and concentration. His critique outlived his failed predictions.
cards.deploy: A structured frame for arguments about exploitation, inequality and recurring financial crises.
cards.counter: How to read this is itself contested. Cold-War liberals point to the shortages and repression of Soviet-style central planning. Western Marxists (David Harvey) and market socialists (Oskar Lange) reply that Marx analysed capitalism, not a blueprint for command economies, and that his crisis theory is distinct from Stalinist planning; dependency theorists add that capitalism exports its crises to the periphery. Whether the USSR refutes Marx, or only one statist version of socialism, is disputed.

quiz.q: For Marx, profit ('surplus value') comes from…
choices: Value workers produce above their wage

quiz.q: Under Marx's account, suppose a worker's daily wage covers the value they create in the first 5 hours of a 9-hour shift. How many hours of surplus value does the capitalist appropriate that day?
Which 20th-century geographer and Marxist scholar argued that Marx analysed capitalism itself rather than offering a blueprint for Soviet-style command economies?
A debater claims 'the collapse of the USSR proves Marx was wrong.' Which response best reflects the contested reading of Marx's Capital?
choices: Marx critiqued capitalism's dynamics, so a failed statist planning system may refute one version of socialism without refuting his analysis of capitalism
Marx wrote Capital as a detailed operating manual for central planning, so the USSR is a direct test of it
Marx predicted the USSR specifically, so its fall confirms his crisis theory
Marx denied that crises occur, so the USSR is irrelevant to his work

cards.title: Historical materialism
cards.fact: Marx's big bet: to understand history, follow how people make their living.
cards.detail: Historical materialism holds that the economic base shapes a society's politics and ideas, and that history advances as productive forces outgrow old ownership arrangements. Powerful as a habit of analysis, contested as a law of history.
cards.deploy: Prompts the sharp question: 'whose material interests does this idea serve?'.
cards.counter: Culture, religion and ideas have driven huge changes no economic base predicted.

quiz.q: Historical materialism claims history advances through a particular tension. Which best states it?
choices: Growing productive forces strain against the existing ownership and property arrangements
Competing religious doctrines strain against scientific discovery
National identities strain against international institutions
Individual preferences strain against market prices in equilibrium

quiz.q: In historical materialism, what term names the economic foundation of production that is said to shape a society's politics and ideas?
A historian shows the Protestant Reformation reshaped European economies in ways no prior change in production foretold. How does this bear on historical materialism?
choices: It is a standard objection: religion and ideas drove major change the economic base did not predict
It confirms the theory, since religion is part of the economic base
It is irrelevant, because historical materialism only concerns the 20th century
It proves the superstructure always determines the base

cards.title: Keynes and the stuck economy
cards.fact: Keynes argued a market economy can get stuck in a slump — and just sit there.
cards.detail: Keynes (1936) argued economies can settle below full employment when demand collapses, so government should boost demand in slumps. Dominant until 1970s stagflation, revived after 2008.
cards.deploy: The canonical case for stimulus in a recession — private demand can fail to recover by itself.
cards.counter: Sustained deficit spending can stoke inflation and debt; the 1970s showed demand management has limits.

quiz.q: Keynes argued that in a slump, the economy…
choices: Can stay stuck below full employment

quiz.q: Keynes's prescription for a demand-deficient slump was…
choices: Cut public spending to balance the budget
Government spending to lift aggregate demand
Wait for wages to fall on their own

quiz.q: A country's private firms and households cut spending sharply after a financial crisis, and output stays well below capacity for years with no automatic rebound. Whose framework best explains why the economy fails to self-correct?
choices: Keynes, who argued an economy can settle at an equilibrium below full employment
Hayek, who argued dispersed prices coordinate the economy automatically
Friedman, who argued inflation is always a monetary phenomenon
Smith, who argued an invisible hand always restores full output

quiz.q: Keynes laid out his theory of demand-deficient slumps in his 1936 book. What is the one-word concept (starting with 'd') that, when it collapses, his theory says traps the economy below full employment?

Keynesian thinking dominated policy from the publication of his General Theory in 1936 until stagflation discredited it in the 1970s. Taking the 1973 stagflation as the endpoint, for how many years did Keynesian demand management dominate before that setback?

cards.title: The paradox of thrift
cards.fact: If everyone saves more at once, the country can end up saving less.
cards.detail: Saving is prudent for one household but, if everyone does it at once in a slump, spending and incomes fall and total saving can drop — a 'fallacy of composition' Keynes used to justify stimulus.
cards.deploy: Explains why 'everyone should just budget like a household' fails for a whole economy at once.
cards.counter: In normal times saving does finance investment; the paradox is a slump phenomenon, not a general law.

quiz.q: During a recession, a politician argues 'every family tightens its belt when times are hard, so the whole nation should too.' Why does the paradox of thrift say this reasoning can backfire?
choices: When all households cut spending at once, others' incomes fall, so total saving can drop
Higher saving by everyone permanently raises the inflation rate
Banks are legally barred from lending out additional household deposits
Individual budgeting always increases a single household's debt

quiz.q: The paradox of thrift is a classic example of a reasoning error where what is true for one part is wrongly assumed true for the whole. What is the name of this logical fallacy?

Suppose in normal times an economy's households together save 600 billion per year. A panic hits and everyone tries to save more, but spending and incomes fall so much that actual total saving drops to 480 billion. By what percent did total saving fall, illustrating the paradox of thrift?

cards.title: Friedman and monetarism
cards.fact: Milton Friedman's counter-revolution: inflation is always, everywhere, about money.
cards.detail: Friedman argued inflation is fundamentally monetary and government meddling does more harm than good. Strict monetarism failed in practice, but his free-market politics shaped the neoliberal era.
cards.deploy: The standard hawkish case that loose money, not greedy sellers, drives inflation.
cards.counter: Keynesian economists like James Tobin disputed the tight money–inflation link; in practice supply shocks and expectations matter, and central banks abandoned strict monetary targets when they failed to hold. Critics also point to the 'Chicago Boys' in Pinochet's Chile — the view, associated with Naomi Klein's 'shock doctrine', that free-market reforms were imposed under dictatorship rather than chosen democratically.

quiz.q: Two economists debate a country's rising prices. One insists the inflation must trace back to excessive growth in the money supply, not to supply shocks or seller behaviour. Which thinker's position is this?

Naomi Klein popularised a two-word phrase for the idea that free-market reforms were imposed during crises or under dictatorship rather than chosen democratically, citing the U.S.-trained economists who advised Pinochet's Chile. What is this phrase?
Critics of Friedman point to the group of free-market economists, trained at one U.S. university, who advised Pinochet's regime in Chile. By what nickname is this group known?

cards.title: Hayek and the knowledge problem
cards.fact: Hayek's argument against central planning: nobody knows enough — but prices do.
cards.detail: Hayek (1945) argued that dispersed knowledge makes central planning impossible, while prices coordinate it automatically — a deep case for markets that information economists like Joseph Stiglitz later qualified, citing externalities, monopoly and imperfect information.
cards.deploy: The strongest principled argument against detailed central planning — it's a knowledge problem, not just a motivation one.
cards.counter: Information economists like Joseph Stiglitz showed markets with imperfect information aren't efficient either, and prices routinely misprice externalities and public goods — which is why even market economies regulate. The socialist-calculation debate also had another side: Oskar Lange argued planners could simulate prices, and modern computational-planning advocates (and Chile's 1970s Cybersyn experiment) claim better data narrows Hayek's knowledge gap.

quiz.q: Hayek's core objection to detailed central planning is best summarised as which of the following?
choices: The knowledge needed is dispersed among millions of people, so no central body can gather it, while prices convey it automatically
Central planners lack the motivation to act in the public interest
Planning is impossible because money has no intrinsic value
Markets fail whenever there are externalities, so planning is required

quiz.q: In the socialist-calculation debate, one economist argued against Hayek that planners could mimic markets by adjusting administered prices through trial and error. Name this economist.

Information economists argued markets with imperfect information are not efficient, qualifying Hayek's case. Name the Nobel-winning economist most associated with this critique of the price mechanism.

cards.title: The hockey stick
cards.fact: For most of history, ordinary living standards barely moved. Then, around 1800, they exploded.
cards.detail: After millennia of near-flat living standards, sustained growth began with Britain's Industrial Revolution (~1800), lifting output per person many-fold — at an immense early human and environmental cost.
cards.deploy: Anchors any argument about technology and growth — the modern world is a recent, fragile exception.
cards.counter: Why Britain, and why then, is fiercely contested. The Eurocentric 'European genius' story is challenged by Kenneth Pomeranz and the California School (cheap coal and New World land broke the deadlock, not innate superiority) and by Eric Williams and Sven Beckert, who root the take-off in Atlantic slavery and colonial extraction ('war capitalism'). The early human and ecological costs were also immense and unevenly borne.

quiz.q: The 'hockey stick' of economic history refers to…
choices: Living standards flat for millennia then rising sharply

quiz.q: In Kenneth Pomeranz and the California School's account, what broke the ecological deadlock and let Britain industrialise first?
choices: A uniquely European cultural genius for invention
Access to cheap coal and New World land
A superior Protestant work ethic relative to Asia

quiz.q: Which historian rooted Britain's industrial take-off in Atlantic slavery and colonial extraction, a thesis later carried forward by Sven Beckert under the label 'war capitalism'?
If sustained modern growth began around 1800, how many years had passed by the year 2050?

cards.title: Enclosure and the making of workers
cards.fact: Before there were factory workers, common land had to be fenced off — and people pushed into wage labour.
cards.detail: English enclosure (1500s–1800s) privatised common land, creating a wage-dependent workforce — Marx's 'primitive accumulation'. Read either as an efficiency gain or as mass dispossession.
cards.deploy: Reminds us markets in land and labour were created — often by force — not simply 'natural'.
cards.counter: Enclosure also raised food output sharply at a time of rising population; it wasn't pure loss.

quiz.q: What two-word term did Marx use for the process by which enclosure stripped people of common land and pushed them into wage labour?
Which point is the strongest counter to viewing English enclosure as pure dispossession?
choices: It restored common grazing rights to villagers
It sharply raised agricultural food output during a period of rising population
It reduced the supply of wage labourers for early factories
It returned privatised land to communal ownership by 1800

quiz.q: If English enclosure is dated roughly from 1500 to 1850, over how many centuries did the process unfold?

cards.title: Bretton Woods and the end of gold
cards.fact: For 27 years the world's money was anchored to gold through the dollar — until one night in 1971 it wasn't.
cards.detail: Bretton Woods (1944) pegged currencies to a gold-backed dollar; Nixon ended gold convertibility in 1971 and money became pure fiat. Whether money needs a hard anchor is still argued.
cards.deploy: Background for any argument about fiat money, inflation, gold standards or cryptocurrencies.
cards.counter: Whether money needs a hard anchor is genuinely split. Austrian-school 'sound money' advocates (Mises, Rothbard, and today Ron Paul's 'End the Fed' current) argue fiat invites inflation and debt; Keynesians reply gold's discipline deepened the Great Depression. Robert Triffin warned a dollar anchor builds in instability, while Modern Monetary Theory takes the opposite pole — a sovereign fiat issuer faces inflation, not solvency, limits. No camp has won.

quiz.q: The Bretton Woods system was founded in 1944 and lasted 27 years before the US ended gold convertibility. In what year did it end?
Which economist warned that anchoring the world's money to one nation's currency builds in instability, an idea now known by his name as a 'dilemma'?
According to Modern Monetary Theory, what is the true binding constraint on a government that issues its own sovereign fiat currency?
choices: Solvency: it can run out of money and default
Inflation: real resource limits, not insolvency, bind it
Gold reserves: spending is capped by the metal it holds
Foreign approval: it must match the discipline of a gold standard

cards.title: The Great Depression
cards.fact: The 1930s slump was so deep it rewrote economics — and economists still argue about why.
cards.detail: The 1930s Depression — mass unemployment after the 1929 crash — birthed Keynesianism and the activist state. Its causes (demand collapse, monetary contraction, the gold standard) remain contested.
cards.deploy: Every modern crisis response (2008, 2020) is haunted by 'don't repeat the 1930s'.
cards.counter: There's no settled single cause — demand, money, banking and the gold standard all played a part.

quiz.q: The Great Depression gave rise to which school of macroeconomic thought, named after the economist who argued for an activist state managing demand?
The stock market crash that preceded the slump occurred in 1929. How many years separate that crash from the year 1939?
Why is there no single agreed cause of the Great Depression among economists?
choices: Records from the 1930s were almost entirely destroyed
Demand collapse, monetary contraction, banking failures and the gold standard each plausibly contributed
Economists agree it was caused solely by the 1929 stock crash
It only affected the United States, so global data is missing

cards.title: The 1970s stagflation
cards.fact: In the 1970s, prices and unemployment rose together — which the textbooks said couldn't happen.
cards.detail: 1970s stagflation — high inflation and unemployment together — broke the simple Phillips curve and was widely used to discredit Keynesian demand management and usher in monetarism and the free-market turn.
cards.deploy: The go-to counter to naive Keynesianism — and the origin story of modern central banking.
cards.counter: That 'Keynes failed, markets won' lesson is itself contested. Heavy oil shocks drove much of the inflation, and post-Keynesians in Hyman Minsky's tradition read stagflation as distributional conflict — a wage–price spiral — not proof demand management is futile. The turn to monetarism and deregulation was a political choice as much as a technical verdict; Friedman's own strict money targets were abandoned soon after.

quiz.q: The combination of high inflation and high unemployment occurring at the same time is known by what one-word term?
1970s stagflation was widely taken to break which relationship, normally drawn as a downward-sloping trade-off between inflation and unemployment?
Which reading of 1970s stagflation comes from the post-Keynesian tradition associated with Hyman Minsky?
choices: It proved demand management is always futile
It was caused purely by central banks printing too much money
It reflected a distributional wage-price spiral rather than disproving demand management
It showed unemployment and inflation can never move together

cards.title: The neoliberal turn
cards.fact: Around 1980, the rich world swung from 'manage the market' to 'free the market'.
cards.detail: From ~1980, Thatcher and Reagan drove privatisation, tax cuts, deregulation and weaker unions, drawing on Friedman and Hayek. Credited with taming inflation, blamed for inequality and the 2008 crisis.
