cards.deploy: Names the framework most current economic arguments are still reacting for or against.
cards.counter: It's a loose, contested label: its architects (Friedman, Hayek, Thatcher, Reagan) sold it as freeing growth, while critics like Joseph Stiglitz and Naomi Klein blame it for inequality and financial crises — and results varied enormously by country.

quiz.q: Name one of the two economists most often cited as the intellectual sources of the post-1980 free-market turn led by Thatcher and Reagan.
Which set of policies best characterises the post-1980 shift from 'manage the market' to 'free the market'?
choices: Nationalisation, higher tariffs, and stronger union power
Privatisation, tax cuts, deregulation, and weaker unions
Fixed exchange rates, capital controls, and price ceilings
Universal basic income, wage floors, and central planning

quiz.q: Which economist is named in the card as blaming the neoliberal turn for rising inequality and financial crises?

cards.title: The 2008 financial crisis
cards.fact: In 2008 the financial system nearly stopped — and the faith that markets police themselves took a beating.
cards.detail: A 2008 mortgage bubble froze global finance and triggered the worst slump since the 1930s. The bailout-and-stimulus response revived Keynes and dented 'efficient markets' faith; its causes and the later austerity remain contested.
cards.deploy: The modern reference point for financial regulation, bailouts and 'too big to fail'.
cards.counter: Causes are contested — reckless private finance, or government distortions and easy money, or both.

quiz.q: The 2008 crisis was triggered by the collapse of a bubble in which type of lending?
Which idea about financial markets lost the most credibility as a result of the 2008 crisis?
choices: The belief that markets efficiently price assets and police themselves
The belief that governments should run balanced budgets
The belief that inflation is always a monetary phenomenon
The belief that free trade raises total output

quiz.q: The bailout-and-stimulus response to the 2008 crisis is most associated with reviving the ideas of which economist?

cards.title: A letter is a number you don't know yet
cards.fact: A variable like x is just a placeholder standing in for a number.
cards.detail: A variable is a name for a number. Writing \(2x\) means 'two times x', whatever x turns out to be. An expression like \(3x + 5\) is a recipe: feed in a number for \(x\) and it gives one out — if \(x = 4\), then \(3x + 5 = 17\). The point of a letter is generality: \(A = \pi r^2\) gives the area of every circle in one line, instead of a separate sum for each radius.

media.caption: An expression is a recipe; plug in a value.

cards.deploy: Lets one statement cover every case at once — the move from arithmetic to algebra.
cards.counter: A symbol only helps if you track what it stands for and its units; the same letter meaning two different things inside one argument is a classic error.

quiz.q: If x = 4, what is 3x + 5?
Using the rule 3x + 5, what value comes out when you feed in x = 10?
The area of a circle is A = pi times r squared. For a circle of radius r = 3, what is its area? Use pi = 3.14.
In the expression 7y, what single operation is implied between the 7 and the y?

cards.title: An equation is a balance scale
cards.fact: Whatever you do to one side of an equation, do to the other — and it stays true.
cards.detail: An equation says two things are equal. \(x + 3 = 7\) reads 'some number plus 3 equals 7'. Think of \(=\) as the pivot of a balance: the two sides weigh the same. To find \(x\), undo what surrounds it by doing the same thing to both sides. Subtract 3 from each: \(x + 3 - 3 = 7 - 3\), so \(x = 4\). The scale never tips because you changed both sides equally. That single habit — do the same to both sides — solves most of school algebra.

media.caption: Subtract 3 from both sides to isolate x.

cards.deploy: Turns 'solving for x' into a mechanical routine: isolate the unknown by undoing operations symmetrically.
cards.counter: Balance holds only for reversible operations applied equally. Multiplying both sides by zero, or by an unknown that might be zero, can erase real solutions or invent fake ones.

quiz.q: To solve x + 3 = 7, you…
Keeping both sides equal, solve for x in x - 5 = 12. What is x?
Which operation applied to both sides of an equation can destroy a real solution or invent a fake one, breaking the balance-scale guarantee?
choices: Multiplying both sides by an expression that could equal zero
Adding the same constant to both sides
Subtracting the same constant from both sides

quiz.q: To isolate x in 4x = 20 you divide both sides by the same number to keep them balanced. What value of x results?

cards.title: A function is a machine
cards.fact: Put a number in, get exactly one number out — that's a function.
cards.detail: Write \(f(x)\) — read 'f of x' — for the output when the input is \(x\). The rule \(f(x) = 2x + 1\) doubles the input and adds one, so \(f(3) = 7\). 'Exactly one output' is the whole idea: a function never returns two answers for the same input. Lay the input along the bottom and the output up the side and you get a graph — a picture of the rule. Functions are the things calculus and machine learning act on.

media.caption: f(x) = 2x + 1 — one output for every input.

cards.deploy: Names the basic object of all higher maths: a dependable input→output rule you can graph, combine and analyse.
cards.counter: A relation that gives two outputs for one input (like 'a number's square roots', ±) is not a function — distinguishing the two avoids real mistakes.

quiz.q: For f(x) = 2x + 1, what is f(3)?
For the rule g(x) = 3x - 2, what is g(5)?
A rule pairs an input with two different outputs (for example, mapping 9 to both +3 and -3). Why is this not a function?
choices: A function must give exactly one output for each input
A function cannot use negative numbers
A function must always increase as the input grows
A function can only take whole numbers as inputs

quiz.q: When you plot a function with inputs along the horizontal axis and outputs up the vertical axis, what is the resulting picture of the rule called?

cards.title: Powers and roots
cards.fact: A power is repeated multiplication; a root undoes it.
cards.detail: \(a^n\) means multiply \(a\) by itself \(n\) times: \(2^3 = 2\times2\times2 = 8\), and \(2^{10} = 1024\). The square root undoes squaring: \(\sqrt{9} = 3\) because \(3^2 = 9\). Powers of the same base add when you multiply: \(a^m \cdot a^n = a^{m+n}\). This is what lets us write the huge and the tiny compactly — scientific notation: \(6.02\times10^{23}\) particles, or \(10^{-9}\) for a billionth.

media.say: a-to-the-m times a-to-the-n equals a-to-the-(m plus n).
media.caption: Multiplying powers adds the exponents.
2ˣ explodes — each step doubles the last.

cards.deploy: Compresses repeated multiplication and gives a clean way to handle very large or very small numbers.
cards.counter: Sign and fraction rules trip people up: \(a^0 = 1\), a negative exponent means a reciprocal (\(a^{-1} = 1/a\)), and a fractional one means a root (\(a^{1/2} = \sqrt a\)).

quiz.q: What is 2¹⁰?
Using the rule that powers of the same base add when multiplied, what is 3^2 times 3^3? Give the final value.
A negative exponent means a reciprocal. What is the value of 5^-1 as a decimal?
Which statement correctly applies the exponent rules?

cards.title: Logarithms: the inverse of powers
cards.fact: A logarithm answers one question: what power produces this number?
cards.detail: \(\log_{10} 1000 = 3\) because \(10^3 = 1000\). The log is the exponent. Its key trick is turning multiplication into addition: \(\log(ab) = \log a + \log b\). A log scale (decibels, the Richter scale, pH) spaces powers of ten evenly, so 10 and 1000 sit the same distance apart, which tames quantities that span many orders of magnitude. In machine learning logs are everywhere — they turn long products of probabilities into manageable sums.

media.say: log-base-b of x-times-y equals log of x plus log of y.
media.caption: Logs convert products into sums.
The logarithm: quick to rise, then a slow crawl.

cards.deploy: Lets you read quantities that span orders of magnitude, and replace awkward products with sums.
cards.counter: Logs are only defined for positive numbers, and the base matters: base 10, base 2 and the natural base \(e\) differ by a constant factor, so always say which you mean.

quiz.q: What is log₁₀(1000)?
Since a logarithm asks 'what power produces this number?', what is log base 2 of 32?
Using log(ab) = log(a) + log(b): if log(a) = 0.7 and log(b) = 1.3, what is log(a times b)?
Why must you always state the base when working with logarithms?
choices: Base 10, base 2, and the natural base e give values that differ by a constant factor
Logs of the same number are identical in every base
A larger base always gives a larger logarithm

cards.title: The straight line: y = mx + b
cards.fact: Every straight line is y = mx + b: m is the slope, b is where it crosses the axis.
cards.detail: The slope \(m\) is rise over run — how much \(y\) climbs for each step right. The intercept \(b\) is the value of \(y\) when \(x = 0\), where the line meets the vertical axis. So \(y = 2x + 1\) starts at 1 and climbs 2 for every 1 across. A bigger \(m\) tilts the line steeper; a negative \(m\) sends it downhill. This is the simplest model in all of statistics and machine learning — a prediction that changes at a constant rate.

media.caption: Drag m and b: the line tilts and shifts.

cards.deploy: The default first model whenever one quantity changes steadily with another.
cards.counter: Most real relationships aren't straight; a line is a deliberately simple approximation, useful precisely because it has just two numbers to find.

quiz.q: In y = mx + b, what does b represent?
choices: Where the line crosses the y-axis

quiz.q: For the line y = -3x + 7, what is the value of y when x = 4?
If the slope m of a line is negative, in which direction does the line head as you read it from left to right?

cards.title: Curves and the quadratic
cards.fact: Add an x² term and the straight line bends into a parabola.
cards.detail: \(y = ax^2 + bx + c\) traces a parabola — a U-shaped curve. The coefficient \(a\) sets how narrow it is and which way it opens (up if \(a>0\), down if \(a<0\)); \(c\) shifts it vertically. To find where it crosses zero, the quadratic formula gives the answer for any quadratic: \(x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\). Parabolas describe thrown objects, and the U-shape is exactly the kind of curve machine learning slides down to find its best fit.

media.caption: y = ax² + bx + c — change a, b, c to reshape the parabola.

cards.deploy: The first step beyond straight lines, and the shape of the cost surfaces optimisers descend.
cards.counter: The quadratic formula's discriminant \(b^2 - 4ac\) can be negative — then the curve never crosses zero and the (real) solutions don't exist.

quiz.q: The graph of y = ax² + bx + c is a…
Using the quadratic formula, find the larger root of x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0.
For the parabola y = ax^2 + bx + c with a = -2, which statement is true?
Compute the discriminant b^2 - 4ac for the quadratic 2x^2 + 3x + 5.

cards.title: Sigma notation: add up a list
cards.fact: The symbol Σ is shorthand for 'add up all of these'.
cards.detail: \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i\) means add \(x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n\). The \(i\) is a counter that runs from the bottom number to the top one. For example \(\sum_{i=1}^{4} i = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10\). The average of \(n\) numbers is just \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i\). This one symbol runs through all of statistics and machine learning: every total error, mean, and dot product is a sum written this way.

media.say: the sum of x-one, x-two, and so on up to x-n.
media.caption: Sigma says: run the counter and add.
Σ adds the bars: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.

cards.deploy: Compresses 'add up many terms' into one symbol you'll meet in every quantitative field.
cards.counter: The limits and the index matter: \(\sum_{i=0}\) versus \(\sum_{i=1}\), or summing the wrong variable, silently changes the result.

quiz.q: What does Σ (from i=1 to 4) of i equal?
Evaluate the sum from i=1 to 5 of i (that is, 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5).
The numbers 4, 8, 6, 2 are added with sigma notation and then averaged using (1/n) times their sum. What is the average?
In the expression sum from i=1 to n of x_i, what is the role of the letter i?

cards.title: The limit: getting infinitely close
cards.fact: A limit is the value a function heads toward as the input creeps up to a point.
cards.detail: Sometimes a function misbehaves exactly at one point but behaves perfectly all around it. \(\frac{\sin x}{x}\) reads as \(0/0\) at \(x = 0\), yet as \(x\) shrinks toward zero the ratio heads steadily to 1. The limit, written \(\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\sin x}{x} = 1\), captures that destination without ever dividing by zero. Making 'infinitely close' precise is the foundation the rest of calculus stands on.

media.caption: Undefined at 0, yet it heads to 1.
sin(x)/x has a hole at 0, yet heads to 1.

cards.deploy: Lets you reason about behaviour at a point a function can't actually reach — the gateway to derivatives and integrals.
cards.counter: A limit can fail to exist: if a function jumps, or approaches different values from the left and the right, there is no single destination.

quiz.q: A limit describes the value a function…
choices: Heads toward as the input approaches a point

quiz.q: A function jumps to a different value when approached from the left than from the right at a point. What can be said about the limit there?
choices: The limit equals the average of the two sides
The limit always equals the function's value at that point

quiz.q: What is the limit of (sin x)/x as x approaches 0?
Why is a limit useful for evaluating (sin x)/x at x = 0?
choices: It finds the value the ratio heads toward without ever dividing by zero
It changes the function into a straight line
It forces the function to equal its slope
It removes the sine term entirely

cards.title: The derivative: the slope of a curve
cards.fact: The derivative is how fast something is changing right now — the slope of a curve at a point.
cards.detail: A straight line has one slope everywhere. A curve's steepness keeps changing. The derivative \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) (also written \(f'(x)\)) is the slope of the tangent line that just grazes the curve at a single point. You find it by taking the slope between two nearby points and letting them slide together — a limit. For \(f(x) = x^2\), the derivative is \(f'(x) = 2x\): at \(x = 3\) the curve climbs with slope 6. Speed is the derivative of distance; acceleration is the derivative of speed.

media.say: f-prime of x equals the limit, as h shrinks to zero, of the change in f divided by h.
media.caption: The slope between two points, as they merge.
Slide the point — the tangent's slope is the derivative.

cards.deploy: The universal tool for rates of change: speed, growth, marginal cost, and the direction to adjust a model.
cards.counter: A derivative needs a smooth curve. At a sharp corner or a jump the slope isn't defined — the function is not differentiable there.

quiz.q: The derivative of a function at a point is the…
For f(x) = x^2, the derivative is f'(x) = 2x. What is the slope of the curve at x = 7?
A car's position over time is given by a distance function. Which quantity equals the derivative of that distance function?
At a sharp corner in a graph, the slope cannot be pinned to a single value. What one-word property does the function lack at that point?

cards.title: The integral: area under a curve
cards.fact: The integral adds up infinitely many thin slivers to measure the area under a curve.
cards.detail: To find the area under a graph, slice the region into thin rectangles, add their areas, then let the slices grow infinitely thin so the answer becomes exact. That limit is the integral, \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\). The fundamental theorem of calculus ties it to the derivative: integration and differentiation undo each other. Distance is the integral of speed over time; in probability, the chance of landing in a range is the area under a curve.

media.caption: The shaded area is the integral ∫ f(x) dx.

cards.deploy: Turns a rate into a total: accumulate speed into distance, a density into a probability, a flow into a quantity.
cards.counter: Many functions have no tidy antiderivative formula — real integrals are often computed numerically rather than solved on paper.

quiz.q: An integral computes the…
A theorem states that integration and differentiation undo each other. What is this theorem called?
An object moves at a constant speed of 5 m/s. Using the fact that distance is the integral of speed over time, how many metres does it travel between t = 2 s and t = 10 s?
In probability, the chance that a continuous outcome lands within a given range equals the integral of which kind of function over that range?

cards.title: The chain rule: rates that pass through layers
cards.fact: To differentiate a function inside a function, multiply the two rates of change.
cards.detail: If \(y\) depends on \(u\), and \(u\) depends on \(x\), then a small nudge in \(x\) ripples through both: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}\). Take \(y = (3x+1)^2\): the outer squaring contributes \(2(3x+1)\), the inner \(3x+1\) contributes \(3\), and the product is \(6(3x+1)\). The chain rule is how rates compose through nested steps — and it is exactly the mechanism that trains deep neural networks, where the error is passed back layer by layer (backpropagation).

media.say: the rate of f-of-g equals f's rate (at g) times g's rate.
media.caption: Outer rate times inner rate.
A chain x → u → y; the rates multiply along it.

cards.deploy: Differentiates any composition — and underpins backpropagation, the engine of modern AI training.
cards.counter: It's easy to forget the inner derivative \(g'(x)\); leaving it out is one of the most common calculus mistakes.

quiz.q: The chain rule differentiates f(g(x)) as…
Using the chain rule, differentiate y = (2x + 5)^2 and evaluate the derivative at x = 4. (Hint: dy/dx = 2(2x+5) times 2.)
The chain rule passing error backward layer by layer is the mechanism that trains deep neural networks. What is this training algorithm called?
When differentiating a composite function f(g(x)), what is the single most common mistake people make?
choices: Forgetting to multiply by the inner derivative g'(x)
Adding the two derivatives instead of multiplying
Using the quotient rule by mistake

cards.title: The gradient: which way is uphill
cards.fact: The gradient bundles a function's slopes in every direction into one arrow pointing straight uphill.
cards.detail: When a function has several inputs, say \(f(x, y)\), it has a separate slope in the x-direction and in the y-direction — its partial derivatives. The gradient \(\nabla f\) collects them into a vector: \(\nabla f = \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right)\). That vector points in the direction of steepest increase, and its length tells you how steep. Walk in the opposite direction and you go downhill fastest — the single idea behind training almost every machine-learning model.

media.say: grad-f is the pair of slopes: how f changes along x, and along y.
media.caption: A vector of partial slopes, pointing uphill.
On the bowl f = x² + y², ∇f points outward — straight uphill.

cards.deploy: Gives the direction to step when tuning many numbers at once — the basis of gradient descent.
cards.counter: The gradient only shows the best local direction; on a bumpy surface, following it can stall in a dip that isn't the lowest point overall.

quiz.q: The gradient of a function points in the direction of…
For f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2, the gradient is (2x, 2y). At the point (3, 4), what is the length (magnitude) of the gradient vector?
Optimisation methods step in the direction opposite to the gradient to reduce a function as fast as possible. What is this method called?
Following the gradient downhill can get stuck in a dip that is not the overall lowest point. What is the name for such a non-global low point?

cards.title: A vector is an arrow and a list
cards.fact: A vector is at once an arrow with direction and length, and a list of numbers.
cards.detail: In the plane, a vector points from the origin to a spot: \(\vec v = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\) means 'go 3 right and 2 up'. The arrow picture (direction and length) and the column of numbers are the same object — and holding both views at once is what makes linear algebra work. A data point with many features (age, height, income…) is simply a vector with many entries: a single point in a high-dimensional space.

media.caption: The vector [3, 2] as an arrow from the origin.

cards.deploy: The basic unit of data and geometry alike: one object you can picture as an arrow or compute with as numbers.
cards.counter: The arrow picture is honest only up to three dimensions; beyond that you must trust the numbers, since a 300-feature vector has no drawable shape.

quiz.q: The vector [3, 2] describes…
A dataset records each customer with 5 features: age, height, weight, income, and number of orders. As a vector, how many entries does one customer's data point have?
Why can the arrow picture of a vector not be drawn for a 300-feature data point?
choices: Arrows can only be pictured in up to 3 dimensions; a 300-dimensional space has no drawable shape
Vectors with more than 3 entries are no longer valid vectors
The numbers become too large to fit on a page
Only vectors with whole-number entries can be drawn as arrows

quiz.q: A vector starting at the origin and going 4 units left and 7 units down is written as a column. List its two entries, top entry first, then bottom entry.

cards.title: Adding and scaling vectors
cards.fact: Add vectors tip-to-tail; scale one by stretching or flipping it.
cards.detail: To add \(\vec a + \vec b\), set \(\vec b\)'s tail at \(\vec a\)'s tip; the sum runs from the very start to the very end. In numbers you just add matching entries: \(\begin{bmatrix}3\\1\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}4\\3\end{bmatrix}\). Multiplying by a plain number (a scalar) stretches or flips: \(2\vec a\) is twice as long, \(-\vec a\) points the other way. Any weighted mix \(c_1\vec a + c_2\vec b\) — a 'linear combination' — is the core move of the whole subject.

media.caption: a + b, tip-to-tail.

cards.deploy: The two operations every later idea is built from: combine vectors and rescale them.
cards.counter: You can only add vectors of the same length (same number of entries); a 2-D and a 3-D vector have no defined sum.

quiz.q: Compute the second (bottom) entry of the vector 3*[2, 1] + [-1, 4].
Which pair of vectors CANNOT be added together?
What is the name for a weighted mix of the form c1*a + c2*b, where c1 and c2 are scalars?

cards.title: The dot product: how aligned are two vectors
cards.fact: The dot product is one number saying how much two vectors point the same way.
cards.detail: Multiply matching entries and add them up: \(\vec a \cdot \vec b = \sum_i a_i b_i\). The same number also equals \(|\vec a|\,|\vec b|\cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between the vectors and the cosine runs from 1 (pointing the same way), through 0 (a right angle), to −1 (opposite). So the dot product is large when they align, zero when they're perpendicular, and negative when they oppose. It is the standard measure of similarity: search engines and language models compare meanings by taking dot products of vectors.

media.tex: \vec a \cdot \vec b = \sum_i a_i b_i = |\vec a|\,|\vec b|\cos\theta
media.say: a dot b: multiply matching entries and add — also the lengths times the cosine of the angle between them.
media.caption: Two views: entry-by-entry, and angle-based.
Swing θ: the dot product peaks when aligned, hits 0 at 90°.

cards.deploy: The workhorse of similarity and projection — and the operation inside every matrix multiply and attention score.
cards.counter: A dot product near zero means the vectors are merely perpendicular, not that either is small; alignment and magnitude are different things.

quiz.q: The dot product of two perpendicular vectors is…
Compute the dot product of [2, -1, 3] and [4, 5, 1].
Two vectors each have length 5, and the angle between them is 60 degrees (cos 60 = 0.5). What is their dot product?
A dot product between two vectors comes out negative. What does this tell you?
choices: The angle between them is greater than 90 degrees, so they partly oppose each other
At least one of the two vectors has zero length
The two vectors are exactly perpendicular
The two vectors point in exactly the same direction

cards.title: Length and distance
cards.fact: A vector's norm is its length — and the gap between two points is the norm of their difference.
cards.detail: The norm \(\|\vec v\| = \sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2 + \cdots}\) is the Pythagorean theorem in any number of dimensions. The distance between two points is the norm of their difference, \(\|\vec a - \vec b\|\). 'Nearest neighbour' methods, clustering, and the size of an error all rest on this. Neatly, \(\|\vec v\|^2 = \vec v \cdot \vec v\): a vector's squared length is its dot product with itself.

media.say: the length of v is the square root of the sum of its squared entries.
media.caption: Pythagoras, in any number of dimensions.
‖[4, 3]‖ = √(16 + 9) = 5 — the hypotenuse.

cards.deploy: Defines size and closeness for data — the basis of distance, error magnitude and similarity searches.
cards.counter: The straight-line (Euclidean) norm is only one choice; others, like summing absolute values (the 'taxicab' norm), measure distance differently and suit different problems.

quiz.q: The norm of a vector measures its…
What is the Euclidean norm (length) of the vector [6, 8]?
What is the Euclidean distance between the points [1, 2] and [4, 6]?
What name is given to the alternative norm that measures distance by summing the absolute values of a vector's entries rather than taking a straight line?

cards.title: A matrix is a grid of numbers
cards.fact: A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers — a table, or a row of vectors side by side.
cards.detail: A matrix has rows and columns: \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\) is 2 by 2. You can read it as a spreadsheet — each row a record, each column a feature — or as several column vectors standing together. Its real power, though, is as an action: a matrix is a rule that takes a vector in and gives a transformed vector out, which is the next step.

media.caption: A 2×2 matrix: rows and columns.

cards.deploy: The container for data tables and for transformations alike — the central object of linear algebra.
cards.counter: Shape is everything: a 2×3 and a 3×2 matrix hold the same six numbers but behave completely differently, and most operations demand matching shapes.

quiz.q: A matrix is best described as…
choices: A grid of numbers in rows and columns

quiz.q: A matrix has 4 rows and 7 columns. How many individual numbers does it contain in total?
You store a dataset as a matrix where each row is one customer and each column is one measured attribute (age, income, etc.). What do the columns represent?
Two matrices hold the same six numbers, one arranged as 2x3 and one as 3x2. What single property distinguishes them and governs how they behave?

cards.title: A matrix transforms space
cards.fact: Multiplying a matrix by a vector moves the whole grid — it rotates, stretches and shears space.
cards.detail: \(A\vec x\) builds a new vector by combining \(A\)'s columns, each weighted by an entry of \(\vec x\). Picture it geometrically: the matrix moves every point of the plane at once, so the square grid tilts and stretches — yet straight lines stay straight and the origin stays fixed. That is a 'linear transformation'. The columns of \(A\) are nothing more than where the two basis arrows land after the move.

media.caption: Move the matrix [[a, b], [c, d]] — watch the grid transform.

cards.deploy: Reframes a matrix as a verb, not a table: it does something to space. This view unlocks the rest of the subject.
cards.counter: Only transformations that keep grid lines straight and evenly spaced, fixing the origin, are 'linear' — bends, curves and shifts of the origin are not matrix multiplication.

quiz.q: Multiplying a vector by a matrix geometrically…
A 2x2 matrix is applied to every point of the plane. Which of these effects means the operation is NOT a linear transformation?
choices: Every point is shifted 3 units to the right before stretching
The grid is stretched twice as wide horizontally
The grid is rotated 45 degrees about the origin
The grid is sheared so vertical lines tilt

quiz.q: The columns of a 2x2 matrix A say where the basis vectors land. If A sends [1,0] to [3,0] and [0,1] to [0,5], what is the x-coordinate of A times the vector [2,4]?
Under a matrix transformation, which single point of the plane always stays fixed?

cards.title: Matrix multiplication = doing one transform after another
cards.fact: Multiplying matrices means applying one transformation, then the next.
cards.detail: The product \(AB\) is the single transformation 'do \(B\) first, then \(A\)': \((AB)\vec x = A(B\vec x)\). Each entry of the product is a dot product of a row of \(A\) with a column of \(B\). Order matters — \(AB \neq BA\) in general, just as rotating then stretching differs from stretching then rotating. Chaining matrices this way is exactly how a neural network stacks its layers.

media.caption: The product is composition: B first, then A.

cards.deploy: Lets you collapse a whole pipeline of transformations into one matrix — and explains layered models.
cards.counter: Matrix multiplication is not commutative: swapping the order usually changes the result, and often isn't even allowed if the shapes stop matching.

quiz.q: In general, for matrices, AB is…
The product AB acts on a vector x. Which order of operations does (AB)x perform?
choices: Apply A and B simultaneously and add the results
Apply whichever has more columns first

quiz.q: A is the 2x2 diagonal matrix [[2,0],[0,1]] and B is [[1,0],[0,3]]. Their product AB is also diagonal. What is the bottom-right entry of AB?
What one-word property does matrix multiplication LACK, meaning AB and BA are generally different?

cards.title: Identity and inverse: undoing a transformation
cards.fact: The identity matrix changes nothing; the inverse runs a transformation backwards.
cards.detail: The identity matrix \(I\) has 1s down the diagonal and 0s elsewhere, so \(I\vec x = \vec x\) — the linear-algebra version of multiplying by 1. The inverse \(A^{-1}\) reverses whatever \(A\) did: \(A A^{-1} = I\). Not every matrix has one. If a transformation squashes space flat — collapsing a dimension — there is no way back, and no inverse exists. That collapse is detected by the determinant being zero.

media.say: A times A-inverse gives the identity — the do-nothing matrix.
media.caption: The inverse cancels the transformation.

cards.deploy: The formal 'undo' button — and the route to solving equations and reversing models.
cards.counter: Inverting a matrix that is nearly singular (almost flattening) is numerically unstable; in practice solvers avoid forming \(A^{-1}\) directly.

quiz.q: A matrix times its inverse gives the…
The 4x4 identity matrix has 1s on its diagonal and 0s elsewhere. How many of its 16 entries are equal to zero?
A 2x2 transformation squashes the entire plane onto a single line, collapsing one dimension. What does this tell you?
choices: It has no inverse and its determinant is zero
It rotates space without changing area

quiz.q: What single quantity, when equal to zero, signals that a square matrix collapses a dimension and therefore has no inverse?

cards.title: Solving many equations at once: Ax = b
cards.fact: A pile of linear equations packs into one tidy matrix equation, Ax = b.
cards.detail: Two equations like \(2x + y = 5\) and \(x - y = 1\) fold into \(A\vec x = \vec b\), with \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\vec b = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Solving asks: which input \(\vec x\) does \(A\) send to \(\vec b\)? If \(A\) is invertible, \(\vec x = A^{-1}\vec b\); otherwise there may be no solution, or infinitely many. Fitting a model, balancing a chemical equation and rendering 3-D graphics all reduce to solving \(A\vec x = \vec b\).

media.tex: A\vec x = \vec b \;\Rightarrow\; \vec x = A^{-1}\vec b
media.say: A times x equals b, so x equals A-inverse times b.
media.caption: When A is invertible, the system has one solution.
Two equations, two lines — they cross at the solution (2, 1).

cards.deploy: The standard form that an enormous range of practical problems gets rewritten into and solved.
cards.counter: Real systems are often 'overdetermined' — more equations than unknowns, no exact solution — so we settle for the closest fit instead (least squares).

quiz.q: In Ax = b, if A is invertible the solution is…
Solve the system 3x + y = 11 and x - y = 1 by writing it as Ax = b. What is the value of x?
A factory has 5 unknown quantities but its constraints produce 9 linear equations with no single point satisfying all of them. What approach handles this overdetermined situation?
choices: Find the closest fit by least squares
Compute the determinant to read off the answer
Discard equations until the system is square, then invert

quiz.q: In the matrix equation Ax = b, what property of the square matrix A guarantees a unique solution exists for every b?

cards.title: The determinant: how much area gets scaled
cards.fact: The determinant says how much a transformation scales area — and zero means it flattens space.
cards.detail: For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}\), the determinant is \(\det A = ad - bc\). It is the factor by which areas grow or shrink under the transformation: \(\det = 2\) doubles every area, \(\det = 1\) preserves it, and a negative determinant flips orientation (like a mirror). When \(\det A = 0\) the grid has been squashed onto a line — a dimension is lost, information is destroyed, and the matrix has no inverse.

media.caption: The shaded unit square's area equals |det A|.

cards.deploy: A one-number test for whether a transformation is reversible, and by how much it expands or shrinks.
cards.counter: A large determinant doesn't mean a matrix is 'well-behaved' for computation; a separate measure (the condition number) governs numerical reliability.

quiz.q: If det A = 0, the transformation…
For the 2x2 matrix with first row [4, 3] and second row [2, 5], compute the determinant ad - bc.
A 2x2 transformation has determinant -3. What does this tell you about its effect on the plane?
choices: It triples areas and flips orientation
It shrinks areas to one third and flips orientation
It triples areas while preserving orientation
It collapses the plane onto a line

quiz.q: A large determinant does NOT guarantee a matrix is numerically reliable to work with. What separate quantity actually governs that numerical reliability?

cards.title: Eigenvectors: the directions that don't turn
cards.fact: An eigenvector is a direction a transformation only stretches — it never rotates it.
cards.detail: Under a matrix \(A\), most vectors swing off to a new direction. A special few hold their direction and are merely scaled: \(A\vec v = \lambda\vec v\). Such a \(\vec v\) is an eigenvector, and the stretch factor \(\lambda\) is its eigenvalue. These reveal a transformation's natural axes — the skeleton it acts along. Google's original PageRank found an eigenvector of the web's link matrix; principal component analysis finds the eigenvectors of data to compress it.

media.say: A times v equals lambda times v — the matrix only stretches v by the factor lambda.
media.caption: Same direction, scaled by λ.
Look for an arrow that stays on its own line — that's an eigenvector.

cards.deploy: Finds the hidden axes of a transformation or dataset — behind PCA, PageRank, and stability analysis.
cards.counter: Not every real matrix has real eigenvectors — a pure rotation turns every direction, so its eigenvalues are complex numbers, with no real axis it leaves alone.

quiz.q: For an eigenvector v of A, Av equals…
A vector v is an eigenvector of matrix A with eigenvalue 4. If Av is then scaled by 1/2, by what total factor has v been stretched compared to its original length?
Why does a matrix that rotates every vector in the plane by 90 degrees have no real eigenvectors?
choices: Every direction is turned, so no real direction is merely scaled
Its determinant is zero, destroying all directions
It scales every vector by zero
Rotations have infinitely many real eigenvectors, not none

quiz.q: Which data-compression technique works by finding the eigenvectors of a dataset to identify its dominant axes of variation?

cards.title: Probability: a number from 0 to 1
cards.fact: A probability scores how likely something is, from 0 (never) to 1 (certain).
cards.detail: List everything that could happen — the 'sample space'. If each outcome is equally likely, the probability of an event is just the share that counts as a success: \(P(A) = \frac{\text{favourable outcomes}}{\text{all outcomes}}\). A fair die has six faces, so \(P(\text{roll a 4}) = \tfrac{1}{6}\). 0 means impossible, 1 means certain, and 0.5 is an even chance. Everything else in probability builds on this.

media.caption: A fair die: six equally likely outcomes, each 1/6.

cards.deploy: Turns vague talk of 'likely' and 'rare' into a number you can compare and combine.
cards.counter: The 'equally likely' shortcut only works for symmetric setups like dice; for real events (rain tomorrow) probability means a long-run frequency or a degree of belief — a split between the frequentist and Bayesian schools.

quiz.q: A probability of 1 means an event is…
A fair eight-sided die has faces numbered 1 through 8. What is the probability of rolling a number greater than 5? Give the answer as a decimal.
The formula favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes assumes each outcome is equally likely. For which situation is this assumption valid?
choices: Drawing one card at random from a well-shuffled standard deck
Whether it rains in a particular city tomorrow
Whether a startup succeeds within five years
Which team wins an unevenly matched football game

quiz.q: Interpreting the probability of rain tomorrow as a personal degree of belief rather than a long-run frequency reflects which school of probability?

cards.title: Adding and multiplying probabilities
cards.fact: Use OR to add chances, AND to multiply them.
cards.detail: For the chance of A or B, add — then subtract the overlap so it isn't counted twice: \(P(A\text{ or }B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A\text{ and }B)\). For A and B both happening, multiply — and if they're independent (one doesn't affect the other), it's simply \(P(A\text{ and }B) = P(A)\,P(B)\). Two fair coins both landing heads: \(\tfrac12 \times \tfrac12 = \tfrac14\).

media.say: the chance of both, when neither affects the other, is the two chances multiplied.
media.caption: Independent events: multiply.
Two fair coins: each combination is ½ × ½ = ¼.

cards.deploy: Lets you build the odds of complex events from simple ones.
cards.counter: The multiply rule fails when events are linked: P(rain) and P(I carry an umbrella) aren't independent, so multiplying understates the truth.

quiz.q: For two independent events, P(A and B) equals…
A spinner has a 0.3 chance of landing red and a 0.5 chance of landing on an even number; the chance of landing on a red even number is 0.2. What is the chance it lands red OR on an even number?
You roll a fair six-sided die three times. What is the probability of getting a 6 on all three rolls? Give the answer as a decimal.
Why must you subtract P(A and B) when computing P(A or B) by adding P(A) and P(B)?
choices: Outcomes where both occur are otherwise counted twice
The two probabilities are always negatively correlated
Subtracting it makes the events independent
It corrects for the events being mutually exclusive

cards.title: Conditional probability: given that…
cards.fact: The probability of A changes once you know B has happened.
cards.detail: Written \(P(A \mid B)\) — 'the probability of A given B' — it narrows the world to the cases where B is true: \(P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A\text{ and }B)}{P(B)}\). Knowing it rained (B) changes the chance the ground is wet (A). When \(P(A \mid B) = P(A)\), knowing B told you nothing — that's exactly what independence means.

media.plain: P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B)
media.say: the chance of A given B is the chance of both, divided by the chance of B.
media.caption: Restrict the world to the cases where B happened.
Knowing it rained lifts the chance the ground is wet.

cards.deploy: The formal way to update a probability when new information arrives.
cards.counter: People routinely confuse P(A|B) with P(B|A) — the 'prosecutor's fallacy'; the chance of a match given innocence is not the chance of innocence given a match.

quiz.q: P(A | B) is read as…
In a deck, P(card is a face card) = 12/52 and P(card is a face card AND a spade) = 3/52. Given a card is a face card, what is the probability it is a spade? Give the answer as a decimal.

A medical expert states that the probability a positive test result occurs given the patient is sick is high, then concludes the patient is almost certainly sick after a positive test. What error is this?
choices: Confusing P(positive | sick) with P(sick | positive)
Failing to subtract the overlap of the two events
Using a prior instead of a posterior

quiz.q: If learning that B has happened leaves the probability of A completely unchanged, so that P(A | B) = P(A), what relationship do A and B have?

cards.title: Bayes' theorem: updating beliefs with evidence
cards.fact: Bayes' rule flips a conditional probability — turning a test result into an updated belief.
cards.detail: It connects \(P(H \mid E)\) (a hypothesis given the evidence) to \(P(E \mid H)\) (the evidence given the hypothesis): \(P(H \mid E) = \frac{P(E \mid H)\,P(H)}{P(E)}\). The starting belief \(P(H)\) is the 'prior'; the answer \(P(H \mid E)\) is the 'posterior'. Its sting is the base rate: a 99%-accurate test for a disease that 1 in 1000 people have still gives mostly false alarms, because healthy people vastly outnumber sick ones.

media.say: the updated belief is the evidence's likelihood times the prior, divided by how likely the evidence was overall.
media.caption: Prior belief × evidence → updated (posterior) belief.
A rare disease (1%): even a positive test leaves you far from certain.

cards.deploy: The engine of rational updating — and of spam filters, medical screening and Bayesian machine learning.
cards.counter: Bayesians treat the prior as a real degree of belief to be updated; frequentists object that priors are subjective. The maths is agreed; what a probability *means* is not.

quiz.q: In Bayes' theorem, the starting belief P(H) before seeing evidence is the…

A disease affects 1 in 200 people. A test gives a positive result for 100% of sick people and for 4% of healthy people. If someone tests positive, what is the probability they actually have the disease? Give the answer as a decimal rounded to two places.
In Bayes' theorem, the updated belief P(H | E) obtained after incorporating the evidence is called the what?
A 99%-accurate test for a rare disease produces mostly false alarms among positives. What is the main reason?
choices: The low base rate means healthy people far outnumber sick ones
The test's accuracy is actually below 50% in practice
P(E | H) is smaller than P(H | E)
The prior and posterior must always be equal

cards.title: Random variables: numbers from chance
cards.fact: A random variable attaches a number to each uncertain outcome.
cards.detail: Call it \(X\). For one die roll, \(X\) is the face shown; for a coin, you might set heads \(= 1\), tails \(= 0\). A discrete random variable takes separate values (0, 1, 2…); a continuous one can be any value in a range (a height, a wait time). Its 'distribution' lists how much probability sits on each value — the bridge from single outcomes to averages and spread.
cards.deploy: Lets you do arithmetic — averages, sums, spreads — on the outcomes of chance.
cards.counter: The number you assign is a modelling choice: coding categories as 1, 2, 3 can smuggle in a false sense that the gaps between them are equal.

quiz.q: A random variable that can take any value in a range is…
Which of these is best modelled as a continuous random variable?
choices: The exact time in seconds until a bus arrives
The number of emails received in an hour
The result of a single die roll
The count of heads in ten coin flips

quiz.q: What is the name for the description of how much probability sits on each value a random variable can take?
A survey codes the categories 'bus', 'train' and 'bike' as 1, 2 and 3. What hidden assumption does treating these numbers as a random variable risk smuggling in?
choices: That the gaps between the categories are equal and meaningful
That the categories are mutually exclusive
That the variable must be continuous
That each category has the same probability

cards.title: Expected value: the long-run average
cards.fact: The expected value is the average you'd get from many repeats — each outcome weighted by its probability.
cards.detail: Multiply each value by its probability and add: \(E[X] = \sum_i x_i\,p_i\). A fair die's expected roll is \(\tfrac16(1+2+\dots+6) = 3.5\) — a value you can never actually roll, but the long-run average. It's the foundation of fair prices, insurance and betting: a bet is 'fair' when its expected gain is zero.

media.say: the expected value is each outcome times its probability, all added up.
media.caption: Each outcome, weighted by how likely it is.

cards.deploy: The single best summary of a random quantity — and the thing rational decisions try to maximise.
cards.counter: Expected value ignores risk: a 1-in-a-million shot at a billion has a high expectation, but few would stake their house on it. That gap is why utility, not raw money, often guides choices.

quiz.q: The expected value of a fair six-sided die is…
A game pays 10 dollars with probability 0.2, pays 3 dollars with probability 0.5, and pays 0 with probability 0.3. What is the expected payout in dollars?
A bet costs 4 dollars to enter and pays out an amount whose expected value is exactly 4 dollars. In the language of expected value, this bet is best described as:
choices: A bet you should always avoid
Guaranteed to break even on any single play
A bet with positive expected profit

quiz.q: A risky venture has a high expected monetary value yet almost everyone refuses it because it could ruin them. What concept, used instead of raw money, explains why people decline such bets?

cards.title: Variance and standard deviation: the spread
cards.fact: Variance measures how far outcomes typically stray from the average.
cards.detail: Take each value's distance from the mean \(\mu\), square it (so positives and negatives don't cancel), and average: \(\sigma^2 = E[(X-\mu)^2]\). The standard deviation \(\sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}\) brings it back to the original units. Two classes can share a mean score of 60 yet feel completely different — one tightly bunched, the other spread from 20 to 95. That difference is the standard deviation.

media.say: variance is the average squared distance from the mean.
media.caption: Square the distances from the mean, then average.
Same mean, different spread: σ sets the width.

cards.deploy: Quantifies risk, noise and consistency — the second number (after the mean) you reach for.
cards.counter: Squaring makes variance hypersensitive to outliers; a single freak value can dominate it, which is why robust measures (like the interquartile range) are sometimes preferred.

quiz.q: The standard deviation is the…
A random variable takes the value 2 with probability 0.5 and the value 8 with probability 0.5. What is its standard deviation?
If every value in a dataset is multiplied by 3, how does the standard deviation change?

Because squaring distances makes variance react sharply to a single extreme value, analysts sometimes prefer a robust spread measure based on the 25th and 75th percentiles. What is that measure called?

cards.title: Distributions: uniform, Bernoulli, binomial
cards.fact: A distribution is the shape of how probability is spread across outcomes.
cards.detail: A few shapes recur everywhere. The uniform puts equal weight on each outcome (a fair die). The Bernoulli is a single yes/no trial with success probability \(p\) (one coin flip). The binomial counts successes in \(n\) independent trials — flip 4 coins and the number of heads follows it, peaking in the middle. Recognising the shape tells you what to expect.

media.caption: Heads in 4 coin flips (binomial): the middle is likeliest.

cards.deploy: Names the common patterns so you can pick the right model instead of starting from scratch.
cards.counter: Reaching for a textbook distribution can impose a shape the data doesn't have — real counts are often more skewed or heavy-tailed than the binomial or normal assume.

quiz.q: The number of heads in several independent coin flips follows the…
You flip 6 fair coins. On average, how many heads do you expect?
What distribution describes a single trial with only two outcomes, success or failure, with success probability p (for example, one coin flip)?
A spinner is divided into 8 equal sectors, and you record which sector it lands on. Which distribution best models this outcome?

cards.title: The normal (Gaussian) distribution
cards.fact: The bell curve: a smooth hump set by just two numbers — its mean and its spread.
cards.detail: The normal distribution's density is \(f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}\). The mean \(\mu\) slides the peak left or right; the standard deviation \(\sigma\) makes it wide or narrow. About 68% of values land within one \(\sigma\) of the mean, 95% within two. It appears so often because sums of many small independent effects tend toward it — the reason it underpins so much of statistics.

media.caption: Slide μ to move the peak, σ to widen or narrow it.

cards.deploy: The default model for measurement error, natural variation and sample averages.
cards.counter: Assuming normality is dangerous in the tails: finance learned in 2008 that 'impossible' extreme moves happen far more often than the bell curve allows (fat tails).

quiz.q: Two numbers fully define a normal distribution: the mean and the…

Adult heights are normally distributed with mean 170 cm and standard deviation 8 cm. Using the rule that about 95% of values fall within two standard deviations of the mean, what is the lower bound of that central 95% range, in cm?
Test scores are normal with mean 500 and standard deviation 100. Approximately what fraction of scores fall between 400 and 600?
What is the name of the result explaining why sums or averages of many small independent effects tend toward a normal distribution?

cards.title: Mean, median, and mode
cards.fact: Three ways to name the 'typical' value — and they can tell different stories.
cards.detail: The mean is the arithmetic average (add up, divide by how many). The median is the middle value when sorted. The mode is the most common value. They agree for symmetric data, but a few extreme values pull the mean while leaving the median put: most people earn below the mean income, because a handful of huge earners drag the average up. The median is the fairer 'typical' there.

media.caption: A long right tail (like incomes) drags the mean past the median.

cards.deploy: The first summary of any dataset — and choosing mean vs median can change the headline.
cards.counter: Any single number hides the shape: the same mean can describe steady data or wildly volatile data. Always ask about spread too.

quiz.q: For incomes with a few very high earners, the 'typical' value is best given by the…
Five houses on a street sold for 200, 210, 220, 230, and 1140 (thousands). What is the median sale price, in thousands?
A dataset is heavily right-skewed by a few very large values. How will its mean and median typically compare?
choices: The mean is larger than the median
The median is larger than the mean
The mean and median are equal
The mode is always larger than both

quiz.q: For the values 3, 7, 7, 7, 9, 12, which single measure of central tendency equals 7 because it is the most frequently occurring value?

cards.title: Population vs sample: estimating from a piece
cards.fact: Statistics infers the whole from a part — and a biased part lies.
cards.detail: You rarely measure everyone (the 'population'), so you take a 'sample' and estimate. The catch is sampling error: any sample differs from the whole by chance, and that wobble shrinks roughly as \(1/\sqrt{n}\) — to halve the error you need four times the data. Worse than random error is bias: a sample that systematically over-represents some group. The 1936 Literary Digest poll surveyed millions yet called the US election wrongly, because its phone-and-car owners skewed wealthy.
cards.deploy: The basis of all polling, testing and science: how to learn about the many from the few.
cards.counter: A bigger sample cuts random error but not bias — a huge skewed sample is confidently wrong. Size is no substitute for representativeness.

quiz.q: To halve a sample's random error, you roughly need to…
Random sampling error shrinks roughly as 1/sqrt(n). If a sample of 400 people gives a certain error, how many people are needed to cut that error to one third of its size?
A survey collects 5 million responses but only from people who own both a phone and a car, a group skewed toward the wealthy. What is the main problem with this survey?
choices: Sampling bias, which a large sample size does not fix
Too small a sample, fixable by collecting more responses
Random sampling error, which 5 million responses cannot reduce
The mean was used instead of the median

quiz.q: What is the general term for the entire group you want to draw conclusions about, as opposed to the smaller subset you actually measure?

cards.title: Hypothesis testing and the p-value
cards.fact: A p-value asks: if nothing were going on, how surprising would this data be?
cards.detail: Start with a 'null hypothesis' — no effect. The p-value is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme if the null were true. A small p (often \(p < 0.05\)) means the data would be surprising under 'no effect', so researchers reject the null. It does not give the probability that the hypothesis is true, nor the size or importance of an effect.

media.tex: p = P(\text{data this extreme} \mid \text{null is true})
media.plain: p = P(data this extreme | null hypothesis true)
media.say: the p-value is the chance of data this extreme, assuming nothing is going on.
media.caption: Small p → the data is surprising if there's really no effect.

cards.deploy: The standard gatekeeper for 'is this result more than noise?' across the sciences.
cards.counter: The American Statistical Association warned in 2016 that p-values are widely misused: p < 0.05 is an arbitrary line, says nothing about effect size, and 'p-hacking' can manufacture it. A small p is not proof.

quiz.q: A small p-value means the data would be… if the null hypothesis were true.
A study reports p = 0.5. Under the standard null hypothesis of no effect, what does this value indicate about the observed data?
choices: Data this extreme is quite ordinary under no effect, so there is no basis to reject the null
There is a 50% chance the hypothesis is true
The effect is large but uncertain
The null hypothesis is proven correct

quiz.q: What name is given to the default starting assumption in a significance test that there is no effect or no difference?
A researcher tries 20 different outcome measures and reports only the one that reached p < 0.05. What practice does this describe?

cards.title: Confidence intervals: the margin of error
cards.fact: A confidence interval reports a range for an estimate, not a single false-precise number.
cards.detail: Rather than '52% support', a poll says '52% ± 3%'. The 95% confidence interval is built so that, across many repeated samples, about 95% of such intervals would contain the true value. A wider interval means more uncertainty; more data narrows it. It keeps you honest about how much the single estimate could be off.
cards.deploy: Communicates uncertainty alongside an estimate — essential for reading polls and studies.
cards.counter: The 95% refers to the long-run behaviour of the method, not to one interval: it's wrong to say 'there's a 95% chance the truth is in this particular range' — a subtlety frequentists stress and Bayesians sidestep with credible intervals.

quiz.q: A wider confidence interval indicates…
A poll reports 47% support with a 95% confidence interval of 47% plus or minus 4%. What is the upper bound of that interval, as a percentage?
What does the '95%' in a 95% confidence interval correctly refer to?
choices: The long-run fraction of such intervals, over many repeated samples, that would contain the true value
The probability that the true value lies inside this particular computed interval
The probability that the sample is unbiased
The fraction of the population that was surveyed

quiz.q: What is the name for the Bayesian counterpart to a confidence interval, for which it is valid to say there is a 95% probability the true value lies within the range?

cards.title: Least-squares regression: the best-fit line
cards.fact: Regression draws the straight line that comes closest to a cloud of points.
cards.detail: Fit a straight line \(\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) — an intercept and a slope — through a cloud of points. The standard method is ordinary least squares (OLS): pick the line that makes the total squared vertical gap between the points and the line as small as possible, \(\sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\). Why square the gaps rather than just add them up? Squaring punishes big misses far more than small ones and — crucially — leaves exactly one best line. The fitted slope \(\beta_1\) then estimates how much \(y\) rises per unit of \(x\). It is the workhorse of empirical science and the simplest machine-learning model there is.

media.caption: The line that minimises the total squared gap to the points.

cards.deploy: The standard tool for measuring how one quantity moves with another, and predicting from it.
cards.counter: A fitted line can mislead: it assumes a straight relationship, is dragged by outliers, and — as the correlation/causation card warns — a good fit never proves x causes y.

quiz.q: Least-squares regression chooses the line that minimises the total…
choices: Squared vertical distance to the points

quiz.q: A least-squares line is fit to four points. The fitted line gives predictions of 5, 8, 11, and 14, while the true y-values are 6, 7, 13, and 13. What is the sum of squared residuals for this fit?
Why does ordinary least squares minimize the sum of SQUARED vertical gaps rather than the sum of the raw signed gaps?
choices: Raw signed gaps can cancel to zero for many different lines, while squaring penalizes large misses heavily and yields a single unique best line
Squaring is the only operation that keeps the slope positive
Summing raw gaps is impossible to compute without calculus
Squaring guarantees the line passes through every data point

quiz.q: In the fitted model y-hat = b0 + b1*x, what does the coefficient b1 estimate about the relationship between x and y?
accept: the change in y per unit x
rise in y per unit increase in x
how much y rises per unit of x

cards.title: Machine learning: fitting a function to data
cards.fact: Instead of writing the rule by hand, you let the machine find a function that fits examples.
cards.detail: A model is a function \(f\) with adjustable numbers inside it, called parameters (or weights). 'Training' means tuning those numbers until \(f\) maps inputs to the right outputs on example data — learning the rule from cases rather than being told it. Show it thousands of labelled photos and it adjusts its weights until it separates cats from dogs. The input is a vector of features; the output is a prediction.

media.caption: Learning = finding the function that best fits the examples.

cards.deploy: The core idea behind modern AI: learn the function from data instead of programming it.
cards.counter: A model only learns patterns present in its training data — including the biases and gaps in that data, which it will faithfully reproduce and even amplify.

quiz.q: In machine learning, 'training' adjusts a model's…
A team trains a hiring model only on resumes from past hires at a firm that historically favored one demographic. The deployed model strongly prefers that same group. What does this best illustrate?
choices: A model reproduces and can amplify the biases present in its training data
The model needs a larger learning rate
Squared error was the wrong loss to use
The model has too few parameters to learn the rule

quiz.q: In machine learning, what name is given to the adjustable internal numbers of the model that training tunes to fit the examples?
What is the key difference between traditional hand-coded programming and the machine-learning approach to building a classifier?
choices: In ML the rule is learned by adjusting a function to fit labelled examples, rather than written out explicitly by a programmer
ML never uses any numerical computation, only logic rules
Hand-coded programs require labelled data but ML does not
ML always produces a function with no inputs

cards.title: Linear regression as your first model
cards.fact: Predict with a weighted sum of the inputs: ŷ = w·x + b.
cards.detail: Give each input feature a weight, multiply, add them up, and add a bias: \(\hat{y} = \vec{w}\cdot\vec{x} + b\). That dot product is the whole model — a price predicted from size, location and age is just their weighted sum. 'Learning' means finding the weights \(\vec{w}\) and bias \(b\) that fit the data best, by making the error as small as possible. With a handful of features you can solve for them exactly with ordinary least squares; with millions you instead descend the error surface step by step (gradient descent) — both routes chase the same minimum. Simple, fast, and the template every fancier model extends.

media.say: the prediction is the weights dotted with the inputs, plus a bias.
media.caption: A prediction is a weighted sum of the features.
One feature: the model is just the best-fit line.

cards.deploy: The clearest place to see what 'a model' and 'weights' actually mean before things get deep.
cards.counter: A straight weighted sum can't capture curves or interactions; its honesty about that limit is also why it rarely overfits and stays easy to interpret.

quiz.q: In ŷ = w·x + b, the vector w holds the…
A linear regression model predicts house price with weights w = (3, 5) on features x = (size, rooms) and bias b = 20. For a house with size 10 and 4 rooms, what price does y-hat = w·x + b give?
When a linear regression has only a handful of features versus millions, which pair of solution methods is typically used, respectively?
choices: Ordinary least squares (exact closed-form solve) for few features; gradient descent (iterative steps down the error surface) for very many
Gradient descent for few features; ordinary least squares for very many
Both cases require gradient descent because no exact solution exists
Both cases use ordinary least squares because it scales to any size

quiz.q: In the model y-hat = w·x + b, what is the single added term 'b' called?

cards.title: The loss function: scoring how wrong you are
cards.fact: A loss function turns 'how bad is this model?' into a single number to minimise.
cards.detail: Compare each prediction \(\hat{y}_i\) to the truth \(y_i\), and summarise the misses in one number. The common choice for regression is the mean squared error: \(L = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i (\hat{y}_i - y_i)^2\). Squaring punishes big mistakes harder and keeps the loss positive. Training becomes a clear goal: choose the weights that make this number as small as possible.

media.say: the loss is the average of the squared gaps between prediction and truth.
media.caption: Mean squared error: average of the squared misses.
Loss as the weight changes: a valley to roll into.

cards.deploy: Defines 'best' precisely, so training is just minimising one number.
cards.counter: The loss you pick is a value judgement: squared error chases outliers, while other losses (absolute error, cross-entropy) reward different behaviour — optimise the wrong loss and you get the wrong model.

quiz.q: Mean squared error squares the errors mainly to…
choices: Punish big mistakes more and stay positive

quiz.q: A regression model makes 3 predictions with errors (prediction minus truth) of -2, 4, and 0. Using mean squared error L = (1/n) * sum of (y-hat - y)^2, what is the loss?

Two models have the same total absolute error, but model A makes one huge mistake while model B spreads the error evenly across many small misses. Under mean squared error, which is judged worse and why?
choices: Model A, because squaring penalizes a single large miss far more than several small ones
Model B, because more individual errors always raise squared loss
They tie, because squared error only depends on the total absolute error
Model A, because squared error ignores small errors entirely

quiz.q: Which loss function is commonly used to train a classifier, rather than the squared-error loss used for regression?

cards.title: Gradient descent: rolling downhill to the best fit
cards.fact: Take small steps in the downhill direction of the loss until you reach the bottom.
cards.detail: The gradient \(\nabla L\) points uphill on the loss surface, so step the opposite way: \(\vec{w} \leftarrow \vec{w} - \eta\,\nabla L\). The learning rate \(\eta\) sets the step size — too small and training crawls, too large and it overshoots and diverges. Repeat, and the weights roll down into a valley of low loss. This one rule trains almost every model in modern machine learning.

layers.body: The gradient \(\nabla L\) points uphill on the loss surface, so step the opposite way: \(\vec{w} \leftarrow \vec{w} - \eta\,\nabla L\). The learning rate \(\eta\) sets the step size — too small and training crawls, too large and it overshoots and diverges. Repeat, and the weights roll down into a valley of low loss. This one rule trains almost every model in modern machine learning.

Say the loss is \(L(w)=(w-3)^2\), so its slope is \(L'(w)=2(w-3)\). Start at \(w=0\) with learning rate \(\eta=0.1\).

Step 1: slope \(=2(0-3)=-6\), so \(w \leftarrow 0-0.1\times(-6)=0.6\). Step 2: slope \(=-4.8\), so \(w \leftarrow 1.08\). Step 3: \(w\approx1.46\)… each step slides \(w\) toward 3, where the slope is 0 — the bottom. Pick \(\eta=1.1\) instead and the steps overshoot and blow up.

media.say: new weights equal old weights minus the learning rate times the uphill gradient.
media.caption: Step against the gradient — downhill on the loss.
Press step: the ball rolls toward the minimum. Try a big η.

cards.deploy: The universal training algorithm — understand this and you understand how models learn.
cards.counter: On a bumpy, non-convex loss it can stall in a local dip or a saddle far from the best solution; momentum and adaptive methods (like Adam) are patches for that, not cures.

quiz.q: Gradient descent updates weights by stepping…
A weight currently equals 5.0. The gradient of the loss with respect to it is +8.0, and the learning rate is 0.1. What is the weight after one gradient-descent update?
Training loss oscillates wildly and then blows up to larger and larger values instead of settling. Which single change is the most direct fix?
choices: Flip the sign of the gradient before stepping

quiz.q: On a non-convex loss surface, gradient descent can get stuck at a point that is the lowest loss in its immediate neighborhood but not the globally lowest. What is the name for such a point?

cards.title: Logistic regression and the sigmoid
cards.fact: Squash a weighted sum through an S-curve to get a probability between 0 and 1.
cards.detail: For yes/no questions you want a probability, not an unbounded number. The sigmoid \(\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\) takes any value and bends it into the range 0 to 1: large positive \(z\) → near 1, large negative → near 0, zero → exactly 0.5. Feed it the weighted sum \(z = \vec{w}\cdot\vec{x} + b\) and you have logistic regression — a classifier that outputs calibrated probabilities.

media.caption: The sigmoid squashes any number into a 0–1 probability.

cards.deploy: The standard way to turn a score into a probability — and the classic activation in a neuron.
cards.counter: Its probabilities are only as honest as the model: a confident sigmoid output can still be badly miscalibrated if the features or data are skewed.

quiz.q: The sigmoid function maps any input to a value between…
A logistic regression neuron produces a weighted sum plus bias of z = 0. Using the sigmoid 1/(1+e^-z), what probability does it output?
For a single feature x, a logistic model uses weight w = 2 and bias b = -1, so z = 2x - 1. Evaluate the output probability sigmoid(z) at x = 0.5. (e^0 = 1.)
A trained sigmoid classifier outputs 0.97 for an input, but among the many inputs it scores at 0.97, only about 60% actually belong to the positive class. What does this reveal?
choices: The model's probabilities are poorly calibrated
The sigmoid was applied with the wrong sign
The learning rate during training was too small
The output cannot be a probability because it exceeds 0.5

cards.title: The artificial neuron
cards.fact: A neuron weighs its inputs, adds them up, and fires through an activation function.
cards.detail: The basic unit: take inputs \(\vec{x}\), weight and sum them with a bias, then pass the result through a non-linear activation: \(y = \sigma(\vec{w}\cdot\vec{x} + b)\). The weighted sum is a dot product; the activation (a sigmoid, or today usually a ReLU) lets the unit bend, not just draw a straight line. One neuron is a tiny logistic regression — the Lego brick everything bigger is built from.

media.say: the output is the activation of the weighted sum of inputs plus a bias.
media.caption: Weigh, sum, then squash: one artificial neuron.
Three weighted inputs feed one neuron.

cards.deploy: The atom of neural networks — every deep model is millions of these wired together.
cards.counter: The brain analogy is loose marketing: a biological neuron is vastly more complex, and this unit is better understood as a tunable mathematical function than as a model of a cell.

quiz.q: An artificial neuron applies an activation function to the…
choices: Weighted sum of inputs plus bias

quiz.q: A neuron has weights (2, -1, 3) and bias 1. For input (1, 4, 2), compute the pre-activation value z = w.x + b.
If an artificial neuron used no activation function (just the weighted sum plus bias), what single class of functions could a stack of such units ever represent?
Which statement best describes the relationship between a single artificial neuron with a sigmoid activation and logistic regression?
choices: A single sigmoid neuron computes exactly the same thing as logistic regression
A neuron has no bias term, unlike logistic regression
Logistic regression cannot output probabilities, but a neuron can
A neuron skips the weighted sum and applies the activation to raw inputs

cards.title: A neural network: layers of neurons
cards.fact: Stack neurons into layers and a network becomes matrices squashed through activations.
cards.detail: A layer computes many neurons at once: collect their weights into a matrix \(W\) and the whole layer is \(\vec{h} = \sigma(W\vec{x} + \vec{b})\) — a matrix-vector product, then an activation, applied entry by entry. Stack layers and the output of one feeds the next. Without the non-linear activations the stack would collapse into a single linear map; with them, the network can approximate almost any function. This is deep learning's core.

layers.body: A layer computes many neurons at once: collect their weights into a matrix \(W\) and the whole layer is \(\vec{h} = \sigma(W\vec{x} + \vec{b})\) — a matrix-vector product, then an activation, applied entry by entry. Stack layers and the output of one feeds the next. Without the non-linear activations the stack would collapse into a single linear map; with them, the network can approximate almost any function. This is deep learning's core.

Take one layer with 2 inputs feeding 3 neurons. The weights form a \(3\times2\) matrix \(W\); the inputs are a length-2 vector \(\vec x\). Then \(W\vec x\) is length-3 (one weighted sum per neuron), you add a length-3 bias \(\vec b\), and squash each of the 3 entries.

So '3 neurons on 2 inputs' is exactly: multiply by a \(3\times2\) matrix, add 3 numbers, squash 3 numbers. The next layer takes those 3 outputs as its own inputs — another matrix, another squash.

media.say: a layer is the activation of a matrix times the inputs, plus a bias vector.
media.caption: One layer: a matrix multiply, a bias, then a squash.
Inputs flow through hidden layers to outputs — every arrow is a weight.

cards.deploy: Explains why linear algebra and calculus are the language of AI: a net is matrices and activations composed.
cards.counter: 'Can approximate any function' is an existence result, not a recipe — it says nothing about how much data, compute, or luck it takes to actually find the right weights.

quiz.q: A neural-network layer is essentially a matrix multiply followed by…
A neural-network layer maps a 5-dimensional input vector to a 3-dimensional output vector via h = sigma(W x + b). How many entries does the weight matrix W contain?
Why does removing all non-linear activations from a deep network make extra layers pointless?
choices: The composition of linear maps is itself a single linear map
The matrices can no longer be multiplied together
The bias vectors cancel out to zero
Gradient descent can no longer compute a gradient

quiz.q: The result that a sufficiently large network with non-linear activations can approximate almost any continuous function goes by what name (the theorem)?

cards.title: Backpropagation: the chain rule that trains the net
cards.fact: Backprop sends the error backwards through the layers to find every weight's gradient.
cards.detail: Gradient descent needs the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight — and a deep net has millions. Backpropagation computes them all efficiently by applying the chain rule layer by layer, from the output error back toward the input. Each layer passes the blame for the error to the one before it. It's just the chain rule, organised — and its rediscovery in the 1980s is what made training deep networks practical.

layers.body: Gradient descent needs the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight — and a deep net has millions. Backpropagation computes them all efficiently by applying the chain rule layer by layer, from the output error back toward the input. Each layer passes the blame for the error to the one before it. It's just the chain rule, organised — and its rediscovery in the 1980s is what made training deep networks practical.

Chain one neuron: \(z=wx\), then \(a=\sigma(z)\), then loss \(L=(a-y)^2\). To adjust \(w\), multiply the rates along the chain:

\(\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial w}=\underbrace{2(a-y)}_{\text{loss}\to a}\cdot\underbrace{\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))}_{a\to z}\cdot\underbrace{x}_{z\to w}\).

Each layer passes that running product back to the layer before it — backprop just does this for every weight at once, output-side first.

media.say: a weight's effect on the loss is the chain of how it changes the output, times how that changes the loss.
media.caption: The chain rule, applied backwards through every layer.
Training sends the error backward, right to left, tuning every weight.

cards.deploy: The reason deep networks are trainable at all — the algorithm that powers the whole field.
cards.counter: Backprop finds gradients, not good solutions: it can suffer vanishing or exploding gradients in deep stacks, which architectures (ReLUs, residual connections, normalisation) were invented to tame.

quiz.q: Backpropagation is fundamentally an application of the…

cards.title: Softmax and cross-entropy
cards.fact: Softmax turns a list of scores into probabilities that sum to 1; cross-entropy scores how good they are.
cards.detail: For many classes, softmax exponentiates each score and divides by the total: \(\text{softmax}(z)_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}\). The biggest score gets the most probability, but all stay positive and sum to 1. Cross-entropy then measures the gap from the true label — heavily punishing confident wrong answers via the logarithm. Together they are the standard output and loss for classification, from image labels to the next-word predictions of a language model.

media.say: each score is exponentiated, then divided by the total — giving probabilities that add to one.
media.caption: Scores in, probabilities (summing to 1) out.
Raw scores → softmax probabilities that sum to 1.

cards.deploy: The standard final layer of a classifier — including the token probabilities an LLM samples from.
cards.counter: Softmax always returns a confident-looking distribution even on nonsense input; it never says 'none of the above', which is one root of AI models' overconfidence.

quiz.q: Softmax converts a list of scores into…

cards.title: Overfitting and the bias–variance trade-off
cards.fact: A model that memorises its training data can fail completely on new data.
cards.detail: Push a model hard enough and it fits the training points perfectly — including their noise. That's overfitting: low error on data it has seen, high error on data it hasn't. The opposite, underfitting, is a model too simple to catch the real pattern. This is the bias–variance trade-off: too simple misses the signal (bias), too flexible chases the noise (variance). You judge a model on held-out test data, and rein in flexibility with regularisation.

media.caption: The simple straight line generalises; a wiggly curve through every point would not.

cards.deploy: The central discipline of machine learning: build models that generalise, not memorise.
cards.counter: More data and bigger models complicate the neat trade-off — very large networks can fit noise yet still generalise ('double descent'), a phenomenon classical theory didn't predict.

quiz.q: A model with low training error but high test error is…

cards.title: Attention and transformers: the maths behind LLMs
cards.fact: Attention lets each word pull in the others most relevant to it — by dot products and softmax.
cards.detail: A transformer represents each token as a vector and lets tokens look at one another. Each forms a query \(Q\), key \(K\) and value \(V\). The relevance of one token to another is their dot product (alignment); softmax turns those scores into weights that sum to 1; the output is the weighted blend of values: \(\text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d}}\right)V\). Stacked in layers, this is the architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) behind GPT and modern large language models.
