People rush to spend before prices rise again, velocity explodes, and the spiral feeds itself: Weimar Germany (1923), Zimbabwe (2008) and Venezuela (2010s) all printed their way into it. It usually ends only with a new currency or a hard fiscal anchor.
cards.deploy: The cautionary extreme of monetary finance — and why central-bank independence is prized.
cards.counter: Pure monetarists blame the money printing alone; others (the 'fiscal theory of the price level') argue hyperinflation is ultimately a collapse of confidence in the government's solvency, with printing the symptom rather than the root cause.

quiz.q: Hyperinflation is typically triggered by governments…

cards.title: What GDP misses
cards.fact: GDP counts market output — not wellbeing, unpaid work, inequality, or the environment.
cards.detail: GDP adds up the market value of what a country produces, and it rises whether the spending is on schools or on cleaning up an oil spill. It ignores unpaid care and housework, says nothing about how income is shared, and treats depleting forests or fisheries as pure gain. Even Simon Kuznets, who helped build it, warned in 1934 that 'the welfare of a nation can scarcely be inferred from' it. Alternatives include the Human Development Index and the Genuine Progress Indicator.
cards.deploy: Arms you to question 'growth = progress' and to ask what a rising GDP is actually counting.
cards.counter: Defenders (the IMF, most statisticians) reply that GDP was never meant to measure welfare, that it correlates strongly with health and education, and that the proposed alternatives are more subjective and harder to compare. The debate is about what to measure, not whether to.

quiz.q: Which does GDP NOT capture?

cards.title: Growth vs degrowth
cards.fact: Can a finite planet sustain endless economic growth — or must rich economies stop chasing it?
cards.detail: The mainstream view holds that growth lifts living standards and can be 'decoupled' from environmental harm through clean technology and efficiency. 'Degrowth' scholars like Jason Hickel and Giorgos Kallis argue that absolute decoupling at the needed scale isn't happening, so rich countries should deliberately shrink resource use and reorganise around wellbeing rather than GDP. Ecomodernists counter that technology and growth are the way out, not the problem.
cards.deploy: Frames the deepest argument in environmental economics: grow greener, or grow less?
cards.counter: The dispute is empirical and contested: defenders of growth point to falling emissions per dollar in some rich economies (relative decoupling), while degrowthers stress that absolute global resource use keeps rising. Neither side has settled the evidence.

quiz.q: 'Degrowth' advocates argue that rich economies should…

cards.title: Why nations fail: institutions
cards.fact: Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson argue prosperity hinges on whether institutions include or extract.
cards.detail: Why are some countries rich and others poor? Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James Robinson (2024 Nobel) argue the decisive factor is institutions. 'Inclusive' institutions — secure property rights, broad political voice, rule of law — let ordinary people invest and innovate; 'extractive' ones funnel wealth to a narrow elite and choke growth. Their natural experiment: colonisers built inclusive institutions where they settled and extractive ones where they merely plundered, and that split still shapes incomes today.
cards.deploy: Shifts the development question from geography or culture to who holds power and how it's constrained.
cards.counter: Critics (Jeffrey Sachs) insist geography and disease still matter hugely, and others note the inclusive/extractive labels can be circular — defined partly by the prosperity they're meant to explain. China's growth under extractive politics is a standing puzzle for the theory.

quiz.q: Acemoglu and Robinson argue prosperity depends most on…

cards.title: Dependency and world-systems theory
cards.fact: Dependency theorists argue poor countries stay poor because the global system is built to drain them.
cards.detail: Against the idea that poor nations simply lag behind, Latin American economists Raúl Prebisch and Andre Gunder Frank argued the world is split into a wealthy 'core' and a 'periphery' locked into supplying cheap raw materials, their terms of trade steadily worsening. Immanuel Wallerstein's world-systems theory generalised this into a single capitalist system that develops the core by underdeveloping the periphery. The prescription was often to industrialise behind tariffs rather than specialise in commodities.
cards.deploy: A counter to free-trade optimism: names who gains and who is structurally held back.
cards.counter: The East Asian 'tigers' — which grew rich through export-led trade, not withdrawal from it — are the standard rebuttal; mainstream economists also note that import-substitution policies often produced inefficient, protected industries. Dependency theorists reply that East Asia had unusual geopolitical backing.

quiz.q: Dependency theory describes the world economy as a…

cards.title: The developmental state
cards.fact: Ha-Joon Chang and Joe Studwell argue today's rich countries got rich by guiding markets, not freeing them.
cards.detail: East Asia's rise — Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, then China — was led by an activist state: protecting infant industries, directing cheap credit, and forcing firms to export and compete abroad ('export discipline'). Ha-Joon Chang argues the now-rich West used the same protectionist tools while climbing, then 'kicked away the ladder' by preaching free trade to others. Joe Studwell adds that land reform and disciplined finance were decisive.
cards.deploy: A powerful case that industrial policy, not laissez-faire, built every late industrialiser.
cards.counter: Free-market economists reply that state direction also produced costly failures (much of Latin America, India's licence raj) and crony capitalism, and that East Asia succeeded partly despite, not because of, intervention. Picking winners is easy to romanticise after the fact.

quiz.q: Ha-Joon Chang's 'kicking away the ladder' accuses rich countries of…
choices: Denying others the protectionist tools they themselves used

cards.title: Feminist economics: the work that doesn't count
cards.fact: The unpaid care that sustains every economy is invisible to the standard measures of it.
cards.detail: Feminist economists point out that mainstream economics ignores the enormous unpaid labour — childcare, cooking, eldercare, housework — done largely by women, without which no paid economy could function. Marilyn Waring showed national accounts count a forest only when it's felled, and a person only when they're paid; care work registers as nothing. The field also studies how gendered assumptions shape models of 'rational' choice and the household.
cards.deploy: Reframes 'the economy' to include the unpaid foundation it actually rests on.
cards.counter: Critics argue assigning market prices to care work is arbitrary and that including it would make GDP even noisier; feminist economists respond that leaving it at zero is the more distorting choice — the dispute is over what counts as economic value at all.

quiz.q: Feminist economics highlights that standard measures ignore…

cards.title: The colonial drain
cards.fact: Empires didn't just rule colonies — they ran them as engines of wealth extraction.
cards.detail: Colonial economies were reshaped to feed the metropole: land turned to cash crops, local industry suppressed, and surpluses siphoned abroad. The Indian nationalist Dadabhai Naoroji formulated the 'drain of wealth' thesis in the 19th century, estimating how much Britain pumped out of India each year; recent work by Utsa Patnaik puts the cumulative figure in the trillions. The mirror image is the Atlantic system, where enslaved labour built plantation wealth.
cards.deploy: Grounds 'why are some nations poor?' in a history of extraction, not just bad luck or culture.
cards.counter: The scale and lasting effect are debated: some economic historians (Tirthankar Roy) argue colonialism's impact is overstated relative to internal factors and that the counterfactual is murky, while others (Patnaik, the dependency school) see extraction as decisive. The numbers turn on contested assumptions.

quiz.q: Dadabhai Naoroji's 'drain of wealth' described…
choices: Wealth siphoned from India to Britain

cards.title: The East Asian miracle
cards.fact: In a generation, the 'Asian tigers' went from poor to rich — the fastest catch-up in history.
cards.detail: From the 1960s, South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore (the 'Four Tigers'), followed by Southeast Asia and China, grew at extraordinary rates, lifting hundreds of millions out of poverty. The recipe is disputed but the ingredients recur: high savings and investment, mass education, land reform, and export-oriented industrialisation. The World Bank's 1993 report 'The East Asian Miracle' tried, awkwardly, to reconcile this with free-market orthodoxy.
cards.deploy: The central case study for every theory of development — and the rebuttal to dependency pessimism.
cards.counter: The 1997 Asian financial crisis exposed the model's fragility, and economists still split: the World Bank credits markets and openness, while Alice Amsden and Robert Wade credit the guiding hand of the state. Paul Krugman argued the growth was mostly 'perspiration' (more inputs), not 'inspiration' (productivity).

quiz.q: A common ingredient in the East Asian growth model was…

cards.title: The Washington Consensus
cards.fact: In the 1980s–90s, the IMF and World Bank prescribed one package to the developing world: liberalise, privatise, stabilise.
cards.detail: Coined by John Williamson in 1989, the 'Washington Consensus' named a set of market reforms — fiscal discipline, privatisation, deregulation, free trade and open capital markets — attached as conditions to IMF and World Bank loans (structural adjustment). It reshaped Latin America, Africa and the post-Soviet states. Results were mixed at best: growth often disappointed and inequality frequently rose.
cards.deploy: The label for the era when market liberalisation was exported worldwide as loan conditions.
cards.counter: Joseph Stiglitz attacked it for forcing premature liberalisation that triggered crises; William Easterly mocked top-down 'planning' for the poor. Defenders reply that the worst failures came where reforms were half-done or corruptly applied, not from the prescription itself. Even Williamson said his term was widely misused.

quiz.q: The Washington Consensus prescribed mainly…

cards.title: The Marshall Plan
cards.fact: After 1945, the US poured aid into Western Europe — and helped rebuild both its economies and its alliances.
cards.detail: From 1948, the United States transferred some $13 billion (a vast sum then) to rebuild Western Europe under the European Recovery Program, named for Secretary of State George Marshall. It funded reconstruction, restarted trade, and was explicitly geopolitical — binding Western Europe to the US and against Soviet influence as the Cold War set in. Recipients were nudged toward cooperation, seeding what became the European common market.
cards.deploy: The canonical example of aid serving reconstruction and strategy at once.
cards.counter: Its size-of-effect is debated — Alan Milward argued Europe's recovery was already under way — but so is its framing. From Moscow the Plan was an instrument of US economic empire and dollar dominance, which is why Stalin forced Eastern Europe to refuse it and built Comecon in reply; dependency-school writers read conditional aid as binding recipients to American markets. The 'generous reconstruction' story is told mostly from Washington's side.

quiz.q: The Marshall Plan was US aid to rebuild…

cards.title: The CIA triad: what security protects
cards.fact: Security has three goals: confidentiality, integrity, and availability.
cards.detail: Almost every security measure serves one of three aims. Confidentiality keeps data secret from those who shouldn't see it (encryption, access control). Integrity keeps it from being altered without detection (hashes, signatures). Availability keeps it reachable when needed (backups, defence against denial-of-service). The three pull against each other — locking something down tighter can make it harder to reach — so security is always a balance, not a maximum.
cards.deploy: A checklist for any system: which of confidentiality, integrity and availability matters most here, and what threatens it?
cards.counter: The triad is a useful frame, not a complete one; practitioners add goals like authenticity, non-repudiation and privacy, and some argue it's too data-centric for modern threats like disinformation.

quiz.q: The 'A' in the CIA triad stands for…

cards.title: Threat, vulnerability, risk
cards.fact: A vulnerability is a weakness; a threat is who'd exploit it; risk is the chance and cost if they do.
cards.detail: These three words are often muddled but mean different things. A vulnerability is a flaw — an unpatched server, a weak password. A threat is an actor or event that could exploit it — a criminal, an insider, a flood. Risk combines them: how likely is exploitation, and how bad would it be? The sum of all the ways in is the 'attack surface'. Security spends scarce effort where risk — not just vulnerability — is highest.
cards.deploy: Stops 'we found a flaw, panic' thinking: a vulnerability with no plausible threat or low impact may not be worth fixing first.
cards.counter: Risk numbers are estimates dressed as facts — probabilities of rare attacks are hard to know — so risk scoring can give false precision and miss the 'unknown unknowns' that cause the worst breaches.

quiz.q: An unpatched, exploitable flaw in software is a…

cards.title: Authentication vs authorization
cards.fact: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you're allowed to do.
cards.detail: Logging in is authentication — proving identity by something you know (a password), something you have (a phone or token), or something you are (a fingerprint). Authorization is the next step: now that we know who you are, which files or actions may you access? Multi-factor authentication (MFA) combines two of those categories, so a stolen password alone isn't enough — one of the single most effective defences there is.
cards.deploy: Clarifies a constant confusion and explains why MFA blocks the bulk of account-takeover attacks.
cards.counter: Not all factors are equal: SMS codes can be intercepted (SIM-swapping), and 'push fatigue' attacks spam approval prompts until a tired user taps yes — so MFA reduces risk but doesn't end it.

quiz.q: Multi-factor authentication combines factors from…

cards.title: How passwords should be stored
cards.fact: Never store passwords as text — store a salted hash you can check but can't reverse.
cards.detail: A cryptographic hash turns any input into a fixed fingerprint that can't be run backwards. So a site stores the hash of your password, not the password; at login it hashes what you typed and compares. To stop attackers pre-computing hashes (rainbow tables), each password gets a unique random 'salt' mixed in before hashing, and a deliberately slow algorithm (bcrypt, Argon2) makes mass guessing expensive. A breach then leaks hashes, not your actual password.
cards.deploy: The reason a well-run site can be breached without your password itself leaking — and why reuse across sites is dangerous.
cards.counter: Hashing only buys time: weak or common passwords still fall to guessing, and NIST's 2017 guidance reversed old habits — it now advises against forced periodic changes and complexity rules, which pushed users toward predictable patterns.

quiz.q: A 'salt' is added before hashing a password to…

cards.title: Symmetric encryption: one shared key
cards.fact: Symmetric encryption scrambles data with a key; the same key unscrambles it.
cards.detail: With a symmetric cipher like AES, sender and receiver share one secret key: the key plus the message produces ciphertext, and the same key reverses it. It's fast and used for the bulk of encrypted data — files, disks, the actual content of a secure connection. The hard part isn't the maths; it's the logistics: how do two parties who've never met agree on a shared secret key without an eavesdropper learning it? That problem is what public-key cryptography solves.
cards.deploy: The workhorse that actually encrypts your data; understanding its key-sharing snag motivates everything that follows.
cards.counter: A symmetric scheme is only as safe as its key handling: reuse a key or a 'nonce', or leak the key, and strong maths gives no protection — most real-world crypto failures are key-management failures, not broken ciphers.

quiz.q: In symmetric encryption, the key used to decrypt is…
choices: The same as the encryption key

cards.title: Public-key cryptography
cards.fact: A public key locks; only the matching private key unlocks — so strangers can exchange secrets.
cards.detail: Public-key (asymmetric) cryptography gives everyone two linked keys: a public one they share freely and a private one they guard. Anyone can encrypt to you with your public key, but only your private key decrypts. It rests on 'one-way' maths — easy to do, brutally hard to reverse. RSA, for example, encrypts as \(c = m^{e} \bmod n\), and reversing it requires factoring a huge number, which is believed to be infeasible. This solves symmetric encryption's key-exchange problem.

media.say: the ciphertext is the message raised to the public exponent, wrapped around a big modulus n.
media.caption: RSA: easy to compute, hard to reverse without the private key.

cards.deploy: The breakthrough behind secure websites, signed software and encrypted messaging.
cards.counter: Its security rests on problems merely *believed* hard (factoring, discrete logs), not proven so — and a large quantum computer running Shor's algorithm would break RSA outright, which is why post-quantum cryptography is being rolled out now.

quiz.q: In public-key cryptography, a message encrypted with your public key can be decrypted with…

cards.title: TLS: what the padlock means
cards.fact: HTTPS uses public-key crypto to agree a secret key, then switches to fast symmetric encryption.
cards.detail: When you connect to an HTTPS site, TLS does a 'handshake': the site presents a certificate (signed by a trusted authority) vouching for its identity and public key, the two sides use public-key crypto to agree on a fresh shared secret, and then they switch to fast symmetric encryption for the actual data. The padlock means the connection is encrypted and the site's certificate checks out — not that the site itself is honest.
cards.deploy: Explains exactly what the browser padlock does and doesn't promise.
cards.counter: The whole system trusts a web of certificate authorities; a compromised or coerced CA can issue fraudulent certificates, and a padlock on a phishing site only proves the connection is encrypted, not that the site is who you want.

quiz.q: The HTTPS padlock guarantees that…
choices: The connection is encrypted and the certificate checks out
No one can hack the site

cards.title: Hashes and digital signatures
cards.fact: A hash detects tampering; signing it with a private key proves who sent it.
cards.detail: A cryptographic hash (like SHA-256) reduces any file to a fixed fingerprint where the tiniest change yields a wildly different output and you can't work backwards — that gives integrity: re-hash a file and compare to spot tampering. A digital signature goes further: the sender encrypts the hash with their private key, and anyone can verify it with the matching public key, proving both that the file is unaltered and who signed it. This is how software updates and documents are authenticated.
cards.deploy: The mechanism behind 'verified' downloads, signed code, and tamper-evident records.
cards.counter: A signature only proves possession of a private key, not that the right person held it — stolen signing keys (as in the Stuxnet and SolarWinds attacks) let malware masquerade as trusted software.

quiz.q: A digital signature proves a message is unaltered AND…

cards.title: Phishing and social engineering
cards.fact: The easiest way past strong security is to trick a human into opening the door.
cards.detail: Social engineering attacks people, not machines: a convincing email, text or call that pressures you into clicking a link, entering a password, or wiring money. Phishing casts a wide net; 'spear-phishing' targets a specific person with tailored detail; 'business email compromise' impersonates a boss or supplier. It works because it exploits trust, urgency and authority — and no firewall stops a user who volunteers their credentials.
cards.deploy: Names why training, verification habits and MFA matter as much as technical defences.
cards.counter: Blaming 'gullible users' is a cop-out: well-designed systems reduce the damage a tricked human can do (MFA, payment call-backs, least privilege), so repeated breaches often point to bad system design, not bad people.

quiz.q: Phishing primarily exploits…

cards.title: Malware: viruses, worms, ransomware
cards.fact: Malware is software written to harm — and its types differ by how they spread and what they do.
cards.detail: A virus attaches to a file and spreads when that file is run; a worm spreads by itself across networks with no help; a trojan hides inside something that looks useful; ransomware encrypts your files and demands payment for the key. Spyware watches, botnets hijack machines into a remote army. The category matters because it shapes the defence — patching for worms, backups for ransomware, vetting downloads for trojans.
cards.deploy: A taxonomy that tells you which defence fits which threat.
cards.counter: The neat categories blur in practice: modern attacks chain several types, and the bigger shift is economic — ransomware-as-a-service turned malware into a criminal industry, so the threat is now organised business, not lone hackers.

quiz.q: Which malware spreads across networks on its own, without user action?

cards.title: Injection attacks: never trust input
cards.fact: If user input is treated as a command, attackers can rewrite what your program does.
cards.detail: Injection happens when data from a user is fed into an interpreter as if it were trusted code. The classic is SQL injection: type a crafted string into a login box and, if the app glues it straight into a database query, you can make the query return everything or delete the table. Cross-site scripting (XSS) does the same with JavaScript in a web page. The fix is the same idea everywhere: keep data and code separate (parameterised queries, output encoding).
cards.deploy: The root cause behind a huge share of web breaches — and why 'sanitise your inputs' is a mantra.
cards.counter: 'Sanitising' by blocklisting bad characters is fragile and keeps losing; the durable fix is structural (parameterised queries, safe APIs) — yet injection has topped the OWASP risk list for two decades because the unsafe pattern is so easy to write.

quiz.q: SQL injection works when user input is…
choices: Treated as part of a database command

cards.title: Man-in-the-middle attacks
cards.fact: If an attacker sits between you and a server, they can read or alter everything — unless it's authenticated.
cards.detail: In a man-in-the-middle attack, the adversary secretly relays your traffic, posing as the server to you and as you to the server. On open Wi-Fi or a compromised router they can capture passwords and inject content. TLS defeats this by authenticating the server with a certificate and encrypting the channel — so even a relay in the middle sees only scrambled data and can't impersonate the real server without a valid certificate.
cards.deploy: Explains why public Wi-Fi without HTTPS is dangerous and why certificate warnings must never be clicked through.
cards.counter: TLS only helps if certificate checking is sound; 'SSL stripping', fake certificates from a rogue CA, or users who dismiss browser warnings all reopen the door — the maths is strong, the trust decisions around it are the weak point.

quiz.q: TLS stops a man-in-the-middle mainly by…
choices: Authenticating the server and encrypting the channel

cards.title: Denial of service
cards.fact: You don't have to break in to take a service down — just drown it in traffic.
cards.detail: A denial-of-service attack overwhelms a system so real users can't reach it, attacking the 'availability' leg of the CIA triad. A distributed version (DDoS) uses a botnet of thousands of hijacked devices to flood a target from everywhere at once, which makes it hard to block by source. Defences absorb or filter the flood (content-delivery networks, scrubbing services, rate limits) rather than stopping the attackers directly.
cards.deploy: Explains outages that aren't 'hacks' in the data-theft sense, and why big sites sit behind traffic-scrubbing networks.
cards.counter: DDoS is increasingly a smokescreen or extortion tool rather than the goal itself, and the rise of insecure IoT devices (the Mirai botnet) has made huge attacks cheap — defence is now an arms race of capacity, not a one-time fix.

quiz.q: A DDoS attack targets which part of the CIA triad?

cards.title: Buffer overflows and memory safety
cards.fact: Write past the end of a memory buffer and you can overwrite the program's own instructions.
cards.detail: Low-level languages like C let a program write data into a fixed-size block of memory without checking the size. Feed in more than fits and the excess spills into adjacent memory — including, classically, the address the program will jump to next. A crafted overflow can redirect execution into the attacker's own code. It's one of the oldest and most powerful bug classes; modern defences (stack canaries, ASLR, non-executable memory) and memory-safe languages (Rust) blunt it.
cards.deploy: Explains a whole family of severe vulnerabilities and the industry push toward memory-safe languages.
cards.counter: Mitigations raise the bar but get bypassed (return-oriented programming defeats non-executable memory); agencies like the NSA and CISA now argue the real fix is rewriting critical code in memory-safe languages, which is slow and contested for legacy systems.

quiz.q: A buffer overflow lets an attacker overwrite…

cards.title: Zero-days and the exploit market
cards.fact: A zero-day is a flaw the defenders don't yet know about — so there's no patch on day zero.
cards.detail: A zero-day vulnerability is one unknown to the software's maker, giving defenders 'zero days' to have fixed it before attacks begin. Because they're unpatched, they're extremely valuable — there's a market where brokers and governments pay six or seven figures for working exploits. 'Responsible disclosure' asks researchers to tell the vendor and allow time to patch before going public; not everyone does.
cards.deploy: Explains why even fully-updated systems can be breached and why patch speed matters so much.
cards.counter: Governments face a dilemma: stockpiling zero-days for spying leaves everyone exposed, since the same flaw can be found or stolen by others — the NSA's hoarded EternalBlue exploit leaked and powered the 2017 WannaCry ransomware that hit hospitals worldwide.

quiz.q: A 'zero-day' vulnerability is one that…
choices: Is unknown to the vendor, so unpatched

cards.title: Defence in depth
cards.fact: Don't rely on one wall — stack independent layers so a single failure isn't fatal.
cards.detail: Defence in depth assumes any one control will eventually fail, so it layers many: a firewall, then network segmentation, then strong authentication, then least-privilege access (everyone gets the minimum rights they need), then logging and encryption of the data itself. An attacker who slips past one layer still faces the next. The aim isn't perfection at any layer but resilience across all of them.
cards.deploy: The organising principle of real-world security architecture — no single point of failure.
cards.counter: Layers add cost, complexity and friction, and poorly chosen ones give 'security theatre' — the feeling of protection without the substance; more controls aren't automatically more security if they don't address the real risks.

quiz.q: The principle of 'least privilege' means giving each user…

cards.title: Threat modelling: think like an attacker
cards.fact: Before defending, ask: what are we protecting, from whom, and how might they get in?
cards.detail: Threat modelling is the disciplined version of 'what could go wrong?'. You map what's valuable (assets), who might attack (adversaries and their capabilities), and the paths in (attack vectors), then prioritise defences against the most plausible, damaging threats. A common prompt is STRIDE — Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege. It turns vague worry into a ranked to-do list.
cards.deploy: The first step of any serious security design: defend against your actual adversaries, not imaginary ones.
cards.counter: A threat model is only as good as its assumptions — it's blind to adversaries or paths you didn't imagine, and a model built once and never revisited rots as the system and threats change.

quiz.q: Threat modelling primarily asks…
choices: What we protect, from whom, and how they'd attack

cards.title: Zero trust: never trust, always verify
cards.fact: Drop the idea of a safe inside network — verify every request, wherever it comes from.
cards.detail: The old model trusted anything inside the corporate firewall — a 'hard shell, soft centre' that an attacker who got in could roam freely. Zero trust (formalised in NIST SP 800-207) discards the trusted interior: every request to every resource is authenticated, authorised and encrypted on its own merits, regardless of network location. Access is least-privilege and continuously re-checked, so a breached laptop can't pivot across the whole network.
cards.deploy: The architecture behind modern remote work and cloud security — location no longer grants trust.
cards.counter: 'Zero trust' has become a marketing label slapped on products; the real thing is an architecture and a discipline, not a box you buy, and retrofitting it onto sprawling legacy systems is hard, slow and easy to do badly.

quiz.q: Zero trust assumes that being inside the network…
choices: Does not by itself confer trust

cards.title: Supply-chain attacks
cards.fact: Why break into the target when you can poison something it already trusts?
cards.detail: Modern software is built from countless third-party components and update channels. A supply-chain attack compromises one of those trusted upstream sources, so the malicious code rides in through a legitimate, signed update. The 2020 SolarWinds attack slipped a backdoor into a network-management tool that pushed it to thousands of organisations, including US government agencies. Open-source dependencies are another route — one tampered package can spread everywhere it's imported.
cards.deploy: Explains why securing your own perimeter isn't enough — you inherit the security of everything you depend on.
cards.counter: Defences (signed builds, software bills of materials, dependency pinning) help but can't fully solve a trust problem that's also social and economic — much critical open-source code is maintained unpaid by a handful of volunteers (the 'nobody's job' problem laid bare by Log4Shell).

quiz.q: A supply-chain attack compromises a target by…
choices: Poisoning a trusted upstream supplier or update

cards.title: The quantum threat to encryption
cards.fact: A large quantum computer would break today's public-key crypto — so the world is migrating now.
cards.detail: Public-key systems like RSA rest on problems (factoring large numbers, discrete logarithms) that ordinary computers can't crack in any reasonable time. Peter Shor's 1994 algorithm shows a sufficiently large quantum computer could solve them quickly, breaking RSA and elliptic-curve crypto. No such machine exists yet, but the fear is 'harvest now, decrypt later' — adversaries storing encrypted data today to crack once one does. NIST standardised the first post-quantum algorithms (built on harder lattice problems) in 2024.
cards.deploy: Explains why governments and tech firms are already swapping out encryption that still works fine today.
cards.counter: Timelines are deeply uncertain — a code-breaking quantum computer may be decades away or never practical at the needed scale — and the new post-quantum schemes are themselves young and less battle-tested, so the migration trades a known future risk for present-day implementation risk.

quiz.q: Shor's algorithm threatens RSA because a quantum computer could…

cards.title: Ordinary least squares: solving for the line
cards.fact: OLS doesn't search for the best-fit line — it solves for it in one shot.
cards.detail: Ordinary least squares finds the line by calculus, not trial and error. Write the total squared error as a function of the slope and intercept; its minimum sits exactly where the derivative is zero, and that condition gives two linear 'normal equations' you can solve directly. For many features at once, the entire solution collapses to one matrix formula, \(\hat{\beta} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y\). The Gauss–Markov theorem adds a guarantee: under standard assumptions, OLS is the 'best linear unbiased estimator' — no other unbiased straight-line fit has smaller variance.

media.say: the best-fit coefficients are X-transpose-X, inverted, times X-transpose-y.
media.caption: The closed-form OLS solution — one linear-algebra computation.
OLS picks the single line that minimises the squared vertical gaps (the residuals).

cards.deploy: Shows that fitting a line is exact maths, not guesswork — and ties regression straight to solving a linear system (Ax = b).
cards.counter: Its optimality rests on assumptions real data often breaks: errors that are independent, equal-variance, and uncorrelated with the predictors. Outliers wreck it (squared errors over-weight them), and when predictors move together ('multicollinearity') \(X^\top X\) becomes nearly impossible to invert — which is why ridge, LASSO and robust regressions exist.

quiz.q: OLS chooses the line's coefficients by minimising the…

cards.title: Firewalls: the gate on the wire
cards.fact: A firewall decides which network traffic may pass, by rules on where it's from, where it's going, and how.
cards.detail: A firewall sits between networks and inspects each packet against a rulebook, allowing or blocking by source, destination, port and protocol. Early ones judged each packet alone; 'stateful' firewalls track whole conversations, so they only let in replies to traffic you started. Modern 'next-generation' firewalls look deeper, into the application and content. It's the classic first layer of network defence — the gate, not the whole castle.
cards.deploy: The first control most networks reach for, and the model for 'default deny, allow what you need'.
cards.counter: A firewall only sees traffic that crosses it: it does nothing against an attacker already inside, encrypted traffic it can't inspect, or a user who invites malware in — which is exactly why perimeter defence gave way to zero trust.

quiz.q: A 'stateful' firewall improves on a basic one by…
choices: Tracking whole connections, not just single packets

cards.title: VPNs: an encrypted tunnel
cards.fact: A VPN wraps your traffic in an encrypted tunnel to a server, hiding it from the local network.
cards.detail: A virtual private network builds an encrypted tunnel between your device and a VPN server; everything inside is scrambled, so the café Wi-Fi or your ISP sees only traffic to the VPN, not what you're doing. Companies use VPNs to let remote staff reach internal systems as if on-site. Crucially, a VPN moves your trust, it doesn't remove it — the VPN provider now sees everything the local network used to.
cards.deploy: Clarifies what a VPN actually protects (the local hop) versus the marketing claim of total anonymity.
cards.counter: Consumer-VPN ads wildly overpromise: HTTPS already encrypts most traffic, the VPN provider can log you, and a VPN does nothing against malware, phishing, or sites tracking your account — security researchers widely criticise the 'a VPN keeps you safe' pitch.

quiz.q: A VPN mainly protects your traffic from…
choices: The local network and your ISP

cards.title: Intrusion detection and prevention
cards.fact: An IDS watches for attacks and alerts; an IPS goes further and blocks them in real time.
cards.detail: An intrusion detection system (IDS) monitors network or host activity for signs of attack and raises alerts; an intrusion prevention system (IPS) sits in-line and can drop malicious traffic itself. They spot trouble two ways: 'signature' detection matches known-bad patterns (fast, but blind to anything new), and 'anomaly' detection flags departures from normal behaviour (catches novelty, but cries wolf). Both feed the alerts that defenders triage.
cards.deploy: The layer that watches inside the gate, not just at it — turning silent intrusions into signals.
cards.counter: Signature systems miss every zero-day; anomaly systems drown teams in false positives, causing alert fatigue where real attacks get ignored among the noise — the 2013 Target breach famously tripped alerts that no one acted on.

quiz.q: The key difference between an IDS and an IPS is that an IPS can…
choices: Block the attack in real time

cards.title: DNS attacks and spoofing
cards.fact: The internet's address book can be poisoned to send you to an attacker's server.
cards.detail: The Domain Name System translates names like example.com into the numeric IP addresses computers actually use. Because it was built without authentication, attackers can forge replies ('DNS spoofing' or cache poisoning) so a correct-looking address quietly leads to their server — perfect for phishing or interception. DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures so resolvers can verify answers, and encrypted DNS (DoH/DoT) hides the lookups from eavesdroppers.
cards.deploy: Explains how you can type the right address and still land on a fake site — and why DNSSEC matters.
cards.counter: DNSSEC has been slow to deploy (decades on, much of the web still skips it) because it's complex and adds fragility, and encrypted DNS shifts trust to whoever runs the resolver — security gains that come with new centralisation worries.

quiz.q: DNS spoofing lets an attacker…
choices: Redirect a correct-looking address to their own server

cards.title: Access control models
cards.fact: Once you know who someone is, access control decides exactly what they may touch.
cards.detail: Access control enforces the rules of who can do what. The common models: discretionary (DAC), where owners grant access to their own files; mandatory (MAC), where a central policy and security labels decide, regardless of owners (used in high-security systems); and role-based (RBAC), where permissions attach to job roles, not individuals — the workhorse of most organisations. All aim at the same goal: least privilege, granting each identity the minimum it needs.
cards.deploy: The framework behind file permissions, admin rights and 'you don't have access to this'.
cards.counter: Over time real systems suffer 'privilege creep' — people accumulate access as they change roles and nobody revokes the old grants — so the elegant models decay into sprawling, over-permissioned messes that audits keep rediscovering.

quiz.q: In role-based access control (RBAC), permissions are attached to…

cards.title: Privilege escalation
cards.fact: Attackers rarely land where they want — they break in low, then climb to admin.
cards.detail: A foothold is rarely the goal; power is. Privilege escalation is the move from limited access to greater rights. 'Vertical' escalation climbs from an ordinary user to administrator or root — often via an unpatched bug or misconfiguration. 'Horizontal' escalation hops sideways into another user's account at the same level. Once an attacker reaches admin, the usual game is over, which is why limiting and monitoring privileged accounts is central to defence.
cards.deploy: Explains why a 'minor' low-level breach can become total compromise — and why admin accounts are guarded hardest.
cards.counter: The lesson isn't just 'patch faster': because escalation paths are so common, modern defence assumes breach and limits the blast radius (least privilege, segmentation, just-in-time admin) rather than hoping to keep every attacker out at the door.

quiz.q: 'Vertical' privilege escalation means gaining…
choices: Another user's account at the same level
Higher rights, e.g. admin or root

cards.title: Sandboxing and isolation
cards.fact: Run risky code in a sealed box so that if it misbehaves, the damage stays inside.
cards.detail: A sandbox is a confined environment where a program runs with tightly limited access to the rest of the system — its files, network and other processes walled off. Browsers run each tab sandboxed, phones isolate every app, and analysts detonate suspected malware in sandboxes to watch it safely. The principle is containment: assume code may be hostile or buggy, and bound what it can reach so a compromise can't spread.
cards.deploy: The idea behind app isolation on phones, browser tab separation, and safe malware analysis.
cards.counter: Sandboxes leak: 'escape' bugs that break out of the box are prized and pricey (a working browser-sandbox escape can fetch a fortune), and sophisticated malware detects when it's in a sandbox and stays dormant to avoid analysis.

quiz.q: The point of a sandbox is to…
choices: Limit what risky code can reach

cards.title: Incident response: assume you'll be breached
cards.fact: Security isn't only prevention — it's a rehearsed plan for when something gets through.
cards.detail: Mature security plans for failure. The incident-response lifecycle (codified in NIST's guidance) runs: prepare in advance, detect and analyse the incident, contain it to stop the spread, eradicate the attacker's foothold, recover systems to normal, and review lessons learned. The slogan is 'it's not if, but when' — so the difference between a minor scare and a catastrophe is often how fast and well-rehearsed the response is.
cards.deploy: Reframes security from a wall to be perfected into a fire drill to be practised.
cards.counter: Plans that live only in a binder fail under pressure; the breaches that spiral (Equifax, 2017) usually do so through slow detection and chaotic, unpractised response — not a lack of written procedure.

quiz.q: Containment, in incident response, aims to…

cards.title: Logs and the SIEM
cards.fact: You can't respond to what you can't see — logging and a SIEM turn scattered events into alerts.
cards.detail: Every system emits logs — logins, file access, network connections. A security information and event management (SIEM) platform pulls these together from across an organisation, correlates them, and raises alerts when patterns look like an attack. Good logging is also what makes investigation possible after the fact: no logs, no idea what happened. The catch is signal-to-noise — too much data, too few analysts.
cards.deploy: The nervous system of a security team: where detection, alerting and investigation actually happen.
cards.counter: SIEMs are notorious for alert overload and high cost, and attackers who reach admin often delete or tamper with logs to cover their tracks — which is why logs are increasingly shipped off-box to write-once storage the intruder can't reach.

quiz.q: A SIEM's main job is to…
choices: Collect and correlate logs to raise alerts

cards.title: Digital forensics
cards.fact: After an attack, forensics reconstructs what happened — and preserves evidence that will hold up.
cards.detail: Digital forensics is the careful collection and analysis of digital evidence: disk images, memory captures, logs and timelines that reveal how an attacker got in, what they touched, and what they took. Its discipline is the 'chain of custody' — documenting who handled each piece of evidence and how, so it stays trustworthy for an investigation or court. Work on copies, never the original, and record everything.
cards.deploy: The practice behind breach investigations, insider cases and any evidence that must survive scrutiny.
cards.counter: Evidence is fragile and contestable: anti-forensics tools wipe or fake traces, encrypted and cloud-hosted data may be unreachable, and timestamps can be forged — so forensic findings are reasoned inferences, not certainties, and sloppy handling can void them entirely.

quiz.q: 'Chain of custody' in forensics means documenting…
choices: Who handled each piece of evidence and how

cards.title: The cloud's shared responsibility
cards.fact: In the cloud, the provider secures the platform — but securing what you put on it is still your job.
cards.detail: Moving to the cloud doesn't outsource security wholesale. The 'shared responsibility model' splits it: the provider (AWS, Azure, Google) secures the physical data centres and core infrastructure, while you remain responsible for your data, your access settings and your configuration. Most cloud breaches aren't the provider being hacked — they're customers leaving a storage bucket public or access keys exposed.
cards.deploy: Cuts the dangerous assumption that 'it's in the cloud, so it's secure' — the riskiest line in the misconfiguration.
cards.counter: The model is real but its boundary is fuzzy and shifts by service type (more is yours with raw servers, less with managed services), and critics note providers market 'security' while quietly leaving the most breach-prone parts — configuration — to often-undertrained customers.

quiz.q: Most cloud data breaches are caused by…

cards.title: Container security
cards.fact: Containers share the host's kernel — lighter than virtual machines, but a thinner wall between them.
cards.detail: Containers (Docker, orchestrated by Kubernetes) package an app with its dependencies and run many to a machine, sharing one operating-system kernel. That makes them fast and cheap — but the isolation is weaker than a full virtual machine, so a kernel bug or a misconfigured, over-privileged container can let an attacker 'break out' onto the host or into neighbours. Security means minimal images, no running as root, scanning for known-vulnerable dependencies, and locking down the orchestrator.
cards.deploy: Explains the security trade-off behind modern cloud-native deployment and why 'don't run as root' is repeated.
cards.counter: The convenience pulls against safety: teams ship images riddled with outdated, vulnerable libraries, and Kubernetes' sprawling configuration is so easy to get wrong that misconfiguration, not exotic kernel escapes, causes most real container incidents.

quiz.q: Compared with a virtual machine, a container's isolation is…

cards.title: Secrets management
cards.fact: Passwords, API keys and certificates are 'secrets' — and hard-coding them into your app is a classic disaster.
cards.detail: Modern systems are full of secrets: database passwords, API keys, signing certificates, encryption keys. The cardinal sin is putting them in source code or config files, where they leak into version control, logs and backups — bots scan public code repositories for exposed keys within minutes. Secrets managers (vaults) store them encrypted, hand them out only to authorised services at run time, rotate them regularly, and log every access.
cards.deploy: Names a leak source behind countless breaches — and the vault-based discipline that prevents it.
cards.counter: Vaults centralise the problem rather than removing it: the vault itself becomes a crown-jewel target, and 'secret sprawl' across code, CI pipelines and developer laptops means leaked keys keep turning up despite the best tooling.

quiz.q: The cardinal sin of secrets management is…

cards.title: German reunification — or annexation?
cards.fact: On 3 October 1990 East Germany joined the West. Whether that was a reunion of equals or a takeover is genuinely disputed.
cards.detail: The German Democratic Republic (East) dissolved and its territory joined the Federal Republic (West). In the dominant Western and West German account — Helmut Kohl, most liberal historians — this 'Wiedervereinigung' was a democratic homecoming: East Germans had toppled their regime and, in the GDR's first free election (March 1990), voted decisively for rapid unification. Others read it closer to an annexation: legally the GDR 'acceded' to the existing West German state under Article 23 of the Basic Law, rather than the two negotiating a new joint constitution (Article 146, the route Jürgen Habermas urged), so Western law, currency and elites were adopted wholesale. The Treuhand agency privatised or shut most Eastern industry within a few years, bringing mass unemployment; decades on, an East–West gap in wages, wealth and political voice — and the politics of 'Ostalgie' — persists.
cards.deploy: A clean test of whose word a source picks — 'reunification' or 'annexation' — and what that choice smuggles in.
cards.counter: The accession was lawful and electorally backed: East German voters chose the pro-unification parties, so 'annexation' is a judgement about how it was done — imposed terms, no new constitution, the Treuhand selloff — not about whether there was consent. The PDS/Die Linke and East German writers like Stefan Heym pressed the annexation reading; Kohl's camp and most Western historians reject it.

quiz.q: Legally, the 1990 unification happened when the GDR…
choices: wrote a new joint constitution with the FRG
acceded to the existing Federal Republic under Article 23

cards.title: Information economics: the invisible hand loosens its grip
cards.fact: Adam Smith's invisible hand only works under perfect information — and Bruce Greenwald and Joseph Stiglitz proved that once information is imperfect, markets stop being efficient.
cards.detail: Smith's claim that self-interested trade yields a socially good outcome was later formalised as the 'first welfare theorem': competitive markets reach a Pareto-efficient result — but only on the assumption that everyone has full information and every market exists. Bruce Greenwald and Joseph Stiglitz showed the catch: whenever information is imperfect or asymmetric, or some markets are simply missing (which is essentially always), that efficiency breaks down, and there generically exist interventions — taxes, subsidies, regulation — that could in principle make everyone better off. On Stiglitz's reading market failure is therefore the rule, not a rare exception to patch, which reframes the whole case for what governments are for.
cards.deploy: The rigorous reply to 'just leave it to the market': the efficiency theorem everyone invokes quietly assumes information conditions that never actually hold.
cards.counter: Free-market economists in the Chicago tradition, and Friedrich Hayek's knowledge argument, reply that markets adapt to information problems through reputation, signalling and intermediaries, and that 'government failure' — capture, poor information, unintended effects — often does worse than the imperfection it tries to fix. Whether the cure beats the disease is the live dispute.

quiz.q: Greenwald and Stiglitz showed competitive markets are efficient only when…
choices: information is perfect and markets are complete

cards.title: Efficiency wages: why some unemployment never clears
cards.fact: Firms often pay above the market-clearing wage on purpose — and Carl Shapiro and Joseph Stiglitz showed that this leaves a pool of people involuntarily unemployed by design.
cards.detail: In the textbook labour market the wage falls until everyone who wants a job has one. Carl Shapiro and Joseph Stiglitz (1984) explained why it doesn't: because employers can't perfectly watch effort, they pay above the going rate so that being fired actually hurts — the threat of losing a well-paid job and not being quickly rehired is what stops workers shirking. But if every firm does this, wages stay above market-clearing and a residue of involuntary unemployment remains as a 'worker-discipline device'. It is unemployment born of hidden action (moral hazard), not of irrational wages. George Akerlof's 'gift-exchange' version is gentler: paying generously buys loyalty and effort.
cards.deploy: Explains persistent involuntary unemployment and 'sticky' wages without blaming workers or assuming markets are irrational.
cards.counter: New classical and real-business-cycle economists (Robert Lucas, Edward Prescott) argue most unemployment is voluntary or frictional and that wages are flexible enough that markets broadly clear; the real-world size of efficiency-wage effects is contested.

quiz.q: Efficiency-wage theory says firms pay above the market-clearing wage to…
choices: discourage shirking by making the job worth keeping

cards.title: Stiglitz: inequality is a choice
cards.fact: Joseph Stiglitz argues today's extreme inequality is not an iron law of markets but the product of politics — rules written by and for those at the top.
cards.detail: In 'The Price of Inequality' (2012) Stiglitz argues the runaway gains at the very top owe less to pure market reward ('marginal product') than to rent-seeking: the wealthy use political power to bend the rules — monopoly protections, financial deregulation, favourable taxes, bailouts — capturing income rather than creating it. Because it is driven by policy, inequality is a choice, not destiny; and he argues it is economically costly as well as unfair, sapping demand, mobility and trust. It is a head-on rejection of 'trickle-down'.
cards.deploy: Shifts the inequality argument from 'markets reward talent' to 'who gets to write the rules' — and ties inequality to growth, not only fairness.
cards.counter: Greg Mankiw's 'Defending the One Percent' argues top incomes largely do reflect higher productivity in a skill- and technology-driven economy, and that heavy redistribution dulls incentives; others note that global inequality between countries has fallen even as inequality within rich countries rose.

quiz.q: Stiglitz's central claim in 'The Price of Inequality' is that inequality is driven mainly by…

cards.title: What international relations studies
cards.fact: International relations studies how states and other actors interact in a world with no government standing above them.
cards.detail: International relations (IR) is the study of politics beyond a single country's borders: war and peace, trade, alliances, diplomacy, international law and global institutions. Its defining feature is that there is no world government to enforce rules over sovereign states, so order has to emerge some other way. To organise explanations, Kenneth Waltz, in his 1959 book Man, the State, and War, sorted the causes of war into three 'images' or levels of analysis: the individual (leaders' psychology and human nature), the state (a country's domestic politics, regime type and economy — for example Lenin's claim that capitalist economies drive imperial wars), and the international system (the arrangement of states and the distribution of power among them). Asking which level is doing the explanatory work is one of the first moves in any IR argument. Today IR also studies non-state actors — firms, NGOs, terrorist networks and bodies like the UN.
cards.deploy: When you hear a claim about why a war happened, ask: is this a 'first image' story about a leader, a 'second image' story about a regime, or a 'third image' story about the structure of power?
cards.counter: Waltz himself argued the third (systemic) image does most of the explaining, treating leaders and regimes as secondary — a structural-realist bias that critics reject. Alexander Wendt, in his 1992 article "Anarchy Is What States Make of It," replies that the levels are not independent: anarchy has no fixed logic, and who counts as a 'state' or a 'threat' is constituted by shared ideas, so you cannot cleanly separate the system from the actors inside it. Postcolonial and feminist scholars push further: writers like Mohammed Ayoob argue the whole 'anarchy among equal sovereign states' picture fits great powers far better than post-colonial states whose main security threats are internal, and feminists like J. Ann Tickner argue the three images leave out gender and everyday life entirely.

quiz.q: In Kenneth Waltz's framework, explaining a war by pointing to the anarchic structure of the state system is which 'image'?

cards.title: International anarchy
cards.fact: International anarchy means there is no authority above sovereign states — not that world politics is chaotic.
cards.detail: In IR, 'anarchy' is a technical term: an-arkhia, the absence of a ruler. It means no body sits above states that can make law, settle disputes by force and enforce verdicts the way a domestic government does over its citizens. This is the near-universal starting premise of the field. The key nuance is that anarchy is the absence of hierarchy, not the presence of disorder — international politics can be highly ordered, with stable borders, trade and treaties, even though no one is in charge. What states make of anarchy is where the schools diverge: neorealists like Kenneth Waltz read it as a self-help world where each state must provide its own security, while liberal institutionalists like Robert Keohane argue institutions, trade and law let states cooperate despite it.
cards.deploy: Use it to separate two claims people conflate: 'there is no world police' (true, that's anarchy) does not by itself imply 'so it's every state for itself' (a realist inference, not a fact).
cards.counter: Constructivist Alexander Wendt, in his 1992 article 'Anarchy is what states make of it', rejects the idea that anarchy has any fixed logic at all: the same structural fact can produce a war-prone world (a Hobbesian culture) or a peaceful one (a Kantian culture) depending on the identities and shared understandings states develop. For Wendt, anarchy therefore explains far less than Waltz's neorealism claims.

quiz.q: In IR theory, 'anarchy' most precisely means:
choices: A state of violent chaos between nations
The absence of any authority above sovereign states
The collapse of a national government

cards.title: Realism: power and survival
cards.fact: Realism holds that states pursue power and security in a dangerous, anarchic world, putting the national interest ahead of morality.
cards.detail: Classical realism is one of IR's oldest traditions. It starts from a sober reading of human nature and the brute fact of anarchy: because no overarching authority protects states, each must look out for itself, and the currency of survival is power. Realists trace the lineage to Thucydides, whose Athenians tell the Melians that 'the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must' (Melian Dialogue, 416 BC), and to Thomas Hobbes, whose 1651 Leviathan pictures life without a sovereign as a war of all against all. In the 20th century E.H. Carr's The Twenty Years' Crisis (1939) attacked 'utopian' faith in the League of Nations and a presumed harmony of interests, and Hans Morgenthau's Politics Among Nations (1948) argued the statesman 'thinks and acts in terms of interest defined as power.' Realists judge foreign policy by prudence and consequences rather than abstract moral ideals, and doubt that universal ethics can safely guide states; many, like Morgenthau, still insist this is not pure amoralism but a prudent ethic of statecraft.
cards.deploy: When a leader says a moral-sounding war or alliance was really 'in the national interest,' you are hearing the realist frame: power and survival first, principle second.
cards.counter: Liberals and neoliberal institutionalists such as Robert Keohane argue realism is too pessimistic — it cannot explain the durable cooperation, trade and institutions that persist even under anarchy. Constructivists like Alexander Wendt counter that 'anarchy is what states make of it': realism treats a fixed human nature and a single meaning of anarchy as given, when both are historically variable and socially constructed. Feminist scholars such as J. Ann Tickner add that realism's 'power and survival' lens encodes a narrowly masculine view of security and erases human and economic security, while postcolonial critics note the tradition was theorised mostly from the vantage of great powers, not the weaker states on the receiving end of power politics.

quiz.q: Which work is the seminal 20th-century statement of classical realism, defining the national interest 'in terms of power'?
choices: Wendt's Social Theory of International Politics
Keohane and Nye's Power and Interdependence

cards.title: Neorealism: it's the structure
cards.fact: Neorealism explains state behaviour by the anarchic structure of the international system, not by human nature.
cards.detail: Kenneth Waltz's Theory of International Politics (1979) reworked realism on scientific lines, giving 'structural realism' or neorealism. His key move: drop the appeal to flawed human nature that classical realists like Hans Morgenthau relied on, and explain conflict from the system's structure alone — anarchy (no authority above states) plus how power is distributed (one, two or many great powers). In this view, similarly placed states behave alike regardless of their leaders or regimes, because anarchy forces them to. Within neorealism a split opened over how much power states want. Defensive realists (Waltz, and Robert Jervis in his 1978 article on the security dilemma) argue states seek just enough power to be secure; grabbing too much provokes others and is self-defeating. Offensive realists, above all John Mearsheimer in The Tragedy of Great Power Politics (2001), counter that because intentions can never be known, the safest bet is to maximise relative power and aim for regional hegemony.
cards.deploy: Use the defensive/offensive split to read great-power moves: is a rising power (e.g. China) seeking enough security to survive, or all the power it can grab? Your answer is basically Waltz vs Mearsheimer.
cards.counter: Liberals (Robert Keohane, Joseph Nye) and constructivists object that pure structure under-predicts: the same bipolar or unipolar configuration has produced very different outcomes, so domestic politics, institutions and ideas must matter. Constructivist Alexander Wendt argues Waltz's 'structure' is too thin — 'anarchy is what states make of it', so the shared ideas states hold decide whether others count as rivals or friends. Classical realists like Morgenthau, in turn, fault Waltz for stripping out statecraft and prudence.

quiz.q: What chiefly distinguishes John Mearsheimer's offensive realism from Kenneth Waltz's defensive realism?
choices: Offensive realism blames human nature, not structure
Offensive realism says great powers should maximise power, not just seek enough security
Offensive realism denies that anarchy exists

cards.title: The balance of power
cards.fact: States tend to balance against the strongest power to avoid being dominated, rather than join it.
cards.detail: The balance of power is the idea that, in an anarchic system, states act to stop any one power from becoming so strong it could dominate the rest. Faced with a rising giant, a state has two basic choices: balance — build up arms or form a counter-alliance against it — or bandwagon — join the strong side hoping for safety or spoils. Hans Morgenthau (Politics Among Nations, 1948) treated the balance of power as a recurring pattern of statecraft that prudent leaders must manage, while Kenneth Waltz (Theory of International Politics, 1979) argued balances form almost automatically under anarchy, whether or not anyone intends them. Stephen Walt refined this into balance of threat — first in a 1985 International Security article, then in The Origins of Alliances (1987): states balance not against raw power alone but against the most threatening state, where threat combines aggregate power, geographic proximity, offensive capability and perceived aggressive intentions. This explains why a weaker-but-scarier neighbour gets balanced against while a distant superpower sometimes does not.
cards.deploy: When countries form a coalition against a rising or aggressive state, ask whether they are responding to its sheer power (balance of power) or to how threatening it seems — proximity, intentions, offensive arms (Walt's balance of threat).
cards.counter: Whether balances reliably form is empirically contested. Robert Gilpin's hegemonic-stability theory holds that states often bandwagon with or free-ride under a dominant power that supplies order rather than ganging up to topple it. Randall Schweller argues states frequently "underbalance" — failing to react to threats for domestic-political reasons — and Stephen Brooks and William Wohlforth note that no great-power coalition formed to balance US unipolar dominance after the Cold War, contrary to what the theory predicts.

quiz.q: Stephen Walt's 'balance of threat' refines balance-of-power theory by arguing that states balance against:
choices: The most threatening state, factoring in proximity and intentions
Whichever state has the largest economy

cards.title: Liberalism: cooperation is possible
cards.fact: Liberal IR argues that cooperation, trade and institutions can produce peace and progress even under anarchy.
cards.detail: Liberalism accepts the realist premise of anarchy but rejects the conclusion that states are trapped in endless rivalry. Its roots are in Immanuel Kant's 1795 essay Perpetual Peace, which argued that republican constitutions, a federation of free states and international law could make peace durable. Modern liberalism comes in strands: republican liberalism holds that representative governments, accountable to citizens who bear war's costs, fight less; commercial liberalism holds that trade and economic interdependence raise the cost of war and so dampen it. Robert Keohane and Joseph Nye, in Power and Interdependence (1977), described 'complex interdependence' — a world with three features: states linked by multiple channels (economic, social, institutional), no fixed hierarchy among issues (security no longer always on top), and military force less usable. There, international institutions matter because they supply information, reduce cheating and let states reach gains they could not reach alone.
cards.deploy: When you see rival states still trading, signing treaties and staffing the same organisations, that's the liberal mechanism at work: interdependence and institutions raising the cost of conflict and the payoff of cooperation.
cards.counter: Realists reply that liberalism mistakes calm for a change in the rules. Kenneth Waltz argues institutions and trade reflect the underlying distribution of power and last only while great powers tolerate them; Joseph Grieco adds that even when cooperation pays, states fear relative gains (who gains more), which institutions cannot dissolve. From a different angle, dependency and world-systems writers such as Immanuel Wallerstein read 'interdependence' as asymmetric dependence: trade ties bind a poorer periphery to a richer core on unequal terms, so the same links liberals call pacifying can entrench hierarchy and can be weaponised by the stronger side.

quiz.q: Keohane and Nye's idea of 'complex interdependence' describes a world in which:
choices: States are linked by many channels and military force is less usable
A single hegemon enforces all the rules
Anarchy has been abolished by world government
Trade is irrelevant to questions of war

cards.title: The democratic peace
cards.fact: Democracies very rarely, if ever, go to war with other democracies — one of IR's most robust empirical regularities, though why it holds is contested.
cards.detail: The democratic peace is the finding that pairs of democracies almost never fight each other, even though democracies are not generally less war-prone overall. The idea descends from Kant's Perpetual Peace (1795), where citizens who must consent to war and pay its price restrain their rulers; political scientist Michael Doyle revived it in a two-part 1983 essay, "Kant, Liberal Legacies, and Foreign Affairs," noting that constitutionally secure liberal states had not gone to war with one another. Two versions are distinguished. The monadic claim — that democracies are more peaceful in general — is weakly supported, since democracies fight non-democracies readily. The dyadic claim, which most evidence backs, says the peace holds specifically between democracies. Bruce Russett is the leading proponent and sets out two mechanisms: normative (democracies externalise habits of peaceful, lawful dispute resolution and a learned norm against fighting each other) and institutional (elections, checks and divided power slow the rush to war and make peaceful intentions credible to other democracies).
cards.deploy: Treat it as a dyadic, not monadic, regularity: don't expect democracies to be peaceful in general, only to avoid war with each other — and watch how borderline cases get coded as "democracy" or "war".
cards.counter: Sebastian Rosato's 2003 critique (American Political Science Review 97:4) argues the causal logic fails: democratic norms did not stop liberal states waging colonial and Cold War wars against weaker peoples, leaders can manufacture consent through nationalism as easily as be restrained by it, and the apparent peace may be an artefact of how 'democracy' and 'war' are defined plus shared interests and US hegemony. Rosato credits geography and power imbalances over regime type — echoing realists like John Mearsheimer, who attribute the pattern to common alliances and the distribution of power.

quiz.q: The best-supported version of the democratic peace is the:
choices: Monadic claim: democracies are more peaceful in general
Dyadic claim: democracies rarely fight each other specifically
Claim that democracies never fight anyone
Claim that all wars are between democracies

cards.title: Institutions and regimes
cards.fact: Neoliberal institutionalists argue that international institutions and regimes let even self-interested states cooperate by lowering the costs and risks of doing so.
cards.detail: An international regime, in Stephen Krasner's standard 1982 definition, is a set of principles, norms, rules and decision procedures around which expectations converge in an issue area — trade (the WTO), money (the IMF), the sea (UNCLOS). Robert Keohane's 'After Hegemony' (1984) borrows from new institutional economics: states often want to cooperate but fear being cheated, so institutions help by reducing transaction costs, supplying information, monitoring compliance, and lengthening 'the shadow of the future' so that cheating today costs you trust tomorrow. Cooperation can then persist even after the dominant power that built the order declines — institutions outlive the hegemon that created them. Keohane shares realism's starting assumption (states are rational egoists under anarchy) but reaches a more cooperative conclusion, which is why the view is called neoLIBERAL rather than idealist. Constructivists like Alexander Wendt push back from the opposite side of realism: by treating state interests as fixed and given, Keohane and the realists share a thin rationalist frame and miss how institutions can reshape what states want and who they think they are.
cards.deploy: Explains why states keep funding the WTO or the climate regime even when no single power forces them to: the institution makes mutual restraint credible and cheap.
cards.counter: John Mearsheimer, in 'The False Promise of International Institutions' (International Security, 1994), gives the realist rebuttal: institutions are mostly a reflection of the underlying balance of power, not an independent cause of peace. On his offensive-realist account, institutions matter only when great powers find them useful and are discarded the moment vital interests collide, so they cannot make states stop behaving as power-maximisers.

quiz.q: On Keohane's neoliberal institutionalist view, how do regimes help self-interested states cooperate?
choices: By replacing anarchy with a world government that enforces rules
By lowering transaction costs and supplying information so cheating becomes riskier
By making states altruistic rather than self-interested
By abolishing the balance of power

cards.title: Constructivism: anarchy is what states make of it
cards.fact: Constructivists hold that anarchy has no single fixed logic: states' interests and identities are built up by ideas, norms and interaction, not handed down by the material structure.
cards.detail: Alexander Wendt's 1992 article 'Anarchy Is What States Make of It', in the journal International Organization, attacks the realist claim that the mere absence of a world government forces states into a self-help struggle. For Wendt, self-help and power politics are institutions states build, not features baked into anarchy — what fills the empty container is the shared understandings states form through interaction. His own example: British nuclear weapons mean something different to the United States than North Korean ones, because the meaning of the arms depends on the relationship, not the megatonnage. Identities and interests are therefore endogenous: a state can come to see others as rivals, friends or enemies, and those self-images shape what it wants. Martha Finnemore and Kathryn Sikkink (1998) add a dynamic story — the 'norm life cycle', in which 'norm entrepreneurs' promote a new standard (say, banning landmines), it reaches a tipping point and cascades as states pressure each other to conform, then becomes so taken-for-granted that it is internalised. The school is not only Western: Qin Yaqing's 'relational' constructivism draws on Chinese thought to argue interests grow out of relations rather than fixed selves, and feminist constructivists trace how gendered ideas shape what states treat as security.
cards.deploy: Use it to explain change realism struggles with — why the slave trade or colonial conquest, once normal great-power behaviour, became unthinkable, or why some nuclear states alarm us and others do not.
cards.counter: Structural realists led by Kenneth Waltz reply that the material logic is not so plastic: under anarchy any state that ignores relative power and survival risks being conquered, so ideas operate only within hard limits set by capabilities. John Mearsheimer puts it more bluntly — ideas and norms 'matter only on the margins', and great-power competition persists whatever states believe. A further limitation, raised by rationalist critics, is that 'soft' constructivism can struggle to predict WHICH ideas will win out, making it strong on explanation after the fact but weaker on forecasting.

quiz.q: What does Wendt mean by 'anarchy is what states make of it'?
choices: Anarchy is a myth; there is in fact a hidden world government
The absence of world government has no single fixed logic — interests and identities are socially constructed
States should embrace chaos as a strategy
Material power has no effect whatsoever on outcomes

cards.title: Marxist and critical IR
cards.fact: Marxist and critical theorists read world politics as a structure of global capitalism and hierarchy, not a level field of sovereign equals.
cards.detail: Immanuel Wallerstein's world-systems analysis takes the whole capitalist world economy, not the single state, as the unit of analysis. It is split into a wealthy 'core' running high-skill, capital-intensive production, a poor 'periphery' supplying cheap labour and raw materials, and a 'semi-periphery' in between that buffers the two; surplus flows from periphery to core through an unequal division of labour. This builds on dependency theory (Raul Prebisch and Andre Gunder Frank), which argued poor regions are not simply 'behind' but were actively underdeveloped by their place in the system. Robert Cox brought in Antonio Gramsci: dominance works partly through hegemony, where the ruling order's ideas come to seem like plain common sense. Cox's line, from his 1981 essay, is that 'theory is always for someone and for some purpose', so apparently neutral IR theory quietly serves existing power. Cox split 'problem-solving theory', which takes the present order as given, from 'critical theory', which asks how that order arose and how it could be changed.
cards.deploy: Use it to question who benefits when 'free trade' or 'global governance' is presented as natural — and to read North-South inequality as built into the system rather than a stage everyone passes through.
cards.counter: W. W. Rostow's modernisation theory ('stages of economic growth') gives the rival liberal reading: poor countries are 'behind' on a common ladder, not trapped, and can climb it. The rise of South Korea and Taiwan is the stock counter-example. But the developmental-state scholars who study those cases (Chalmers Johnson, Alice Amsden, Robert Wade) credit strong state intervention, not free markets, so they undercut Rostow's laissez-faire reading as much as Wallerstein's determinism. Realists such as Kenneth Waltz add that the system is driven less by class and capital than by states' enduring security competition under anarchy.

quiz.q: In Wallerstein's world-systems analysis, what is the 'semi-periphery'?
choices: A region with no role in the capitalist world economy
An intermediate zone that buffers between the wealthy core and the poor periphery
The same thing as a great power

cards.title: The English School: a society of states
cards.fact: Hedley Bull's 'The Anarchical Society' (1977) argues that states, despite having no government above them, form an international SOCIETY bound by shared rules and institutions.
cards.detail: The English School threads a 'via media' (middle way) between realism and liberalism. Against realists, Bull denies that anarchy means a pure war of all against all; against liberals, he denies that order requires a world government or the spread of democracy. Instead states form a society when, conscious of common interests, they agree to common rules and work shared institutions: diplomacy, international law, the balance of power, the management role of the great powers, and even war as an instrument of order. Order — predictable, rule-governed coexistence — is the system's primary good, but Bull sets it against justice: rules that keep the peace may freeze in place an unjust distribution, and pressing too hard for justice (say, by armed intervention) can wreck order. Martin Wight gave the school its scaffolding with 'three traditions' — Hobbesian/realist (international politics as conflict), Grotian/rationalist (the English School's own society-of-states view), and Kantian/revolutionist (a community of humankind).
cards.deploy: Use it to explain why sovereign states with no overlord still mostly keep treaties, respect embassies and recognise borders — and to frame debates over humanitarian intervention as a clash between order and justice.
cards.counter: Realist Kenneth Waltz argues the 'society' is thin window-dressing over a balance of power that does the real work, and collapses whenever great-power interests clash.
