From within the school's own tradition, Gerrit Gong ('The Standard of "Civilisation" in International Society', 1984) and Edward Keene ('Beyond the Anarchical Society', 2002) show that this 'society of states' began as a club of European empires whose 'standard of civilisation' admitted some peoples and licensed conquering others; postcolonial critics such as John M. Hobson, drawing on Edward Said's account of Orientalism, argue its claimed universality masks a Eurocentric pedigree.

quiz.q: What is the central claim of Hedley Bull's 'The Anarchical Society'?
choices: World government is necessary for any international order
Anarchy makes a permanent war of all against all inevitable
States with no overlord still form a society bound by shared rules and institutions
International law has no influence on state behaviour

cards.title: Hegemonic stability and power transition
cards.fact: Hegemonic stability theory holds that an open, stable international order depends on one dominant power willing to underwrite it; power-transition theory warns that the decline of that power, or the rise of a challenger, breeds instability and war.
cards.detail: An open economic order — free-ish trade, a usable reserve currency, open sea lanes — is a public good: everyone benefits and no one can easily be excluded, so each state is tempted to free-ride rather than pay for it. Charles Kindleberger, in 'The World in Depression' (1973), argued the Great Depression spiralled because Britain could no longer act as system stabiliser and the United States was not yet willing to, so no one supplied liquidity or open markets. Robert Gilpin and Stephen Krasner generalised this beyond trade: a hegemon shoulders a disproportionate share of providing such goods because it gains most from the order it polices (Robert Keohane coined the label 'hegemonic stability theory' in 1980). A.F.K. Organski's power-transition theory, from his 1958 textbook 'World Politics', adds the conflict dynamic: the danger point comes when a fast-rising challenger approaches parity while dissatisfied with the rules the incumbent wrote — that overtaking moment, not a wide power gap, is when major war is most likely.
cards.deploy: Frames worries about US relative decline and China's rise: the question becomes whether a rising China is satisfied with the existing order or wants to rewrite it, and whether the transition can stay peaceful.
cards.counter: Robert Keohane's neoliberal institutionalism is the standing rebuttal: in 'After Hegemony' (1984) he argues cooperation can persist after the hegemon fades because the institutions it built lower the costs of cooperating on their own; Duncan Snidal similarly shows smaller states will help fund institutions they benefit from. Power-transition fatalism is also contested: Graham Allison's 'Thucydides Trap' (12 of 16 historical rivalries ended in war) is criticised by Joseph Nye and others as overstating inevitability — Allison's own list counts the early-1900s US overtaking of Britain as a peaceful transition. And Susan Strange ('The Persistent Myth of Lost Hegemony', 1987) attacks the premise itself, arguing US structural power was never actually declining the way the theory assumes.

quiz.q: According to power-transition theory, when is major war between great powers most likely?
choices: When one power is overwhelmingly dominant and unchallenged
When a dissatisfied rising challenger approaches parity with the leading state
Only when there is no hegemon at all
When two powers share identical values and institutions

cards.title: Soft power
cards.fact: Soft power, a term coined by Joseph Nye, is the ability to get the outcomes you want by attraction — through culture, values and legitimacy — rather than by coercion or payment.
cards.detail: Joseph Nye introduced the idea in 'Bound to Lead' (1990) and developed it in 'Soft Power' (2004). He splits power into hard power, which works by sticks (military or economic coercion) and carrots (payment and bribes), and soft power, which works by getting others to WANT what you want. Soft power rests on three resources: a country's culture (where it is attractive to others), its political values (when it actually lives up to them at home and abroad), and its foreign policies (when others see them as legitimate and moral). It is co-optive and slow-acting — you cannot simply buy or order it, and it can evaporate when a state's actions contradict its stated values. The related term 'smart power', for the deliberate combination of hard and soft instruments into an effective strategy, is usually credited to Suzanne Nossel (Foreign Affairs, 2004); Nye says he introduced it in 2003 and he did most to popularise it, notably when Hillary Clinton adopted it under the Obama administration.
cards.deploy: Explains why Hollywood, universities, the BBC or K-pop can advance a country's interests, and why heavy-handed propaganda or hypocrisy can drain soft power faster than any rival's effort.
cards.counter: The attribution and the value of the concept are both contested. On value, Niall Ferguson argues soft power is overrated and derivative — admiration without tanks rarely changes a state's vital decisions, and 'attraction' tends to follow hard power rather than substitute for it. Neorealists hold that states respond to force and economic incentives, not appeal. Janice Bially Mattern argues much 'attraction' is actually coercive (e.g. 'you are either with us or against us' rhetoric), so the hard/soft line blurs. Others note the concept resists measurement, making its effects hard to falsify, and that what counts as attractive 'values' is culturally loaded rather than universal — a Western liberal yardstick presented as neutral.

quiz.q: In Nye's framework, soft power works mainly by…
choices: Military coercion and the threat of force
Attraction through culture, values and legitimacy

cards.title: Deterrence and MAD
cards.fact: Deterrence prevents an attack not by physically stopping it but by making the attacker believe retaliation will cost more than any gain.
cards.detail: Deterrence works on the mind of the adversary: you hold something they value at risk and credibly threaten to destroy it if they strike. In the nuclear age this hardened into Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD) — if both sides keep a 'second-strike' capability (enough hidden missiles, submarines and bombers to survive a surprise hit and still annihilate the attacker), then striking first is suicide, so neither does. Thomas Schelling, in 'The Strategy of Conflict' (1960) and 'Arms and Influence' (1966), recast this as bargaining: the key variable is not raw firepower but credibility — the threat must be believable, which is hard when carrying it out would be irrational (would the US really trade New York for Berlin?). Schelling's answer was to make threats partly automatic, or to deliberately leave the outcome to chance (his 'threat that leaves something to chance'), shifting the risk of catastrophe onto the opponent. Glenn Snyder named the resulting 'stability–instability paradox': precisely because all-out war is unthinkable, states feel safer waging smaller proxy wars and crises beneath the nuclear threshold.
cards.deploy: Explains why two nuclear rivals rarely fight directly but clash through proxies, and why arms-control debates obsess over 'second-strike survivability' and missile defence (which can destabilise by undermining the other side's confidence in retaliating).
cards.counter: Whether deterrence actually 'works' is contested. Kenneth Waltz argued nuclear weapons are a powerful stabiliser and that even their spread tends to induce caution; Scott Sagan, in 'The Limits of Safety' (1993) and their joint debate 'The Spread of Nuclear Weapons', counters that organisations, false alarms, rogue commanders and accidents make safety fragile, and that Cold War near-misses (1962 Cuban crisis, the 1983 Petrov false alarm) suggest survival owed much to luck and individual judgement, not tidy MAD logic. Anti-nuclear and just-war critics (e.g. the US Catholic bishops' 1983 'The Challenge of Peace') add that 'stability' is purchased by permanently holding millions of civilians hostage to mass slaughter.

quiz.q: Why does 'Mutually Assured Destruction' require a survivable second-strike force?
choices: So a state can win a nuclear war by striking first
So that even after absorbing a surprise attack a state can still retaliate and destroy the aggressor, making a first strike suicidal
Because international law sets a minimum arsenal size
To make missile defence systems unnecessary

cards.title: Collective security
cards.fact: Collective security means every state in a system pledges to treat an attack on any one of them as an attack on all, and to respond together.
cards.detail: The idea, central to liberal internationalism, is to replace shifting alliances with one universal commitment: any aggressor faces the combined weight of everyone else, so aggression never pays. This differs sharply from an alliance. An alliance like NATO points outward at a known enemy and binds a fixed bloc; collective security points inward, has no designated foe, and is meant to discipline whichever member turns aggressor, even a former friend. The League of Nations (Covenant in force 1920) was the first large-scale attempt; the UN Charter's Chapter VII, which lets the Security Council authorise sanctions and force against threats to peace, is the second. It repeatedly underdelivers for two structural reasons. First, enforcement is a collective-good problem: each state would rather others bear the blood and treasure of confronting an aggressor, so they free-ride and the response stalls. Second, the great powers wrote in escape hatches: the five permanent Security Council members each hold a veto, so the system is paralysed exactly when a permanent member, or its client, is the aggressor.
cards.deploy: Use it to see why the UN can act decisively over a small state's aggression (Korea 1950, Kuwait 1991) yet does nothing when a permanent member invades a neighbour: the veto, not the principle, is doing the work.
cards.counter: E.H. Carr, in The Twenty Years' Crisis (1939), attacked interwar faith in collective security as a "utopian" illusion that ignored power: states will not risk much for distant quarrels that don't touch their interests, so it collapses into inaction or into great-power policing dressed in universal language. (Carr did not embrace pure realism either; he wanted realism tempered by some moral and institutional order.) Inis Claude, in Power and International Relations (1962), is more sympathetic, treating it as a worthy but only partially achievable middle ground between pure balance-of-power and world government. A further, often non-Western objection: because enforcement runs through the P5, "collective" security can legitimise selective great-power intervention, so which aggressions get punished tracks the permanent members' interests rather than any impartial rule.

quiz.q: How does collective security differ from a military alliance?
choices: It is aimed at a specific, named external enemy
It binds a fixed bloc of members permanently
It has no designated enemy and is meant to act against whichever member commits aggression

cards.title: Why states obey international law
cards.fact: International law has no world police, yet states obey most of it most of the time — the puzzle is why.
cards.detail: International law is built on consent. Its core maxim is 'pacta sunt servanda' — agreements must be kept — and it has two main sources: treaties (written agreements states sign and ratify) and customary international law (rules that bind because states consistently follow them out of a sense of legal obligation, called 'opinio juris'). There is no central enforcer above sovereign states, so why comply at all? Realists like Hans Morgenthau ('Politics Among Nations', 1948) answer that compliance is mostly cheap: law largely codifies what powerful states already want, and it gives way the moment it cuts against a vital interest — so the law is shaped by power more than it constrains it. Liberal and rational-choice accounts (Robert Keohane, Andrew Guzman's 'How International Law Works', 2008) point instead to reputation and reciprocity: a state that breaks deals finds others won't deal with it, and most international life is repeated cooperation where today's defection raises tomorrow's costs. Constructivists like Friedrich Kratochwil ('Rules, Norms, and Decisions', 1989) and Martha Finnemore go further: states internalise norms and come to see themselves as law-abiding members of an international society, so compliance becomes a matter of identity, not just calculation.
cards.deploy: Lets you read a treaty violation correctly: ask whether the rule was ever more than a paper-thin reflection of power (realist), whether the violator is burning reputational capital it will need later (liberal), or whether it is being shamed as a norm-breaker (constructivist).
cards.counter: The hard case for any compliance theory is the great power that simply breaks the law and absorbs the reputational hit — the US over Iraq 2003, Russia over Ukraine. For realists this confirms law tracks power; defenders reply, with Louis Henkin ('How Nations Behave', 1979), that 'almost all nations observe almost all principles of international law almost all of the time', and the dramatic breaches are the rare exceptions, not the rule. Third World Approaches to International Law (TWAIL) scholars such as Antony Anghie and Makau Mutua reject the framing itself: they argue the doctrine was forged through the colonial encounter — sovereignty and the 'standard of civilisation' were tools to mark European states off from 'uncivilised' others — so asking why states 'obey' a neutral law obscures whose interests that law was built to serve.

quiz.q: What does the principle 'pacta sunt servanda' mean?
choices: Agreements must be kept — treaties create binding obligations through consent
A world government enforces all treaties

cards.title: Global governance
cards.fact: Global governance is how the world manages shared problems — trade, finance, climate, disease — through overlapping institutions, even though no world government exists.
cards.detail: Many problems spill across borders and no single state can solve them alone, yet there is no sovereign above states to impose solutions. Governance fills the gap through a patchwork: formal international organisations (the UN, the World Trade Organization for trade rules, the IMF for financial crises), 'regimes' (sets of agreed rules and expectations around an issue, like the climate treaties), and looser transgovernmental networks of regulators and experts. James Rosenau and Ernst-Otto Czempiel captured the idea in their 1992 book title 'Governance without Government' — steering and rule-making without a central ruler. A common critique names a 'democratic deficit': these bodies make decisions that bind billions, but the people affected never elect their officials and cannot vote them out. Weighted voting at the IMF and World Bank gives rich states outsized control — the US alone holds about 16% of IMF votes, and since major changes need 85%, that is effectively a veto — and negotiations happen far from any public that could hold them accountable, so legitimacy comes from expertise and bargaining among governments rather than from citizens.
cards.deploy: Use it to judge any global body by two questions: is it effective at the cross-border problem (a public-good question), and is it legitimate — who is in the room, who is bound, and who never got a vote?
cards.counter: Robert Keohane and Joseph Nye argue the 'democratic deficit' charge misfires (Keohane, 'Global Governance and Democratic Accountability', 2003): global bodies are accountable in other ways — to their member governments, to markets, through peer review and transparency — and demanding direct election misunderstands what they are. From the global South, scholars and movements (e.g. Oxfam and the Tricontinental Institute) counter that the deeper problem is not a missing ballot but skewed power: institutions like the IMF and WTO lock in advantages for wealthy states, so reform of voting weights matters more than electing officials.

quiz.q: What does the 'democratic deficit' critique of global governance claim?
choices: Global bodies have too many elected officials
Bodies like the IMF and WTO make binding decisions but their officials are unelected and largely unaccountable to affected populations
There are not enough international organisations
Global governance requires a single world government to function

cards.title: Feminist IR
cards.fact: Feminist IR asks 'where are the women?' in world politics and argues that gender is built into war, security and the state itself.
cards.detail: Mainstream IR (realist and liberal alike) treats the state as a unitary, rational actor and 'high politics' as wars and diplomacy among such states. Feminist scholars argue this picture quietly writes women out and smuggles in a masculine ideal of the cold, self-interested, autonomous actor. Cynthia Enloe, in 'Bananas, Beaches and Bases' (Pandora Press, 1989; US edition 1990), keeps asking 'where are the women?' and finds them everywhere the textbooks don't look — as diplomats' wives, military-base sex workers, banana-plantation and textile labour on global supply chains, migrant domestic workers — doing the invisible work that makes international politics run. J. Ann Tickner reworks the core concepts: 'security' is not just defending borders but freedom from poverty and violence including domestic violence, and the supposedly neutral 'rational state' encodes traits culturally coded masculine (autonomy, toughness) while devaluing those coded feminine (care, interdependence). The shared move is to make the invisible visible: by asking how gender structures who fights, who is protected and who is exploited, feminist IR claims to reveal power that gender-blind theory misses.
cards.deploy: Apply it to any security story by asking what gendered work and assumptions are off-page: who staffs the bases, whose unpaid labour absorbs the shock of sanctions or war, and why 'rational' and 'strong' are taken to mean the same thing.
cards.counter: Feminist IR is itself internally divided, not a single line. Liberal feminists want women added to existing institutions (more women in militaries and foreign ministries); standpoint/difference feminists like Tickner argue women's experience yields different knowledge; poststructural feminists (e.g. Christine Sylvester) deny any fixed 'women's experience' to speak from, treating gender as discursively produced. Mainstream IR pushed back directly: Robert Keohane urged feminists to formulate testable hypotheses and gather data scientifically. Tickner replied in 'You Just Don't Understand' (International Studies Quarterly, 1997) that the disagreement is really about epistemology — what counts as legitimate knowledge — not feminists failing at positivist method; Keohane answered in 1998 ('Beyond Dichotomy').

quiz.q: What is the central claim behind Cynthia Enloe's question 'where are the women?'
choices: Women should be barred from military service
Gender is irrelevant to international politics
Women are everywhere in world politics doing invisible work that mainstream IR overlooks, and gender structures war, security and the state
Only women can study international relations

cards.title: Postcolonial and Global IR
cards.fact: Postcolonial and Global IR argue that mainstream IR was built from a European vantage point and erases race, empire and the experience of the colonised world.
cards.detail: Standard IR dates the modern system to the 1648 Peace of Westphalia and tells its story through European great powers, treating colonialism as a footnote rather than as the central engine of world politics. Postcolonial scholars reject this. Edward Said's 'Orientalism' (1978) showed how Western scholarship constructed 'the East' as exotic, irrational and in need of rule — a body of knowledge that justified empire. Gayatri Spivak's essay 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' (1988), drawing on the Subaltern Studies historians, presses the further point that the colonised were not merely misrepresented but denied a voice in the very categories that describe them. Decolonial and race-centred writers, recovering W.E.B. Du Bois (who named the 'global colour line') and Frantz Fanon, put empire and race back at the centre of how power, hierarchy and 'sovereignty' actually work. Amitav Acharya's 'Global IR', set out in his 2014 ISA presidential address 'Global International Relations (IR) and Regional Worlds', is a constructive response: rather than just critiquing the discipline, it calls for a worldwide field that draws on the histories and ideas of Asia, Africa and Latin America as theory, not just as raw cases to plug into Western models.
cards.deploy: Use it to interrogate the discipline's own categories: when a textbook says 'the international system began in 1648' or calls some states 'failed', ask whose history that centres and whose empire it hides.
cards.counter: The two impulses pull apart. Acharya explicitly wants Global IR to supplement and pluralise mainstream IR rather than supplant it; more radical critics such as Robbie Shilliam argue that merely adding non-Western thinkers to a Eurocentric discipline leaves its colonial foundations intact, so IR should be decolonised at the root, not broadened. Mainstream realists, for their part, contend that anarchy and the balancing of power are real constraints that operate regardless of cultural standpoint.

quiz.q: What is Edward Said's 'Orientalism' arguing in the context of postcolonial IR?
choices: That Eastern states are inherently irrational
That Western knowledge constructed 'the East' as exotic and inferior, producing a body of ideas that helped justify empire
That IR theory is fully universal and culture-neutral
That the Westphalian system began in Asia

cards.title: What political science studies
cards.fact: Political science is the systematic, evidence-based study of power, the state, and how collective decisions get made — captured by Harold Lasswell's phrase, 'who gets what, when, how'.
cards.detail: Political scientists study how groups of people govern themselves: how power is gained, used and constrained; how states, parties, courts and electorates behave; and what shapes who wins and who loses. Harold Lasswell distilled politics in the title of his 1936 book 'Politics: Who Gets What, When, How' — a fight over scarce goods like money, status and rights. The discipline draws a working line between positive analysis (explaining what is, empirically — why turnout falls, why wars start) and normative analysis (arguing what ought to be — what justice or legitimacy requires). The positive side leans on surveys, statistics, case studies, process tracing and experiments; the aim is to test claims against evidence, not just to express opinions. It overlaps with political philosophy (which is mostly normative) and with economics, sociology and history.
cards.deploy: When a debate stalls, ask whether the disagreement is positive (a factual claim you could check) or normative (a value judgment) — they need different kinds of argument, and conflating them produces talking past each other.
cards.counter: The 'science' label is contested. Behaviouralists like David Easton pushed for a systematic, methods-driven discipline modelled on natural science. But the positive/normative line is porous, and several named camps say so: Leo Strauss, in 'Natural Right and History' (1953), traced Max Weber's fact/value distinction toward a corrosive relativism; interpretive social scientists in the Weberian 'verstehen' tradition (e.g. Charles Taylor) argue that choosing what to measure and how to interpret human action already carries values; and W.B. Gallie's idea of 'essentially contested concepts' explains why a term like 'democracy' cannot be defined neutrally. On these views a fully value-free political science is an illusion.

quiz.q: In political science, a 'positive' question is one that…
choices: Asks what is, empirically, and can be tested against evidence
Asks what ought to be done

cards.title: The three faces of power
cards.fact: Power has three "faces": winning open decisions (Dahl), keeping issues off the agenda (Bachrach & Baratz), and shaping what people even want (Lukes).
cards.detail: Robert Dahl's first face, set out in his 1957 essay "The Concept of Power" and his New Haven study Who Governs? (1961), defines power behaviourally: A has power over B to the extent A can get B to do something B would not otherwise do, visible in who wins observable conflicts over decisions. Peter Bachrach and Morton Baratz added a second face in their 1962 article "Two Faces of Power" (American Political Science Review): power also works through "non-decision-making" — controlling the agenda so that grievances threatening to the powerful are quietly suppressed before they ever reach a vote. Steven Lukes, in Power: A Radical View (1974), added a third, more radical face: power can shape people's very wants and perceptions so they accept a situation against their own real interests, with no visible conflict at all. Lukes himself framed all three as variants of one underlying idea — A getting B to act against B's interests — that differ in how visible the conflict is; the third face leaves no overt losers to point to, which is why it is the most disputed. It hinges on the contested notion of "real interests".
cards.deploy: When something looks like consensus, check the deeper faces: is an issue simply absent from debate (second face), or have people been taught not to want it (third face)? Apparent agreement can mask suppressed conflict.
cards.counter: Dahl and the pluralists resist the third face: if there is no observable conflict and no expressed preference, claiming people have hidden "real interests" the analyst can read off looks unfalsifiable and paternalistic — who is the theorist to decide what citizens "really" want? Lukes conceded in his 2005 second edition that the third face needs a worked-out account of domination and is hard to operationalise. Feminist theorists (e.g. Amy Allen) push the other way: Lukes still treats power mainly as one agent dominating another ("power over") and misses the structural, internalised power in gender and other social relations that no single A imposes on a single B.

quiz.q: Steven Lukes' 'third face' of power refers to…
choices: Winning votes in open political contests
Keeping certain issues off the agenda entirely
Shaping people's wants so they accept things against their real interests

cards.title: The modern state
cards.fact: Max Weber defined the state as the human community that successfully claims a monopoly on the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory.
cards.detail: In his 1919 lecture 'Politics as a Vocation', Max Weber argued you cannot define the state by what it does — almost every task has at some point been handled by something else — only by its specific means: force. The state is the organisation whose administrative staff upholds a successful claim to the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical violence over a territory. Three things are bundled here. Territory: a bounded patch of land the claim covers. Sovereignty/monopoly: in principle no rival (mafia, militia, neighbouring state) may legitimately use force inside it, and private violence is allowed only by the state's permission. And administration: a standing bureaucracy and coercive apparatus (police, army, courts, tax collectors) that makes the claim stick day to day. The word 'legitimate' carries the weight — others may use force, but only the state claims the recognised right to.
cards.deploy: Use this as a diagnostic: where armed groups openly tax, police and fight without the government's leave (failed states, contested borderlands), the Weberian monopoly has broken down, which is often a better description of 'state failure' than economic measures.
cards.counter: The monopoly is an ideal-type, not a fact everywhere. Joel Migdal's 'state-in-society' work ('Strong Societies and Weak States', 1988; 'State in Society', 2001) shows states routinely share real authority with chiefs, clans and local strongmen, so many functioning polities never matched the monopoly. Catharine MacKinnon, in 'Toward a Feminist Theory of the State' (1989), adds that defining the state by public force obscures the coercion inside the household that states long declined to police.

quiz.q: Weber's definition of the state hinges on its claim to a monopoly over…
choices: The legitimate use of physical force within a territory

cards.title: Sovereignty
cards.fact: Sovereignty is supreme authority within a territory — a final say with no higher earthly power above it (Bodin, Hobbes).
cards.detail: Jean Bodin, in his Six livres de la République (1576), gave the first systematic theory: sovereignty is the absolute, perpetual and indivisible power to make law in a commonwealth, a final authority that is not itself bound by the laws it makes. Thomas Hobbes radicalised it in Leviathan (1651): to escape the war of all against all, people contract to transfer their rights to a sovereign whose word is law and who stands above that law. Two directions matter. Internal sovereignty is supreme authority over everyone inside the borders — the buck stops with the state. External sovereignty is the flip side: independence from any higher authority abroad, so no other state may legitimately command you. The 'Westphalian' ideal — a world of equal, mutually non-interfering territorial states — is named for the 1648 Peace of Westphalia, but historian Andreas Osiander argues that link was largely read back into the treaties by later writers. Today scholars debate erosion: human-rights regimes, the WTO, the EU's 'pooling' of sovereignty, and the Responsibility to Protect doctrine all let outside bodies reach inside the once-sealed state.
cards.deploy: When a government invokes 'sovereignty' to block outside criticism (over human rights, trade rules or borders), recognise it is leaning on the external face — the Westphalian norm of non-interference — which is exactly the norm contemporary international law has been chipping away at.
cards.counter: Stephen Krasner (Sovereignty: Organized Hypocrisy, 1999) argues the Westphalian story is largely myth: sovereignty is a 'longstanding norm that is frequently violated' through intervention, conditional recognition and great-power coercion, so its supposed recent 'erosion' overstates a golden age that never existed. Postcolonial legal scholar Antony Anghie adds that the equal-sovereignty norm was, for centuries, withheld from colonised peoples by a 'standard of civilization' — sovereignty was a club non-European societies had to be admitted to, not a right they held.

quiz.q: The distinction between 'internal' and 'external' sovereignty is between…
choices: Supreme authority over those inside the territory vs. independence from any higher authority abroad

cards.title: Legitimate authority
cards.fact: Legitimacy is what makes power feel rightful rather than mere force; Max Weber named three pure types — traditional, charismatic, and legal-rational.
cards.detail: A regime that rules by raw coercion alone is fragile and expensive; legitimacy is the belief, among the ruled, that the rulers have a rightful claim to be obeyed, which makes them obey more or less voluntarily. Max Weber distinguished three 'pure types' of legitimate domination by their source. Traditional authority rests on custom and the sanctity of long-standing arrangements — 'we obey the king because there has always been a king' (monarchy, patriarchy, inherited chieftaincy). Charismatic authority rests on devotion to the extraordinary personal gifts of a leader — a prophet, a revolutionary, a demagogue — and is unstable, since it must be 'routinised' into office or tradition to outlast the founder. Legal-rational authority rests on belief in impersonal rules: you obey the office and the law, not the person, and officials are bound by the same rules. Modern bureaucratic states lean mainly on the third, though Weber held that real regimes always mix all three.
cards.deploy: Read leaders by their legitimacy claim: a strongman who builds a personality cult is banking on charisma (and faces the succession problem when he goes), whereas one who endlessly invokes 'the constitution' or 'the rule of law' is claiming legal-rational authority — and can be held to those rules.
cards.counter: Weber's typology is descriptive (why people in fact accept rule), not normative. The Stanford Encyclopedia (Fabienne Peter) marks the split: liberal social-contract theorists — John Rawls, who ties legitimacy to the justification of coercive power, and Joseph Raz, whose 'service conception' grants authority only where obeying it helps you better follow the reasons that already apply to you — hold that whether authority is genuinely rightful is a separate moral question, so a regime widely believed rightful (Weberian legitimacy) can still be unjust and owed no real obedience. A sharper challenge comes from outside that liberal frame: feminist theorist Carole Pateman (The Sexual Contract, 1988) argues the contract tradition itself conceals an 'original' patriarchal subordination of women, so it cannot be the neutral yardstick of legitimate authority that Rawls and Raz assume.

quiz.q: Weber's 'charismatic' authority is grounded in…
choices: Devotion to the extraordinary personal qualities of a leader
Belief in impersonal rules and offices

cards.title: Regime types
cards.fact: Political systems are classed roughly as democracies, authoritarian regimes, totalitarian regimes, and 'hybrid' ones — including competitive authoritarianism, where elections are real but the field is tilted.
cards.detail: A 'regime' is the basic rules deciding who holds power and how it is gained and kept. The classic poles: democracy, where rulers are chosen through free and fair, competitive elections with civil liberties intact; and authoritarianism, where power is held without genuine electoral accountability and dissent is limited. Totalitarianism is an extreme subtype that goes further — a single ideology, a mass party, terror and the attempt to control all of society and private life (Nazi Germany, Stalin's USSR). Hannah Arendt theorised it in The Origins of Totalitarianism (1951); Carl Friedrich and Zbigniew Brzezinski (Totalitarian Dictatorship and Autocracy, 1956) defined it as a six-point 'syndrome': an official ideology, a single mass party, terroristic police, monopoly of communications, monopoly of weapons, and a centrally directed economy. The big late-20th-century insight is that many regimes sit in between. Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way's 'competitive authoritarianism' (Journal of Democracy article 2002; book 2010) names regimes that hold real, contested multiparty elections — opposition can and sometimes does win — yet so abuse state power, media and the courts that the playing field is heavily, unfairly tilted toward incumbents. For Levitsky and Way these are not flawed democracies but a distinct authoritarian type wearing democratic clothes.
cards.deploy: Don't ask only 'are there elections?' Ask whether the field is level: if the opposition can run but faces a captured media, weaponised tax authorities and stacked courts, Levitsky and Way would call it competitive authoritarianism, not a young democracy.
cards.counter: Where to draw the boxes is contested. Giovanni Sartori ('Concept Misformation in Comparative Politics', 1970) warned against 'concept stretching' — overloading a category until it no longer discriminates; in that spirit, projects like V-Dem (led by Staffan Lindberg and colleagues) and Freedom House grade regimes on continuous democracy scales rather than sorting them into discrete types. Others argue the labels themselves carry a Western, liberal-democratic benchmark in which competitive elections are the test of legitimate rule. China's government advances a rival yardstick — Xi Jinping's 'whole-process people's democracy', judged by governing outcomes and consultation rather than contested elections — and academics such as Daniel A. Bell (The China Model) defend meritocratic alternatives, while critics like Larry Diamond counter that such framings relabel authoritarian control as democracy.

quiz.q: In Levitsky and Way's framework, a 'competitive authoritarian' regime is one that…
choices: Holds genuinely contested elections but tilts the playing field heavily toward incumbents
Is simply a young, imperfect democracy on its way to consolidating

cards.title: What democracy is
cards.fact: Democracy can be defined thinly (just competitive elections) or thickly (real participation, rights and equality) — and the two pull in different directions.
cards.detail: Joseph Schumpeter, in Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942), offered the minimalist view: democracy is just a method, 'that institutional arrangement for arriving at political decisions in which individuals acquire the power to decide by means of a competitive struggle for the people's vote'. On this reading you have democracy if rulers compete for votes and losers hand over power — nothing more. Robert Dahl, in Polyarchy (1971), set a higher but still procedural bar he called 'polyarchy', requiring both contestation (free, fair, regular elections among rival candidates) and inclusive participation (near-universal suffrage plus free speech, free press and the right to form associations). Against both, participatory theorists like Carole Pateman and substantive thinkers like Amartya Sen hold that elections are hollow if citizens cannot really shape decisions or if basic capabilities and social goods are denied, so they judge democracy partly by its outcomes. The deep split is procedure versus outcomes: is a system democratic because of how decisions are made, or because of what they deliver?
cards.deploy: Tells you why people argue past each other about which countries 'count' as democracies — they are using thin (electoral) versus thick (substantive) yardsticks.
cards.counter: Dahl deliberately avoided calling real systems 'democracies', reserving that word for an unreachable ideal of full government responsiveness and using 'polyarchy' for actual regimes. William I. Robinson (Promoting Polyarchy, 1996) goes further, arguing polyarchy is a managed, elite-dominated 'low-intensity democracy' that legitimates inequality while limiting genuine popular power — so meeting the procedural checklist is not the same as rule by the people.

quiz.q: What distinguishes Robert Dahl's 'polyarchy' from Schumpeter's bare minimalist definition of democracy?
choices: Polyarchy requires both electoral contestation AND inclusive participation with civil liberties, not just a competitive struggle for votes
Polyarchy requires that the government deliver good social outcomes
Polyarchy abolishes elections in favour of direct citizen assemblies
Polyarchy applies only to one-party states

cards.title: How autocracies survive
cards.fact: Dictatorships endure not by being uniquely evil but by following a survival logic: repress threats, buy off key supporters, and manufacture legitimacy.
cards.detail: Johannes Gerschewski (2013) synthesises the literature into three pillars of authoritarian durability: repression (jailing, surveilling or killing opponents), co-optation (rewarding potential rivals with money, jobs and access so they stay loyal), and legitimation (claiming a right to rule via performance, nationalism, religion or rigged elections). The selectorate theory of Bruce Bueno de Mesquita, Alastair Smith, Randolph Siverson and James Morrow — set out in The Logic of Political Survival (2003) — sharpens the co-optation piece: every leader survives by satisfying a 'winning coalition', the supporters whose backing is essential to staying in power. In an autocracy that coalition is tiny (a handful of generals, financiers or party bosses), so the cheapest strategy is to funnel private rewards (bribes, contracts, posts) to those few rather than provide public goods for everyone. Information control is the connective tissue: Sergei Guriev and Daniel Treisman (Spin Dictators, 2022) argue that many modern 'informational autocrats' lean less on mass terror and more on censorship, propaganda and faked competence to stop ordinary people from coordinating a revolt. The point is that these are intelligible incentives, not mere villainy — change the size of the winning coalition and the behaviour changes.
cards.deploy: Explains why pouring aid into a dictatorship often funds the regime rather than the people: a small winning coalition makes it rational to buy loyalty with private spoils.
cards.counter: Selectorate theory's clean win-set logic has been criticised as hard to measure: Jessica Weeks notes it wrongly assumes coalition members lose their independent power bases when a leader falls, and that all actors read the world the same way. Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way offer a different account — what actually keeps many regimes alive is the organisational strength and cohesion of the ruling party and coercive apparatus. A revolutionary or party-built state (their work on competitive authoritarianism and revolutionary regimes) can survive crises that a pure spoils model would predict should topple it.

quiz.q: According to selectorate theory (Bueno de Mesquita, Smith, Siverson and Morrow), why do autocrats tend to provide private rewards rather than public goods?
choices: Because international law forbids them from spending on public goods
Because their 'winning coalition' is small, so buying off those few essential supporters is cheaper than serving everyone
Because autocrats are inherently more corrupt by personality
Because public goods are illegal under one-party rule

cards.title: Waves of democratization
cards.fact: Democracy has spread in "waves" followed by partial "reverse waves" — and whether wealth reliably brings democracy is hotly disputed.
cards.detail: Samuel Huntington, in The Third Wave (1991), argued that democratization has come in three big waves. A long first wave (roughly 1828–1926, US and European suffrage) peaked with about 29 democracies, then ebbed after Mussolini's 1922 rise. A second wave came after World War II (decolonisation and reconstruction), cresting around 1962. A third began with Portugal's Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974, sweeping through Southern Europe, Latin America, Asia and the post-Soviet bloc. Each wave was followed by a "reverse wave" in which some new democracies collapsed back into authoritarian rule. A separate strand, modernization theory, asks what causes democracy: Seymour Martin Lipset's 1959 article "Some Social Requisites of Democracy" claimed that economic development — wealth, education, a large middle class, urbanisation — makes democracy more likely and more stable. The link is real on average but disputed on direction and exceptions. Oil-rich states (Saudi Arabia, the Gulf monarchies) grow wealthy yet stay authoritarian: rentier-state theorists Hazem Beblawi and Giacomo Luciani argue that rulers funded by resource rents need not tax citizens, so citizens demand less accountability. China has become rich without democratizing, straining the simple "wealth brings democracy" story.
cards.deploy: Frames debates about whether economic growth will eventually "democratize" a country like China — and warns that resource wealth can entrench autocracy instead.
cards.counter: Adam Przeworski and Fernando Limongi (1997) reanalysed the data and argued modernization gets the mechanism wrong: wealth does not reliably trigger transitions to democracy (they reject the "endogenous" account), but once a democracy exists, higher income powerfully prevents it from dying (the "exogenous" survival story). On the wave imagery, Huntington's three-wave periodisation is one historian's frame, not a fixed fact, and can read history as a Western-led march. Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way counter that many third-wave transitions did not stall and "ebb" so much as settle into durable hybrid "competitive authoritarian" regimes — holding real but unfair elections — rather than completing the journey to liberal democracy.

quiz.q: Why do oil-rich states pose a challenge to Lipset's modernization theory?
choices: They are too poor to sustain elections
They grow wealthy from resource rents yet often remain authoritarian, weakening the 'wealth brings democracy' link
They were excluded from all three of Huntington's waves
They democratize faster than any other type of state

cards.title: Democratic backsliding
cards.fact: Modern democracies usually die not by tanks but by elected leaders slowly bending the rules in their own favour while keeping a democratic facade.
cards.detail: The political scientist Nancy Bermeo named the shift in her 2016 article 'On Democratic Backsliding' (Journal of Democracy): the open military coup has largely given way to 'executive aggrandizement', where a leader wins power legitimately, then weakens the checks on that power one by one. Steven Levitsky and Daniel Ziblatt popularised the same idea in 'How Democracies Die' (2018). The typical playbook is to 'capture the referees' (pack courts, election commissions and regulators with loyalists), sideline or co-opt opponents and independent media, and rewrite the rules of the game (gerrymander, change term limits, restrict who can vote) — each move framed as legal and even popular. Because the steps are gradual and dressed in legal language, there is rarely a single dramatic moment that triggers resistance; by the time the system is hollowed out, elections may still happen but can no longer be lost. Levitsky and Ziblatt stress that written constitutions are not enough: democracy also depends on unwritten 'soft guardrails', especially 'mutual toleration' (accepting rivals as legitimate) and 'forbearance' (not using every legal power to the hilt). The V-Dem Institute reports that since around 2010 more countries have been autocratizing than democratizing, with Hungary, Turkey, India, Poland, Brazil and the United States cited as cases.
cards.deploy: Gives you a checklist for spotting erosion early — watch for capture of courts and election bodies and the breaking of norms, not just for soldiers in the streets.
cards.counter: The framework can over-diagnose. Comparativists such as Adam Przeworski argue democracy is more resilient than alarmist accounts assume — strong institutions and voters sometimes reverse erosion, as in Poland's 2023 turnover, when a coalition under Donald Tusk ousted Law and Justice. But International IDEA and writers in the Journal of Democracy caution that one election does not undo capture: repairing packed courts and politicised media may force the new government toward the same hardball it condemned. Separately, scholars of comparative democratization like Sheri Berman and critics of the 'global democratic recession' thesis (e.g. work questioning Freedom House and V-Dem framings) note the norms-erosion story is built largely on US and European cases; it can treat liberal-democratic norms as a fixed baseline while ignoring how those same democracies' histories of exclusion, colonialism and external interference shaped which norms ever existed.

quiz.q: What do Levitsky and Ziblatt mean by 'capturing the referees' in democratic backsliding?
choices: Bribing sports officials to influence elections
Staging a military coup to seize the presidency
Packing courts, election commissions and regulators with loyalists so they no longer constrain the leader
Inviting foreign monitors to certify elections

cards.title: Separation of powers
cards.fact: Split government into legislative, executive and judicial branches that can each block the others, so no single hand holds all the power.
cards.detail: The doctrine is most associated with Montesquieu, who in 'The Spirit of the Laws' (1748) warned that 'when the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person... there can be no liberty.' His fix was to divide state power into three functions — making law (legislature), enforcing it (executive), and judging disputes under it (judiciary) — and house them in distinct, independent bodies. He drew on earlier ideas: Polybius described the Roman Republic as a mixed government, and John Locke (Two Treatises, 1690) had already split legislative from executive power. Montesquieu's aim was liberty through structure: by arming each branch with some power to check the others (a veto, the power of the purse, judicial review, confirmation of appointments), 'power should be a check to power' so no faction can dominate. Pure separation is rare; most constitutions blend it with 'checks and balances' in which branches share and contest powers rather than work in sealed compartments. The US Constitution is the textbook embodiment, but the logic shapes courts, legislatures and executives across many democracies.
cards.deploy: Explains why a court can strike down a law or a legislature can refuse a budget — these frictions are designed in, not malfunctions.
cards.counter: Walter Bagehot argued the opposite for Britain in 'The English Constitution' (1867): he praised the 'efficient secret' of fusing executive and legislature in the cabinet, which lets a unified majority govern decisively rather than gridlock. From another angle, Woodrow Wilson ('Congressional Government', 1885) held that the US separation diffused responsibility so much that real power drifted to unaccountable committees; legal realists and later critics make the broader point that a three-branch chart can hide where power actually sits — strong executives, party discipline, militaries, central banks or concentrated wealth can hollow out the paper separation.

quiz.q: What was Montesquieu's core reason for separating government into legislative, executive and judicial branches?
choices: To make government cheaper to run
To prevent tyranny by stopping any one person or body from holding all powers, letting each branch check the others
To guarantee that the executive always wins disputes
To abolish the judiciary's role in lawmaking

cards.title: Presidential vs parliamentary
cards.fact: Either you elect a president separately for a fixed term, or you draw the executive from the legislature and let it fall when it loses the legislature's confidence — and Juan Linz argued the first is the riskier design.
cards.detail: These are two basic blueprints for the executive. In a presidential system the head of government is elected directly (or via an electoral college) for a fixed term, separately from the legislature, so the two can be held by opposing parties. In a parliamentary system the head of government (a prime minister) is chosen by and from the legislature and stays in office only while commanding its majority — a lost vote of confidence can bring the government down and trigger a new one or an election. Juan Linz, in "The Perils of Presidentialism" (Journal of Democracy, 1990), argued presidentialism is more prone to breakdown for two main reasons. First, dual legitimacy: when a president and a legislative majority from rival parties both claim a popular mandate, no constitutional umpire can resolve the deadlock, so each side is tempted to escalate. Second, rigidity: a president's fixed term cannot easily remove a failing or radical leader before the clock runs out, whereas a parliament can swap a prime minister mid-stream. Linz also argued presidential elections are "winner-take-all," which can sharpen polarisation.
cards.deploy: Helps you read constitutional design choices in new or reforming democracies — and why coalition-friendly parliamentary systems are often recommended for divided societies.
cards.counter: Linz's thesis is contested. José Antonio Cheibub (Presidentialism, Parliamentarism, and Democracy, 2007) argues the correlation between presidentialism and collapse is largely spurious: presidential regimes cluster in countries with a legacy of powerful, politically involved militaries, and it is that legacy — not the constitutional form — that drives the instability. Defenders of presidentialism (and of semi-presidential hybrids like France's) add that fixed terms give stability and direct accountability, and that well-designed parties and electoral rules can blunt the deadlock and rigidity Linz feared. Even sympathetic critics like Scott Mainwaring argued the real danger is the specific combination of presidentialism with a fragmented multiparty system, not presidentialism as such.

quiz.q: What is the 'dual legitimacy' problem Juan Linz identified in presidential systems?
choices: Two presidents are elected at the same time
Both a directly elected president and the legislature can claim a popular mandate, with no umpire to resolve deadlock between them
The judiciary and executive share the same election
Voters cast two ballots for the same office

cards.title: Federalism
cards.fact: Federalism splits sovereign authority between a central government and regional units, so each has powers the other cannot simply override.
cards.detail: In a unitary state (France, Japan) all authority flows from the centre, which can create or abolish local bodies at will. A federation (the United States, Germany, India, Brazil) instead divides sovereignty by a constitution: the central government runs things like defence and currency, while states or provinces keep guaranteed powers over matters such as schooling or policing, and neither level can unilaterally strip the other's domain. A common guide for who decides what is subsidiarity — the principle that a task should sit at the lowest level able to handle it, with the centre stepping in only when the smaller unit cannot. Large or diverse countries often federate because it lets distinct regions, languages or religions govern their own affairs while staying in one state, defusing pressure to break apart.
cards.deploy: Use it to explain why a US state or German Land can defy national policy on, say, drug law or immigration enforcement, and why secession crises (Catalonia, Quebec) are partly fights over the federal bargain.
cards.counter: William Riker (Federalism: Origin, Operation, Significance, 1964) argued federalism is less about high principle than a bargain struck by elites expanding territory, usually to meet a military or external threat, and that it can entrench the powerful: in the antebellum US, 'states' rights' shielded slavery. Alfred Stepan ('Federalism and Democracy: Beyond the U.S. Model', 1999) added that over-representing small units — as the US Senate does — makes some federations 'demos-constraining', letting a minority block the national majority.

quiz.q: What most distinguishes a federation from a unitary state?
choices: It always has a written constitution
Regional units hold constitutionally guaranteed powers the centre cannot simply abolish
Its regions are larger than in a unitary state

cards.title: Veto players
cards.fact: A veto player is any actor whose agreement is needed to change policy; the more of them there are, and the further apart their views, the harder it is to change anything.
cards.detail: George Tsebelis built this framework (most fully in his 2002 book Veto Players: How Political Institutions Work) to compare political systems on one dimension: how easy is it to depart from the status quo? Some veto players are institutional — a president, a second chamber, a constitutional court — and some are partisan, like the parties in a coalition. Using spatial models of bargaining, where each actor has an ideal point in policy space and any change must be preferred by all of them, Tsebelis showed that policy stability rises as you add veto players and as the ideological distance between them grows. He also stressed that the count alone says little; what matters is how the number interacts with the distances between ideal points. This explains why a fragmented coalition or a divided US government produces gridlock, and why systems with few veto players can swing policy sharply. The framework deliberately cuts across the usual labels, letting you compare a presidential system and a parliamentary coalition on the same yardstick.
cards.deploy: Reach for it to predict where reform will stall: count who can say no and how far apart they are, rather than just asking whether a country is presidential or parliamentary.
cards.counter: The theory predicts stability but says little about the direction or quality of policy, and Tsebelis himself concedes that actors' preferences are hard to measure. Ellen Immergut, whose 1990 article and 1992 book on health-care politics introduced the rival language of 'veto points,' argued the blocking opportunities depend on shifting parliamentary majorities and the rules of each decision stage, not on a fixed roster of actors. Critics such as Mark Hallerberg point out that agenda-setting power and informal norms can let a determined government route around nominal veto players, so the same institutional map can yield very different reform records.

quiz.q: According to Tsebelis, policy is hardest to change when…
choices: There is a single strong leader
There are many veto players who are ideologically far apart

cards.title: Bureaucracy
cards.fact: Max Weber described modern bureaucracy as rule-bound, hierarchical and impersonal — powerful precisely because it is predictable, yet hard for politicians to control.
cards.detail: Writing in the late 1910s (the work was published posthumously in 1921-22, after his death in 1920), Weber distinguished rational-legal authority — obeying impersonal rules — from rule by tradition or charisma, and saw bureaucracy as its purest form. Its features are an 'ideal type', a deliberate simplification rather than a snapshot of any real office: a clear hierarchy, fixed jurisdictions, decisions made by written rules and kept in files, officials hired for qualifications and paid salaries, and the separation of the office from the person who holds it, so you obey the post, not the individual. This makes administration calculable, which is why modern states and large firms are built on it. But it concentrates expertise and information in the officials' hands, creating a principal-agent problem: elected politicians (the principals) set goals, while the administrators (the agents) who carry them out know more and may quietly pursue their own ends, so steering them is genuinely hard. Weber also feared this efficiency could harden into an 'iron cage' (Talcott Parsons' rendering of Weber's stahlhartes Gehäuse) that even rulers cannot escape.
cards.deploy: Use it to see why a newly elected minister cannot just snap their fingers and change a department, and why sluggish or unresponsive agencies are partly a structural feature — concentrated expertise, fixed rules, career officials who outlast ministers — and not simply sabotage by a hostile 'deep state'.
cards.counter: Weber's bureaucracy is an ideal type, and named critics pull against it from different directions. Robert Merton ('Bureaucratic Structure and Personality', 1940) argued rules produce 'goal displacement', where obeying the rule becomes the goal and the actual purpose suffers. Michael Lipsky (Street-Level Bureaucracy, 1980) found that front-line staff — teachers, police, caseworkers — exercise wide discretion the hierarchy never sees, so policy is really made at the counter. William Niskanen (Bureaucracy and Representative Government, 1971) claimed agencies systematically over-expand their budgets; but Patrick Dunleavy's bureau-shaping model (1991) counters that senior officials prefer interesting, low-conflict work over raw budget size, so the budget-maximizing claim is overstated. From a feminist and anarchist angle, Kathy Ferguson (The Feminist Case Against Bureaucracy, 1984) rejects the whole frame: bureaucracy is not a neutral tool that occasionally malfunctions but a structure of domination that subordinates clients and officials alike, which adding women to management will not fix.

quiz.q: For Weber, what makes bureaucratic authority 'rational-legal'?
choices: Officials are obeyed personally because of their charisma
Authority rests on impersonal rules attached to offices, not on the person
Decisions are handed down by tradition over generations
Officials are elected by the public

cards.title: The rule of law
cards.fact: The rule of law means the government itself is bound by law applied equally and predictably — not just that it uses law to control everyone else.
cards.detail: The key contrast is with 'rule by law', where rulers use law as a tool to command subjects but stand above it themselves; the rule of law instead subjects the rulers to the same general, public, stable rules as everyone, enforced by independent courts. Theorists split it into two conceptions. A thin or formal/procedural conception asks only about form: are laws clear, public, prospective, consistent and impartially applied? Lon Fuller's eight principles (his 'inner morality of law') and Joseph Raz's account both sit here — though they disagree on whether meeting those formal demands is itself a moral achievement (Fuller) or just the law working efficiently as an instrument (Raz). On the thin view even a harsh regime can satisfy the rule of law if it follows its own rules. A thick or substantive conception adds content: the laws must also protect basic rights and human dignity, so a regime that lawfully oppresses (Arthur Chaskalson and Tom Bingham cite apartheid South Africa) fails the test. The thin version is more neutral and easier to agree on; the thick version captures more of what people want but builds in contested claims about which rights count.
cards.deploy: Use the thin/thick distinction to cut through debates about authoritarian states that have 'lots of law': they may score well on procedure while failing any rights-based test.
cards.counter: Joseph Raz defends the thin view, warning that loading every good thing (democracy, rights, social justice) into the rule of law empties the phrase of distinct meaning — for him it is 'just one of the virtues' a legal system can have. From the left, the Marxist historian E.P. Thompson (in Whigs and Hunters, 1975) and the critical legal studies movement note the ideal can mask power: equal rules can still entrench unequal property and class relations — yet Thompson still judged it 'an unqualified human good' worth defending. Postcolonial critics add a further angle: rule-of-law language was used to legitimise colonial administration, so its export today can carry the same imperial baggage.

quiz.q: What is the central difference between 'rule of law' and 'rule by law'?
choices: Rule of law requires a written constitution; rule by law does not
Under rule of law the government itself is bound by the law; under rule by law the rulers stand above it
Rule by law applies only in democracies
There is no real difference; the terms are synonyms

cards.title: The left–right spectrum
cards.fact: 'Left' and 'right' come from where deputies sat in France's 1789 National Assembly — supporters of revolution to the president's left, defenders of the old order to his right.
cards.detail: In 1789 the National Assembly debated how much power to leave the king — chiefly whether he should keep an absolute veto. Deputies who wanted to limit the monarchy and push change sat to the president's left; those loyal to the king and the old regime sat to his right. The deputy Baron de Gauville recorded that royalists took the right "to avoid the shouts" from the other side. The seating label stuck and spread worldwide. Three ideological families are usually placed along the line. Liberalism (rooted in John Locke) prizes individual liberty and limits on state power. Conservatism (whose founding figure is conventionally Edmund Burke, though some historians dispute the label) prizes order, tradition and gradual change, distrusting grand redesigns of society. Socialism (Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels and many earlier figures) prizes equality and collective provision, willing to use state power to redress economic inequality. Roughly, the left favours equality and change while the right favours order and tradition — but compressing every political belief onto one line is a simplification, because it cannot separate economic views from social ones.
cards.deploy: Use it as quick shorthand, but watch its limits: a libertarian (economically 'right', socially permissive) or a religious socialist breaks the single line, which is why analysts often add a second axis.
cards.counter: The libertarian activist David Nolan — a co-founder of the US Libertarian Party, not a political scientist — popularised a two-axis 'Nolan chart' (1969) splitting economic freedom from personal freedom, arguing the single line hides where libertarians and authoritarians actually stand. Political scientists more broadly have long held that one axis is too crude to capture the real range of beliefs. And cross-national work like the World Values Survey finds that what counts as 'left' or 'right' shifts sharply across countries and eras, so the labels — born in revolutionary France — travel poorly outside that original European context.

quiz.q: Where do the political terms 'left' and 'right' originate?
choices: From the seating in France's 1789 National Assembly
From the layout of the British House of Commons

cards.title: Nationalism
cards.fact: Modernist theorists argue nationalism is a recent invention that creates nations, not an ancient bond that nations naturally express.
cards.detail: A nation is a large group that imagines itself a single people deserving its own state. Benedict Anderson, in Imagined Communities (1983), called nations "imagined communities": members will never meet most of their compatriots, yet feel deep kinship, a feeling he tied to print capitalism and mass vernacular literacy that let strangers picture themselves as one public. Ernest Gellner (Nations and Nationalism, 1983) pushed the modernist claim further: industrial society needs a mobile, literate workforce sharing one standardised culture, so nationalism is a product of modernity that manufactures nations, rather than nations giving rise to nationalism. Against this, Anthony D. Smith's ethnosymbolism (The Ethnic Origins of Nations, 1986) argues modern nations did not appear from nowhere — they grow from older ethnic cores ("ethnies") with shared myths, memories and symbols, so the modern nation reworks genuinely old material. The debate is essentially about timing and roots: invented yesterday, or built on something ancient?
cards.deploy: Use it to read separatist and unification movements: ask whether a group's national identity is being newly constructed (Gellner/Anderson) or revived from deep ethnic memory (Smith), since each implies different politics.
cards.counter: Primordialists (the position Clifford Geertz described and Smith critiqued) hold that ethnic attachments are far older and more visceral than the modernists allow. Anthony D. Smith's ethnosymbolism is the disciplined middle position. From a postcolonial angle, Partha Chatterjee (The Nation and Its Fragments, 1993; his essay "Whose Imagined Community?") objects that Anderson's "modular" forms treat European and American nationalism as the template the colonised world merely borrows, leaving it "nothing left to imagine" — and misses how anticolonial nationalism first claims a sovereign spiritual or cultural domain of its own before the political fight.

quiz.q: What is the central claim of the modernist view of nationalism (Gellner, Anderson)?
choices: Nations are ancient and biologically rooted
Nationalism is a modern phenomenon that creates nations, rather than the reverse
Every ethnic group inevitably becomes a nation

cards.title: Populism
cards.fact: Populism is a 'thin' ideology that splits society into 'the pure people' against 'the corrupt elite', and says politics should enact the people's will.
cards.detail: Cas Mudde defines populism as a 'thin-centred ideology' that divides society into two morally opposed, homogeneous camps — 'the pure people' versus 'the corrupt elite' — and holds that politics should express 'the general will' of the people. 'Thin' means it carries no full programme of its own, so it attaches to a fuller 'host' ideology: paired with nationalism and anti-immigration on the right (Marine Le Pen, Donald Trump), or with anti-austerity and redistribution on the left (Hugo Chavez, Spain's Podemos). What unites them is the anti-elite, 'us versus them' frame, not a shared policy package. Because populists claim to be the sole voice of a unified people, Mudde and co-authors (e.g. Cristobal Rovira Kaltwasser) argue they are ambivalent toward democracy: they champion popular sovereignty and majority rule, yet often attack the checks — courts, an independent press, minority rights — that liberal democracy uses to restrain majorities.
cards.deploy: Lets you classify a movement by its frame ('people vs elite') rather than its policies, and see why left and right populists can look alike structurally while pushing opposite agendas.
cards.counter: Ernesto Laclau and Chantal Mouffe reject the ideational view. In their Hegemony and Socialist Strategy (1985), and Laclau's On Populist Reason (2005), populism is not a thin ideology but a 'logic' of politics: 'a people' is constructed by linking many unmet demands into a shared chain held together by an 'empty signifier'. They treat populism as a healthy democratic resource for contesting entrenched power, not a pathology — and charge that Mudde's framework quietly defends the liberal status quo. Latin American scholars such as Carlos de la Torre push back on the implicit Western frame too, noting that populism there (e.g. Peronism) has often been inclusionary, extending rights and recognition to previously excluded poor and indigenous majorities, not simply a threat to democracy.

quiz.q: In Cas Mudde's definition, what makes populism a 'thin-centred' ideology?
choices: It appeals only to a thin slice of the electorate
It has no full programme of its own and attaches to a fuller 'host' ideology
It is held only weakly by its followers
It avoids taking any position on the economy

cards.title: Social movements
cards.fact: Movements turn grievance into sustained action through resources, political openings, and shared 'repertoires' of protest — not raw discontent alone.
cards.detail: A social movement is sustained, organised collective action by people outside formal power pushing for (or against) change. The puzzle is that grievances are everywhere but movements are rare, so theory asks what converts discontent into durable mobilisation. The resource-mobilization school (sociologists John McCarthy and Mayer Zald) argues movements need resources — money, members, organisations, media access, leadership — and that the supply of resources matters more than the level of grievance. Political-process theory (Doug McAdam, Sidney Tarrow) adds 'political opportunity structures': movements surge when the system opens up, through elite splits, new allies, or weakened repression. Charles Tilly contributes the 'repertoire of contention' — the limited menu of protest forms a society knows how to perform at a given time (the petition, the strike, the demonstration, the boycott), which actors draw on and slowly modify rather than inventing afresh.
cards.deploy: Explains why a movement erupts in one moment and not another: look for new resources or a political opening, and read its tactics as drawn from an inherited repertoire.
cards.counter: Cultural and 'new social movement' theorists such as Alberto Melucci and Francesca Polletta argue the resource/opportunity approach explains the 'how' of mobilization better than the 'why'. By treating interests as given and structural, it sidelines collective identity, emotion, meaning and the framing work by which people come to see a situation as unjust and themselves as the ones to fix it — the very things that motivate participation. Melucci makes collective identity, not resources, the central variable.

quiz.q: What does Charles Tilly's 'repertoire of contention' refer to?
choices: The list of demands a movement issues to the state
The limited menu of protest forms a society knows how to perform at a given time
The financial resources available to a movement
The set of allies a movement recruits among elites

cards.title: Theories of revolution
cards.fact: Theda Skocpol argues social revolutions come from state breakdown plus peasant capacity to revolt — structures, not ideology — against the deprivation tradition that roots revolt in a rising-then-thwarted sense of frustration.
cards.detail: Why do revolutions happen? One tradition locates the cause in mass psychology. James C. Davies' 'J-curve' (in 'Toward a Theory of Revolution', 1962) holds that revolt erupts not in steady misery but when a long rise in expectations is suddenly reversed, opening an unbearable gap between what people expect and what they get; Ted Robert Gurr generalised this as 'relative deprivation' in 'Why Men Rebel' (1970) — rebellion tracks the felt gap between expectation and attainment. In 'States and Social Revolutions' (1979), Theda Skocpol mounts a structural counter-argument built on France (1789), Russia (1917) and China (1911 onward). Quoting Wendell Phillips, she insists revolutions 'are not made; they come': they require two structural conditions to coincide, neither of which anyone wills. First, the old regime's state breaks down — typically under international military and fiscal pressure it cannot meet, often blocked by a landed upper class. Second, peasants must have the autonomous community organisation and capacity to revolt once central control slips. Ideology and revolutionary intent, for Skocpol, are not the engine; they ride on structural openings.
cards.deploy: Gives you rival lenses for any uprising: ask whether expectations recently outran reality (deprivation, Davies/Gurr), whether the state was already cracking and society could exploit it (structural, Skocpol), or why individuals chose to join once revolt looked likely to win (Kuran's cascades).
cards.counter: Skocpol's structuralism drew sharp named replies. William H. Sewell Jr. argued she wrongly demotes ideology and culture, which do real causal work in the French Revolution rather than just decorating structural shifts (Skocpol answered him in 'Social Revolutions in the Modern World', 1994). Rational-choice scholars such as Timur Kuran stress individual decisions, preference falsification and information cascades — why a person joins once a revolt looks likely to win, and why the 1989 collapses surprised everyone — which a purely structural account leaves dark.

quiz.q: What two conditions must coincide for a social revolution, in Theda Skocpol's account?
choices: A charismatic leader and a unifying ideology
State breakdown and peasant capacity to revolt
Economic growth and an expanding middle class

cards.title: Clientelism
cards.fact: Clientelism trades material favours — jobs, cash, services — for votes and loyalty, distributing benefits to supporters rather than by public policy.
cards.detail: Clientelism is politics run as an exchange: a patron (a politician, party or 'boss') gives clients material goods — public jobs, cash, food, building permits, help with the bureaucracy — and in return clients deliver votes and support. The relationship is asymmetric (patron above client), often mediated by 'brokers' who know the neighbourhood, and it is iterated and contingent: you keep getting benefits as long as you keep delivering, and can be cut off if you don't. Classic 'machine politics' — the patronage machines of 19th-century US cities, or party machines across Latin America, southern Italy and parts of Africa and Asia — runs on exactly this logic. The contrast, as political scientists Herbert Kitschelt and Steven Wilkinson frame it, is programmatic politics, where benefits flow by public, formalised rules (a pension everyone over 65 receives) regardless of how you voted. Clientelism tends to thrive where the state is weak, poverty makes small payments decisive, and parties can monitor or credibly enforce the bargain; it is corrosive of democratic accountability because it rewards loyalty over good policy.
cards.deploy: Lets you read a party that wins through favours and patronage networks rather than its platform, and explains why anti-poverty 'programmatic' reforms (universal transfers) are partly attempts to break clientelist machines.
cards.counter: Javier Auyero, in his study of Peronist survival networks in Argentina (Poor People's Politics, 2000), warns against the elite reflex of dismissing clientelism as mere vote-buying by ignorant poor: seen from the clients' side it can be a rational survival strategy and a real, reciprocal social relationship, not just a cash-for-vote trade. Susan Stokes adds a structural caveat: because the secret ballot hides how people actually vote, machines face a commitment problem and work best only where they can monitor voters — dense small towns and tight social networks — so the coercive 'perverse accountability' she models is conditional on surveillance, not automatic.

quiz.q: How does clientelism differ from programmatic politics?
choices: Clientelism uses public, rule-based benefits; programmatic politics uses favours
Clientelism trades targeted material favours for support; programmatic politics distributes benefits by public rules regardless of vote
Clientelism happens only in dictatorships; programmatic politics only in democracies
There is no real difference between the two

cards.title: Political culture and social capital
cards.fact: A line from Almond & Verba to Putnam argues that citizens' shared attitudes — trust, civic engagement, dense association — are what make democracy work.
cards.detail: Political culture means the pattern of attitudes, beliefs and habits citizens hold toward politics. In 'The Civic Culture' (1963), Gabriel Almond and Sidney Verba surveyed five countries and sorted orientations into three types: 'parochial' (barely aware of national politics), 'subject' (aware but passive, expecting things to be done to them), and 'participant' (active, expecting to help shape outcomes). Stable democracy, they argued, rests on a mixed 'civic culture' that blends participation with enough deference and trust to keep the system manageable. Robert Putnam pushed this into 'social capital' — the networks, norms of reciprocity and trust generated by people associating. In 'Making Democracy Work' (1993) he traced the better performance of northern and central over southern Italian regional governments to centuries of denser horizontal civic association; in 'Bowling Alone' (2000) he argued American social capital was eroding as people withdrew into private life. The through-line: self-governance depends less on formal institutions than on whether citizens trust and join with one another.
cards.deploy: Offers a cultural explanation for why two countries with identical constitutions can have very different democratic quality, and frames worries about declining trust and civic membership.
cards.counter: Critics attack the causal arrow and what it hides.
