Sidney Tarrow (American Political Science Review, 1996) argued Putnam reverses cause and effect: over centuries it may be institutions that built civic culture, not the other way round, and the historical reconstruction is hard to test. Carole Pateman, in 'Participation and Democratic Theory' (1970), argued the civic-culture tradition treats passive deference as healthy and quietly takes Anglo-American norms as the democratic ideal. Feminist scholars such as Vivien Lowndes show Putnam's measures are gendered — counting formal club membership while ignoring the informal care and community networks women generate — so that inequality and power, not a thin stock of 'trust', shape who counts as civically engaged.

quiz.q: In Almond and Verba's 'The Civic Culture', a 'participant' orientation describes citizens who…
choices: are barely aware of national politics
are aware of politics but passively expect things to be done to them
are active and expect to help shape political outcomes

cards.title: Civil society
cards.fact: Civil society is the space of voluntary association between the state and the family — clubs, unions, churches, NGOs — where citizens organise on their own.
cards.detail: Civil society names the realm of organised life that is neither the state nor the household: voluntary associations people form themselves — sports clubs, trade unions, churches, charities, professional bodies, NGOs, neighbourhood groups. Watching 1830s America for 'Democracy in America' (1835/1840), Alexis de Tocqueville argued such associations are a school of democracy: by joining together for shared purposes, citizens learn cooperation and self-rule and build a counterweight to an overbearing state, guarding against the 'tyranny of the majority'. Jurgen Habermas adds a different strand — the 'public sphere' (from 'The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere', 1962): the arena (coffee houses, the press, now online forums) where private citizens come together to debate public matters and form public opinion through reasoned argument, which can then hold power to account. Robert Putnam's 'Bowling Alone' (2000) carries the Tocquevillean line into modern survey data, treating dense membership as 'social capital' that makes democracy work. All three treat civil society as a foundation for democratic life: a space where people build the trust, skills and collective voice that self-government needs.
cards.deploy: Gives you the middle layer between citizen and state, so you can ask whether a country's associations are dense and independent — a standard yardstick for democratic health and a first target of authoritarian crackdowns.
cards.counter: The benign picture has named critics. Sheri Berman ('Civil Society and the Collapse of the Weimar Republic', World Politics, 1997) showed that Weimar Germany had unusually dense civic associations, yet weak parties and a discredited state let those networks feed the Nazi rise rather than democracy — so association is not automatically pro-democratic. Antonio Gramsci instead split the capitalist order into 'political society' (the coercive state — army, police, courts) and 'civil society' (schools, churches, press, unions), where the ruling class wins 'hegemony', consent to its own dominance; civil society is a terrain of class struggle, not a neutral good. And the very category is a contested liberal export: scholars such as Partha Chatterjee argue it fits a narrow Western associational model and ignores the 'political society' of the postcolonial poor, who bargain with the state outside formal civic forms.

quiz.q: Civil society is best described as…
choices: the elected branches of the state
the space of voluntary association between the state and the family

cards.title: Knowledge as justified true belief
cards.fact: On the classical analysis, you know something only if you believe it, it is true, and you are justified in believing it.
cards.detail: The idea traces to Plato's dialogue Theaetetus, where Socrates and Theaetetus test whether knowledge is 'true belief with an account (logos)' — though the dialogue ends in aporia, rejecting that definition rather than endorsing it. The modern slogan breaks knowledge into three conditions. Belief: you have to actually accept the claim — you can't know what you don't even think is so. Truth: a belief can't count as knowledge if it's false, however confident you are. Justification: a lucky true guess isn't knowledge; you need good reasons, evidence, or grounds for holding it. The point of the third condition is to rule out beliefs that just happen to be right. So 'the Earth is round' is knowledge for you only if it's true, you believe it, AND you have grounds (you've seen the evidence) rather than a coin-flip hunch.
cards.deploy: A clean three-part checklist for pressing any knowledge claim: is it actually true, do you really believe it, and what are your grounds?
cards.counter: Edmund Gettier (1963) showed all three conditions can be met without knowledge, when a justified belief is true only by luck. Timothy Williamson's 'knowledge-first' program goes further, arguing knowledge is a basic mental state that can't be built up from belief plus extra conditions at all. The tripartite analysis is also not uniquely Western: classical Indian Nyaya epistemology, systematized by Gangesa (14th c.), defines knowledge as cognition produced by a reliable source (pramana) and likewise rules out accidentally-true belief — locating the same anti-luck worry in a different framework. Per the SEP, no analysis of knowledge is widely accepted, so JTB is a contested starting point, not a settled definition.

quiz.q: On the classical 'justified true belief' analysis, which is NOT one of the three required conditions for knowledge?
choices: You are certain beyond all possible doubt
You are justified in believing it

cards.title: The Gettier problem
cards.fact: Edmund Gettier showed you can have a justified true belief that still isn't knowledge, because its truth is a matter of luck.
cards.detail: In a three-page 1963 paper, Edmund Gettier built cases where the belief, truth and justification conditions are all met yet we balk at calling it knowledge. In his Case I, Smith has strong evidence that Jones will get a job and that Jones has ten coins in his pocket, so Smith infers 'the man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket'. As it happens, Smith himself gets the job, and Smith too has ten coins in his pocket without realising it. Smith's inferred belief is true and was well justified, but it is true by accident: his justification ran through Jones, not through the man (himself) who made it true. The lesson is that justification can be disconnected from what makes the belief true, so justified-true-belief is not sufficient for knowledge. This launched decades of attempts to add a fourth condition that screens out luck.
cards.deploy: A precise tool for spotting 'right answer, wrong reasons' — cases where someone lands on the truth by accident, not by their evidence actually tracking it.
cards.counter: Whether the cases sink JTB is itself disputed. Linda Zagzebski (1994, 'The Inescapability of Gettier Problems') argues that any analysis allowing justification to fall short of guaranteeing truth will face such cases, so the fix must be structural, not a patch. On how universal the reaction is, the experimental-philosophy work of Weinberg, Nichols and Stich (2001) reported that intuitions about Gettier cases varied across cultures and groups, casting doubt on the 'we wouldn't call it knowledge' response — but later attempts to replicate them mostly failed, and the large cross-cultural study by Machery, Stich and colleagues (2017, 'Gettier Across Cultures', testing Brazil, India, Japan and the USA) found the core Gettier intuition fairly robust.

quiz.q: What do Gettier cases demonstrate?
choices: That true beliefs are always justified
That a belief can be justified and true yet fail to be knowledge
That nothing can ever be known
That justification is unnecessary for knowledge

cards.title: Reliabilism
cards.fact: On Alvin Goldman's reliabilism, a belief is justified if it was produced by a reliable process — whether or not you can spell out your reasons.
cards.detail: Goldman's 1979 paper 'What Is Justified Belief?' proposed that justification depends on the track record of the cognitive process that formed the belief: perception, memory, and good inference tend to produce true beliefs, while wishful thinking and guessing don't. This is a form of EXTERNALISM — the thing that makes your belief justified (the process's reliability) is a fact about the world, and you needn't have any access to it. A child or an animal can have justified beliefs just by perceiving well, even with no story to tell about why. This contrasts with INTERNALISM — the position of evidentialists like Earl Conee and Richard Feldman — on which justification must consist of factors you could in principle become aware of by reflection: your evidence and reasons, accessible 'from the inside'. Reliabilism also offers a Gettier diagnosis: lucky true beliefs often come from unreliable or accidentally-right processes.
cards.deploy: A way to credit knowledge that can't be articulated — the expert's snap judgement or trained perception — by asking 'is the process that produced this belief actually reliable?' rather than 'can you justify it in words?'
cards.counter: Laurence BonJour's clairvoyant case is the famous counterexample: imagine Norman, a reliable clairvoyant who has no evidence he has the power and no reason to trust the resulting belief — reliabilism says he's justified, but intuitively he isn't. There's also the 'generality problem' (anticipated by Goldman and pressed by Richard Feldman and by Conee and Feldman): any belief is produced by a process describable at many levels of generality, some reliable and some not, and reliabilism gives no principled way to pick the relevant one.

quiz.q: What does Goldman's reliabilism say makes a belief justified?
choices: That you can articulate good reasons for it from the inside
That it was produced by a reliable belief-forming process
That it coheres with all your other beliefs
That it feels certain to the believer

cards.title: Skepticism
cards.fact: If a perfect deception would feel exactly like reality, the skeptic asks how you could ever know you aren't being deceived.
cards.detail: In his First Meditation (1641), René Descartes imagined an 'evil demon' bent on deceiving him about everything — the external world, his own body, even simple arithmetic. The modern update is the 'brain in a vat': a brain kept alive and fed electrical signals that perfectly simulate ordinary life. The argument runs: if you can't tell the difference between the real world and the deception, then you don't know you're in the real one; and since you can't rule the deception out, you don't really know the everyday things you take for granted. This isn't idle paradox — Descartes used radical doubt as a method to find something indubitable to build knowledge on, and skeptical hypotheses set the agenda for what any theory of knowledge has to answer.
cards.deploy: A stress test for confidence: ask what would look the same whether a claim were true or false — if nothing distinguishes them, your grounds are thinner than they feel.
cards.counter: Descartes thought he defeated the demon (via the cogito and a non-deceiving God), but later philosophers answer differently. G. E. Moore simply insisted his knowledge that 'here is a hand' is more certain than any skeptical premise, so the argument should be run in reverse. Hilary Putnam argued from semantic externalism that 'I am a brain in a vat' is self-refuting — a vat-brain's words couldn't refer to real vats. And the ancient Pyrrhonists (Sextus Empiricus) treated skepticism not as a problem to solve but as a way of life: suspend judgement (epoché) and gain tranquillity (ataraxia).

quiz.q: What is the core move in Cartesian skeptical arguments like the evil demon or brain-in-a-vat?
choices: Proving that the external world does not exist
Showing that a perfect deception would be indistinguishable from reality, so you can't rule it out
Demonstrating that all beliefs are false
Arguing that knowledge requires no justification

cards.title: Rationalism vs empiricism
cards.fact: Rationalists say some substantive knowledge comes from reason alone; empiricists say all of it ultimately traces back to the senses.
cards.detail: The dispute is about the SOURCE of substantive knowledge. The rationalists usually grouped together — Descartes, Spinoza and Leibniz — hold that reason can deliver truths about the world independently of experience, often via innate ideas the mind brings with it. In his New Essays (written 1704, published 1765), Leibniz answered Locke's 'blank slate' with the image of a veined block of marble: experience reveals a structure already latent in the mind. The empiricists usually paired against them — Locke, Berkeley and Hume — deny innate content; Locke's Essay (1689) argues the mind starts as a tabula rasa and every idea is built from sensation or reflection. Hume sharpened this: ideas are faded copies of impressions, so any concept that can't be traced to an impression (he targeted causation and the self) is suspect. The clash sets up Kant's later attempt to synthesise the two.
cards.deploy: A lens for any debate about where a belief comes from: is the claim being defended by appeal to what we can observe, or by appeal to what reason or 'common sense' supposedly delivers on its own?
cards.counter: The neat 'Continental rationalists vs British empiricists' textbook split is itself contested. Markie and Folescu's SEP entry warns that the labels oversimplify: the real disagreements are over specific theses (innate knowledge, innate concepts, a priori knowledge of the world), almost no thinker falls cleanly into one camp, and figures like Hobbes, Berkeley, Anne Conway, Émilie du Châtelet and Mary Shepherd resist the grouping. Kant argued both camps were half-right: knowledge requires sensory content AND the mind's own organising categories, so neither reason alone nor experience alone suffices. W. V. O. Quine's 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism' (1951) later attacked the analytic/synthetic distinction that much of the a priori side leaned on.

quiz.q: What is the central disagreement between rationalists and empiricists?
choices: Whether some knowledge can come from reason alone or must all ultimately trace to sense experience

cards.title: A priori and the analytic–synthetic divide
cards.fact: Two cuts: knowable without experience vs only through it, and true-by-meaning vs true-about-the-world. Kant said some truths are both a priori and substantive; Quine doubted the second cut exists at all.
cards.detail: Two distinctions get tangled together. The first is about how a belief is justified: a priori means knowable independent of experience (you don't run an experiment to know 'all bachelors are unmarried'), a posteriori means justified by experience ('it rained yesterday'). The second is about what makes a sentence true: analytic means true purely by the meanings of its words ('a vixen is a female fox'), synthetic means its truth also depends on how the world is. Immanuel Kant, in the Critique of Pure Reason (1781), claimed the interesting cases are 'synthetic a priori' — substantive truths known without experience, his examples being arithmetic ('7+5=12') and geometry, which he held were not mere unpacking of definitions yet needed no observation. W.V.O. Quine's 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism' (Philosophical Review, 1951) attacked the analytic side, targeting Rudolf Carnap's logical-empiricist program: Quine argued that 'analytic' can only be explained via a circle of equally unclear notions (synonymy, definition, meaning) with no non-circular grounding, and that our beliefs face experience 'only as a corporate body' — confirmation holism — so no statement is immune from revision, collapsing the supposedly sharp line.
cards.deploy: Lets you separate two questions people blur: 'how do you know that?' (a priori vs experience) from 'is that just a definition or a real claim about the world?' (analytic vs synthetic).
cards.counter: Quine's obituary for the distinction is contested. H.P. Grice and P.F. Strawson ('In Defense of a Dogma', 1956) argued that a notion ordinary speakers apply confidently and agree on can't be incoherent merely because it resists a tidy reductive definition. Many later philosophers (e.g. Frank Jackson's defense of conceptual analysis, and formal/lexical semanticists who build analytic meaning-relations into their theories) still treat analyticity as a workable notion. Georges Rey's SEP survey judges the debate genuinely open: Quine's challenge is serious but has not been shown to be decisive.

quiz.q: Kant's 'synthetic a priori' claims that some truths are…
choices: True by definition and learned through experience
Substantive (not mere definitions) yet knowable without experience

cards.title: Hume's problem of induction
cards.fact: We assume the future will resemble the past, but David Hume showed any argument for that assumption either begs the question or relies on the very habit it's meant to justify.
cards.detail: Induction is reasoning from observed cases to unobserved ones: the sun has risen every day, so it will rise tomorrow. David Hume (1748) pressed a simple question: what justifies that leap? He laid out a dilemma. You can't justify it by pure logic ('demonstrative reasoning'), because a future where nature changes its habits involves no contradiction — it's conceivable. And you can't justify it by experience ('probable reasoning'), because every appeal to 'it has always worked before' already assumes that past regularities carry over to the future — the Uniformity of Nature — which is exactly the principle in question. That makes any experiential defence circular. Hume's own diagnosis is psychological, not logical: induction isn't grounded in reason at all but in 'custom' or habit — repeated exposure conditions us to expect the usual, and we mistake that pull of habit for rational insight.
cards.deploy: A reminder that 'it's always worked so far' is a psychological habit, not a proof — useful for spotting overconfident extrapolation from track records.
cards.counter: Many think the problem dissolves rather than threatens. Karl Popper accepted that induction is unjustifiable but argued science doesn't need it — it proceeds by conjecture and falsification. Bayesians (developed from Frank Ramsey and Bruno de Finetti) recast the issue as updating rational degrees of belief, and Peter Strawson argued that demanding an external 'justification' of induction is a confusion, since being reasonable just means proportioning belief to evidence.

quiz.q: Why does Hume say you can't justify induction by appealing to its past success?
choices: Because doing so assumes the future resembles the past — the very point in question
Because induction always fails in practice
Because only deductive logic counts as reasoning

cards.title: Theories of truth
cards.fact: Four rival answers to 'what makes a belief true?': it matches reality (correspondence), it coheres with a system (coherence), it works in inquiry (pragmatist), or 'true' adds nothing beyond asserting the claim (deflationary).
cards.detail: The question is what truth consists in, not how we check it. The correspondence theory (Aristotle, G.E. Moore, and Bertrand Russell from around 1910) says a belief is true when it matches the way things actually are — 'snow is white' is true because snow is white; truth is a relation between thought and world. The coherence theory (the British idealist H.H. Joachim, and later the American Brand Blanshard) says a belief is true when it fits into a maximally consistent, comprehensive web of beliefs, since on this view we can never step outside our beliefs to compare them with a 'naked' reality. The pragmatist theory (Charles Peirce, William James) ties truth to inquiry: for Peirce truth is the opinion inquiry would converge on in the long run, while James more loosely said true beliefs are those that 'work' — that prove useful and survive testing. Deflationism (anticipated by Frank Ramsey's redundancy theory, developed as 'minimalism' by Paul Horwich) denies truth is a substantive property at all: saying 'p is true' just re-asserts p, so the word 'true' is a convenient device for endorsing claims, not a deep nature to analyse.
cards.deploy: Helps you ask, when someone calls a claim 'true', which standard they mean — matching the facts, fitting a worldview, or just being useful — which are not the same test.
cards.counter: The theories trade objections rather than one winning. Russell objected that coherence can't distinguish reality from an internally consistent fairy tale; Russell also charged that 'useful' beliefs (in James's sense) can be false, so usefulness isn't truth. Defenders of substantive truth (e.g. realists about science) argue deflationism throws away truth's role in explaining why successful theories track the world, while deflationists like Horwich reply that no such heavyweight property is needed. Each camp answers in kind, and the field remains divided.

quiz.q: Deflationism about truth holds that…
choices: Calling 'p' true adds nothing beyond asserting p — 'true' isn't a deep property
Truth is whatever beliefs cohere best

cards.title: Bayesian epistemology
cards.fact: Treat belief as a degree of confidence — a credence between 0 and 1 — that obeys the probability axioms and gets revised by Bayes' rule as evidence comes in. Dutch-book arguments show why deviating leaves you exploitable.
cards.detail: Instead of treating belief as all-or-nothing (you believe it or you don't), Bayesian epistemology models it as a credence: a number from 0 (certain false) to 1 (certain true). The view has two core norms. Probabilism says your credences should obey the probability axioms — be non-negative, sum to 1 over exhaustive alternatives, and add for mutually exclusive cases. Conditionalization says when you learn evidence E, you update by Bayes' rule, shifting toward hypotheses that predicted E and away from those that didn't, weighted by your prior confidence. Why obey the axioms? The Dutch-book argument (Frank Ramsey 1926, Bruno de Finetti 1937) shows that if your credences violate them, a clever bookmaker can offer you a set of bets you'll each accept as fair yet that together guarantee you lose money — incoherence is a practical defect, not just an aesthetic one. This is a modern reply to Hume: induction isn't a leap needing external proof but the rational updating of credences as data accumulates.
cards.deploy: Reframes 'do you believe X?' as 'how confident, and how should this evidence move you?' — and explains why ignoring base rates or refusing to update is literally incoherent.
cards.counter: The framework has real soft spots its own proponents debate. The 'problem of the priors' bites: Bayes' rule tells you how to update but not where your starting credences come from, so two reasonable agents can reach different conclusions from identical evidence. Subjective Bayesians (de Finetti, Savage) accept this, holding any coherent prior is permitted; objective Bayesians (Harold Jeffreys, E. T. Jaynes) try to pin priors down via principles like indifference or maximum entropy, which critics say are ill-defined or arbitrary. And the 'problem of old evidence' (Clark Glymour 1980) shows the rule struggles to credit evidence already known when a theory was proposed — Einstein's use of Mercury's long-known perihelion shift is the stock case.

quiz.q: A Dutch-book argument shows that if your credences violate the probability axioms…
choices: You will always make true predictions
A set of bets each acceptable to you can be combined to guarantee you lose

cards.title: Testimony and social knowledge
cards.fact: Almost everything you know — history, geography, science — you were told. The fight is whether trust in testimony must be earned by track record (Hume) or is a basic source of knowledge in its own right (Reid).
cards.detail: Testimony is believing something because someone told you, whether in conversation, a textbook, or the news. Since you've personally verified almost none of what you know, testimony does enormous epistemic work, which raises the question of what justifies believing what others say. Reductionism, traced to David Hume (whose "Of Miracles" in the 1748 Enquiry is the standard source), says testimony is not a basic source: a hearer is entitled to believe a speaker only on the strength of independent reasons — chiefly one's own observed track record that testimony of that kind tends to be reliable. So trust must be earned and reduces to ordinary inductive evidence. Anti-reductionism (also called non-reductionism), traced to Thomas Reid's Inquiry into the Human Mind (1764), denies this: Reid says humans have an innate 'principle of credulity' — a disposition to believe what we're told, paired with a 'principle of veracity' to speak truly — and absent specific red flags (the speaker is shifty, the claim is implausible) the hearer has a default, defeasible entitlement to trust. On this view testimony is a basic source alongside perception and memory. Either way, the moral is that knowledge is irreducibly social: it lives in a web of speakers and hearers, not in the lone inquirer.
cards.deploy: Sharpens how you handle second-hand claims: do you (Humean) demand the source prove its track record, or (Reidian) extend default trust until something specific defeats it?
cards.counter: Both camps face pointed objections. C.A.J. Coady (Testimony: A Philosophical Study, 1992) argued the reductionist can't actually run the project — no individual has checked enough testimony first-hand to build the required track record, and you'd need testimony even to learn that others are generally reliable, making the inductive base circular. Against anti-reductionism, Elizabeth Fricker defends 'local reductionism': a blanket default right to believe is too permissive and licenses gullibility, so hearers should monitor each source for trustworthiness. A third option treats testimony as interpersonal: Richard Moran's 'assurance' view says a speaker, by asserting, gives the hearer their word and assumes responsibility, so trust rests on that relationship rather than on either inference or bare credulity.

quiz.q: On the anti-reductionist (Reidian) view of testimony, a hearer…
choices: Must first establish the speaker's track record before believing
Has a default, defeasible entitlement to believe absent specific red flags
Can never gain knowledge from testimony
Should treat all testimony as equally false

cards.title: Fallibilism
cards.fact: Charles Peirce's stance: you can genuinely know things while admitting any of your beliefs might turn out wrong. Knowledge doesn't require certainty — and demanding certainty is what hands the skeptic an easy win.
cards.detail: Fallibilism, a term from the American philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce in the late 1800s, is the view that knowledge does not require certainty: a belief can count as knowledge even though it could, in principle, turn out false. Jason Stanley puts the standard version sharply — you can know that p even when your evidence for p is logically consistent with p being false. Peirce framed it against Cartesian foundationalism — René Descartes' project of rebuilding all knowledge on indubitable, certain foundations. Peirce argued no inquiry ever reaches that bedrock; science advances by self-correction, holding its best-tested results as provisionally settled while staying open to revision. The payoff is escaping a trap: if you assume knowing X means being unable to be wrong about X, the skeptic only has to show error is conceivable to deny you any knowledge at all. The fallibilist blocks the move by lowering the bar — knowledge needs good justification, not a guarantee — so ordinary empirical claims can qualify even though they fall short of certainty.
cards.deploy: Lets you hold a position firmly while genuinely conceding it might be wrong — defusing the bad-faith 'but can you be 100% sure?' demand without collapsing into 'so nobody knows anything'.
cards.counter: Fallibilism faces a sharp puzzle. If you can know p while granting p might be false, you seem committed to saying 'I know p, but possibly not-p' — what Patrick Rysiew (2001) named a 'concessive knowledge attribution', and what sounds like a contradiction. David Lewis (1996) calls such a sentence the plain, explicit statement of fallibilism; if so, its oddness suggests knowledge really must be infallible, the line infallibilists press. Rysiew's own reply is that these sentences can be true but are merely infelicitous to say — pragmatically awkward, not contradictory; other fallibilists deny the fallibilist is committed to their truth at all.

quiz.q: Fallibilism, as Peirce held it, says that knowledge…
choices: Can be genuine even though the belief might turn out false

cards.title: Occam's razor
cards.fact: Among hypotheses that fit the evidence equally well, prefer the one that posits fewer entities or assumptions.
cards.detail: The razor is a rule of thumb for choosing between explanations: when two accounts cover the same data, lean toward the leaner one — the one that invents fewer unseen causes, forces or entities. It is named for William of Ockham, a 14th-century English Franciscan friar, who wrote "plurality must never be posited without necessity"; the famous Latin slogan "entities must not be multiplied beyond necessity" is not in his works but was coined by the Irish friar John Punch in 1639, and the idea itself goes back further (Aristotle, Ptolemy, Duns Scotus). It is best read as a tie-breaker, not a truth detector: a simpler theory may be easier to test, but reality is sometimes genuinely complicated, so the leaner story can be the wrong one. "Simpler" is also slippery — cutting entities can force messier equations, so fewer entities and fewer equations pull in different directions.
cards.deploy: When someone's explanation needs a pile of special add-ons to survive each objection, ask whether a plainer account fits the same facts — extra epicycles are a warning sign.
cards.counter: Philosophers split on what the razor is worth. Karl Popper defends it instrumentally: simpler theories say more and so are more falsifiable, easier to test and refute. Richard Swinburne goes further, calling simplicity "an ultimate a priori epistemic principle that simplicity is evidence for truth." Elliott Sober pushes back: there is no global justification for parsimony — its force depends on local, subject-specific background assumptions, and where those assumptions fail, preferring the simpler hypothesis tracks nothing about the world.

quiz.q: What does Occam's razor actually license you to do?
choices: Prove that simpler theories are true
Prefer the hypothesis with fewer assumptions among those that fit the evidence equally well
Reject any theory that posits unobservable entities
Accept whichever theory is most popular among experts

cards.title: Scientific realism vs anti-realism
cards.fact: Realists say science's unobservables (electrons, fields) are really out there; anti-realists say theories are just tools for predicting what we can observe.
cards.detail: Scientific realism is the view that our best mature theories are at least approximately true, including their claims about things no one can see directly — electrons, quarks, electromagnetic fields. Its headline argument is the 'no-miracles argument', named after Hilary Putnam's 1975 line that realism 'is the only philosophy that doesn't make the success of science a miracle': if electrons weren't real, why does electron theory keep working so well? Anti-realists push back from two directions. Larry Laudan's 1981 'pessimistic meta-induction' points out that the history of science is full of once-successful theories now known to be false (phlogiston, caloric, the luminiferous ether), so by induction today's best theories are probably also false about their deep posits. Instrumentalists go further: a theory is a calculating device for organizing observations, and asking whether its hidden machinery is 'real' is a question we needn't answer.
cards.deploy: When a debate turns on whether a model's hidden variables 'really exist' or just 'work', you're standing on the realism/anti-realism fault line — name which question is actually being asked.
cards.counter: Bas van Fraassen's constructive empiricism (The Scientific Image, 1980) offers a disciplined middle path: science aims only at theories that are 'empirically adequate' — true about the observable — while you stay agnostic, neither believing nor disbelieving, about the unobservable. You keep all the predictive power without betting that electrons are literally real, sidestepping both the no-miracles overreach and the pessimistic induction. Critics counter that van Fraassen's sharp observable/unobservable line is itself hard to draw and arguably arbitrary.

quiz.q: What does Laudan's 'pessimistic meta-induction' argue against scientific realism?
choices: No theory can ever be tested in isolation
Many past theories were empirically successful yet are now known to be false, so today's may be too
Simpler theories are always preferable to complex ones

cards.title: Kuhn's paradigms
cards.fact: Kuhn argued science isn't steady accumulation but long stretches of 'normal science' inside a paradigm, broken by crises and revolutions.
cards.detail: In The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), Thomas Kuhn rejected the textbook picture of science as facts piling up steadily. Most science is 'normal science': puzzle-solving within an accepted 'paradigm' — a reigning framework of theory, exemplary problems and shared standards (think Newtonian mechanics) that tells researchers what counts as a question and a good answer. Anomalies that resist the paradigm accumulate until they trigger a 'crisis', and a 'scientific revolution' swaps in a new paradigm (relativity, quantum theory). Kuhn's most radical claim is 'incommensurability': rival paradigms don't share a neutral measuring stick, because they redefine key terms and even what scientists 'see', so the choice between them isn't settled by logic and evidence alone. This directly opposes Karl Popper, for whom a single decisive refutation should topple a theory; Kuhn replies that during normal science researchers don't try to falsify the paradigm at all — they protect it and blame the anomaly on themselves.
cards.deploy: When a field seems to ignore data that 'should' refute it, ask whether you're watching normal science defend a paradigm — and what crisis would have to build before it flips.
cards.counter: In his 1970 essay 'Falsification and the Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes', Imre Lakatos charged that Kuhn made theory change a matter of 'mob psychology' — an irrational conversion rather than a reasoned judgment — and proposed 'research programmes' that are appraised rationally over time by whether they keep predicting novel facts; Popper similarly held that even paradigm shifts can be defended with reasons, not just sociology.

quiz.q: On Kuhn's view, what mainly happens during 'normal science'?
choices: Scientists constantly try to falsify the reigning theory
Scientists solve puzzles within an accepted paradigm rather than testing it
Rival paradigms are compared on a neutral measuring stick
Theories accumulate steadily with no framework guiding them

cards.title: Underdetermination
cards.fact: The evidence never fully pins down one theory: incompatible theories can fit exactly the same data.
cards.detail: Underdetermination is the claim that any body of evidence can be accommodated by more than one mutually incompatible theory, so data alone can't single out the true one. One root is the Duhem-Quine thesis (after the French physicist-historian Pierre Duhem and the American logician W.V.O. Quine): you never test a hypothesis in isolation, only bundled with auxiliary assumptions (the instrument works, no hidden forces, the background physics holds). So when a prediction fails, logic alone can't say which link in the web broke -- you can always save the cherished hypothesis by revising an auxiliary instead. Kyle Stanford, summarizing the debate, separates this 'holist' (confirmational) underdetermination from 'contrastive' underdetermination, where two whole rival theories fit identical evidence with no experiment that could ever decide between them; Duhem and Quine, he notes, ran the two problems together. Because evidence leaves slack, other factors must do the choosing -- which is why underdetermination is a lever both for anti-realists like Bas van Fraassen (believe only what the data fix; stay agnostic about unobservables) and for sociologists of science in the 'strong programme' (David Bloor, Barry Barnes) who hold that social interests fill the gap.
cards.deploy: Before treating 'the data prove it' as decisive, ask which auxiliary assumptions a contrary result could be pinned on instead -- the data rarely point at a single culprit.
cards.counter: Larry Laudan and Jarrett Leplin (1991) argue the threat is overblown: which empirical consequences a theory has depends on the auxiliaries currently available, so 'empirical equivalence' must be relativized to a state of science -- rivals tied today can come apart tomorrow as new auxiliaries are added. They add that equivalent theories can still differ in evidential support (e.g. one is derivable from a better-confirmed general theory), and that simplicity, explanatory power and consilience routinely break ties. On their view underdetermination is a logical possibility, not the standing scientific predicament anti-realists need.

quiz.q: Why does the Duhem-Quine point make a single failed prediction inconclusive?
choices: Because experiments can never be repeated
Because the hypothesis is tested bundled with auxiliary assumptions, so logic can't say which one failed
Because all observation is theory-laden and so unreliable
Because simpler theories must always be preferred

cards.title: Standpoint epistemology
cards.fact: Knowledge is socially situated, and the marginalized can hold an epistemic advantage on truths about how power works.
cards.detail: Standpoint epistemology holds that what you can know depends on where you stand in society: your position shapes which questions occur to you and which facts are visible. Drawing on a Marxist idea that the worker sees the labour system more clearly than the boss, Nancy Hartsock (1983) and Sandra Harding argued that those marginalized along lines of gender, race or class can have an epistemic advantage about how systems of power actually operate, precisely because they have to navigate them. Harding's 'strong objectivity' turns the usual worry on its head: real objectivity requires examining the social position of the knower, including the invisible biases of the privileged, rather than pretending to a 'view from nowhere' (Thomas Nagel's phrase, which Harding rejects). Donna Haraway's 'situated knowledges' (1988) makes the parallel case that all vision is from a body and a location; she calls the pretence of detached neutrality 'the god trick', and argues that owning one's partiality yields more honest, accountable knowledge. Patricia Hill Collins extended the tradition to race: in 'Black Feminist Thought' (1990) she argues Black women's 'outsider within' position and their intersecting oppressions generate a distinctive standpoint, anticipating intersectional analysis. A standpoint here is an achievement, won through critical reflection and political struggle, not just an identity you are born with.
cards.deploy: When a claim of 'neutral' expertise overlooks how things look to the people affected, standpoint theory gives you the question: whose situated knowledge is missing from this 'view from nowhere'?
cards.counter: Susan Haack presses the objectivity worry head-on: she argues social disadvantage confers no automatic epistemic privilege, and that tying knowledge to political position risks turning inquiry into advocacy for a foregone conclusion. A separate internal problem, raised by Bat-Ami Bar On, is adjudication: if several oppressed groups' standpoints conflict, which is privileged, and how do we rule out internalized oppression distorting any one of them? Helen Longino keeps the social insight but relocates objectivity: in her critical contextual empiricism it comes from the critical scrutiny of a diverse community, not from any single privileged standpoint, since heterogeneous communities are better at exposing each other's hidden background assumptions.

quiz.q: What does Sandra Harding's 'strong objectivity' demand?
choices: Stripping all social context from inquiry to reach a view from nowhere
Critically examining the social position and biases of the knower, including the privileged
Accepting whatever the marginalized assert without scrutiny
Replacing evidence with personal lived experience

cards.title: The regress problem
cards.fact: Every reason needs a reason — so how does justification ever stop? That regress is epistemology's oldest headache.
cards.detail: If a belief is justified by another belief, and that one needs justifying too, you face the regress problem — sharpened by the ancient skeptic Agrippa into a trilemma (also called Münchhausen): a chain of reasons must either run on forever, circle back on itself, or stop at something itself unjustified. The two main escapes name two camps. Foundationalists, in the spirit of Descartes, say the chain halts at 'basic' beliefs justified non-inferentially — by direct experience or self-evidence. Coherentists, such as the early Laurence BonJour, deny any belief is basic and locate justification in how well a belief coheres with the whole web of one's beliefs. Each accepts the cost the other calls fatal: an arbitrary stopping point, or a suspiciously circular web.
cards.deploy: When someone demands you 'justify' a claim all the way down, name the trilemma — every body of knowledge must either stop somewhere or loop.
cards.counter: Reliabilists like Alvin Goldman sidestep the regress entirely: a belief can be justified by being produced by a reliable process, even if the believer can articulate no chain of reasons at all — shifting the question from 'what reasons do you have?' to 'how was the belief formed?'.

quiz.q: Agrippa's trilemma says a chain of justifying reasons must do one of three things — which is NOT one of them?
